## Community Gotchas — Cycle 31

### Gotcha 186 — `device.appLaunchArgs.modify()` changes are silently ignored if called after `reloadReactNative()` has already been awaited [community]

**Root cause**: `device.appLaunchArgs.modify()` queues a patch to be applied on the *next* app launch or JS reload. If you call `modify()` *after* `await device.reloadReactNative()` returns, the patched args are buffered for the *following* reload — the reload that already completed does not see the change. The test proceeds with stale launch args and the feature under test is silently misconfigured.

```ts
// BAD — modify() called after reload; args are stale for the current run
await device.reloadReactNative();
device.appLaunchArgs.modify({ FEATURE_FLAG: '1' }); // Too late — already reloaded
// App runs with FEATURE_FLAG absent; test may silently pass for the wrong reason

// GOOD — always modify() BEFORE the reload that reads the args
device.appLaunchArgs.modify({ FEATURE_FLAG: '1' });
await device.reloadReactNative(); // Now the app reads FEATURE_FLAG = '1'
await waitFor(element(by.id('new-feature-panel'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

// WHY this matters: the ordering constraint is non-obvious — modify() looks like
// a synchronous setter, so developers assume it takes effect immediately. In reality
// it sets a "pending args" state that is flushed only on the next launch event,
// causing silent feature-flag misconfiguration that is hard to debug without
// inspecting device.getLaunchArgs() after the reload.
```

---

### Gotcha 187 — `by.ancestor()` / `by.descendant()` match zero elements when the ancestor's `testID` is on a View with `accessible={true}` that collapses its subtree into a single accessibility node [community]

**Root cause**: React Native's accessibility system can merge a View and all its children into a single accessibility node when `accessible={true}` is set on the parent. In this mode, the children are no longer individually addressable via the accessibility tree. Detox's `by.ancestor()` walks the accessibility tree, not the React component tree — so `by.id('delete-button').withAncestor(by.id('list-item-1'))` returns zero matches because `list-item-1`'s children are collapsed.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — by.ancestor() finds zero matches; element exists in component tree
await element(by.id('delete-button').withAncestor(by.id('list-item-1'))).tap();
// Throws: "Element not found: by.id('delete-button').withAncestor(by.id('list-item-1'))"

// ROOT CAUSE IN COMPONENT:
// <View testID="list-item-1" accessible={true}> ← collapses children
//   <Text>Item title</Text>
//   <TouchableOpacity testID="delete-button">...</TouchableOpacity>
// </View>

// FIX — remove accessible={true} from the container View, or set
// importantForAccessibility="no" on the container and "yes" on interactive children
// <View testID="list-item-1" importantForAccessibility="no-hide-descendants">

// WHY this matters: many list-row components set accessible={true} to improve
// TalkBack/VoiceOver UX (reads the whole row as one element), which simultaneously
// breaks any by.ancestor()/by.descendant() selector that targets children of that row
```

---

### Gotcha 188 — `element.multiTap(2)` fires as two separate taps instead of a system double-tap on Android when the element is inside a `GestureDetector` with `onDoubleTap` [community]

**Root cause**: Android's system double-tap detector uses a `ViewConfiguration.getDoubleTapTimeout()` window (~300 ms). `element.multiTap(2)` sends two tap events in rapid succession at the Espresso layer, but the inter-tap delay used by Espresso (~100–150 ms) is shorter than the system detector's minimum inter-tap threshold on some Android 14+ emulators with touch smoothing enabled. The two taps are treated as two single taps, and `onDoubleTap` is never triggered.

```ts
// BAD — multiTap(2) may not trigger GestureDetector onDoubleTap on Android 14+
await element(by.id('zoomable-image')).multiTap(2);
// onDoubleTap fires only on iOS; Android GestureDetector sees two taps

// FIX (option A) — use sequential taps with platform guard
if (device.getPlatform() === 'android') {
  await element(by.id('zoomable-image')).tap();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('zoomable-image'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(200);
  await element(by.id('zoomable-image')).tap();
} else {
  await element(by.id('zoomable-image')).multiTap(2);
}

// FIX (option B — preferred) — expose a testID-gated double-tap handler in the app:
// onDoubleTap={() => triggerZoom()} — replace with a dedicated test-only button
// <Button testID="zoom-in-button" onPress={triggerZoom} />

// WHY this matters: GestureDetector (RNGH v2+) double-tap is a common mobile gesture
// and teams that test it with multiTap(2) see 30–50% intermittent failures on Android CI
// with API 34+ images — the component itself works correctly for real users
```

---

### Gotcha 189 — `element.clearText()` on a `TextInput` with `onChangeText` triggers an extra empty-string change event that may fire form validation prematurely [community]

**Root cause**: `clearText()` internally calls `element.replaceText('')` on iOS (using `Obj-C KVO setText:`) and fires a synthetic change event with value `''`. If the component's `onChangeText` handler includes a validation trigger that fires on every change (e.g., Formik's `handleChange`), the empty string may trigger a premature validation error banner before the test types the new value. This error banner can obscure subsequent UI elements and cause `toBeVisible()` to fail on the field below it.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — validation error banner appears after clearText(), blocking next field
await element(by.id('email-input')).clearText();
// onChangeText fires with '' → Formik validates → error banner slides in
await element(by.id('email-input')).typeText('new@example.com');
// error banner blocks by.id('password-input') which is now partially off-screen
await element(by.id('password-input')).tap(); // FAILS — obscured by error banner

// FIX — use replaceText() for a single atomic clear+fill to minimize change events
await element(by.id('email-input')).replaceText('new@example.com');
// Only one change event fires with the final value; validation sees a non-empty value

// ALTERNATIVE — dismiss the validation banner explicitly if replaceText is not viable
await element(by.id('email-input')).clearText();
await waitFor(element(by.id('email-validation-error'))).toExist().withTimeout(1000).catch(() => {});
await element(by.id('email-input')).replaceText('new@example.com');

// WHY this matters: controlled-input forms with real-time validation (Formik, React Hook Form
// with mode:'onChange') are ubiquitous — clearText() causing a spurious validation event
// is the #2 cause of form-interaction test failures after stale-element selectors
```

---

### Gotcha 190 — `device.getLaunchArgs()` returns `undefined` for args set via `.detoxrc.ts` `configurations[].launchArgs` after `reloadReactNative()` [community]

**Root cause**: `.detoxrc.ts` `configurations[N].launchArgs` are injected as process-level environment variables on app startup. `device.getLaunchArgs()` merges static config args with runtime `appLaunchArgs`. However, `reloadReactNative()` does NOT re-read the static config args — it only re-runs the React JS bundle. If a test calls `device.getLaunchArgs()` after a `reloadReactNative()`, the returned object reflects the runtime `appLaunchArgs` snapshot only, and static config args that were not also set via `device.appLaunchArgs.modify()` appear as `undefined`.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — getLaunchArgs() returns undefined for static config args after reloadReactNative
// .detoxrc.ts sets: launchArgs: { API_ENV: 'staging' }
await device.reloadReactNative();
const args = await device.getLaunchArgs();
console.log(args.API_ENV); // undefined — static config arg is absent after JS-only reload

// FIX — replicate all static config args that tests need to assert on via appLaunchArgs.modify()
device.appLaunchArgs.modify({ API_ENV: 'staging' }); // mirrors .detoxrc.ts launchArgs
await device.reloadReactNative();
const args2 = await device.getLaunchArgs();
console.log(args2.API_ENV); // 'staging' ✓

// ALTERNATIVE — read args from NativeModules.RNConfig instead of device.getLaunchArgs()
// NativeModules.RNConfig.API_ENV is available regardless of reload strategy

// WHY this matters: teams use device.getLaunchArgs() in guard assertions to verify
// test configuration before proceeding (Pattern 150 pattern) — silent undefined returns
// cause guard assertions to pass vacuously, letting tests proceed with a misconfigured
// app environment and producing false positives
```

---

## Updated Anti-Patterns Checklist (Cycle 31 additions)

| Anti-Pattern | Fix |
|---|---|
| Calling `device.appLaunchArgs.modify()` after `await device.reloadReactNative()` | `modify()` must be called before the reload it targets — the completed reload will not see the change (Gotcha 186) |
| Using `by.ancestor()` on a View with `accessible={true}` set on the parent container | `accessible={true}` collapses the accessibility subtree — children are not individually addressable; remove or use `importantForAccessibility` (Gotcha 187) |
| Using `element.multiTap(2)` for `GestureDetector onDoubleTap` on Android | Espresso inter-tap delay may not satisfy Android's double-tap threshold — use a platform-conditional tap sequence or expose a test-only handler (Gotcha 188) |
| Using `element.clearText()` on a Formik `mode:'onChange'` field before `typeText()` | `clearText()` fires an empty-string change event triggering premature validation — use `replaceText()` for a single atomic update (Gotcha 189) |
| Asserting `device.getLaunchArgs()` for static config args after `reloadReactNative()` | Static config args are not re-injected on JS-only reloads — mirror them via `appLaunchArgs.modify()` or read from `NativeModules.RNConfig` (Gotcha 190) |

---

## Cycle 32 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 158 — `element.scroll()` with `whileElement` for infinite-scroll list item discovery [official]

**Description:** When testing infinite-scroll lists (FlatList, FlashList) where target items are not yet rendered, `waitFor(element(by.id('target-item'))).toBeVisible().whileElement(by.id('list-container')).scroll(200, 'down')` scrolls the list incrementally until the item becomes visible or the timeout elapses. This avoids brittle `scrollTo` calls with hard-coded offsets that break when list data changes.

```ts
// Scroll a FlatList until a dynamically-loaded item appears
it('finds an item loaded on page 3 of the infinite list', async () => {
  await element(by.id('home-screen')).waitFor(element(by.id('product-list'))).toBeVisible();

  await waitFor(element(by.id('product-item-42')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .whileElement(by.id('product-list'))
    .scroll(250, 'down', NaN, 0.5);

  await expect(element(by.id('product-item-42'))).toBeVisible();
  await element(by.id('product-item-42')).tap();

  await waitFor(element(by.id('product-detail-screen')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(4000);

  await expect(element(by.id('product-title'))).toHaveText('Item 42');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use when the list is dynamically paginated and item render position is unpredictable. Do NOT use on short static lists — `element(by.id('item')).tap()` directly is faster and less flaky. Do NOT set an unbounded timeout without a `withTimeout` on the outer `waitFor` — the scroll loop will run indefinitely if the item never loads. Named alternative: `element.scrollTo('bottom')` (one-shot, no waiting, risks overshooting). [official]

---

### Pattern 159 — `by.web(element(by.id('webview'))).element(by.web.id('submit-btn'))` for hybrid WebView interaction [official]

**Description:** Detox 20+ exposes a `by.web()` API for driving DOM elements inside `WebView` components. Scope the web matcher to a specific WebView by wrapping it in `by.web(element(by.id('webview-id')))`, then chain `.element(by.web.id(...))` / `.element(by.web.cssSelector(...))` to target the DOM node. Supports `tap()`, `typeText()`, `replaceText()`, `clearText()`, `selectAllText()`, `getText()`, `scrollToView()`, and `focus()`.

```ts
import { by, device, element, expect, waitFor } from 'detox';

it('submits a payment form inside the embedded WebView', async () => {
  await waitFor(element(by.id('payment-webview')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(8000);

  const webview = by.web(element(by.id('payment-webview')));

  await webview.element(by.web.id('card-number')).typeText('4111111111111111');
  await webview.element(by.web.id('expiry')).typeText('12/28');
  await webview.element(by.web.id('cvv')).typeText('123');
  await webview.element(by.web.id('submit-btn')).tap();

  await waitFor(element(by.id('payment-success-banner')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(10000);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use for embedded payment forms, OAuth sign-in WebViews, and content editors rendered in WKWebView/WebView. Do NOT use on cross-origin iframes — `by.web()` cannot cross the security origin boundary; instrument the OAuth redirect URI instead. Named alternative: `by.web.cssSelector()` (more flexible for non-id DOM elements, but fragile to class-name churn). [official]

---

### Pattern 160 — `device.setStatusBar()` for precise iOS status-bar state in screenshot regression tests [official]

**Description:** `device.setStatusBar(options)` (iOS simulator only) overrides time, battery level, WiFi bars, and cellular signal so that screenshot baselines are deterministic. Call it in `beforeAll` to pin to a known state before any visual snapshot; call `device.resetStatusBar()` in `afterAll` to restore defaults. Without this, CI screenshots taken at different times of day have different clock values and fail pixel-diff comparisons.

```ts
import { device } from 'detox';

beforeAll(async () => {
  // Pin status bar to a known deterministic state for screenshot baselines
  await device.setStatusBar({
    time: '9:41',
    batteryLevel: 100,
    batteryState: 'charging',
    wifiMode: 'active',
    wifiBars: 3,
    cellularMode: 'active',
    cellularBars: 4,
    operatorName: 'TestCo',
    dataNetwork: '5G',
  });
});

afterAll(async () => {
  await device.resetStatusBar();
});

it('renders the dashboard header correctly', async () => {
  const screenshot = await device.takeScreenshot('dashboard-header-baseline');
  // Compare with stored baseline using your image-diff library
  expect(screenshot).toMatchImageSnapshot({ threshold: 0.01 });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use for any pixel-level or layout screenshot test on iOS simulator. Do NOT use on Android — `device.setStatusBar()` is iOS-only; Android emulators expose `adb shell settings` for demo mode but Detox does not wrap this. Named alternative: `element.takeScreenshot()` (element-scoped, avoids status bar entirely if the status bar is not in scope). [official]

---

### Pattern 161 — `device.shake()` to trigger iOS motion events in shake-to-report and undo-shake flows [official]

**Description:** `device.shake()` sends a simulated device shake to the iOS simulator, which raises `UIApplication.willResignActiveNotification` briefly and fires the `motionEnded(_:with:)` event chain. This is the correct way to test shake-to-undo, shake-to-report-a-bug, and accelerometer-gated features without physical hardware.

```ts
it('opens the shake-to-report dialog when the device is shaken', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });

  await waitFor(element(by.id('main-screen')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(5000);

  // Trigger shake event on the simulator
  await device.shake();

  // The bug-report dialog should appear within 2 seconds
  await waitFor(element(by.id('shake-report-modal')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(2000);

  await expect(element(by.text('Report a Problem'))).toBeVisible();

  // Dismiss and verify the modal can be closed
  await element(by.id('dismiss-report-modal')).tap();
  await expect(element(by.id('shake-report-modal'))).not.toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use for shake-gated features on iOS. Do NOT use on Android — `device.shake()` is iOS-simulator-only; on Android, use `adb shell sendevent` via `device.executeShellCommand()` or expose a test-only trigger button. Named alternative: a testID-gated `__DEV__` button that calls the same handler (skips platform inconsistency entirely). [official]

---

### Pattern 162 — `element.getAttributes()` for asserting computed layout bounds and accessibility label at runtime [official]

**Description:** `element.getAttributes()` returns a snapshot of the element's resolved attributes: `{ frame: { x, y, width, height }, text, label, placeholder, value, enabled, focused, identifier }`. This is the correct approach for asserting that an element has a minimum tap target size (≥44×44 pt on iOS, ≥48×48 dp on Android) or confirming that a dynamic `accessibilityLabel` was set correctly by the component.

```ts
it('confirms the CTA button meets minimum tap-target size', async () => {
  await waitFor(element(by.id('cta-button')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(5000);

  const attrs = await element(by.id('cta-button')).getAttributes();

  if (!('frame' in attrs)) {
    throw new Error('getAttributes returned a multi-element result; refine the matcher');
  }

  expect(attrs.frame.width).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(44);
  expect(attrs.frame.height).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(44);
  expect(attrs.label).toBe('Continue to checkout');
  expect(attrs.enabled).toBe(true);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use for layout-compliance, accessibility-label regression, and placeholder-text assertions. Do NOT use `getAttributes()` as a polling mechanism inside a `setInterval` — it issues a synchronous IPC call to the app process each time and will slow the test if called in a tight loop. Named alternative: `toHaveAccessibilityLabel()` matcher (declarative, no manual attribute extraction needed when only the label is under test). [official]

---

### Pattern 163 — `device.reverseTcpPort()` for directing Android emulator network traffic to the host machine's mock server [official]

**Description:** When running E2E tests against a local mock API server, the Android emulator's `localhost` resolves to the emulator, not the host. `device.reverseTcpPort(8080)` (wraps `adb reverse tcp:8080 tcp:8080`) makes the emulator's port 8080 forward to the host port 8080, so `http://localhost:8080` in the app reaches the host's mock server. Place this in `globalSetup` or `beforeAll` rather than per-test.

```ts
import { device } from 'detox';
import { startMockServer, stopMockServer } from '../support/mockServer';

let mockServer: { port: number; stop: () => Promise<void> };

beforeAll(async () => {
  mockServer = await startMockServer({ port: 8080 });

  if (device.getPlatform() === 'android') {
    await device.reverseTcpPort(8080);
  }
  // iOS simulator shares the host network directly; no reversal needed

  await device.launchApp({
    newInstance: true,
    launchArgs: { API_BASE_URL: 'http://localhost:8080' },
  });
});

afterAll(async () => {
  if (device.getPlatform() === 'android') {
    await device.unreverseTcpPort(8080);
  }
  await mockServer.stop();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use when running a local mock server on the host alongside Android emulator E2E tests. Do NOT use in CI pipelines that run the app against a shared staging URL — `reverseTcpPort` has no effect when the device under test is a real physical device connected via USB unless it is explicitly adb-connected to the CI agent. Named alternative: hard-code `10.0.2.2:8080` (Android emulator's well-known alias for host loopback) to avoid the `reverseTcpPort` call entirely. [official]

---

### Pattern 164 — `detox test --inspect-brk` with VS Code attach for stepping through flaky test scenarios interactively [community]

**Description:** Running `detox test --inspect-brk --testNamePattern="<flaky test name>"` pauses test execution on the first line and exposes a Node.js inspector endpoint. Attach VS Code's Node debugger (`.vscode/launch.json` with `"request": "attach"`) to set breakpoints inside spec files, inspect `element()` return values, and single-step through `waitFor` chains without restarting the whole suite. This is the fastest way to diagnose the exact IPC call that times out on a flaky test.

```ts
// .vscode/launch.json snippet for attaching to Detox inspector
// {
//   "type": "node",
//   "request": "attach",
//   "name": "Detox: Attach to running test",
//   "port": 9229,
//   "skipFiles": ["<node_internals>/**", "**/node_modules/detox/**"]
// }

// Example spec with a deliberate breakpoint via debugger statement
it('debuggable: verifies checkout flow timing', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });

  await waitFor(element(by.id('cart-icon'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
  await element(by.id('cart-icon')).tap();

  debugger; // Execution pauses here when --inspect-brk is active in VS Code

  await waitFor(element(by.id('checkout-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
  await expect(element(by.id('order-total'))).toHaveText('$42.00');
});

// Run with: npx detox test --inspect-brk -t "verifies checkout flow timing"
```

**Tradeoff:** Use exclusively during local debugging of flaky or complex scenarios. Do NOT commit specs with `debugger` statements — the test hangs in CI when no debugger is attached. Named alternative: `console.log(await element(by.id('foo')).getAttributes())` inline logging (no IDE integration required, but less interactive). [community]

---

### Pattern 165 — `jestCircus` `handleTestEvent` hook for emitting per-step Detox timing metrics to CI observability systems [community]

**Description:** Detox uses Jest Circus as its runner. `DetoxCircusEnvironment` exposes `handleTestEvent` which fires for `test_start`, `test_done`, `test_fn_start`, `test_fn_failure`, and `hook_*` events. Instrument this hook in a custom environment extending `DetoxCircusEnvironment` to emit step durations to Datadog, Grafana, or a local JSON artifact — enabling trend analysis of which `waitFor` steps are slowest across runs.

```ts
import { DetoxCircusEnvironment } from 'detox/runners/jest';
import type { Circus } from '@jest/types';

export default class InstrumentedDetoxEnvironment extends DetoxCircusEnvironment {
  private stepStart = 0;

  override async handleTestEvent(
    event: Circus.Event,
    state: Circus.State,
  ): Promise<void> {
    await super.handleTestEvent(event, state);

    if (event.name === 'test_fn_start') {
      this.stepStart = Date.now();
    }

    if (event.name === 'test_fn_success' || event.name === 'test_fn_failure') {
      const duration = Date.now() - this.stepStart;
      const testName = state.currentlyRunningTest?.name ?? 'unknown';
      // Emit to your observability sink
      process.stdout.write(
        JSON.stringify({ event: 'detox_step', test: testName, durationMs: duration }) + '\n',
      );
    }
  }
}
// jest.config.ts: testEnvironment: './support/InstrumentedDetoxEnvironment'
```

**Tradeoff:** Use in mature test suites that need CI performance budgets or SLO tracking. Do NOT add complex I/O (HTTP calls, database writes) inside `handleTestEvent` — it executes synchronously in the runner event loop and slow I/O will skew timings and block test teardown. Named alternative: Detox built-in `--record-logs all` artifact + post-process with a log parser (simpler, but timing granularity is per-test, not per-step). [community]

---

### Pattern 166 — `device.installApp()` / `device.uninstallApp()` for testing app update migration flows [official]

**Description:** `device.installApp()` installs the app binary without launching it; `device.uninstallApp()` removes it while preserving the device state. This pair enables testing upgrade scenarios: install v1, seed data, uninstall and install v2, launch, and verify that data migration ran correctly — all within a single E2E spec without needing two separate CI pipelines.

```ts
it('migrates user preferences from v1 schema to v2 schema on first launch', async () => {
  // Step 1: install and seed v1 app
  await device.installApp(); // uses binaryPath from current config
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true, launchArgs: { SCHEMA_VERSION: '1' } });

  await waitFor(element(by.id('settings-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
  await element(by.id('theme-toggle')).tap(); // set dark mode in v1
  await device.terminateApp();

  // Step 2: install v2 over the top (no uninstall — simulates OTA update)
  await device.installApp(); // replace with v2 binary path via env override
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: false }); // retain v1 user data

  // Step 3: verify migration
  await waitFor(element(by.id('settings-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(6000);
  await expect(element(by.id('theme-toggle'))).toHaveToggleValue(true); // dark mode preserved
  await expect(element(by.id('migration-success-banner'))).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use for migration-regression tests when schema changes are shipped. Do NOT rely on `device.installApp()` to test install-time permissions dialogs — the app must be fully uninstalled first for the OS to re-show permission prompts. Named alternative: `device.launchApp({ delete: true })` (clears data but does not simulate a binary-level upgrade). [official]

---

### Pattern 167 — `by.system` system dialog dismissal for OS-level permission and alert sheets [official]

**Description:** `element(by.system.label('Allow'))` / `element(by.system.label('Don\'t Allow'))` targets native OS permission dialogs (camera, location, notifications, microphone) that appear outside the React Native view hierarchy. These system dialogs cannot be matched with standard `by.id()` or `by.text()` matchers. For iOS, Detox intercepts the `SpringBoard` layer; for Android, it uses UiAutomator2.

```ts
it('grants camera permission and opens the scanner on first launch', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({
    newInstance: true,
    permissions: { camera: 'unset' }, // force the OS dialog to appear
  });

  await waitFor(element(by.id('scan-button'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
  await element(by.id('scan-button')).tap();

  // iOS: "Allow 'MyApp' to access your camera?" dialog
  if (device.getPlatform() === 'ios') {
    await waitFor(element(by.system.label('Allow'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
    await element(by.system.label('Allow')).tap();
  } else {
    // Android: "Allow MyApp to take pictures and record video?"
    await waitFor(element(by.system.label('While using the app'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
    await element(by.system.label('While using the app')).tap();
  }

  await waitFor(element(by.id('camera-preview'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use when the feature flow requires the actual OS permission dialog to appear. Do NOT use `by.system` as a fallback for in-app custom permission rationale dialogs — those use standard React Native views and should be targeted with `by.id()`. Named alternative: `device.launchApp({ permissions: { camera: 'YES' } })` (pre-grants permission at launch time, skips dialog entirely — preferred when permission-granting UX is not under test). [official]

---

### Pattern 168 — `element.longPress()` with `duration` for press-and-hold context menus and haptic triggers [official]

**Description:** `element(by.id('list-item')).longPress(800)` sends a press-and-hold gesture lasting 800 ms, which is the standard iOS context-menu trigger threshold. The `duration` parameter (milliseconds, default 1000) must be tuned per platform: iOS UIKit menus activate at ~500 ms, Android context menus at ~300 ms, and custom `onLongPress` handlers at whatever `delayLongPress` prop is set on the `Pressable`.

```ts
it('opens the context menu on long-press of a message bubble', async () => {
  await waitFor(element(by.id('message-bubble-7')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(5000);

  // Use platform-appropriate duration
  const longPressDuration = device.getPlatform() === 'ios' ? 600 : 400;
  await element(by.id('message-bubble-7')).longPress(longPressDuration);

  // Context menu should appear
  await waitFor(element(by.id('context-menu'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);

  await expect(element(by.text('Copy'))).toBeVisible();
  await expect(element(by.text('Delete'))).toBeVisible();
  await expect(element(by.text('React'))).toBeVisible();

  // Select "React" option
  await element(by.text('React')).tap();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('emoji-picker'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use for any gesture that differs from a normal tap: context menus, drag handles, swipe-to-reveal triggers, press-and-hold animations. Do NOT use the default 1000 ms duration if the component's `delayLongPress` is set below 500 ms — the default will feel slow and introduce unnecessary test latency. Named alternative: expose a `__testLongPressHandler` testID prop on the component that triggers the handler directly without a gesture (avoids duration tuning entirely). [official]

---

### Pattern 169 — `detox-copilot` `pilot.perform()` natural-language step execution for exploratory smoke tests [community]

**Description:** `detox-copilot` (Detox's optional LLM-assisted layer) exposes `pilot.perform(instruction: string)` which translates a plain-English step into one or more Detox API calls at runtime. This is useful for rapid smoke-test scripts where the exact element IDs are unknown, and for onboarding new team members who are not yet fluent in Detox's matcher API.

```ts
import { pilot } from 'detox/plugins/detox-copilot';

// Precondition: DETOX_COPILOT_API_KEY is set in the environment
// and pilot.init() was called in globalSetup

it('smoke: user can log in and reach the dashboard', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });

  // Natural-language steps — copilot resolves to actual Detox API calls
  await pilot.perform('Tap the "Sign In" button on the welcome screen');
  await pilot.perform('Enter "testuser@example.com" in the email field');
  await pilot.perform('Enter "P@ssword123" in the password field');
  await pilot.perform('Tap the "Log In" button');
  await pilot.perform('Verify that the dashboard screen is visible');
  await pilot.perform('Verify that the "Hello, Test User" greeting is visible');

  // Standard Detox assertions can be mixed in freely
  await expect(element(by.id('dashboard-screen'))).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use for exploratory, smoke, and demo tests where speed of authorship outweighs step precision. Do NOT use `pilot.perform()` for assertions in critical-path regression tests — LLM output is non-deterministic and may resolve to a different API call on repeat runs if the prompt is ambiguous. Named alternative: standard `element(by.id(...)).tap()` chain (deterministic, CI-safe, no external API dependency). [community]

---

### Pattern 170 — `device.enableSynchronization()` / `device.disableSynchronization()` for tests involving WebSocket-driven real-time updates [official]

**Description:** Detox's synchronization engine tracks pending network requests, JS timers, and animation frames. WebSocket connections keep an open async channel that the synchronization engine never considers "idle," causing `waitFor()` and action calls to timeout waiting for a quiescence that never arrives. `device.disableSynchronization()` bypasses this; explicit `waitFor(...).withTimeout()` guards replace automatic idle detection.

```ts
it('shows real-time chat messages delivered over WebSocket', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });

  // WebSocket connection is established on app start — disable sync to avoid
  // Detox hanging waiting for the socket to close
  await device.disableSynchronization();

  try {
    await waitFor(element(by.id('chat-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);

    // Simulate an incoming WS message from the test harness (via mock server)
    // The mock WS server pushes a message; app renders it within 1 second
    await waitFor(element(by.id('message-from-alice')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(3000);

    await expect(element(by.text('Hello from Alice!'))).toBeVisible();
  } finally {
    // Always re-enable synchronization to avoid leaking disabled state to other tests
    await device.enableSynchronization();
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use for any feature that holds a persistent async channel (WebSockets, SSE, long-polling, Bluetooth LE peripheral scanning). Do NOT disable synchronization globally in `beforeAll` as a catch-all fix for flaky tests — it removes Detox's idle detection entirely and masks genuine timing issues. Named alternative: `jest.fakeTimers()` (only suppresses JS timer-based async; does not help with native network activity). [official]

---

### Pattern 171 — `device.captureViewHierarchy()` for diagnosing element-not-found failures in CI artifact logs [official]

**Description:** `device.captureViewHierarchy(name)` saves a `.viewhierarchy` file (iOS) or an XML layout dump (Android) to the Detox artifacts directory. Calling it in the `afterEach` hook when a test fails provides a complete snapshot of the accessibility tree at the moment of failure — far more diagnostic than a screenshot alone because it shows every element's `testID`, bounds, and enabled state.

```ts
import { device } from 'detox';

afterEach(async () => {
  const testName = expect.getState().currentTestName ?? 'unknown';
  const testFailed = expect.getState().assertionCalls === 0 ||
    (expect.getState() as any).numPassingAsserts <
    (expect.getState() as any).assertionCalls;

  if (testFailed) {
    // Capture the full view hierarchy as a diagnostic artifact
    await device.captureViewHierarchy(`failure-${testName.replace(/\s+/g, '-')}`);
    await device.takeScreenshot(`failure-screenshot-${testName.replace(/\s+/g, '-')}`);
  }
});

it('navigates to the profile screen via the bottom tab', async () => {
  await element(by.id('tab-profile')).tap();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('profile-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
  // If this fails, the afterEach hook captures full hierarchy for diagnosis
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use in any suite that runs in CI where interactive debugging is impossible. Do NOT call `captureViewHierarchy` on every test pass — writing `.viewhierarchy` files is expensive on iOS (serializes the entire UIKit hierarchy to XML) and inflates artifact storage. Named alternative: `--record-videos failed` Detox CLI flag (captures video for visual replay, but does not expose the accessibility tree for selector debugging). [official]

---

### Pattern 172 — `expect(element(by.id('list'))).toHaveCount(n)` for asserting rendered list item count without scrolling [official]

**Description:** `toHaveCount(n)` asserts that exactly `n` elements match the given matcher in the currently rendered viewport (for visible elements) or in the full accessibility tree (for elements with `accessibilityViewIsModal` off). This is more reliable than counting text occurrences with `by.text()` in a list because each list item has a unique `testID` generated from the index or item ID, making miscount assertions deterministic.

```ts
it('renders exactly 5 pinned messages in the pinned panel', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({
    newInstance: true,
    launchArgs: { SEED_PINNED_COUNT: '5' },
  });

  await waitFor(element(by.id('pinned-panel'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);

  // Assert exact count of pinned message rows
  await expect(element(by.id('pinned-message-row'))).toHaveCount(5);

  // Verify first and last items are both visible
  await expect(element(by.id('pinned-message-row')).atIndex(0)).toBeVisible();
  await expect(element(by.id('pinned-message-row')).atIndex(4)).toBeVisible();

  // Remove one pin and verify count decreases
  await element(by.id('pinned-message-row')).atIndex(0).swipe('left', 'fast', 0.7);
  await element(by.id('unpin-action')).tap();
  await expect(element(by.id('pinned-message-row'))).toHaveCount(4);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use when asserting that a specific number of list items is rendered (pagination boundaries, filtered results, empty-state transitions). Do NOT use `toHaveCount` on FlatList items when the list is virtualized and only renders a window of items — only items in the render window are in the accessibility tree, so the count will be less than the total data length. Named alternative: assert on `by.id('empty-state')` visibility (indirect count check when only zero vs. non-zero matters). [official]

---

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 32

### Gotcha 191 — `element.scroll()` with `whileElement` silently stops scrolling when `ScrollView` has `scrollEnabled={false}` set programmatically mid-test [community]

**Root cause**: If the app sets `scrollEnabled={false}` on a `ScrollView` in response to a modal appearing or a loading state, Detox's `whileElement().scroll()` loop does not throw an error — it simply fires scroll events that the ScrollView ignores. The `waitFor` loop exhausts its timeout waiting for the target element to appear, while the list sits frozen. The failure message is an unhelpful timeout error, not "scroll disabled," making this very hard to diagnose.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — waitFor with whileElement times out even though item exists in data
await waitFor(element(by.id('product-item-99')))
  .toBeVisible()
  .whileElement(by.id('product-list'))
  .scroll(300, 'down'); // silent no-op if scrollEnabled is false

// DIAGNOSIS — add a guard before the scroll loop
const listAttrs = await element(by.id('product-list')).getAttributes();
// Check: if the scroll indicator is absent or frame.height matches content.height,
// the list may have scroll disabled

// FIX — ensure the app re-enables scrollEnabled before entering the scroll loop:
// await waitFor(element(by.id('loading-overlay'))).not.toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
// Only then run the whileElement scroll

// WHY this matters: loading states commonly set scrollEnabled=false to prevent
// scroll-during-fetch jank, and tests that begin the whileElement loop before the
// fetch completes will reliably time out on CI where network latency is higher
```

---

### Gotcha 192 — `by.web()` `getText()` returns an empty string for text nodes rendered inside a Shadow DOM component [community]

**Root cause**: `by.web().getText()` uses the WebView's JavaScript bridge to call `element.textContent`. Shadow DOM roots are isolated from the document's main query selectors — `document.querySelector('[id="shadow-text"]')` returns `null` if the element is inside a `<shadow-root>`. The Detox web driver does not pierce shadow roots by default, so `getText()` resolves the element as an empty node and returns `''`.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — getText() returns '' for a visible text node inside a Web Component
const text = await webview.element(by.web.id('shadow-label')).getText();
console.log(text); // '' — element resolved to shadow root boundary

// WHY: Standard DOM querySelector cannot cross shadow DOM boundaries. The Detox
// web driver builds its element handle via querySelector, which stops at shadow roots.

// FIX (option A) — inject a JS executor via evaluateScript to pierce the shadow root:
// const text = await webview.element(by.web.id('host-element'))
//   .runScript(`el => el.shadowRoot.querySelector('#shadow-label').textContent`);

// FIX (option B) — work with the app team to expose the text via a data attribute
// on the shadow host: <my-component data-display-text="..."> so standard querySelector
// can read it without piercing the shadow root

// FIX (option C) — add a non-shadow fallback element for testing:
// render an aria-hidden <span id="shadow-label-test-mirror"> outside the shadow root
```

---

### Gotcha 193 — `device.setLocation()` does not move the iOS simulator's blue dot on a MapKit map until `CLLocationManager` delivers a second update [community]

**Root cause**: `device.setLocation(lat, lng)` sends a location override to the simulator's location daemon. `CLLocationManager` delivers the first update asynchronously after a ~200–500 ms delay. MapKit's annotation layer only re-renders the blue dot after a second location update is delivered — the first update initializes the internal location state but does not always trigger a UI repaint. Tests that assert on the blue dot position immediately after `setLocation()` will find the dot at the previous location.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — blue dot is still at old position immediately after setLocation()
await device.setLocation(37.7749, -122.4194); // San Francisco
await expect(element(by.id('map-user-location-dot'))).toBeVisible(); // passes
// But the dot visual position has not updated — snapshot comparison fails

// FIX — send a second setLocation() call a short time after the first to force
// a second CLLocationManager update that triggers the MapKit repaint:
await device.setLocation(37.7749, -122.4194);
await waitFor(element(by.id('map-accuracy-ring'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(1500);
await device.setLocation(37.7750, -122.4194); // tiny delta forces second update
await waitFor(element(by.id('map-user-location-dot')))
  .toHaveId('map-user-location-dot')
  .withTimeout(2000);

// WHY this matters: map-based features (ride hailing, delivery tracking, store locator)
// are very common in React Native apps and setLocation() is the only non-hardware
// way to test them — the two-update pattern is not documented and is discovered
// through CI flakiness
```

---

### Gotcha 194 — `element.typeText()` on a `TextInput` with `autoCorrect={true}` inserts autocorrect-substituted text instead of the literal string typed [community]

**Root cause**: On iOS simulator, `typeText()` simulates keystrokes through the software keyboard. If `autoCorrect` is enabled, the iOS text system applies autocorrections (e.g., typing `teh` becomes `the`). The Detox IPC layer does not disable autocorrect before dispatching keystrokes — the text that lands in the field depends on iOS system spell-check dictionaries, which differ between OS versions and simulator configurations. This causes `toHaveText('teh test')` to fail with `toHaveText('the test')`.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — typeText() lands different text than the string argument
await element(by.id('search-input')).typeText('teh best restautant');
// Actual value: 'the best restaurant' — autocorrected on iOS 18.x

// FIX (preferred) — set autoCorrect={false} on TextInput elements used in E2E tests
// <TextInput testID="search-input" autoCorrect={false} ... />

// FIX (alternative) — use replaceText() which bypasses the keyboard layer entirely
// and sets the field value directly via KVO, skipping autocorrect:
await element(by.id('search-input')).replaceText('teh best restautant');
// Value is exactly 'teh best restautant' — no autocorrect applied

// WHY this matters: search bars, comment inputs, and address fields commonly have
// autoCorrect enabled for real-user UX — tests that use typeText() on these fields
// see different values per OS version, creating cross-version CI failures that look
// like regressions in text-handling logic
```

---

### Gotcha 195 — `device.terminateApp()` on Android does not trigger `onDestroy()` lifecycle on all Activities; some background services keep running and corrupt the next test's initial state [community]

**Root cause**: `device.terminateApp()` sends `SIGKILL` to the app's main process on Android. Activities are destroyed, but `Service` subclasses running in a separate process (declared with `android:process=":background"` in `AndroidManifest.xml`) survive the kill because they run in their own PID. When the app relaunches for the next test, the surviving service may reconnect and push stale state (cached data, WebSocket events, notification badges) before the new Activity renders, corrupting the test's initial condition.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — second test starts with a notification badge count > 0 even though
// device.terminateApp() was called between tests

// BAD teardown — leaves background service alive
afterEach(async () => {
  await device.terminateApp(); // kills main process; :background service survives
});

// FIX — use device.launchApp({ newInstance: true }) in beforeEach rather than
// terminateApp() in afterEach. newInstance:true forces a cold start via full
// process replacement, which also kills any :background process:
beforeEach(async () => {
  await device.launchApp({
    newInstance: true,
    launchArgs: { RESET_SERVICES: '1' }, // app-side hook that stops services on launch
  });
});

// ALTERNATIVE — add a native module reset command callable from tests:
// await NativeModules.TestUtils.stopBackgroundServices();
// await device.terminateApp();

// WHY this matters: push notification services, analytics SDKs, and sync managers
// are commonly in separate Android processes — this pattern is very frequent in
// production apps but the multi-process survival of terminateApp() is not documented
// in Detox's teardown guidance
```

---

### Gotcha 196 — `waitFor(element(by.id('modal'))).not.toBeVisible()` resolves immediately while the dismissal animation is still running, causing the next action to interact with the half-dismissed modal [community]

**Root cause**: Detox's `not.toBeVisible()` checks the element's `isVisible` property in the accessibility tree. On iOS, a modal's container view is marked `isVisible = false` as soon as the UIKit dismissal animation begins — before the animation completes (~300 ms for the default spring curve). If the test proceeds immediately after `not.toBeVisible()` resolves, it may tap an element that is visually partially obscured by the still-sliding-down modal, causing the tap to land on the modal overlay instead of the intended target.

```ts
// BAD — proceeds the instant the modal is marked non-visible, before animation ends
await element(by.id('dismiss-modal-button')).tap();
await waitFor(element(by.id('modal-container'))).not.toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
await element(by.id('main-cta-button')).tap(); // taps modal overlay during animation

// FIX (option A) — wait for the element behind the modal to become visible/hittable
// instead of waiting for the modal to become non-visible:
await element(by.id('dismiss-modal-button')).tap();
await waitFor(element(by.id('main-cta-button'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
await element(by.id('main-cta-button')).tap(); // now the modal is fully gone

// FIX (option B) — wait for the target to be hittable after the non-visible guard
await element(by.id('dismiss-modal-button')).tap();
await waitFor(element(by.id('modal-container'))).not.toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
await waitFor(element(by.id('main-cta-button'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);
await element(by.id('main-cta-button')).tap();

// WHY this matters: modal dismiss animations are present in nearly every React Native
// app (bottom sheets, alert dialogs, action sheets) and the isVisible / animation-done
// gap is the #1 cause of tap-lands-on-wrong-element failures in modal-heavy test suites
```

---

## Updated Anti-Patterns Checklist (Cycle 32 additions)

| Anti-Pattern | Fix |
|---|---|
| Starting `whileElement().scroll()` before a loading overlay is dismissed | `scrollEnabled` may be `false` during loading; wait for overlay to disappear before entering the scroll loop (Gotcha 191) |
| Using `by.web().getText()` on text inside a Shadow DOM component | Shadow DOM isolates nodes from `querySelector`; pierce via `runScript()` or expose a data attribute on the shadow host (Gotcha 192) |
| Asserting map blue-dot position immediately after `device.setLocation()` | `CLLocationManager` requires two updates before MapKit repaints the dot; send a second `setLocation()` with a tiny delta (Gotcha 193) |
| Using `element.typeText()` on a `TextInput` with `autoCorrect={true}` | iOS autocorrect substitutes literals; use `replaceText()` or set `autoCorrect={false}` on test-facing inputs (Gotcha 194) |
| Relying on `device.terminateApp()` to stop Android `:background` process services | `SIGKILL` on the main PID leaves separate-process services alive; use `newInstance: true` in `beforeEach` for a clean cold start (Gotcha 195) |
| Using `waitFor(...).not.toBeVisible()` to gate actions after a modal dismissal | `isVisible` flips before animation ends; wait for the target behind the modal to become visible instead (Gotcha 196) |
