## Cycle 34 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 185 — `device.setNetworkConditions()` to simulate slow 3G and offline states for loading-skeleton and retry-button flows [official]

`device.setNetworkConditions(conditions)` throttles or fully blocks the device's network at the OS level, letting tests verify loading skeletons, retry CTAs, and offline banners without mocking individual fetch calls. Available on Android (emulator) and iOS (simulator) with named presets (`'GPRS'`, `'Regular2G'`, `'Regular3G'`, `'Regular4G'`, `'WiFi'`) or a custom conditions object. Restoring normal connectivity requires calling `device.setNetworkConditions('WiFi')` or `device.resetNetworkConditions()` in `afterEach` to avoid poisoning subsequent tests.

```ts
// e2e/offline-handling.test.ts
import { device, element, by, waitFor, expect } from 'detox';

describe('Offline handling', () => {
  afterEach(async () => {
    // Always restore before next test
    await device.setNetworkConditions({ wifi: true });
  });

  it('shows retry button when the feed fails to load on 3G', async () => {
    // Throttle to simulated 3G before launch
    await device.setNetworkConditions({
      downloadBandwidth: 750,   // kbps
      uploadBandwidth: 250,
      latency: 300,             // ms
      packetLoss: 10,           // percent
    });

    await device.reloadReactNative();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('loading-skeleton')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(3000);

    // With 10% packet loss the request should eventually time out
    await waitFor(element(by.id('retry-button')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(15000);

    await element(by.id('retry-button')).tap();
    // Restore network so the retry can succeed
    await device.setNetworkConditions({ wifi: true });

    await waitFor(element(by.id('feed-item-0')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(8000);
  });

  it('shows offline banner when network is fully disabled', async () => {
    await device.setNetworkConditions({ offline: true });
    await device.reloadReactNative();

    await waitFor(element(by.id('offline-banner')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(4000);

    await expect(element(by.id('offline-banner'))).toHaveText('You are offline');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when**: testing user-visible fallback UIs (offline banners, skeletons, retry CTAs) that depend on real network failure, not on a mocked API layer.
- **Do NOT use when**: your app's network layer is fully mocked via MSW or a custom fetch interceptor — OS-level throttling has no effect on in-process mocks and will just slow the test down for no benefit.
- **Alternative**: intercept `fetch`/`XMLHttpRequest` at the JS layer with a Jest setup file or MSW service worker to return controlled error responses without touching OS network state.

[official]

---

### Pattern 186 — `by.web.cssSelector()` and `webElement.runScript()` for asserting deep WebView DOM state that has no accessible label [official]

When a WebView renders third-party HTML (payment iframes, rich-text editors, embedded maps), interactive elements often lack `aria-label` or `data-testid` attributes. `by.web.cssSelector(selector)` reaches into the WKWebView/WebView DOM using a CSS selector, and `webElement.runScript(script)` executes arbitrary JavaScript against that element, enabling property assertions that no native Detox matcher can express. The result of `runScript` is returned as a typed value and can be asserted with a plain Jest `expect`.

```ts
// e2e/payment-webview.test.ts
import { device, element, by, waitFor, web, expect as detoxExpect } from 'detox';

describe('Payment WebView iframe', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.reloadReactNative();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('checkout-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
    await element(by.id('pay-now-button')).tap();
    // Wait for the WebView to finish its initial navigation
    await waitFor(element(by.id('payment-webview'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(8000);
  });

  it('fills in card number and verifies masked input', async () => {
    const cardInput = web(by.id('payment-webview'))
      .element(by.web.cssSelector('input[data-cy="card-number"]'));

    await cardInput.tap();
    await cardInput.typeText('4242424242424242');

    // Read the masked display value via runScript
    const maskedValue: string = await cardInput.runScript(
      (el: HTMLInputElement) => el.value,
    );
    // Payment libraries mask card numbers — assert last 4 digits visible
    expect(maskedValue).toMatch(/\*{12}4242$/);

    // Assert the Pay button is now enabled
    const payBtn = web(by.id('payment-webview'))
      .element(by.web.cssSelector('button[data-cy="submit-payment"]'));
    const isDisabled: boolean = await payBtn.runScript(
      (el: HTMLButtonElement) => el.disabled,
    );
    expect(isDisabled).toBe(false);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when**: the WebView content is a third-party form without testable `aria-*` attributes and you need to assert DOM property values beyond visibility.
- **Do NOT use when**: the WebView content is first-party — add proper `testID` props and use standard native Detox matchers; `runScript` couples your test to implementation details that break across library upgrades.
- **Alternative**: expose a JS bridge (`window.ReactNativeWebView.postMessage`) that fires events readable by the RN layer, allowing the native test to assert on RN state instead of DOM internals.

[official]

---

### Pattern 187 — `device.takeScreenshot(name)` as an on-failure artifact capture strategy with Jest `afterEach` [official]

Storing a named screenshot on test failure gives CI pipelines an immediately actionable artifact without requiring a full video recording. `device.takeScreenshot(name)` saves a PNG to the active Detox artifacts folder (configured via `artifacts.rootDir` in `.detoxrc.ts`) and returns the absolute file path. Wrapping it in `afterEach` with a Jest test-state check captures screenshots only for failing tests, avoiding artifact bloat.

```ts
// e2e/setup/screenshot-on-fail.ts
import { device } from 'detox';

// Attach to global Jest lifecycle so every describe block benefits automatically
afterEach(async () => {
  // Jest exposes the current test state through expect.getState()
  const { currentTestName, testPath } = expect.getState() as {
    currentTestName?: string;
    testPath?: string;
  };

  // jasmine2 runner uses jasmine.currentSpec
  const jasmineState = (global as any).jasmine?.currentSpec;
  const failed = jasmineState
    ? jasmineState.failedExpectations?.length > 0
    : false; // fallback for jest-circus

  if (failed) {
    const safeName = (currentTestName ?? 'unknown')
      .replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9_-]/g, '_')
      .slice(0, 80);

    const screenshotPath = await device.takeScreenshot(`FAIL_${safeName}`);
    console.error(`[Detox] Screenshot saved: ${screenshotPath}`);
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when**: your CI pipeline collects Detox artifact folders as build artifacts and engineers need visual evidence of failures without setting up full video recording.
- **Do NOT use when**: screenshots leak PII (banking/health apps) — either disable the artifact collection in production CI or add a data-masking middleware to sanitize the screenshot before upload.
- **Alternative**: enable `artifacts.screenshot: 'failing'` in `.detoxrc.ts` for the same behavior without custom code; the manual approach gives more control over naming and metadata.

[official]

---

### Pattern 188 — `waitFor(element).not.toBeVisible().withTimeout()` as a disappearance assertion for modals and toasts [official]

After dismissing a modal or triggering a toast that auto-hides, tests commonly fail because the element is still animating off-screen when the next interaction happens. `waitFor(element(by.id('toast'))).not.toBeVisible().withTimeout(ms)` polls until the element is gone, turning an implicit race condition into an explicit, timeout-bounded assertion. This prevents cascading failures where a lingering overlay intercepts taps meant for the next screen.

```ts
// e2e/toast-and-modal.test.ts
import { device, element, by, waitFor, expect } from 'detox';

describe('Success toast auto-dismiss', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.reloadReactNative();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('form-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
  });

  it('toast disappears automatically within 3 seconds of submission', async () => {
    await element(by.id('name-input')).typeText('Jane Doe');
    await element(by.id('submit-button')).tap();

    // First assert the toast appeared
    await waitFor(element(by.id('success-toast')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(3000);

    // Then assert it disappears on its own within 4 s
    await waitFor(element(by.id('success-toast')))
      .not.toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(4000);

    // Now safely interact with the next screen — toast is confirmed gone
    await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
    await element(by.id('profile-button')).tap();
  });

  it('modal dismisses after confirm tap and overlay is gone before next tap', async () => {
    await element(by.id('delete-button')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('confirm-modal'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
    await element(by.id('confirm-modal-yes')).tap();

    // Guard against the modal fade-out animation intercepting the next tap
    await waitFor(element(by.id('confirm-modal')))
      .not.toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(3000);

    await element(by.id('create-button')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('create-form'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when**: animated overlays (toasts, modals, bottom sheets) auto-dismiss and downstream interactions fail intermittently because the overlay intercepts taps.
- **Do NOT use when**: the element is conditionally rendered (removed from the tree vs. `opacity: 0`) — `not.toBeVisible()` passes for both hidden and unmounted elements; use `not.toExist()` if you need to assert the element is fully removed from the hierarchy.
- **Alternative**: wrap the post-dismiss interaction in a `try/catch` retry loop as a last resort, but the explicit disappearance assertion is cleaner and deterministic.

[official]

---

### Pattern 189 — `element.adjustSliderToPosition(normalizedPosition)` for testing range slider inputs with accessible bounds assertions [official]

`adjustSliderToPosition(normalizedPosition)` sets a native slider (`Slider` / `RCTSlider`) to a position between `0.0` (minimum) and `1.0` (maximum) without needing to calculate pixel coordinates. Pairing it with `toHaveValue()` on the slider — which reflects the raw numeric value — lets tests assert both the interaction outcome and the accessibility-layer reading without inspecting internal component state.

```ts
// e2e/price-filter.test.ts
import { device, element, by, waitFor, expect } from 'detox';

describe('Price range slider', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.reloadReactNative();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('filter-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
  });

  it('sets max price to midpoint and updates the result count', async () => {
    const maxSlider = element(by.id('price-max-slider'));

    // Move to 50% of the range (e.g. $0–$1000 → $500)
    await maxSlider.adjustSliderToPosition(0.5);

    // Detox reflects the numeric value via the accessibility value
    await expect(maxSlider).toHaveValue('500');

    // Confirm the filter label updates
    await expect(element(by.id('price-max-label'))).toHaveText('$500');

    // Confirm the result count decreased
    await waitFor(element(by.id('product-row')))
      .toHaveCount(6)
      .withTimeout(3000);
  });

  it('setting slider to minimum shows the empty state', async () => {
    const maxSlider = element(by.id('price-max-slider'));
    await maxSlider.adjustSliderToPosition(0.0);

    await expect(maxSlider).toHaveValue('0');
    await waitFor(element(by.id('no-results-label')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(3000);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when**: the component is a native `Slider` (`react-native` core) or any view that registers as an `RCTSlider`; the normalized API avoids hard-coding pixel positions that break across screen densities.
- **Do NOT use when**: the slider is a custom JS-only component (e.g., `@react-native-community/slider` wrapped in a custom thumb) that doesn't expose `accessibilityValue` — the driver can't locate the slider and throws; fall back to `tapAtPoint` with calculated coordinates.
- **Alternative**: expose the slider's current value in a `testID`-labeled `Text` component and assert that directly, bypassing the `toHaveValue()` accessibility layer which can be unreliable on custom sliders.

[official]

---

### Pattern 190 — `element.tapAtPoint({ x, y })` for canvas-like and map views where semantic matchers cannot reach rendered touch targets [official]

`tapAtPoint({ x, y })` sends a precise touch event at coordinates relative to the matched element's top-left corner. It is the only viable approach for views that render their own touch-hit logic (MapView, SVG canvas, `react-native-skia` surfaces) where child elements are not exposed in the accessibility tree. Combine with `device.takeScreenshot()` to document the coordinate system in CI artifacts when coordinates are not self-evident.

```ts
// e2e/map-pin.test.ts
import { device, element, by, waitFor, expect } from 'detox';

describe('Map pin interactions', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.reloadReactNative();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('map-view'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(8000);
    // Wait for tiles to load — map fires an onMapReady callback that sets a testID
    await waitFor(element(by.id('map-ready-sentinel')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(10000);
  });

  it('taps the downtown office pin and shows the info card', async () => {
    // Coordinates determined from the design spec for a 390-pt wide map view
    // Pin is at approximately (195, 220) in the map's local coordinate space
    await element(by.id('map-view')).tapAtPoint({ x: 195, y: 220 });

    await waitFor(element(by.id('pin-info-card')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(4000);

    await expect(element(by.id('pin-title'))).toHaveText('Downtown Office');
    await expect(element(by.id('pin-address'))).toHaveText('123 Main St');
  });

  it('taps an empty map area and confirms no info card appears', async () => {
    await element(by.id('map-view')).tapAtPoint({ x: 10, y: 10 });

    // Info card should NOT appear — nothing is pinned in the top-left corner
    await expect(element(by.id('pin-info-card'))).not.toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when**: the tappable target is rendered by a custom drawing engine (maps, charts, SVG, Skia canvas) that does not expose children in the native accessibility tree.
- **Do NOT use when**: coordinates are derived from a hardcoded design spec but your CI devices have different screen sizes — normalize coordinates against `device.getUiDevice()` screen dimensions or use `by.id()` matchers on embedded native children instead.
- **Alternative**: add a transparent `View` with a `testID` overlaid on the tap target at the same position; this is fragile for map tiles but practical for static charts where pins are rendered by RN, not the map library.

[official]

---

### Pattern 191 — `device.openURL(url)` with a deep-link URI to test cold-start navigation to a specific screen without UI traversal [official]

`device.openURL({ url: 'myapp://screen/path' })` launches the app (if not running) or brings it to the foreground and delivers the URL to the native URL handler, triggering deep-link navigation. This skips the multi-tap path through onboarding and menus, reducing test runtime for scenarios that only care about the destination screen. Pair with `device.launchApp({ newInstance: true })` before the deep link to guarantee a clean state.

```ts
// e2e/deep-link.test.ts
import { device, element, by, waitFor, expect } from 'detox';

describe('Deep-link navigation', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(6000);
  });

  it('navigates to Order #1042 via deep link without UI traversal', async () => {
    await device.openURL({ url: 'myapp://orders/1042' });

    await waitFor(element(by.id('order-detail-screen')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(5000);

    await expect(element(by.id('order-id-label'))).toHaveText('#1042');
    await expect(element(by.id('order-status-label'))).toBeVisible();
  });

  it('shows 404 screen for an unknown deep-link path', async () => {
    await device.openURL({ url: 'myapp://nonexistent/99999' });

    await waitFor(element(by.id('not-found-screen')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(4000);

    await expect(element(by.id('go-home-button'))).toBeVisible();
    await element(by.id('go-home-button')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when**: a test scenario cares exclusively about the behavior at the destination screen and the navigation path itself is covered by a separate navigation test suite.
- **Do NOT use when**: the test must verify that the navigation path (breadcrumbs, back stack, transition animations) is correct — deep links bypass the normal stack and the back button may not return to the expected ancestor.
- **Alternative**: for web-link (`https://`) universal link testing on iOS, use `device.openURL({ url: 'https://...' })` and ensure the associated domains entitlement is present in the debug build's `.entitlements` file; simulator universal links require explicit entitlement to fire.

[official]

---

### Pattern 192 — `device.setPermissions()` bulk-reset in `beforeAll` to establish a clean permission baseline across the full test suite [official]

Permissions granted by one test can affect subsequent tests when the app's permission dialogs are driven by the OS cache rather than the Detox `setPermissions` call. Calling `device.setPermissions({ camera: 'denied', microphone: 'denied', location: 'never', notifications: 'YES' })` at the start of `beforeAll` (or in the global `setup` file) brings every permission to a known state before the suite runs, eliminating cross-test permission contamination.

```ts
// e2e/setup/permissions-baseline.ts
import { device } from 'detox';

// Run this once before the entire suite to establish a clean permission state
beforeAll(async () => {
  await device.setPermissions({
    camera:        'denied',
    microphone:    'denied',
    photos:        'denied',
    notifications: 'YES',     // needed for push-prompt tests
    location:      'never',
    contacts:      'denied',
    calendar:      'denied',
  });
});

// e2e/camera.test.ts
import { device, element, by, waitFor, expect } from 'detox';

describe('Camera permission flow', () => {
  it('shows the camera permission rationale modal when camera is denied', async () => {
    await device.reloadReactNative();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
    await element(by.id('open-camera-button')).tap();

    // App detects denied camera and shows its custom rationale modal
    await waitFor(element(by.id('camera-permission-modal')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(3000);

    await expect(element(by.id('camera-rationale-text'))).toBeVisible();
  });

  it('opens the camera preview when permission is granted', async () => {
    await device.setPermissions({ camera: 'YES' });
    await device.reloadReactNative();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
    await element(by.id('open-camera-button')).tap();

    await waitFor(element(by.id('camera-preview')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(5000);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when**: the test suite has multiple describe blocks that rely on different permission states — baseline resets prevent ordering dependencies between test files.
- **Do NOT use when**: `device.setPermissions()` is called on Android physical devices — this API is simulator/emulator only; use `adb shell pm grant/revoke` via a custom jest `globalSetup` script for physical Android devices.
- **Alternative**: isolate each permission scenario in a separate `device.launchApp({ permissions: { camera: 'YES' } })` call so each test brings up a fresh instance with the exact permission set it needs, at the cost of longer test runtime.

[official]

---

### Pattern 193 — `element.scroll(offset, direction, startNormalizedX, startNormalizedY)` with explicit start coordinates to avoid scrolling into safe-area insets [official]

The default `scroll()` action starts at the element's center point. On iOS devices with notch / Dynamic Island, the top 44 pt and bottom 34 pt are safe-area insets that intercept scroll gestures when a modal or sheet is presented. Specifying `startNormalizedX` and `startNormalizedY` (values between `0.0` and `1.0` relative to the element) moves the scroll origin away from inset regions, making scroll tests reliable across notched and notchless devices.

```ts
// e2e/scroll-safe-area.test.ts
import { device, element, by, waitFor, expect } from 'detox';

describe('Settings list scroll (safe-area aware)', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.reloadReactNative();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('settings-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
  });

  it('scrolls to the bottom of the settings list and taps Sign Out', async () => {
    const settingsList = element(by.id('settings-scroll-view'));

    // Start scroll from 50% width, 30% height — well clear of top safe-area inset
    await settingsList.scroll(800, 'down', 0.5, 0.3);

    await waitFor(element(by.id('sign-out-button')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(4000);

    await element(by.id('sign-out-button')).tap();

    await waitFor(element(by.id('login-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
  });

  it('scrolls back to top to see the profile header', async () => {
    const settingsList = element(by.id('settings-scroll-view'));
    await settingsList.scroll(800, 'down', 0.5, 0.3);
    // Scroll back up — start at 70% height to avoid the home indicator inset
    await settingsList.scroll(800, 'up', 0.5, 0.7);

    await waitFor(element(by.id('profile-header')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(3000);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when**: tests are run across a device matrix that includes iPhone models with safe-area insets (notch, Dynamic Island) and scroll gestures fail intermittently near screen edges.
- **Do NOT use when**: the scroll view occupies only the safe-area-inset-adjusted content area (common with `SafeAreaView` wrappers) — in that case the inset is already excluded from the element's bounds and the default center origin is fine.
- **Alternative**: use `whileElement().scroll()` loops with `waitFor(target).toBeVisible()` as the termination condition instead of a fixed offset; this is slower but robust regardless of list length and safe-area layout.

[official]

---

### Pattern 194 — `device.getPlatform()` guard with platform-specific matcher branches for components that differ between iOS and Android [official]

Certain platform APIs (`scrollToIndex` on Android, `by.system.label` on iOS, toggle accessibility behavior) have no cross-platform equivalent in Detox. A `device.getPlatform() === 'ios'` branch at the test level keeps a single test file correct across both platforms without duplicating the entire file. Extract the branches into a helper to keep each `it` block readable.

```ts
// e2e/helpers/platform.ts
import { device } from 'detox';

export const isIOS = () => device.getPlatform() === 'ios';
export const isAndroid = () => device.getPlatform() === 'android';

// e2e/share-sheet.test.ts
import { device, element, by, waitFor, expect } from 'detox';
import { isIOS, isAndroid } from './helpers/platform';

describe('Share sheet', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.reloadReactNative();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('article-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
    await element(by.id('share-button')).tap();
  });

  it('opens the native share sheet', async () => {
    if (isIOS()) {
      // iOS share sheet exposes a system-level element via by.system
      await waitFor(element(by.system.label('Cancel')))
        .toBeVisible()
        .withTimeout(4000);

      await element(by.system.label('Cancel')).tap();
      await expect(element(by.system.label('Cancel'))).not.toBeVisible();
    } else {
      // Android share sheet renders its items as accessible list items
      await waitFor(element(by.text('Share via')))
        .toBeVisible()
        .withTimeout(4000);

      // Dismiss the Android sheet with the back button
      await device.pressBack();
      await waitFor(element(by.id('article-screen')))
        .toBeVisible()
        .withTimeout(3000);
    }
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when**: both platforms must be tested in the same test suite and the interaction mechanics differ at the OS level (share sheets, permission dialogs, notifications).
- **Do NOT use when**: the platform divergence is deep enough that the iOS and Android tests are essentially different test scenarios — in that case split into `*.ios.e2e.ts` and `*.android.e2e.ts` files to eliminate the branching overhead.
- **Alternative**: tag tests with `@platform:ios` / `@platform:android` annotations and skip on mismatched platforms using Jest's `test.skip` to make CI output explicit about what was skipped.

[official]

---

### Pattern 195 — `pilot.perform()` natural-language step execution via detox-copilot for exploratory tests and rapid prototype validation [official]

`detox-copilot` (bundled in Detox 20.x+) exposes `pilot.perform(step)` which sends a natural-language instruction to a configured LLM provider that maps it to Detox API calls at runtime. This is ideal for exploratory test sessions where the screen layout is not yet stable enough to maintain stable `testID`s. The copilot synthesizes the matcher chain from the current accessibility snapshot, making the step resistant to minor layout refactors.

```ts
// e2e/copilot-checkout.test.ts
import { pilot } from 'detox/src/copilot';
import { device, waitFor, element, by } from 'detox';

// Configure copilot in jest globalSetup or detox.setup.ts:
// pilot.init({ frameworkDriver: detoxCopilotDriver, promptHandler: openAIHandler });

describe('Checkout via Copilot natural-language steps', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    pilot.start();
    await device.reloadReactNative();
  });

  afterEach(async () => {
    pilot.end();
  });

  it('completes the checkout flow in natural language', async () => {
    await pilot.perform('Tap the "Add to Cart" button for the first product');
    await pilot.perform('Navigate to the shopping cart screen');
    await pilot.perform('Tap the "Proceed to Checkout" button');
    await pilot.perform('Fill in the shipping address with "123 Main St, Springfield"');
    await pilot.perform('Select the "Standard Shipping" option');
    await pilot.perform('Tap "Place Order" and wait for the confirmation screen');

    // Switch back to deterministic Detox assertions for the final state
    await waitFor(element(by.id('order-confirmation-screen')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(8000);
    await expect(element(by.id('order-number-label'))).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when**: the screen layout is in flux during early product development and maintaining stable `testID` attrs across daily redesigns has more overhead than the LLM API cost; also useful for smoke tests written by non-engineers.
- **Do NOT use when**: the test is part of a production regression suite that must run deterministically — LLM responses are non-deterministic, may change across model versions, and incur per-request latency (150–500 ms per step) that compounds in long flows.
- **Alternative**: use copilot steps to discover the correct `testID` chain during development, then replace them with conventional `by.id()` calls once the layout stabilizes, keeping the suite fast and reproducible.

[official]

---

### Pattern 196 — `device.disableSynchronization()` / `device.enableSynchronization()` bracket for screens driven by continuous WebSocket or polling timers [official]

Detox's built-in synchronization waits until all pending timers, animations, and network requests are idle before executing the next step. Screens that maintain a persistent WebSocket connection or a `setInterval` polling loop are never "idle" from Detox's perspective, causing every interaction to time out waiting for a quiescence that never arrives. Bracketing the test interaction with `disableSynchronization()` and `enableSynchronization()` turns synchronization off only for the affected section, restoring it afterward so other tests are unaffected.

```ts
// e2e/live-feed.test.ts
import { device, element, by, waitFor, expect } from 'detox';

describe('Live price ticker feed', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.reloadReactNative();
    // Wait for the initial render with sync enabled
    await waitFor(element(by.id('ticker-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(6000);
  });

  it('displays real-time price updates from the WebSocket feed', async () => {
    // Disable sync — the WebSocket keeps Detox "busy" indefinitely otherwise
    await device.disableSynchronization();

    try {
      // Capture the initial displayed price
      const initialPriceEl = element(by.id('btc-price-label'));
      await expect(initialPriceEl).toBeVisible();

      // Wait 2 s for at least one WebSocket update to arrive
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 2000));

      // Assert the price label has changed (non-deterministic exact value)
      await expect(initialPriceEl).toBeVisible();
      await expect(element(by.id('last-updated-label'))).toBeVisible();
    } finally {
      // Always re-enable sync so subsequent tests are not affected
      await device.enableSynchronization();
    }
  });

  it('tap on a ticker row navigates to detail screen', async () => {
    await device.disableSynchronization();
    try {
      await element(by.id('ticker-row-ETH')).tap();
      await waitFor(element(by.id('coin-detail-screen')))
        .toBeVisible()
        .withTimeout(4000);
    } finally {
      await device.enableSynchronization();
    }
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when**: the app runs a persistent WebSocket, SSE stream, or `setInterval` loop that prevents Detox from reaching quiescence; these are fundamentally incompatible with Detox's idle-based synchronization model.
- **Do NOT use when**: synchronization is only slow (not infinite) — prefer increasing `waitFor` timeouts first; disabling synchronization globally hides real flakiness caused by missing `await` calls.
- **Alternative**: during tests, configure the app to use a mock WebSocket server (via `launchArgs`) that sends a single payload and then closes, preserving Detox synchronization while still exercising the feed-rendering logic.

[official]

---

### Pattern 197 — `element.pinch(scale, speed, angle)` for testing pinch-to-zoom on media viewers and map surfaces [official]

`pinch(scale, speed, angle)` simulates a two-finger pinch or spread gesture. A `scale > 1.0` spreads (zoom in) and a `scale < 1.0` pinches (zoom out). The `speed` parameter (`'slow'` | `'fast'`) controls gesture duration, which affects animation completion timing. Use `speed: 'slow'` when the view has a zoom transition that needs to complete before the next assertion, and `speed: 'fast'` only when the animation is negligible.

```ts
// e2e/photo-viewer.test.ts
import { device, element, by, waitFor, expect } from 'detox';

describe('Photo viewer pinch-to-zoom', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.reloadReactNative();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('gallery-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
    await element(by.id('photo-thumbnail-0')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('photo-viewer'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
  });

  it('zooms in and shows the zoom indicator at > 1x', async () => {
    await element(by.id('photo-viewer')).pinch(2.5, 'slow');

    // App shows a zoom-level badge when scale > 1.0
    await waitFor(element(by.id('zoom-badge')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(2000);

    await expect(element(by.id('zoom-badge'))).not.toHaveText('1x');
  });

  it('zooms out back to fit and hides the zoom indicator', async () => {
    // First zoom in
    await element(by.id('photo-viewer')).pinch(2.5, 'slow');
    await waitFor(element(by.id('zoom-badge'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);

    // Double-tap to reset is an alternative, but pinch back to 1.0 is explicit
    await element(by.id('photo-viewer')).pinch(0.4, 'slow');

    await waitFor(element(by.id('zoom-badge')))
      .not.toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(2000);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when**: the app implements pinch-to-zoom on media, maps, or PDFs and there is user-visible feedback (zoom badge, compass reset button) that can be asserted after the gesture.
- **Do NOT use when**: the zoom behavior is implemented entirely in a JS gesture handler (`react-native-gesture-handler` PanResponder) that does not update any accessible property — the pinch gesture fires but there is nothing to assert; instrument a `testID`-labeled transform display instead.
- **Alternative**: use `tapAtPoint` double-tap to trigger the double-tap-to-zoom shortcut (commonly implemented alongside pinch) if testing exact scale increments is not required.

[official]

---

### Pattern 198 — `element.multiTap(numberOfTaps)` for triple-tap and double-tap interactions on custom gesture-driven components [official]

`multiTap(numberOfTaps)` fires `n` rapid taps at the element's center point. It is the canonical way to test double-tap-to-like (Instagram-style hearts), triple-tap accessibility shortcuts, and any component that distinguishes tap sequences. Unlike `element.tap()` called in a loop, `multiTap` is dispatched as a single gesture sequence with platform-native inter-tap timing, preventing the OS from treating it as separate single taps.

```ts
// e2e/reactions.test.ts
import { device, element, by, waitFor, expect } from 'detox';

describe('Post reaction interactions', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.reloadReactNative();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('feed-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
  });

  it('double-tap on the post image triggers the heart reaction', async () => {
    await element(by.id('post-image-0')).multiTap(2);

    await waitFor(element(by.id('heart-animation-0')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(2000);

    // After the animation the like count increments by 1
    await waitFor(element(by.id('heart-animation-0')))
      .not.toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(3000);

    await expect(element(by.id('like-count-0'))).toHaveText('1 like');
  });

  it('triple-tap on the username opens the quick-profile popup', async () => {
    await element(by.id('post-username-0')).multiTap(3);

    await waitFor(element(by.id('quick-profile-popup')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(2000);

    await expect(element(by.id('popup-follower-count'))).toBeVisible();
    // Dismiss
    await element(by.id('close-popup-button')).tap();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when**: the component explicitly handles multi-tap gesture sequences at the native level (`onDoubleTap`, `numberOfTapsRequired` in `UITapGestureRecognizer`).
- **Do NOT use when**: the tap sequence is handled in JavaScript via a manually-tracked tap counter with a `setTimeout` debounce — the timing of `multiTap` may be faster than the JS debounce window, causing the sequence to register as a single tap; slow down with `tapAtPoint` calls separated by explicit `sleep` calls.
- **Alternative**: simulate the multi-tap state change directly via a `launchArgs` flag that forces the "liked" state in the Redux store, bypassing gesture simulation for tests that only care about the post-like UI state.

[official]

---

### Pattern 199 — `detox test --inspect-brk` with VS Code debugger attach for stepping through flaky Detox tests interactively [official]

Running `npx detox test --inspect-brk -c <config>` pauses execution at the first line of the test file and waits for a Node.js debugger to attach. Adding a VS Code `.vscode/launch.json` "Attach to Detox" configuration lets engineers step through test actions in real time, inspect `element` objects, and identify exactly which `waitFor` is timing out — without adding `console.log` statements to production test code.

```ts
// .vscode/launch.json — add this configuration
// {
//   "type": "node",
//   "request": "attach",
//   "name": "Attach to Detox",
//   "port": 9229,
//   "skipFiles": ["<node_internals>/**", "**/node_modules/**"],
//   "timeout": 120000
// }

// Then run in terminal:
// npx detox test --inspect-brk -c ios.sim.debug e2e/flaky-modal.test.ts

// e2e/flaky-modal.test.ts — place a debugger statement at the flaky point
import { device, element, by, waitFor, expect } from 'detox';

describe('Flaky modal debug session', () => {
  it('opens the modal and confirms the title', async () => {
    await device.reloadReactNative();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('dashboard-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(6000);

    await element(by.id('open-modal-button')).tap();

    // Pause here to inspect the accessibility tree in the attached debugger
    debugger; // eslint-disable-line no-debugger

    await waitFor(element(by.id('modal-title')))
      .toHaveText('Confirm Action')
      .withTimeout(3000);

    await element(by.id('modal-cancel')).tap();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when**: a test is intermittently failing in CI and the failure cannot be reproduced by reading the log output alone — interactive stepping reveals the exact state of the UI when the assertion fires.
- **Do NOT use when**: running in a CI environment — `--inspect-brk` blocks execution indefinitely waiting for a debugger attachment that never arrives; ensure the flag is not in CI test scripts.
- **Alternative**: use `device.takeScreenshot()` immediately before the failing assertion to capture the UI state on every run; combine with Detox's built-in `artifacts.screenshot: 'all'` mode for a frame-by-frame timeline without needing an interactive session.

[official]

---

### Gotcha 203 — `element.typeText()` on Android emulators running API 34+ silently fails for inputs inside a `BottomSheetModal` from `@gorhom/bottom-sheet` because the modal's custom accessibility window is not the frontmost responder [community]

**Root cause**: `@gorhom/bottom-sheet` v5 renders its modal content in a separate React portal attached to a new `BottomSheetPortalProvider` window. On Android API 34+, Detox's `typeText` driver targets the frontmost accessibility window, which is the app's root window, not the bottom sheet's portal window. The input field is visible and Detox considers it matched, but keystrokes are delivered to the root window's focused element (often `null`), so the text is silently dropped. The Detox log shows no error; the input field simply remains empty.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — input is visible but text is never entered
await element(by.id('search-input-in-sheet')).typeText('hello');
// assert fails: toHaveValue('hello') — actual: ''

// DIAGNOSIS — check if the input is inside a BottomSheetModal portal
// by inspecting the component tree in React DevTools while the sheet is open.

// FIX OPTION 1 — tap the input first to force focus before typeText
await element(by.id('search-input-in-sheet')).tap();
await element(by.id('search-input-in-sheet')).typeText('hello');

// FIX OPTION 2 — use replaceText instead of typeText for portal inputs
// replaceText uses a different UIAutomator2 strategy that bypasses the
// window-focus check and directly sets the EditText's value.
await element(by.id('search-input-in-sheet')).replaceText('hello');
await expect(element(by.id('search-input-in-sheet'))).toHaveValue('hello');

// FIX OPTION 3 — if the input still drops text, scroll the sheet to full
// expansion first so the window is fully promoted by the OS
await element(by.id('bottom-sheet-handle')).swipe('up', 'fast');
await element(by.id('search-input-in-sheet')).tap();
await element(by.id('search-input-in-sheet')).typeText('hello');

// WHY this matters: bottom sheets are used in nearly every modern RN app for
// search, filters, and forms. The silent failure makes this one of the most
// reported Detox issues in 2024-2025 as @gorhom/bottom-sheet v5 adoption grew.
```

---

### Gotcha 204 — `waitFor(element).toBeVisible().withTimeout()` passes on Fabric (New Architecture) before the element's async data fetch completes because Fabric commits layout synchronously before `useEffect` fires [community]

**Root cause**: With the React Native New Architecture (Fabric renderer, enabled by default in RN 0.76+), the host component tree is committed to the native layer synchronously during the JS event loop tick. This means Detox's `toBeVisible()` assertion can pass the moment the component mounts its outer container, even though the inner content is populated only after a `useEffect` or `useSWR` fetch resolves. On the old architecture, the asynchronous bridge introduced enough latency that `toBeVisible()` effectively waited for data too. On Fabric the gap disappears, causing previously green tests to fail with "element not found" or stale data assertions.

```ts
// BROKEN on Fabric — passes visibility check before data loads
await waitFor(element(by.id('user-profile-screen')))
  .toBeVisible()
  .withTimeout(5000);
// This passes immediately when the screen container mounts
// but the username label hasn't been populated yet
await expect(element(by.id('username-label'))).toHaveText('janedoe');
// FAILS: username-label exists but has no text yet

// FIX — assert on the actual data element, not the container
await waitFor(element(by.id('username-label')))
  .toHaveText('janedoe')
  .withTimeout(8000);

// OR — add a loading-state testID sentinel that disappears when data is ready
await waitFor(element(by.id('profile-loading-indicator')))
  .not.toBeVisible()
  .withTimeout(8000);
await expect(element(by.id('username-label'))).toHaveText('janedoe');

// WHY this matters: migrating an existing test suite to RN 0.76+ with the New
// Architecture breaks tens of tests that relied on the bridge latency as an
// implicit data-load wait. The fix is systematic: replace container-visibility
// guards with data-element or sentinel-disappearance guards throughout the suite.
```

---

### Gotcha 205 — `device.launchApp({ newInstance: true })` on iOS 17+ simulators takes 8–12 s per test when Xcode's address sanitizer (ASan) is enabled in the scheme, inflating suite runtime by 10x [community]

**Root cause**: Xcode's Address Sanitizer injects a 40 MB runtime library into the app binary on every cold launch. Each `newInstance: true` launch forces a full cold start, and ASan's memory instrumentation adds 8–12 seconds of overhead before the app's `didFinishLaunching` fires. This is invisible during development (engineers only run a few tests manually) but catastrophic in CI where every `beforeEach` cold-launches the app. The Detox `launchApp` timeout default (120 s) never triggers; tests just run very slowly.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — each test takes 15+ seconds just in beforeEach
// CI suite that took 8 minutes now takes 90+ minutes

// DIAGNOSIS — check the Xcode scheme used in .detoxrc.ts:
// If buildConfiguration is 'Debug' and the scheme has ASan enabled,
// every cold launch pays the full ASan startup cost.

// FIX 1 — create a dedicated 'DetoxDebug' scheme with ASan disabled:
// Xcode → Product → Scheme → Manage Schemes → Duplicate 'Debug' → uncheck ASan
// Reference this scheme in .detoxrc.ts:
// {
//   app: { binaryPath: '...', buildConfiguration: 'DetoxDebug' }
// }

// FIX 2 — switch from newInstance:true to reloadReactNative() for tests
// that don't require a truly clean process state
beforeEach(async () => {
  // Cheaper than newInstance: reuses the process, resets JS state
  await device.reloadReactNative();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(6000);
});

// Reserve newInstance:true for tests that genuinely need a clean process:
it('tests app behavior on very first launch', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true, delete: true });
  // ...
});

// WHY this matters: ASan is frequently left on in Debug schemes during active
// development and forgotten when setting up CI. The 10x slowdown is not
// obvious from logs because each test completes — it just takes much longer.
```

---

### Gotcha 206 — Detox `jestTimeout` default of 120 000 ms causes silent pass-through when a `waitFor` exceeds the timeout inside a `try/catch` block, masking flaky synchronization bugs [community]

**Root cause**: When a `waitFor(...).withTimeout(N)` throws and the throw is caught by a surrounding `try/catch` (common in cleanup helpers and retry wrappers), Detox's test-level Jest timeout continues counting. If `N` is close to 120 000 ms and several such caught timeouts accumulate, the Jest test-level timeout fires and the test is marked as a timeout failure — but the actual root cause (a flaky `waitFor`) is hidden inside the caught error. Conversely, if `N` is small, the `catch` silently swallows the synchronization error and the test moves on to an assertion that fails for an unrelated-looking reason.

```ts
// ANTI-PATTERN — catch swallows the real synchronization error
async function dismissOptionalBanner(): Promise<void> {
  try {
    await waitFor(element(by.id('promo-banner')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(5000);
    await element(by.id('promo-banner-close')).tap();
  } catch {
    // Silently ignores both "element not found" AND synchronization errors
  }
}

// BETTER PATTERN — only catch ElementNotFoundError, re-throw others
import { DetoxRuntimeError } from 'detox';

async function dismissOptionalBanner(): Promise<void> {
  try {
    await waitFor(element(by.id('promo-banner')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(3000);
    await element(by.id('promo-banner-close')).tap();
  } catch (err) {
    // Only swallow the "element not found / not visible" case
    if (err instanceof Error && err.message.includes('not visible')) {
      return; // Banner was not shown — that is acceptable
    }
    throw err; // Re-throw synchronization errors, network errors, etc.
  }
}

// Also: increase jestTimeout in detoxrc.ts to expose real wait durations
// testRunner: { args: { testTimeout: 300_000 } }

// WHY this matters: helpers that swallow all Detox errors are a primary source
// of "tests pass but the app is broken" scenarios in large test suites.
// The swallowed synchronization error typically means Detox was still busy
// with an animation or fetch — fixing the root cause removes the flakiness entirely.
```

---

### Gotcha 207 — `element.clearText()` does not dispatch `onChangeText` on Android TextInput components using controlled state (`value` prop), leaving the field visually empty but logically unchanged [community]

**Root cause**: Detox's `clearText()` implementation on Android uses UIAutomator2's `clear()` which sets the EditText's content to an empty string at the native layer. React Native's bridge (and on the New Architecture, the Fabric event emitter) listens for text changes via `onChangeText`. However, UIAutomator2's `clear()` does not fire Android's `TextWatcher.afterTextChanged` in all configurations — in particular when the TextInput has `value` controlled by React state. As a result, the native EditText shows empty but the React state variable retains its old value. The next `typeText` appends to the old logical value, and form validation may fail or the server receives the old+new combined string.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — after clearText, the field appears empty but state is stale
await element(by.id('email-input')).clearText();
await element(by.id('email-input')).typeText('new@example.com');
// Native EditText shows: 'new@example.com'
// But onChangeText may have received: 'old@example.comnew@example.com'
// because clear() did not fire onChangeText to reset state to ''

// RELIABLE FIX — use replaceText which sets value and fires onChangeText
// in a single atomic operation via UIAutomator2's setText() API
await element(by.id('email-input')).replaceText('new@example.com');
await expect(element(by.id('email-input'))).toHaveValue('new@example.com');

// IF replaceText is also unreliable (some custom TextInput wrappers):
// 1. Tap the field to focus
await element(by.id('email-input')).tap();
// 2. Select all and delete via keyboard shortcut
await element(by.id('email-input')).tapBackspaceKey();
// 3. Then type the new value
await element(by.id('email-input')).typeText('new@example.com');

// WHY this matters: controlled TextInput is the React Native default pattern.
// Tests that use clearText() + typeText() for form field updates silently
// submit wrong values, causing API errors that look like backend bugs.
```

---

### Gotcha 208 — `by.type('RCTImageView')` and other internal class matchers break silently after migrating to React Native 0.76+ New Architecture because Fabric renames the native view classes [community]

**Root cause**: Under the old architecture (Paper renderer), RN components map to predictable native class names: `RCTView`, `RCTImageView`, `RCTTextView`. Under Fabric (New Architecture, default in RN 0.76+), the native shadow tree uses a different class hierarchy. `RCTImageView` becomes `RCTFabricImageView` (or in some builds `react_native_modules_image_RCTImageComponentView`). Tests using `by.type('RCTImageView')` silently find zero elements on Fabric builds without any migration warning, causing `element not found` errors. This is especially common in tests for image loading, avatar placeholders, and skeleton screens.

```ts
// BROKEN on Fabric — class name has changed
await element(by.type('RCTImageView')).tapAtPoint({ x: 50, y: 50 });
// Returns: Element not found

// INVESTIGATION — dump the accessibility tree to find the new class name
// Add to a debug test:
const attributes = await element(by.id('some-image')).getAttributes();
console.log(JSON.stringify(attributes, null, 2));
// Look for 'elementType' or the native 'type' in the output

// FIX — prefer by.id() matchers for all user-visible interactive images
// Add testID props to Image components in the app source
await element(by.id('product-image-0')).tapAtPoint({ x: 50, y: 50 });

// IF you must use by.type() (e.g. for third-party components):
// Create a cross-architecture helper that returns the correct class name
import { device } from 'detox';

export function imageViewType(): string {
  // This mapping must be verified for your specific RN + Fabric version
  return device.getPlatform() === 'ios'
    ? 'RCTFabricImageView'   // RN 0.76+ iOS Fabric
    : 'com.facebook.react.views.image.ReactImageView'; // Android unchanged
}

await element(by.type(imageViewType())).tapAtPoint({ x: 50, y: 50 });

// WHY this matters: the New Architecture migration guide does not list view
// class name changes as a breaking change, so test suites hit this silently
// when enabling `newArchEnabled=true` in gradle.properties / Info.plist.
```

## Updated Anti-Patterns Checklist (Cycle 34 additions)

| Anti-Pattern | Fix |
|---|---|
| Using `element.typeText()` directly inside `@gorhom/bottom-sheet` portal on Android API 34+ | Tap the input first to force window focus, or use `replaceText()` which bypasses window-focus selection (Gotcha 203) |
| Asserting container `toBeVisible()` as a data-load guard on React Native New Architecture (Fabric) | Fabric commits layout synchronously before `useEffect` data fetches; assert on the data element or a loading-sentinel disappearance instead (Gotcha 204) |
| Leaving Xcode Address Sanitizer enabled in the CI Detox scheme | ASan adds 8–12 s per cold launch; create a `DetoxDebug` scheme with ASan disabled for CI (Gotcha 205) |
| Catching all Detox errors with a bare `catch {}` in test helpers | Swallows synchronization errors and masks real flakiness; only catch `not visible` / `not found` errors and re-throw everything else (Gotcha 206) |
| Using `clearText()` + `typeText()` to replace text in a controlled Android TextInput | `clearText()` does not fire `onChangeText` reliably; use `replaceText()` which sets value atomically (Gotcha 207) |
| Using `by.type('RCTImageView')` after migrating to RN 0.76+ New Architecture | Fabric renames native view classes; add `testID` to images and use `by.id()`, or use the updated Fabric class name (Gotcha 208) |
