## Community Gotchas — Cycle 39

### Gotcha 219 — `pilot.perform()` Detox Copilot steps silently retry on `ElementNotFoundError` up to 3 times by default, causing a test that should fail fast to take 45+ seconds before reporting failure [community]

**Root cause**: Detox Copilot's `pilot.perform()` wraps each step in an internal retry loop (default `maxRetries: 3`, each with `retryDelay: 5000 ms`). When the LLM-translated action targets an element that does not exist (wrong screen, missing `testID`, crashed component), Copilot retries the full LLM prompt + action cycle up to three times before propagating the `ElementNotFoundError`. Each retry costs a full LLM round-trip (1–3 s) plus the wait delay, making a single bad step consume 15–45 s. Teams debugging CI failures see 45-second timeouts with no indication that the test was waiting on Copilot retries, making the root cause invisible in logs.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — pilot.perform() takes 45+ seconds to fail on a wrong screen
await pilot.perform('Tap the delete account button'); // On the home screen, not settings
// Copilot retries 3x × 5s = 45+ seconds before failing

// FIX — set maxRetries: 0 for steps that should fail fast if the element is absent
pilot.init(new AnthropicPromptHandler({
  model: 'claude-sonnet-4-5',
  maxRetries: 0,          // Fail immediately — no silent retry loops
  cacheResponses: true,
}));

// ALTERNATIVE — reduce retryDelay to keep retries but fail faster
pilot.init(new AnthropicPromptHandler({
  maxRetries: 1,
  retryDelay: 500,        // 0.5s between retries — total max wait 1.5s vs 45s
}));

// WHY this matters: Copilot's default retry behavior was designed for
// transient network latency in the LLM API, but teams that use it for
// element interaction get 45-second delays on misconfigured tests
// with no log output indicating retries are occurring.
```

**WHY this matters:** The default 3x retry x 5 s delay converts a fast failing assertion into a 45-second timeout trap that makes CI timeouts appear to be environment flakiness rather than a test logic error. Disabling or reducing retries makes the failure surface at the correct test step immediately.

---

### Gotcha 220 — `element(by.id('x')).getAttributes()` returns `ElementAttributes[]` (an array) when a `FlatList` renders multiple elements with the same `testID` due to list virtualization reuse, silently breaking attribute assertions [community]

**Root cause**: React Native's `FlatList` (and `VirtualizedList`) recycles view cells during virtualization. If an item's `testID` is set to a static value (e.g., `testID="list-item"`) instead of a unique per-index value (e.g., `testID={"list-item-" + index}`), Detox finds multiple elements matching the same ID simultaneously in the native view tree. `getAttributes()` on a multi-match query returns an `ElementAttributes[]` array instead of a single `ElementAttributes` object, and calling `.text` or `.frame` on the array returns `undefined` without any error, silently producing null assertions.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — getAttributes returns an array, attribute access silently returns undefined
const attrs = await element(by.id('list-item')).getAttributes();
console.log(attrs.text); // undefined (attrs is ElementAttributes[], not ElementAttributes)
jestExpect(attrs.text).toBe('Product Name'); // PASSES with undefined — false pass!

// DIAGNOSIS — check if the return value is an array
if (Array.isArray(attrs)) {
  console.warn(`[detox] Multiple elements matched 'list-item': ${attrs.length} elements found`);
}

// FIX OPTION 1 — use unique per-index testIDs in the FlatList renderItem
// <View testID={`list-item-${item.id}`}>

// FIX OPTION 2 — use element(by.id('x')).atIndex(0) to target the first match
const firstItemAttrs = await element(by.id('list-item')).atIndex(0).getAttributes();
if (!Array.isArray(firstItemAttrs)) {
  jestExpect(firstItemAttrs.text).toBe('Product Name');
}

// FIX OPTION 3 — always guard with Array.isArray before reading attributes
const result = await element(by.id('list-item')).getAttributes();
const single = Array.isArray(result) ? result[0] : result;
jestExpect(single?.text).toBe('Product Name');

// WHY this matters: FlatList testID reuse is a pervasive pattern in codebases
// where testIDs were added for debugging rather than testing; the silent
// undefined return from array attribute access creates false-passing assertions
// that only fail in production when a completely different element is matched.
```

**WHY this matters:** The silent `undefined` return from array attribute access means assertions can pass with wrong data. This is one of the hardest bugs to catch because the test produces a green result while asserting nothing meaningful.

---

### Gotcha 221 — `device.setNetworkConditions('offline')` on Android emulators does NOT block localhost traffic, so tests that point `apiBase` to `http://10.0.2.2:4000` (host machine) still succeed even when the test expects network failure [community]

**Root cause**: Android's `setNetworkConditions` throttles the emulator's external network interface but the `10.0.2.2` loopback alias (which routes to the host machine's localhost) bypasses the network interface throttling entirely. Tests that run a local mock server on `localhost:4000` and configure the app to use `http://10.0.2.2:4000` will continue to receive responses from the mock server even when `setNetworkConditions('offline')` is active. The test then asserts on an "offline" state that never occurs, producing a false pass on "should show error screen when offline" tests.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — app still gets responses from mock server despite 'offline' network conditions
await device.setNetworkConditions('offline');
await element(by.id('refresh-button')).tap();
// App sends request to http://10.0.2.2:4000 → host localhost → still responds
await waitFor(element(by.id('network-error-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
// TIMES OUT: app got a response, shows data instead of error screen

// CORRECT APPROACH 1 — stop the mock server instead of setting offline conditions
mockServer.close();  // Kills the local server so 10.0.2.2 connections are refused
await element(by.id('refresh-button')).tap();
await waitFor(element(by.id('network-error-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(8000);
mockServer.listen(4000); // Restart for subsequent tests

// CORRECT APPROACH 2 — use a mock server that can simulate offline by returning 503/network errors
await mockServer.setMode('offline');  // Mock server returns ECONNREFUSED-equivalent
await element(by.id('refresh-button')).tap();
await waitFor(element(by.id('network-error-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(8000);

// WHY this matters: Android loopback bypass is undocumented in the Detox API
// reference for setNetworkConditions; teams discover it only when "offline"
// tests pass in development (where mock server runs locally) and fail in CI
// (where the app points to a real staging URL that IS blocked by offline mode).
```

**WHY this matters:** The `10.0.2.2` loopback bypass makes `setNetworkConditions('offline')` tests meaningless for any app that uses localhost-based mock servers during E2E testing — a very common pattern. The fix requires explicitly stopping the mock server or using a mock that can simulate network errors programmatically.

---

### Gotcha 222 — `element.swipe('up', 'fast')` on iOS 26 with the `liquidGlass` system chrome dismisses the keyboard via the floating keyboard dismiss bar before the swipe gesture reaches the app content [community]

**Root cause**: iOS 26 introduced the `liquidGlass` design language which includes a floating keyboard dismiss handle at the top of the software keyboard. When Detox dispatches a `swipe('up', 'fast')` gesture on an element that is positioned directly above the keyboard, the fast upward gesture velocity triggers the iOS 26 floating dismiss bar gesture recognizer, which intercepts the gesture and dismisses the keyboard before the gesture reaches the application's scroll view. The result is that the scroll/swipe action is consumed by the OS, the application content does not scroll, and subsequent `waitFor().toBeVisible()` assertions on off-screen content fail.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — swipe('up', 'fast') dismisses keyboard instead of scrolling content (iOS 26)
await element(by.id('message-input')).typeText('Hello world');
// Keyboard is now visible
await element(by.id('message-list')).swipe('up', 'fast');
// iOS 26 liquidGlass dismiss bar intercepts the gesture
// Result: keyboard dismissed, list did NOT scroll

// FIX OPTION 1 — dismiss keyboard explicitly first, then scroll
await element(by.id('message-input')).tapReturnKey();  // Or blur the input
await waitFor(element(by.id('keyboard-dismiss-indicator'))).not.toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);
await element(by.id('message-list')).swipe('up', 'slow');

// FIX OPTION 2 — use 'slow' velocity which is below the dismiss bar threshold
await element(by.id('message-list')).swipe('up', 'slow', 0.7);

// FIX OPTION 3 — use device.disableSynchronization around the swipe
// to prevent Detox from waiting on animations (which includes keyboard anim)
await device.disableSynchronization();
await element(by.id('message-list')).swipe('up', 'fast');
await device.enableSynchronization();

// WHY this matters: iOS 26 liquidGlass is the default from Xcode 17+
// simulators; any existing test that pairs typeText() with a fast upward
// swipe will begin failing silently (scroll no-op, not an error) on iOS 26
// simulator targets without any code change in the app or test.
```

**WHY this matters:** iOS 26 changes the interaction model for gestures near the keyboard without any deprecation warning or Detox API change. All existing tests that perform fast upward swipes while the keyboard is visible will silently fail to scroll on iOS 26 simulators, with no obvious connection to the iOS version in the error message.

---

### Gotcha 223 — `waitFor(element(by.id('x'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout()` always times out for elements inside Expo Router's `<Stack>` navigator when the stack transition animation is interrupted by a second navigation event before it completes [community]

**Root cause**: Expo Router (React Navigation v7 under the hood) uses React Native's `LayoutAnimation` for stack screen transitions. If a test dispatches two navigation events in rapid succession (e.g., `tap()` on a nav item followed immediately by `tap()` on a child nav item), the first stack transition animation is interrupted and the native `onTransitionEnd` callback is never called. Detox's synchronization engine waits for all in-flight animations to complete before evaluating `waitFor()` assertions. With the interrupted `LayoutAnimation`, Detox's animation idle check never resolves, and `waitFor()` waits until the full timeout expires rather than failing fast.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — waitFor times out after two rapid navigation taps
await element(by.id('products-tab')).tap();
await element(by.id('product-item-1')).tap();   // Second tap before first transition ends
await waitFor(element(by.id('product-detail-screen')))
  .toBeVisible()
  .withTimeout(5000);
// TIMES OUT: Detox waiting for interrupted LayoutAnimation to finish (never fires onTransitionEnd)

// FIX OPTION 1 — wait for first screen before tapping into second
await element(by.id('products-tab')).tap();
await waitFor(element(by.id('products-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
await element(by.id('product-item-1')).tap();
await waitFor(element(by.id('product-detail-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

// FIX OPTION 2 — disable synchronization around rapid navigation sequences
await device.disableSynchronization();
await element(by.id('products-tab')).tap();
await element(by.id('product-item-1')).tap();
await device.enableSynchronization();
await waitFor(element(by.id('product-detail-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);

// FIX OPTION 3 — use Expo Router's programmatic navigation from launchApp URL
await device.launchApp({ url: 'myapp://products/1' });  // Skip the tap-nav sequence entirely
await waitFor(element(by.id('product-detail-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);

// WHY this matters: Expo Router is the default navigation solution for new
// Expo SDK 50+ projects; the interrupted-transition synchronization deadlock
// affects any test that navigates more than one level deep without waiting
// for each transition to complete, which is a very common test pattern.
```

**WHY this matters:** The synchronization deadlock from an interrupted navigation animation is indistinguishable from a genuine timeout in Detox output. The test log shows "Timeout waiting for element" with no hint that a stuck animation is the cause, sending developers down the wrong debugging path for hours.

## Updated Anti-Patterns Checklist (Cycle 39 additions)

| Anti-Pattern | Fix |
|---|---|
| Using `pilot.perform()` with default `maxRetries: 3` and `retryDelay: 5000` for steps that target specific screens — slow 45-second failure loops | Set `maxRetries: 0` or `retryDelay: 500` in `AnthropicPromptHandler` constructor to fail fast on missing elements (Gotcha 219) |
| Using static `testID="list-item"` in `FlatList.renderItem` — `getAttributes()` returns an array and attribute access silently returns `undefined` | Use `testID={"list-item-" + item.id}` for unique per-item IDs; guard all `getAttributes()` calls with `Array.isArray()` check (Gotcha 220) |
| Using `device.setNetworkConditions('offline')` to test error states when the app points to `http://10.0.2.2:4000` — localhost bypasses Android offline throttling | Stop the mock server explicitly or configure it to return `ECONNREFUSED`-equivalent responses instead of relying on OS-level offline conditions (Gotcha 221) |
| Using `swipe('up', 'fast')` while the iOS 26 software keyboard is visible — liquidGlass dismiss bar intercepts the gesture | Dismiss the keyboard first with `tapReturnKey()` or use `swipe('up', 'slow')` below the dismiss bar threshold (Gotcha 222) |
| Dispatching two navigation taps in rapid succession inside Expo Router — interrupted `LayoutAnimation` causes Detox synchronization deadlock | Wait for each screen transition to complete with `waitFor().toBeVisible()` before dispatching the next navigation action (Gotcha 223) |
| Running iOS 26 simulators on Apple Silicon CI without `simulatorLaunchArchitecture: 'arm64'` — Rosetta translation causes timing differences | Set `simulatorLaunchArchitecture: 'arm64'` in `.detoxrc.ts` device config for Apple Silicon runners (Pattern 235) |
| Using `device.launchApp({ newInstance: true })` without `clearKeychain()` for auth flow tests — stale token from previous run bypasses login screen | Call `device.clearKeychain()` (iOS) in `beforeEach` alongside `delete: true` in `launchApp` to guarantee a blank auth state (Pattern 244) |
| Capturing view hierarchies on every test regardless of pass/fail — significant 0.5–2 s overhead per test | Use `captureViewHierarchy()` only inside a failure-gated `afterEach` check to capture debug data with zero overhead on passing tests (Pattern 234) |

## Cycle 40 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 245 — `element(by.id('x')).tap({ x, y })` coordinate-offset tap for elements with non-uniform hit-test regions in custom `TouchableOpacity` wrappers [official]

React Native's `TouchableOpacity` responder region is derived from the native frame of the outermost view, not the visual hit area defined by padding or `hitSlop`. When a component uses negative margins or overlapping sibling views, the element's touchable region shifts relative to its `testID` anchor, causing a plain `tap()` to land outside the actual responder bounds and be silently ignored. Detox's `tap({ x, y })` accepts a coordinate offset relative to the element's bounding box center, allowing tests to target the exact pixel where the responder is active. Use `getAttributes()` to inspect the `frame` of the element first, then calculate the correct offset from the known layout. This pattern is essential for components that use `hitSlop` expansion or `-margin` tricks to extend touch targets beyond their visual bounds.

```ts
// Inspect the element's frame before tapping to determine the correct offset
const attrs = await element(by.id('floating-action-button')).getAttributes();
if (Array.isArray(attrs)) throw new Error('Multiple FAB matches — use a unique testID');

// FAB uses negative margins; center of touchable is 8px below visual center
const offsetY = 8;
await element(by.id('floating-action-button')).tap({ x: 0, y: offsetY });

// Verify the expected sheet appeared (confirms the tap landed in the responder)
await waitFor(element(by.id('action-sheet'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);

// For precision-critical buttons (e.g., map pins) inspect frame and derive offset:
// const { x, y, width, height } = attrs.frame;
// await element(by.id('map-pin-42')).tap({ x: width / 2, y: height - 4 });
```

**Tradeoff:** Coordinate offsets are brittle when the layout changes — a padding or margin change in the component immediately breaks the hardcoded offset. Reserve `tap({ x, y })` for elements where `hitSlop` or overlapping views make a plain `tap()` unreliable; prefer proper `testID` placement on the innermost touchable view as the long-term fix. [official]

### Pattern 246 — `device.sendUserActivity()` for iOS Handoff / `NSUserActivity` deep-link testing without launching from a URL scheme [official]

iOS Handoff and Spotlight search both deliver content to apps via `NSUserActivity` continuation, which is a distinct code path from URL-scheme deep links. Detox's `device.sendUserActivity(activityPayload)` injects a synthetic `NSUserActivity` directly into the running app, triggering `application(_:continue:restorationHandler:)` without requiring Safari, Spotlight, or another device. The method accepts a plain JSON object that maps to the `NSUserActivity` `userInfo` dictionary along with `activityType`. This allows tests to verify the Handoff acceptance flow, content restoration handlers, and the resulting navigation state in complete isolation from OS-level activity routing. Available from Detox 20.x on iOS only; Android does not have an equivalent API.

```ts
// Send a synthetic NSUserActivity to test Handoff article continuation
await device.sendUserActivity({
  activityType: 'com.myapp.article.view',
  userInfo: {
    articleId: 'article-789',
    scrollPosition: 0.45,
    sourceDevice: 'iPhone16Pro',
  },
});

// App should restore the article at the given scroll position
await waitFor(element(by.id('article-789-content'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);

// Assert scroll position was restored (check visibility of mid-article anchor)
await waitFor(element(by.id('article-789-mid-anchor'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);

// Verify toolbar state reflects continuation (e.g., "Continued from iPhone 16 Pro" banner)
await expect(element(by.id('handoff-continuation-banner'))).toBeVisible();
```

**Tradeoff:** `sendUserActivity()` is iOS-only with no Android equivalent, requiring platform guards in shared test files. The injected activity bypasses the OS routing layer, so tests cannot detect failures in the `NSUserActivityTypes` plist registration — only the handler code path is exercised. [official]

---

### Pattern 247 — `element.pinch(scale, speed, angle)` for testing pinch-to-zoom gestures on map and photo viewer components with multi-touch simulation [official]

React Native map and image viewer components expose pinch-to-zoom through the standard iOS/Android multi-touch gesture recognizer stack. Detox's `element.pinch(scale, speed, angle)` synthesizes a two-finger pinch or spread gesture with configurable scale factor (< 1 = pinch in, > 1 = spread out), speed (`'slow'` | `'fast'`), and angle in radians. The gesture is dispatched to the element's center unless the element has non-standard gesture responder chains (e.g., `MapView` from `react-native-maps` v2 which uses a native gesture recognizer that requires the gesture to originate inside the tile area). Tests should disable synchronization around pinch gestures on animated zoom components to avoid the Detox idle-wait hanging on the zoom interpolation animation.

```ts
// Test pinch-to-zoom on a photo viewer component
await device.disableSynchronization(); // Avoid hanging on zoom animation
await element(by.id('photo-viewer')).pinch(2.5, 'slow', 0); // Spread out (zoom in)
await device.enableSynchronization();

// Verify zoom level indicator updated
await expect(element(by.id('zoom-level-indicator'))).toHaveText('250%');

// Test pinch-in (zoom out) to minimum
await device.disableSynchronization();
await element(by.id('photo-viewer')).pinch(0.4, 'slow', 0); // Pinch in (zoom out)
await device.enableSynchronization();

// Should snap back to minimum zoom level (100%)
await waitFor(element(by.id('zoom-level-indicator')))
  .toHaveText('100%')
  .withTimeout(2000);
```

**Tradeoff:** Pinch gestures on native map components (react-native-maps, Mapbox) may not register because those views use their own native gesture recognizer that Detox cannot drive through the standard touch injection API. In those cases, prefer direct state injection via the `MapView` `region` prop with `testID`-gated assertions on the visible tile set. [official]

---

### Pattern 248 — `device.matchFace()` / `device.unmatchFace()` for Face ID authentication flow testing on iOS simulators without manual intervention [official]

Biometric authentication flows require Face ID or Touch ID simulator enrollment, which Detox can control programmatically through `device.matchFace()` (success path), `device.unmatchFace()` (failure path), `device.enrollTouchId()`, and `device.matchTouchId()`. These APIs work only on iOS simulators; Android biometric simulation uses `device.setBiometricEnrollment()` and `device.matchBiometric()`. The typical pattern is to enroll biometrics in `beforeAll`, call `matchFace()` or `unmatchFace()` in individual tests, and then dismiss any resulting system alert using `by.system.label()`. Without explicit enrollment, the simulator shows a "Face ID not enrolled" error dialog that Detox cannot dismiss without system element access, causing the test to hang.

```ts
beforeAll(async () => {
  // Enroll Face ID on the simulator before auth tests
  await device.setBiometricEnrollment(true); // iOS 16+ API
});

it('should unlock app with Face ID success', async () => {
  await element(by.id('biometric-auth-button')).tap();
  // Simulator Face ID prompt appears — approve it
  await device.matchFace();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
});

it('should show retry screen on Face ID failure', async () => {
  await element(by.id('biometric-auth-button')).tap();
  // Simulate face mismatch
  await device.unmatchFace();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('biometric-retry-prompt'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
  await expect(element(by.id('biometric-retry-prompt'))).toHaveText('Face not recognized. Try again.');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `matchFace()` / `unmatchFace()` only work on simulators — physical device CI agents cannot simulate biometric success/failure. Tests that use these APIs must be tagged and excluded from real-device test runs, and the app should provide a development bypass (e.g., a `__TEST_SKIP_BIOMETRIC__` flag) for physical device CI. [official]

---

### Pattern 249 — `by.text()` combined with `ancestor()` scope filter to disambiguate identically-labelled buttons across multiple rendered list cards [community]

In list-based UIs, action buttons within each card (e.g., "Delete", "Edit", "Share") share the same text label across every rendered card. Using `element(by.text('Delete'))` matches all visible instances, and `atIndex(N)` is fragile because the index depends on scroll position and virtualization. Combining `by.text()` with `.withAncestor(by.id('card-<id>'))` scopes the match to a specific card's subtree, making the selector resilient to list reordering and virtualization. The ancestor matcher traverses the view hierarchy upward from each candidate match, checking whether the specified ancestor is in the ancestor chain. Use the card's unique data ID (from the content, not position) as the ancestor `testID` to keep the test readable and independent of render order.

```ts
// Render each card with a unique testID derived from item ID
// <View testID={`card-${item.id}`}>
//   <Text>{item.title}</Text>
//   <TouchableOpacity testID="delete-btn"><Text>Delete</Text></TouchableOpacity>
// </View>

// Target the Delete button within a specific card by ancestor scope
const cardAncestor = by.id('card-item-42');
const deleteButton  = by.text('Delete').withAncestor(cardAncestor);

await element(deleteButton).tap();

// Confirm the deletion modal shows the correct item title
await waitFor(element(by.id('delete-confirm-modal'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
await expect(element(by.id('delete-confirm-title'))).toHaveText('Delete "Widget Pro 42"?');
await element(by.text('Confirm')).tap();

// Card should be gone
await expect(element(by.id('card-item-42'))).not.toBeVisible();
```

**Tradeoff:** `withAncestor()` requires the ancestor element to be rendered and have the expected `testID` at the time of matching, which means the card must be scrolled into view before the scoped tap. On FlatLists with many items, this requires a scroll-to-item step before the ancestor-scoped action, adding test complexity. [community]

---

### Pattern 250 — `element.typeText()` followed by `element.clearText()` and `expectToHaveText('')` for controlled form field reset testing [official]

Testing form reset, clear, and undo behaviors requires predictable control over a text field's content across sequential test steps. Detox's `element.typeText(text)` appends to the current field value, so calling it without first clearing can accumulate text from prior test steps when `beforeEach` does not fully reset the app state. The correct pattern is: `clearText()` to guarantee an empty field, then `typeText()` to set the desired value, then assert with `toHaveText()` before interacting with related form controls. For fields with input masks (phone, credit card, date), use `replaceText()` instead of `typeText()` because the mask inserts non-typed characters that break the position-based insertion assumption of `typeText()`.

```ts
// Reliable form field population pattern for masked and unmasked inputs
const emailField = element(by.id('email-input'));
const phoneField = element(by.id('phone-input'));

// Clear → type is the safe sequence for unmasked fields
await emailField.clearText();
await emailField.typeText('user@example.com');
await expect(emailField).toHaveText('user@example.com');

// Use replaceText for masked fields (phone mask inserts dashes automatically)
await phoneField.clearText();
await phoneField.replaceText('4155552671');
// Mask transforms to: (415) 555-2671
await expect(phoneField).toHaveText('(415) 555-2671');

// Test the clear button resets both fields
await element(by.id('form-clear-button')).tap();
await expect(emailField).toHaveText('');
await expect(phoneField).toHaveText('');
```

**Tradeoff:** `clearText()` on Android uses the accessibility action `clearText` which may not fire the `onChange` handler for all controlled component patterns (e.g., redux-form). If the clear action does not trigger state updates, use `replaceText('')` instead, which dispatches through the text change pipeline and reliably fires all listeners. [official]

---

### Pattern 251 — `detox test --inspect-brk` with VS Code attach configuration for interactive step-through debugging of flaky Detox tests [official]

Flaky tests that fail intermittently are nearly impossible to debug from CI logs alone. Detox supports Node.js inspector protocol via `--inspect-brk`, which pauses execution at the first line of the test runner and waits for a debugger to attach. Combining this with a VS Code `"type": "node"` launch configuration set to `"request": "attach"` allows developers to set breakpoints inside test files, inspect Detox element state, and evaluate `element(by.id('x')).getAttributes()` calls directly from the VS Code debug console. This workflow eliminates the need to add `console.log` statements and re-run tests. The `--testNamePattern` flag narrows execution to a single test to reduce attach-and-wait time.

```jsonc
// .vscode/launch.json — attach to Detox inspect-brk session
{
  "version": "0.2.0",
  "configurations": [
    {
      "name": "Attach to Detox",
      "type": "node",
      "request": "attach",
      "port": 9229,
      "restart": false,
      "sourceMaps": true,
      "outFiles": ["${workspaceFolder}/e2e/**/*.js"]
    }
  ]
}
```

```bash
# Terminal: run specific flaky test paused at first line
npx detox test --inspect-brk \
  --configuration ios.sim.debug \
  --testNamePattern "should render cart after adding item"
# Then attach the VS Code debugger to port 9229
```

**Tradeoff:** `--inspect-brk` pauses the entire test runner until a debugger attaches, so it cannot be used in unattended CI. The flag must be removed before committing, and the technique requires a local simulator (not a remote CI device). For CI flakiness, use `--record-videos failing` artifact capture instead. [official]

---

### Pattern 252 — `beforeAll` / `afterAll` lifecycle-scoped `device.installApp()` and `device.uninstallApp()` for multi-variant APK/IPA testing within a single test suite [official]

Testing multiple build variants (e.g., free vs. premium, staging vs. production, feature-flagged variants compiled into separate APKs) within a single CI run normally requires separate Detox configurations. Using `device.installApp(binaryPath)` and `device.uninstallApp(bundleId)` inside `beforeAll`/`afterAll` blocks allows a single test file to switch the installed binary between `describe` blocks, avoiding a full `detox test` re-invocation with a different `--configuration`. The pattern is: uninstall the current variant, install the next variant binary, launch the app, run assertions specific to that variant, then clean up. The binary path must be absolute and the bundle ID must match the variant being installed.

```ts
describe('Free variant feature gates', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.uninstallApp();
    await device.installApp('/path/to/MyApp-free.apk');
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  });

  afterAll(async () => {
    await device.terminateApp();
  });

  it('should show upgrade prompt on premium feature tap', async () => {
    await element(by.id('advanced-filters-button')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('upgrade-modal'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
  });
});

describe('Premium variant feature gates', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.uninstallApp();
    await device.installApp('/path/to/MyApp-premium.apk');
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  });

  it('should show advanced filters without upgrade prompt', async () => {
    await element(by.id('advanced-filters-button')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('advanced-filter-panel'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
    await expect(element(by.id('upgrade-modal'))).not.toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `device.installApp()` takes 5–15 seconds per install depending on APK size, making variant-switching suites significantly slower than single-binary suites. This pattern is only worthwhile for dedicated variant-verification runs; routine feature tests should use build flags or `launchArgs` feature injection to avoid the install overhead. [official]

---

### Pattern 253 — `element.scroll(pixels, direction, startPositionX, startPositionY)` anchor-point scroll for tab bars and horizontal pagers that reject top-edge scroll starts [community]

React Native's `ScrollView` and FlatList reject scroll gestures that begin outside their content area. Horizontal pager components (React Native Pager View, Reanimated carousel) often sit flush below a `TabBar`, which means the default Detox scroll start position (element center) may land on the tab bar overlay rather than the pager content. Using `startPositionX` and `startPositionY` as fractional values (0.0–1.0 of element dimensions) allows precise control over where the scroll gesture originates within the element frame. For pagers below a 44-pt tab bar, starting the scroll at `startPositionY: 0.7` (lower 30% of the element) reliably avoids the tab bar hit area.

```ts
// Carousel pager sits below a sticky TabBar — default center scroll lands on tab bar
// Use startPositionY: 0.7 to originate the gesture in the lower portion of the pager

// Scroll the horizontal pager left to reveal the third slide
await element(by.id('product-image-pager')).scroll(
  300,           // pixels to scroll
  'left',        // direction
  0.5,           // startPositionX — center horizontally
  0.7,           // startPositionY — 70% down (below the 44pt tab bar overlay)
);

// Verify the third slide indicator is active
await expect(element(by.id('pager-indicator-2'))).toHaveId('pager-indicator-2--active');

// Scroll back to the first slide
await element(by.id('product-image-pager')).scroll(600, 'right', 0.5, 0.7);
await expect(element(by.id('pager-indicator-0'))).toHaveId('pager-indicator-0--active');
```

**Tradeoff:** The fractional start position must be tuned for each specific layout and is sensitive to tab bar height changes (e.g., when running on devices with dynamic island vs. standard notch). A layout change that shifts the tab bar height will break the offset, requiring a recalibration. Where possible, expose a `testID` on the pager's inner content view to give Detox a scroll anchor that is not obscured. [community]

---

### Pattern 254 — `device.setLocation(lat, lng)` combined with `waitFor` assertions on location-gated UI to test geofence and proximity feature flows [official]

Location-gated features (store locator, proximity notifications, geofence unlock) require the device to report a specific GPS coordinate to trigger the relevant app behavior. Detox's `device.setLocation(latitude, longitude)` injects a synthetic location into the iOS simulator's location service or the Android emulator's GPS mock, causing `CLLocationManager` / `FusedLocationProviderClient` to deliver that position to the app. The location is typically updated within 1–2 seconds; a `waitFor(...).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000)` assertion with a 5-second window reliably captures the UI response. On Android, the emulator must have been launched with the `GPS` hardware profile enabled in `AVD Manager` (or `hw.gps = yes` in the AVD config file).

```ts
it('should show in-store mode UI when user enters store geofence', async () => {
  // Set location outside the geofence first (reset state)
  await device.setLocation(37.3382, -121.8863); // San Jose — outside the fence
  await waitFor(element(by.id('nearby-store-banner'))).not.toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

  // Move into the geofence (Apple Park — 1 Apple Park Way)
  await device.setLocation(37.3349, -122.0090);

  // App should respond to CLRegion enter event and show in-store mode
  await waitFor(element(by.id('in-store-mode-banner'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(6000);
  await expect(element(by.id('in-store-price-toggle'))).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `device.setLocation()` on physical iOS devices is not supported — the API is simulator-only. Physical device geofence testing requires a real GPS walk-through or a mock location app (e.g., `MockGPS`). Additionally, the CoreLocation permission must be granted before the test; combine with `device.launchApp({ permissions: { location: 'always' } })` to grant programmatically. [official]

---

### Pattern 255 — `element.longPress(duration)` with platform-specific duration constants to reliably trigger context menus on both iOS and Android [community]

iOS and Android use different minimum duration thresholds to distinguish a long press from a press-and-hold scroll gesture. On iOS, `UILongPressGestureRecognizer` defaults to `0.5 s` (500 ms); on Android, `ViewConfiguration.getLongPressTimeout()` returns `500 ms` as well, but the actual event fires 100 ms later due to touch classifier debounce, making the effective threshold closer to `600 ms`. Using a hard-coded `500` can intermittently miss the Android threshold. The safe cross-platform duration is `800 ms`: it clears both OS thresholds by at least 200 ms of margin, avoiding flakiness from minor timing variations in emulator scheduling without being so long that it triggers secondary long-press behaviors (text selection cursor on iOS at ~1200 ms).

```ts
// Platform-safe long press duration constants
const LONG_PRESS_DURATION = {
  ios: 600,     // 100 ms above iOS 500 ms minimum
  android: 800, // 200 ms above Android ~600 ms effective threshold
};

const platform = await device.getPlatform();
const duration = LONG_PRESS_DURATION[platform];

// Long-press a list item to reveal the context menu
await element(by.id('message-list-item-3')).longPress(duration);

// Context menu should appear with expected actions
await waitFor(element(by.id('context-menu'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);
await expect(element(by.text('Reply'))).toBeVisible();
await expect(element(by.text('Forward'))).toBeVisible();
await expect(element(by.text('Delete'))).toBeVisible();

// Dismiss by tapping outside
await element(by.id('context-menu-backdrop')).tap();
```

**Tradeoff:** Hardcoding platform-specific constants couples the test to OS timing assumptions that may shift between OS versions. A better long-term approach is to expose a `testID` on the long-press trigger's `onLongPress` handler output element and assert its visibility with `waitFor`, allowing the OS to drive the timing and the test to simply observe the result. [community]

---

### Pattern 256 — `jestExpect.extend()` with custom Detox matchers for domain-specific assertions (e.g., `toBeLoading()`, `toHaveFormErrors()`) [community]

Detox's built-in matchers (`toBeVisible`, `toHaveText`, `toHaveId`) cover structural assertions but require multiple chained assertions to express higher-level domain states like "the form is in a loading state" or "the form has validation errors". Extending `jestExpect` via `jestExpect.extend()` with custom async matchers that internally call `element.getAttributes()` and compose multiple Detox assertions allows test files to read as domain language. Custom matchers also centralize the implementation of multi-step assertion logic, so a component refactor only requires updating the matcher rather than every test that uses it.

```ts
// e2e/matchers/formMatchers.ts
import { jestExpect } from 'detox';

jestExpect.extend({
  async toBeLoading(elementId: string) {
    const el = element(by.id(elementId));
    const attrs = await el.getAttributes() as Detox.ElementAttributes;
    const isLoading = attrs.accessibilityState?.busy === true;
    return {
      pass: isLoading,
      message: () => `expected element "${elementId}" ${isLoading ? 'not ' : ''}to be in loading state`,
    };
  },
  async toHaveFormErrors(formId: string, expectedErrors: string[]) {
    for (const errText of expectedErrors) {
      const errEl = element(by.id(`${formId}-error`).withDescendant(by.text(errText)));
      const attrs = await errEl.getAttributes() as Detox.ElementAttributes;
      if (!attrs.visible) {
        return { pass: false, message: () => `expected form error "${errText}" to be visible` };
      }
    }
    return { pass: true, message: () => 'all expected errors visible' };
  },
});

// e2e/tests/checkout.test.ts
it('shows validation errors on empty submit', async () => {
  await element(by.id('checkout-submit')).tap();
  await jestExpect('checkout-form').toHaveFormErrors(['Email is required', 'Card number required']);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Custom matcher implementations that call `getAttributes()` add async overhead and can create their own flakiness if the attribute check races with animations. Keep custom matchers thin — one `getAttributes()` call per matcher — and guard with `waitFor()` before calling the custom matcher to ensure the element is in its final state. [community]

---

### Pattern 257 — `device.openURL({ url, sourceApp })` for testing universal link disambiguation sheets when multiple apps are registered for the same URL scheme [official]

When both the app under test and another installed app (e.g., a companion app or a system app like Safari) are registered as handlers for the same URL scheme or associated domain, iOS shows a disambiguation sheet asking the user to choose a handler. Detox's `device.openURL({ url, sourceApp })` simulates opening a URL from a specific source app bundle ID, which tells the OS to route the URL through the normal universal link resolution flow including the disambiguation sheet. This is the only supported way in Detox to test the app's behavior as a secondary handler rather than the default handler, and to verify that `application(_:open:options:)` receives the correct `sourceApplication` in its options dictionary.

```ts
it('should accept universal link from Safari with correct source attribution', async () => {
  await device.openURL({
    url: 'https://myapp.example.com/product/123',
    sourceApp: 'com.apple.mobilesafari',
  });

  // App should open and navigate to the product screen
  await waitFor(element(by.id('product-detail-123'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(6000);

  // Source attribution should be recorded in analytics (inspect via test bridge)
  // Or verify via a debug label exposed in dev builds
  await expect(element(by.id('debug-source-app'))).toHaveText('com.apple.mobilesafari');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The disambiguation sheet itself cannot be automated through Detox's element API — Detox always routes the URL directly to the app under test. Tests that need to verify the disambiguation sheet UI (e.g., "Did the correct app name appear?") require XCUITest directly. Use `openURL` only for testing the receiving end of the universal link, not the disambiguation sheet interaction. [official]

---

### Pattern 258 — `element.adjustSliderToPosition(normalizedPosition)` for range sliders with verification of value labels and downstream state changes [official]

`Slider` and `RangeSlider` components in React Native use `adjustSliderToPosition(0.0–1.0)` in Detox to set the slider to a normalized fractional position (0.0 = minimum, 1.0 = maximum). Unlike direct `typeText()`, this API respects the slider's `step` and `minimumValue`/`maximumValue` constraints, snapping to the nearest valid step. After adjusting, the test must wait for the app's `onValueChange` handler to propagate the new value to any dependent UI (e.g., a price range label, a search result count). Without a `waitFor()` between the slider adjustment and the downstream assertion, tests non-deterministically assert stale values from the previous slider position.

```ts
// Set a price range slider to 75% of maximum ($750 out of $1000)
await element(by.id('max-price-slider')).adjustSliderToPosition(0.75);

// Wait for onValueChange to propagate to the price label
await waitFor(element(by.id('max-price-label')))
  .toHaveText('$750')
  .withTimeout(2000);

// Search results should update to reflect the new price filter
await waitFor(element(by.id('search-result-count')))
  .not.toHaveText('Loading...')
  .withTimeout(4000);

// Verify result count is non-zero and within the filtered range
const resultAttrs = await element(by.id('search-result-count')).getAttributes();
if (!Array.isArray(resultAttrs)) {
  const count = parseInt((resultAttrs.text ?? '0').replace(' results', ''), 10);
  jestExpect(count).toBeGreaterThan(0);
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `adjustSliderToPosition()` maps the fractional position to the slider's native value, but the actual text label may show a rounded or currency-formatted value that does not directly correspond to a simple arithmetic conversion. Maintain a `sliderPositionToLabel` helper function in the test utils to document and centralize the slider's value mapping logic. [official]

---

### Pattern 259 — `device.shake()` for triggering React Native's developer menu and shake-to-undo / bug-report flows in debug builds [official]

React Native's shake gesture triggers the in-app developer menu in debug builds and is also used by applications to implement shake-to-undo (iOS UIKit undo support) and custom shake-to-report-bug flows. Detox's `device.shake()` dispatches a synthetic accelerometer shake event to the simulator/emulator. The method is iOS-only in Detox 20.x (Android emulators require a different approach via `adb emu sensor set acceleration`). For apps that use shake for QA/feedback flows, this enables end-to-end testing of the feedback form submission path without requiring a physical device shake.

```ts
it('should show shake-to-report feedback form on device shake', async () => {
  // Navigate to a screen where shake feedback is enabled
  await element(by.id('home-tab')).tap();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);

  // Trigger shake gesture
  await device.shake(); // iOS simulator only

  // Feedback form should appear
  await waitFor(element(by.id('feedback-form-modal'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
  await expect(element(by.id('feedback-screenshot-preview'))).toBeVisible();

  // Fill and submit the report
  await element(by.id('feedback-description-input')).typeText('Button is misaligned');
  await element(by.id('feedback-submit-button')).tap();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('feedback-success-toast'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `device.shake()` is iOS simulator-only in Detox 20.x. Android shake testing requires `adb emu sensor set acceleration 10:10:10` via a `Bash` step in `beforeEach`, which is less portable and requires the test runner to have `adb` in `PATH`. Add a platform guard and skip the test on Android until Detox adds native Android shake support. [official]

---

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 40

### Gotcha 224 — `element(by.id('x')).scroll()` on Android API 34+ `RecyclerView`-backed `FlatList` jumps past the target item when `pixels` value exceeds a single screen height, because `RecyclerView` uses a velocity-based fling instead of a fixed-pixel scroll [community]

**Root cause**: On Android API 34+, React Native's `FlatList` implementation was updated to use `RecyclerView`'s `smoothScrollBy(dx, dy)` path when the scroll delta exceeds the viewport height. `smoothScrollBy` applies velocity-based deceleration physics, meaning that requesting a 1500-pixel scroll on a 900-pixel-tall list results in an unpredictable overshoot or undershoot depending on the current item momentum state. Detox's `element.scroll()` maps directly to this call, so `scroll(1500, 'down')` may land anywhere between 800 and 2000 pixels from the starting position, causing `waitFor(element).toBeVisible()` after the scroll to time out because the target item is off-screen in either direction.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — scroll overshoots on Android API 34+ FlatList
await element(by.id('products-list')).scroll(1500, 'down');
await waitFor(element(by.id('product-item-50'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
// TIMES OUT on Android 34+: item-50 is off-screen due to RecyclerView fling overshoot

// FIX OPTION 1 — scroll in smaller increments (less than half the screen height)
const SAFE_SCROLL_STEP = 400; // < viewport height of 900px
for (let i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
  await element(by.id('products-list')).scroll(SAFE_SCROLL_STEP, 'down');
}
await waitFor(element(by.id('product-item-50'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);

// FIX OPTION 2 — use the Detox scrollTo helper (scroll until visible)
await waitFor(element(by.id('product-item-50')))
  .toBeVisible()
  .whileElement(by.id('products-list'))
  .scroll(400, 'down');

// WHY this matters: the RecyclerView physics change was introduced with the
// React Native 0.74 Android renderer update that ships with Expo SDK 51+;
// any test written against SDK 50 that uses large pixel scrolls will begin
// failing silently on the API 34 emulator target without any change to the
// test or app code.
```

**WHY this matters:** The RecyclerView fling physics change in React Native 0.74+ makes all large-delta `scroll()` calls on Android unreliable without any error message — the scroll completes, but the stopping position is non-deterministic. This causes intermittent CI failures that are very difficult to attribute to the API 34 upgrade because the symptom (timeout on `waitFor`) looks identical to a missing `testID` or a slow server response.

---

### Gotcha 225 — `element(by.text('OK')).tap()` on iOS 17.4+ system alert dialogs silently no-ops when the system alert uses `UIAlertController` presented as `UIAlertControllerStyleActionSheet` rather than `UIAlertControllerStyleAlert`, because Detox's `by.text()` matcher targets the `Alert` accessibility subtree, not the `ActionSheet` subtree [community]

**Root cause**: iOS presents some system permissions dialogs (notably the `PHPhotoLibrary` limited-selection prompt in iOS 17.4+) as `UIAlertControllerStyleActionSheet` rather than `UIAlertControllerStyleAlert`. Detox's `by.text('OK')` matcher traverses the `Alert` accessibility subtree looking for buttons. `ActionSheet`-style system dialogs are rendered in a separate `UIWindow` with the `UIAccessibilityTraitButton` trait but without being part of the `Alert` accessibility chain. The `tap()` call returns without an error but does not interact with the button, and the test proceeds as if the alert was dismissed, leaving the system sheet visible and blocking subsequent element interactions.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — by.text('OK') no-ops on UIAlertControllerStyleActionSheet dialogs
await element(by.id('select-photos-button')).tap();
// iOS 17.4+ shows limited photo selection ActionSheet (not Alert)
await element(by.text('OK')).tap(); // Silent no-op: ActionSheet not in Alert accessibility tree
await waitFor(element(by.id('photo-picker-grid'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
// TIMES OUT: system sheet is still blocking the app

// FIX OPTION 1 — use by.system.label() which targets any system window type
await element(by.system.label('OK')).tap();

// FIX OPTION 2 — grant the permission upfront in launchApp to skip the dialog
await device.launchApp({ permissions: { photos: 'limited' } });

// WHY this matters: the iOS 17.4 limited photo selection prompt changed from
// Alert style to ActionSheet style without a documented Detox compatibility
// note; teams using by.text('OK') to dismiss the legacy prompt silently have
// their tests pass (no error thrown) while the sheet remains visible.
```

**WHY this matters:** The silent no-op means the test does not fail at the `tap()` line — it fails later with a timeout on the next assertion, sending developers to inspect the wrong part of the test. The root cause (ActionSheet vs Alert subtree mismatch) is only discoverable by capturing a view hierarchy dump with `device.captureViewHierarchy()` at the point of failure.

---

### Gotcha 226 — `device.reloadReactNative()` triggers a `codePush` update check on apps integrated with Microsoft CodePush in staging builds, causing a 10–30 second stall in tests that expect immediate UI readiness after reload [community]

**Root cause**: Microsoft CodePush hooks into the React Native `AppRegistry` startup lifecycle to check for pending updates before rendering the root component. When `device.reloadReactNative()` is called, React Native re-triggers the `AppRegistry` startup sequence, which invokes the CodePush update check against the configured deployment key (pointing to the staging CodePush endpoint in staging builds). The check involves a network round-trip to the CodePush service, which takes 5–30 seconds depending on network conditions in CI. Detox's synchronization engine waits for all pending network activity to complete before evaluating subsequent `waitFor()` calls, causing a 10–30 second pause after every `reloadReactNative()` call in affected test suites.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — reloadReactNative() stalls for 10-30s in CodePush-enabled staging builds
await device.reloadReactNative();
await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
// TIMES OUT: CodePush update check is blocking the JS bundle load

// FIX OPTION 1 — launch with a CodePush-disabled env flag in launchArgs
// (requires app to check this flag and skip CodePush initialization)
await device.launchApp({
  newInstance: true,
  launchArgs: { CodePushDisabled: '1' },
});

// FIX OPTION 2 — use disableSynchronization around reloadReactNative + waitFor
await device.disableSynchronization();
await device.reloadReactNative();
// Wait a fixed duration for the bundle to load (fragile, prefer option 1)
await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 3000));
await device.enableSynchronization();
await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(8000);

// WHY this matters: CodePush integration in staging builds is nearly universal
// for RN apps using OTA updates; the 10-30s per reloadReactNative() stall
// adds 5-15 minutes to a full E2E suite run and makes the CI timing appear
// indistinguishable from genuine slow network test failures.
```

**WHY this matters:** CodePush stalls after `reloadReactNative()` are masked as normal network-wait synchronization by Detox's logs — the test output shows "Waiting for app to be idle..." with no indication that a background update check is the cause. Teams only discover this when they notice that tests run much faster on fresh simulator boots (no CodePush state) than on subsequent reloads within the same session.

---

### Gotcha 227 — `element(by.id('x')).getAttributes()` returns stale `accessibilityValue` on Android when the element is inside a `Reanimated` v3 shared-transition container, because the shared transition temporarily unmounts and remounts the element with the animation view's accessibility data [community]

**Root cause**: Reanimated v3's shared-transition API (`sharedTransitionTag`) unmounts the original element and replaces it with a Reanimated animation proxy view during the transition animation. The proxy view inherits the `testID` of the original element but does not inherit all accessibility properties — specifically, `accessibilityValue` may be empty or stale during the transition frame. If `getAttributes()` is called within the ~300 ms transition window, the returned `accessibilityValue` reflects the animation proxy's empty state rather than the post-transition element's final value. Tests that assert on `accessibilityValue` immediately after a navigation-triggered shared transition receive a false-empty value.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — accessibilityValue is empty immediately after a shared transition
await element(by.id('product-card-42')).tap(); // Triggers shared transition to detail screen
const attrs = await element(by.id('product-detail-42')).getAttributes();
// attrs.accessibilityValue is '' or undefined — proxy view's empty state

// FIX OPTION 1 — wait for the transition to complete before calling getAttributes()
await waitFor(element(by.id('product-detail-header'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
// Header is a non-animated element; its visibility confirms transition completion
const finalAttrs = await element(by.id('product-detail-42')).getAttributes();
if (!Array.isArray(finalAttrs)) {
  jestExpect(finalAttrs.accessibilityValue).toBe('In stock: 12 units');
}

// FIX OPTION 2 — disable sync around the transition to avoid hanging on animations
await device.disableSynchronization();
await element(by.id('product-card-42')).tap();
await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 400)); // Wait for Reanimated transition
await device.enableSynchronization();
const stableAttrs = await element(by.id('product-detail-42')).getAttributes();

// WHY this matters: Reanimated v3 shared transitions are the default hero
// animation pattern in Expo Router 3+ apps; any test that uses getAttributes()
// for post-navigation state verification will hit this on any screen that
// uses sharedTransitionTag for a card-to-detail navigation pattern.
```

**WHY this matters:** The stale `accessibilityValue` is returned without any error — `getAttributes()` succeeds, returning an empty or null value that silently fails the assertion. The underlying cause (Reanimated transition proxy) is invisible in the Detox output, and the timing window (300 ms) makes the failure intermittent: on fast simulators the transition completes before `getAttributes()` runs, so the test passes locally but fails on slower CI agents.

---

### Gotcha 228 — `element.swipe('left', 'slow')` on `React Native Gesture Handler` v2.16+ `Swipeable` rows fails to trigger the swipe action because RNGH v2.16 raised the minimum swipe velocity threshold and Detox's `'slow'` velocity now falls below the new minimum [community]

**Root cause**: React Native Gesture Handler v2.16 (bundled with Expo SDK 52) increased `Swipeable`'s minimum velocity threshold from `0.3` (normalized) to `0.5` (normalized) to reduce accidental swipe openings during scroll. Detox's `swipe()` with `'slow'` speed maps to approximately `0.2` normalized velocity, which is now below the updated RNGH threshold. The swipe gesture is dispatched, starts tracking, but never activates the `Swipeable` action — the component snaps back to its closed position. The test then asserts on delete/archive buttons that were never revealed, timing out without an obvious connection to the RNGH version bump.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — swipe('left', 'slow') no longer opens RNGH Swipeable rows in SDK 52+
await element(by.id('message-row-7')).swipe('left', 'slow');
await waitFor(element(by.id('message-row-7-delete-button'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
// TIMES OUT: Swipeable snapped back because velocity was below RNGH v2.16 threshold

// FIX OPTION 1 — use 'fast' speed to exceed the new threshold
await element(by.id('message-row-7')).swipe('left', 'fast', 0.7);
await waitFor(element(by.id('message-row-7-delete-button'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);

// FIX OPTION 2 — lower the RNGH Swipeable threshold in the component for E2E builds
// <Swipeable minVelocityThreshold={0.1} ...> when __E2E__ flag is set

// WHY this matters: 'slow' was the recommended velocity for Swipeable rows in
// all Detox documentation and community examples written before SDK 52/RNGH v2.16;
// an SDK upgrade silently breaks every existing swipe-to-delete test with a
// timeout error that appears identical to a missing testID or hidden element.
```

**WHY this matters:** The velocity threshold change in RNGH v2.16 is a breaking change for Detox tests with no RNGH migration guide entry for E2E testing. The failure mode is identical to a gesture that successfully fired but whose result is not visible — making it very difficult to distinguish from a logic bug in the swipe action handler.

## Updated Anti-Patterns Checklist (Cycle 40 additions)

| Anti-Pattern | Fix |
|---|---|
| Using a plain `tap()` on components with `hitSlop` or negative-margin touch targets — gesture lands outside the responder bounds and is silently ignored | Use `tap({ x, y })` with an offset derived from `getAttributes().frame` to target the actual responder region (Pattern 245) |
| Using `element.typeText()` without preceding `clearText()` on form fields — accumulates text from prior test runs when `beforeEach` does not fully reset app state | Always call `clearText()` before `typeText()`; use `replaceText()` for masked inputs that must fire the `onChange` pipeline (Pattern 250) |
| Scrolling FlatLists on Android API 34+ with `scroll(pixels > viewportHeight)` — RecyclerView fling physics causes unpredictable overshoot or undershoot | Scroll in increments less than half the viewport height, or use `waitFor().whileElement().scroll()` to scroll until the target is visible (Gotcha 224) |
| Using `element(by.text('OK')).tap()` to dismiss iOS 17.4+ `UIAlertControllerStyleActionSheet` system dialogs — silent no-op because ActionSheet is not in the Alert accessibility subtree | Use `element(by.system.label('OK')).tap()` which targets all system window types, or grant the permission upfront via `launchApp({ permissions: {} })` (Gotcha 225) |
| Calling `device.reloadReactNative()` in CodePush-enabled staging builds — CodePush update check triggers on every reload, adding 10–30 seconds of network stall per test | Inject `launchArgs: { CodePushDisabled: '1' }` in `launchApp` to skip CodePush initialization in the E2E environment (Gotcha 226) |
| Calling `element.getAttributes()` immediately after a Reanimated v3 shared-transition navigation — proxy view returns empty `accessibilityValue` during the 300 ms transition window | Wait for a non-animated landmark element to become visible before calling `getAttributes()` to confirm the transition has fully completed (Gotcha 227) |
| Using `element.swipe('left', 'slow')` on RNGH v2.16+ `Swipeable` rows — `'slow'` velocity is now below the updated 0.5 threshold, causing the swipe to snap back without activating | Switch to `swipe('left', 'fast', 0.7)` or add `minVelocityThreshold={0.1}` to the `Swipeable` component in E2E builds (Gotcha 228) |

## Cycle 41 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 260 — `element.tapKey(key)` for cross-platform keyboard key injection to test Return/Done/Search IME actions on text inputs [official]

React Native `TextInput` elements expose keyboard action buttons (Return, Done, Search, Next, Go, Send) whose behavior depends on the `returnKeyType` prop. While `element.tapReturnKey()` covers the common case, some apps use custom `onSubmitEditing` callbacks that only fire when a specific IME key is pressed. Detox provides `element.tapKey(key)` (Detox 20.x) for injecting a named keyboard key with full platform normalization. Unlike `typeText('\n')`, `tapKey` dispatches the correct `KeyboardEvent` type so `onSubmitEditing` callbacks fire with the right `nativeEvent.submittingKey` value. This enables testing multi-step form flows where successive inputs must be navigated via action keys without physically dismissing the keyboard.

```ts
it('navigates through search form fields using keyboard action keys', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });

  // Enter first field and move to next via Next key
  await element(by.id('search-query-input')).tap();
  await element(by.id('search-query-input')).typeText('TypeScript best practices');
  await element(by.id('search-query-input')).tapKey('Next'); // iOS returnKeyType="next"

  // Focus should shift to the second field automatically via onSubmitEditing
  await waitFor(element(by.id('search-filter-input'))).toBeFocused().withTimeout(2000);
  await element(by.id('search-filter-input')).typeText('2026');
  await element(by.id('search-filter-input')).tapKey('Search'); // iOS returnKeyType="search"

  // Assert search results screen appears
  await waitFor(element(by.id('search-results-list')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(5000);
  await expect(element(by.id('search-results-list'))).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `tapKey` fires the keyboard action event but does not automatically move focus — the app must implement `onSubmitEditing` focus chaining for `Next` to shift to the next field. Tests relying on this pattern are tightly coupled to the app's `returnKeyType` configuration; if a field's `returnKeyType` is changed from `'next'` to `'done'`, the focus chain test will pass (key fires) while the UX regression is missed. Always assert on the focused state of the next element after `tapKey('Next')` to catch regressions. [official]

---

### Pattern 261 — `element.swipe('up', 'slow', 0.5, 0.8)` pull-to-refresh trigger with normalized start position for `RefreshControl`-wrapped lists [community]

React Native's `RefreshControl` requires a downward pull that starts well within the list's scroll region and travels at least 60–80 points. Detox's `element.swipe('down')` on a `ScrollView` with `RefreshControl` fails on iOS when the swipe starts near the top status bar (the default `0.5, 0.5` start position), because iOS intercepts the gesture as a notification-center pull. Starting the swipe from 80% down the screen and swiping upward in the component's coordinate space correctly triggers `RefreshControl`. On Android, the standard `swipe('down')` at `startNormalizedY: 0.3` works reliably with the `SwipeRefreshLayout` native component. A cross-platform helper wraps both strategies behind `triggerPullToRefresh(listId)`.

```ts
// Cross-platform pull-to-refresh helper
async function triggerPullToRefresh(listTestId: string): Promise<void> {
  if (device.getPlatform() === 'ios') {
    // Start from 80% down and swipe toward the top to avoid notification-center conflict
    await element(by.id(listTestId)).swipe('up', 'slow', 0.5, 0.8);
    // iOS RefreshControl activates on upward pull within the scroll container
    // using a normalized start 0.8 keeps the gesture origin well inside the list
  } else {
    // Android SwipeRefreshLayout responds to a gentle downward drag from 30% Y
    await element(by.id(listTestId)).swipe('down', 'slow', 0.5, 0.3);
  }
}

it('refreshes the feed list on pull-to-refresh', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await waitFor(element(by.id('feed-list'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

  await triggerPullToRefresh('feed-list');

  // Spinner appears during the refresh
  await waitFor(element(by.id('refresh-spinner'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);
  // Wait for completion
  await waitFor(element(by.id('refresh-spinner'))).not.toBeVisible().withTimeout(10000);
  // First item should now be updated
  await expect(element(by.id('feed-item-0'))).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The `swipe('up', ..., 0.8)` strategy for iOS is counterintuitive — it exploits the fact that iOS `RefreshControl` triggers on an upward pull (pulling the list content downward relative to the viewport). The exact `startNormalizedY` threshold is device-height-dependent: on iPads, 0.8 may need to become 0.7 because the list is taller in absolute points. Consider reading `getAttributes().frame.height` and computing the start Y as `(frame.height - 60) / frame.height` for a device-adaptive start position. [community]

### Pattern 262 — `device.appLaunchArgs.get()` for reading current launch arguments in assertion helpers, enabling test helpers to adapt to active feature-flag combinations without re-specifying flags inline [official]

When tests inject feature flags via `launchArgs`, assertion helpers need to know which flag variant is active to choose the correct expected UI state. Hard-coding the expected state in every assertion couples the helper to a specific flag combination. `device.appLaunchArgs.get()` returns the current launch arguments as a record, allowing shared helpers to branch based on the active flags. This is especially useful for A/B UI tests where the same interaction (e.g., tapping a checkout button) leads to different screens depending on which checkout flow variant is active.

```ts
// Helper that asserts checkout completion based on the active feature flag
async function assertCheckoutSuccess(): Promise<void> {
  const args = await device.appLaunchArgs.get() as Record<string, string>;
  const checkoutVariant = args['CHECKOUT_FLOW'] ?? 'legacy';

  if (checkoutVariant === 'v2') {
    // v2 flow shows an animated success card instead of a modal
    await waitFor(element(by.id('checkout-success-card')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(6000);
    await expect(element(by.id('checkout-success-card'))).toHaveText('Order Confirmed');
  } else {
    // Legacy flow shows a success modal
    await waitFor(element(by.id('checkout-success-modal')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(6000);
    await element(by.id('checkout-success-ok-button')).tap();
  }
}

it('completes checkout with the v2 flow', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true, launchArgs: { CHECKOUT_FLOW: 'v2' } });
  await element(by.id('cart-checkout-button')).tap();
  await element(by.id('payment-confirm-button')).tap();
  await assertCheckoutSuccess();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `device.appLaunchArgs.get()` returns the arguments as set at launch time — it does not reflect runtime modifications made via `device.appLaunchArgs.modify()` after the app has already started. For tests that modify flags mid-run, you must track the active flags in a test-local variable rather than re-reading from `appLaunchArgs.get()`, otherwise the helper will still see the original launch values. [official]

### Pattern 263 — `waitFor(element).not.toExist()` as a strict cleanup assertion to confirm that dismissed modals, popovers, and banners are fully removed from the view hierarchy before proceeding [official]

`waitFor(element).not.toBeVisible()` passes as soon as an element's opacity reaches zero or its frame moves off-screen, but the element may remain in the React tree with `display: none` or a zero alpha. Subsequent `tap()` calls on underlying elements can be intercepted by the invisible element if it still captures touches. `waitFor(element).not.toExist()` waits until the element is fully unmounted from the view hierarchy — no residual touch interception is possible. This guard is essential after dismissing modals, closing bottom sheets, or hiding overlays before tapping elements that were previously covered.

```ts
it('dismisses the onboarding banner and proceeds to interact with the main feed', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });

  // Onboarding banner covers the top of the feed
  await waitFor(element(by.id('onboarding-banner'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
  await element(by.id('onboarding-banner-close')).tap();

  // Wait for full unmount — not just invisible, but removed from the hierarchy
  await waitFor(element(by.id('onboarding-banner')))
    .not.toExist()
    .withTimeout(2000);

  // Now safe to tap elements that were under the banner
  await element(by.id('feed-story-card-0')).tap();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('story-detail-screen')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(4000);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `not.toExist()` is stricter than `not.toBeVisible()` but also slower — the element must complete the full React unmount cycle, which includes `useEffect` cleanup, `LayoutAnimation` callbacks, and any library-managed exit animations. If a library uses `display: none` to hide rather than unmount, `not.toExist()` will never pass. In that case, check if the element still intercepts touches via `getAttributes().enabled === false` and wrap the subsequent interaction in a short retry if necessary. [official]

---

### Pattern 264 — Horizontal `ScrollView` page-width scroll for tab-swipe navigation when the `TabView` does not expose a testID on the page container [community]

Many React Native tab implementations render a `ScrollView` with `horizontal={true}` and `pagingEnabled` as the underlying page container without assigning a testID to each page. When swipe-to-navigate behavior must be tested, `element.scroll(pageWidth, 'right')` on the ScrollView container moves one page to the right. Because `pageWidth` varies by device, using the frame width from `getAttributes()` produces reliable results. This pattern avoids coupling to tab indicator testIDs that may not be present in third-party tab libraries.

```ts
// Page-swipe navigation on a horizontal paged ScrollView
async function swipeToPage(
  scrollViewId: string,
  targetPageIndex: number,
  currentPageIndex: number
): Promise<void> {
  const container = element(by.id(scrollViewId));
  const attrs = await container.getAttributes();
  if (Array.isArray(attrs)) return; // guard against multiple-match result
  const pageWidth = attrs.frame.width;
  const delta = targetPageIndex - currentPageIndex;
  const direction = delta > 0 ? 'right' : 'left';

  for (let i = 0; i < Math.abs(delta); i++) {
    await container.scroll(pageWidth, direction);
  }
}

it('navigates to the third onboarding page via swipe', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await waitFor(element(by.id('onboarding-pager'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);

  await swipeToPage('onboarding-pager', 2, 0); // swipe to page index 2

  await waitFor(element(by.id('onboarding-page-2-content')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(3000);
  await expect(element(by.id('onboarding-cta-button'))).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Using `attrs.frame.width` as the scroll delta assumes the pager is exactly one page wide per scroll step — correct for `pagingEnabled` ScrollViews but wrong for multi-peek carousels that show part of the adjacent page. For multi-peek carousels, calculate the snap step from the `contentOffset` delta by reading `getAttributes()` before and after a known good swipe during test authoring. [community]

---

### Pattern 265 — `element.tapKey('Backspace')` loop to selectively clear parts of a `TextInput` without triggering `onChange` with empty-string intermediates via `clearText()` [official]

`element.clearText()` replaces the field content with an empty string in a single operation, which fires a single `onChange` with `''`. Some apps implement validation or suggestion-list logic that reacts to each individual character deletion — deleting backwards one key at a time triggers a sequence of `onChange` calls with progressively shorter strings. `tapKey('Backspace')` repeated N times simulates this character-by-character deletion, which is essential for testing search autocomplete dismissal, inline validation recovery, and undo stacks that track per-keystroke deltas.

```ts
// Helper that clears N characters by pressing Backspace individually
async function clearCharacters(inputId: string, charCount: number): Promise<void> {
  const inputEl = element(by.id(inputId));
  for (let i = 0; i < charCount; i++) {
    await inputEl.tapKey('Backspace');
  }
}

it('shows the suggestion list rebuilding as the user backspaces through the query', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });

  await element(by.id('search-input')).tap();
  await element(by.id('search-input')).typeText('typescript');

  // Verify final suggestion list with full query
  await waitFor(element(by.id('suggestion-typescript-generics'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);

  // Backspace to 'types' — different suggestion set
  await clearCharacters('search-input', 5); // removes 'cript'
  await waitFor(element(by.id('suggestion-types-of-testing'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);

  // Backspace to 't' — empty or generic suggestions
  await clearCharacters('search-input', 4); // removes 'ypes'
  await waitFor(element(by.id('suggestion-trending-topics'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `tapKey('Backspace')` issues one IPC round-trip per keystroke. Clearing a 40-character field via 40 individual `tapKey` calls adds approximately 2–4 seconds to the test on a slow CI runner because each call must wait for Detox synchronization. For fields requiring bulk deletion, `clearText()` remains faster; reserve `tapKey` loops for the specific cases where per-keystroke `onChange` behavior is under test. [official]

### Pattern 266 — `device.setPermissions()` called at runtime after app launch to test permission-change UI transitions without requiring a full app restart [official]

In production, users can grant or revoke permissions from iOS Settings while the app is backgrounded and then return to the app. Detox's `device.setPermissions()` can be called after `launchApp()` to change a permission mid-session. Combined with `device.sendToBackground()` and `device.bringToForeground()`, this simulates the exact permission-change-while-backgrounded flow. The app's permission-change handler (typically triggered by the `AppState` `change` event to `'active'`) should re-check the permission and update the UI accordingly.

```ts
it('shows the camera re-permission prompt when camera access is revoked while backgrounded', async () => {
  const appId = 'com.example.myapp';

  // Launch with camera permission granted
  await device.launchApp({
    newInstance: true,
    permissions: { camera: 'YES' },
    bundleId: appId,
  });

  await waitFor(element(by.id('camera-viewfinder'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

  // Background the app and revoke camera permission
  await device.sendToBackground();
  await device.setPermissions({ camera: 'NO' });

  // Return to the app — should re-check permissions on AppState active event
  await device.bringToForeground();

  // App should show the re-permission prompt, not the viewfinder
  await waitFor(element(by.id('camera-permission-prompt')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(4000);
  await expect(element(by.id('camera-viewfinder'))).not.toBeVisible();
  await expect(element(by.id('open-settings-button'))).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `device.setPermissions()` is iOS-only in Detox 20.x. On Android, runtime permission revocation requires `adb shell pm revoke <package> android.permission.CAMERA`, which must be wrapped in a custom `beforeEach` Bash step. The Android approach is asynchronous — the permission revocation propagates after a short delay, so a `waitFor` or `new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 500))` is needed before bringing the app to the foreground. [official]

### Pattern 267 — `element.getAttributes()` with a `visibleBounds` intersection check to detect off-screen or safe-area-clipped elements before tapping [community]

On devices with `SafeAreaView` insets, elements near the bottom of the screen can have a non-zero `frame` but be visually clipped by the safe area. `getAttributes().isVisible` returns `false` for these elements, but `waitFor().toBeVisible()` with the default 75% threshold may intermittently pass or fail depending on the exact pixel overlap with the safe area boundary. Reading `visibleBounds` from `getAttributes()` provides the actual visible pixel rectangle, enabling a precise area-based visibility assertion: the intersection of `frame` and `visibleBounds` must meet a minimum area threshold before the tap is issued.

```ts
// Utility to assert an element is at least 50% visible before tapping
async function assertSufficientlyVisible(testId: string, minFraction = 0.5): Promise<void> {
  const el = element(by.id(testId));
  const attrs = await el.getAttributes();
  if (Array.isArray(attrs)) throw new Error(`Multiple elements match ${testId}`);

  const { frame, visibleBounds } = attrs as {
    frame: { x: number; y: number; width: number; height: number };
    visibleBounds: { x: number; y: number; width: number; height: number };
  };

  const visibleArea = visibleBounds.width * visibleBounds.height;
  const totalArea = frame.width * frame.height;
  const fraction = totalArea > 0 ? visibleArea / totalArea : 0;

  if (fraction < minFraction) {
    throw new Error(
      `Element ${testId} is only ${(fraction * 100).toFixed(1)}% visible ` +
      `(min: ${minFraction * 100}%)`
    );
  }
}

it('confirms the submit button is sufficiently visible before tapping', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await element(by.id('long-form-scroll')).scrollTo('bottom');
  await assertSufficientlyVisible('submit-button', 0.8);
  await element(by.id('submit-button')).tap();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `visibleBounds` is only available on iOS in Detox 20.x; Android `getAttributes()` does not return a `visibleBounds` field. On Android, the equivalent check uses the element's `frame.y + frame.height` compared against the device screen height minus the safe area bottom inset. The cross-platform utility must branch on `device.getPlatform()` and implement the Android size-based check separately. [community]
