### Pattern 268 — `waitFor(element(by.id('toast-container'))).toBeVisible()` chained with text assertion for testing transient toast notifications that auto-dismiss after 2–4 seconds [official]

Toast/snackbar components show briefly after user actions (form submission, network errors, clipboard copies) and are difficult to test because they appear and disappear faster than a developer can manually add `waitFor` guards. The correct pattern is: immediately after the triggering action, use `waitFor().toBeVisible()` with a timeout that exceeds the toast's show delay, then assert on the toast text, then `waitFor().not.toBeVisible()` with a timeout that exceeds the toast's auto-dismiss duration. Asserting on text rather than the container testID makes tests resilient to toast component library swaps.

```ts
// Reusable toast assertion helper
async function expectToast(
  expectedText: string,
  showTimeoutMs = 3000,
  dismissTimeoutMs = 6000
): Promise<void> {
  await waitFor(element(by.id('toast-container')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(showTimeoutMs);

  // Assert the text content while the toast is visible
  await expect(element(by.text(expectedText))).toBeVisible();

  // Wait for auto-dismiss to confirm the component handles it correctly
  await waitFor(element(by.id('toast-container')))
    .not.toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(dismissTimeoutMs);
}

it('shows a success toast after saving profile changes', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await element(by.id('profile-name-input')).replaceText('Alice');
  await element(by.id('profile-save-button')).tap();
  await expectToast('Profile saved successfully');
});

it('shows an error toast when the save fails due to network error', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({
    newInstance: true,
    launchArgs: { MOCK_NETWORK_ERROR: '1' },
  });
  await element(by.id('profile-save-button')).tap();
  await expectToast('Failed to save profile. Please try again.', 4000, 8000);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The `by.text(expectedText)` assertion inside `expectToast` requires exact text matching — any trailing punctuation difference, locale-specific string, or dynamic value (e.g., "Saved at 10:42 AM") will cause the assertion to fail. For dynamic toast content, use `by.id('toast-message')` combined with `getAttributes().text` and `jestExpect().toMatch(regex)` to validate a pattern rather than an exact string. [official]

### Pattern 269 — `device.takeScreenshot(name)` with a `beforeEach`/`afterEach` bracket and a deterministic naming convention for per-test evidence collection in CI artifact uploads [official]

Detox's `device.takeScreenshot(name)` saves a PNG to the configured `artifactsLocation` directory. When called in `beforeEach` and `afterEach` with a deterministic naming scheme (e.g., `before_<test-title>` and `after_<test-title>`), every test in the suite gets a before/after screenshot pair stored under `artifacts/<device>/<test-suite>/`. These pairs are invaluable for debugging test failures without rerunning the test: the before screenshot confirms the initial state was correct, and the after screenshot shows the final state that caused an assertion to fail. This pattern works alongside `--take-screenshots failing` but provides screenshots for every test, not just failing ones.

```ts
// e2e/setup.ts — global beforeEach/afterEach screenshot pairs
const sanitize = (s: string): string =>
  s.replace(/[^a-z0-9_-]/gi, '_').slice(0, 80);

beforeEach(async () => {
  const title = sanitize(expect.getState().currentTestName ?? 'unknown');
  await device.takeScreenshot(`before__${title}`);
});

afterEach(async () => {
  const title = sanitize(expect.getState().currentTestName ?? 'unknown');
  await device.takeScreenshot(`after__${title}`);
});

// jest.config.ts — configure artifact storage
// export default {
//   testEnvironment: 'detox/runners/jest/DetoxEnvironment',
//   // Detox config picks up artifactsLocation from .detoxrc.ts:
//   // artifacts: { rootDir: './e2e/artifacts', pathBuilder: './e2e/pathBuilder.js' }
// };
```

**Tradeoff:** Taking screenshots in `beforeEach` and `afterEach` for every test adds approximately 300–600 ms per test per screenshot call. On a 200-test suite this totals 2–4 minutes of added CI time. Gate the screenshot behavior behind a `DETOX_FULL_SCREENSHOTS=1` environment variable so that the default CI run uses `--take-screenshots failing` (faster) while a dedicated evidence-collection run enables the full bracket. [official]

---

### Pattern 270 — `element.longPressAndDrag()` for drag-and-drop reordering in `DraggableFlatList` with full parameter reference for normalized source and target positions [official]

Drag-and-drop list reordering is one of the most complex gestures to test reliably. Detox's `longPressAndDrag` API provides all the parameters needed to replicate a full pick-up-drag-drop sequence: an initial long press to activate drag mode, source normalized position within the source element, a target element reference, target normalized position, drag speed, and hold duration before the drop. For `react-native-draggable-flatlist`, drag mode is activated after a 600–800 ms long press on the drag handle. Using the handle's testID as the source element and the target row's testID as the destination produces reliable reorders across all simulators.

```ts
it('reorders the playlist by dragging item 2 to the top', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await waitFor(element(by.id('playlist-list'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);

  // Verify initial order
  await expect(element(by.id('playlist-item-0-title'))).toHaveText('Track A');
  await expect(element(by.id('playlist-item-2-title'))).toHaveText('Track C');

  // Drag the handle of item-2 to the position of item-0
  await element(by.id('playlist-item-2-drag-handle')).longPressAndDrag(
    800,   // longPressDuration ms — activates DraggableFlatList drag mode
    0.5,   // source normalized X (center of handle)
    0.5,   // source normalized Y (center of handle)
    element(by.id('playlist-item-0')), // target element
    0.5,   // target normalized X
    0.1,   // target normalized Y — drop near the top of item-0
    'slow', // drag speed
    200    // holdDuration ms — time held before release
  );

  // Verify new order after drop
  await waitFor(element(by.id('playlist-item-0-title'))).toHaveText('Track C').withTimeout(3000);
  await expect(element(by.id('playlist-item-2-title'))).toHaveText('Track A');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `longPressAndDrag` is iOS-only in Detox 20.x. Android drag-and-drop reordering must be tested with RNGH gesture composition or via `adb` input injection. Additionally, `DraggableFlatList` uses Reanimated shared values for position tracking — if Reanimated animations are disabled in the test environment via `launchArgs`, the drag gesture may complete instantaneously and bypass drop zone detection logic. Keep `REANIMATED_ANIMATIONS_ENABLED: '1'` in `launchArgs` when testing DnD. [official]

---

### Pattern 271 — `waitFor(element).toBeVisible().whileElement(by.id(list)).scroll()` two-pass strategy for `SectionList` items obscured by sticky section headers under Detox's 75%-visibility threshold [official]

Detox 20.48+ raised the visibility threshold for `toBeVisible()` from 50% to 75% of the element's frame area. `SectionList` section headers that stick to the top of the viewport can obscure the top 25–35% of the first item in a section, causing `waitFor(item).toBeVisible()` to intermittently fail. Using `waitFor().whileElement().scroll()` before asserting repositions the list so that the target element's 75% threshold is clear of the section header. This pattern requires the item to have a testID and the SectionList container to be scrollable.

```ts
// Helper to scroll a SectionList item past sticky header into 75%-visible area
async function scrollItemIntoView(listId: string, itemId: string): Promise<void> {
  // Keep scrolling in small increments until the item passes the 75% threshold
  await waitFor(element(by.id(itemId)))
    .toBeVisible()
    .whileElement(by.id(listId))
    .scroll(150, 'down');
}

it('expands a SectionList section and interacts with the first item', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await waitFor(element(by.id('contacts-section-list'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);

  // Tap section header to expand
  await element(by.id('section-header-favorites')).tap();

  // Scroll the first favorite item past the sticky header into the 75%-visible area
  await scrollItemIntoView('contacts-section-list', 'contact-item-alice');

  await element(by.id('contact-item-alice')).tap();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('contact-detail-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The `whileElement().scroll(150, 'down')` approach will continue scrolling indefinitely if the item never passes the 75% threshold (e.g., item is in a collapsed section, item testID is wrong, or item is genuinely off-screen). Always pair this pattern with a `withTimeout()` on the outer `waitFor` to ensure the test fails with a timeout error rather than an infinite scroll loop. The scroll increment (150) should be smaller than the section header height to prevent scrolling past the target. [official]

---

### Pattern 272 — `by.id().and(by.type())` compound matcher for resolving testID collisions between a composite component and its internal native container that shares the same accessibility tree testID [community]

React Native's `View` component passes `testID` down to the underlying native container. When a composite component assigns a testID that is also propagated to an inner native container via `accessible={true}`, Detox's `by.id()` matcher can match both the composite component and the inner native view. The `by.id().and(by.type())` compound narrows the match to a specific native type, resolving the ambiguity. This pattern is most common when a component wraps `View` with `accessible={true}` and `importantForAccessibility='yes'` on both the outer and inner containers.

```ts
// Resolve testID collision between composite Card and its inner native container
it('taps the correct card element when composite component has testID on both layers', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });

  await waitFor(element(by.id('product-card-list'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);

  // Using by.id() alone matches both the Card composite and its inner RCTView
  // — use by.type() to narrow to the actual touchable native container
  const iosType = 'RCTTouchableOpacity';
  const androidType = 'com.facebook.react.views.touchable.ReactTouchable';
  const nativeType = device.getPlatform() === 'ios' ? iosType : androidType;

  const cardEl = element(by.id('product-card-42').and(by.type(nativeType)));
  await cardEl.tap();

  await waitFor(element(by.id('product-detail-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
});

// Verification: confirm compound matcher resolves to a single element
it('verifies compound matcher avoids multi-match error', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  const nativeType = device.getPlatform() === 'ios'
    ? 'RCTTouchableOpacity'
    : 'com.facebook.react.views.touchable.ReactTouchable';
  const attrs = await element(
    by.id('product-card-42').and(by.type(nativeType))
  ).getAttributes();
  // getAttributes() throws on multiple matches — single match confirmed
  jestExpect(Array.isArray(attrs)).toBe(false);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `by.type()` native class names differ between iOS and Android and can change across React Native versions when the renderer changes. Consider `by.semanticType('touchable')` (Detox 20.47+, Pattern 56) as a more portable alternative when the component is uniformly a touchable element. Reserve `by.type()` compound matching for cases where `by.semanticType()` does not adequately narrow the match. [community]

---

### Pattern 273 — `detox.init()` / `detox.cleanup()` in Jest `globalSetup` / `globalTeardown` for monorepo shared-emulator initialization to eliminate per-package cold-start overhead [official]

In monorepo setups with multiple packages that each have their own Detox test suite, spinning up a new emulator per package adds 3–5 minutes of CI overhead per package. Using Jest's `globalSetup` and `globalTeardown` with `detox.init()` / `detox.cleanup()` allows all packages to share a single running emulator across their test runs. The emulator is started once at the beginning of the CI pipeline step and stopped once at the end, with each package running its `beforeAll` app launch against the already-warm emulator.

```ts
// e2e/global-setup.ts — shared across multiple packages in a monorepo
import { detox } from 'detox';
import detoxConfig from '../.detoxrc';

export default async function globalSetup(): Promise<void> {
  // Initialize Detox without launching the app — warms the emulator only
  await detox.init(detoxConfig, { initGlobals: false, launchApp: false });
  console.log('[globalSetup] Detox initialized — emulator is warm');
}

// e2e/global-teardown.ts
import { detox } from 'detox';

export default async function globalTeardown(): Promise<void> {
  await detox.cleanup();
  console.log('[globalTeardown] Detox cleaned up — emulator shut down');
}

// Each package's jest.config.ts
export default {
  globalSetup: '<rootDir>/../../e2e/global-setup.ts',
  globalTeardown: '<rootDir>/../../e2e/global-teardown.ts',
  testEnvironment: 'detox/runners/jest/DetoxEnvironment',
  // Each package's beforeAll must call device.launchApp({ delete: true }) for isolation
};
```

**Tradeoff:** Sharing an emulator across packages means that one package's test run can leave the emulator in a dirty state (modified keychain, cached network responses, stale app data) that affects the next package. Each package must enforce strict `beforeAll` cleanup via `device.launchApp({ delete: true })` or `device.resetContentAndSettings()` to guarantee isolation. Packages cannot be run in parallel when sharing a single emulator — this pattern improves sequential suite execution time, not parallel throughput. [official]

---

### Pattern 274 — `element.multiTap(2)` for testing double-tap to like/favorite gestures implemented via RNGH `TapGesture` with `numberOfTaps: 2` [official]

Double-tap gestures for liking/favoriting content (Instagram-style) are commonly implemented with RNGH's `TapGesture({ numberOfTaps: 2 })`. Detox's `element.multiTap(2)` dispatches two rapid tap events on the same element within the RNGH gesture recognition window (typically 250 ms between taps). The key implementation note is that Detox's `multiTap` uses a fixed inter-tap interval that must fall within the RNGH recognition window — if the app customizes the recognition window, the timing may need adjustment. Test both the double-tap trigger and the single-tap fallback in separate test cases to fully cover gesture handling.

```ts
it('double-tapping a post image triggers the like animation and persists the like', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await waitFor(element(by.id('feed-post-image-0'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

  // Verify initially not liked
  await expect(element(by.id('like-indicator-0'))).not.toBeVisible();

  // Double-tap to like (RNGH TapGesture numberOfTaps: 2)
  await element(by.id('feed-post-image-0')).multiTap(2);

  // Heart animation appears briefly — wait for it then confirm persistent like indicator
  await waitFor(element(by.id('like-burst-animation-0'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);
  await waitFor(element(by.id('like-burst-animation-0'))).not.toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
  await expect(element(by.id('like-indicator-0'))).toBeVisible();

  // Reload to confirm like was persisted (not just in-memory state)
  await device.reloadReactNative();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('feed-post-image-0'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
  await expect(element(by.id('like-indicator-0'))).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `multiTap(2)` fires both taps with Detox's fixed inter-tap timing. If the RNGH `TapGesture` recognition window is shorter than Detox's inter-tap interval, the double-tap will not register and the test will silently observe a single-tap behavior. Verify the RNGH recognition window in the component (`maxDelay` prop on `TapGesture`), and if the window is customized to be shorter than ~200 ms, add `disableSynchronization: true` around the `multiTap` call to prevent Detox's synchronization from inserting idle-wait time between the two taps. [official]

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 41

### Gotcha 229 — `waitFor(element(by.id('x'))).toHaveText(text)` fails intermittently on `Animated.View` containers on Android API 35+ at high refresh rates because Detox marks the app idle before the native layout pass completes [community]

**Root cause**: On Android API 35+, the `Animated.View` layout pass runs asynchronously on the UI thread and can complete one or two frames after the JavaScript animation driving it has set `opacity` to `1.0`. Detox's synchronization engine marks the app as idle when the JS `Animated.Value` resolves to `1.0` — before the Android compositor has committed the final opacity to the view layer. `waitFor().toHaveText()` fires during this one-frame window when the native view exists but its layout has not been committed to the display list, causing `toHaveText()` to fail with an element-not-visible error despite the JS-side opacity being fully resolved. The failure is intermittent and correlates with API 35+ 90/120 Hz display profiles where the frame gap is shorter and the race more frequent.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — toHaveText() fails intermittently on Animated.View content on Android API 35+
// After animation completes (opacity reaches 1.0), the native layout pass is still pending
await waitFor(element(by.id('animated-label'))).toHaveText('Ready').withTimeout(3000);
// INTERMITTENT FAIL: "element not visible" on Android API 35+ at 90/120 Hz

// FIX OPTION 1 — use a toBeVisible() guard on a non-Animated sibling before asserting text
await waitFor(element(by.id('animated-container-sentinel'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
// sentinel is a plain View inside the Animated.View that becomes visible after layout
await expect(element(by.id('animated-label'))).toHaveText('Ready');

// FIX OPTION 2 — wait for toBeVisible() first, then assert text
await waitFor(element(by.id('animated-label'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(500);
await waitFor(element(by.id('animated-label'))).toHaveText('Ready').withTimeout(2000);

// WHY this matters: any app that uses Animated.View for entrance animations (fade-in,
// slide-in) and follows it with an immediate text assertion will see this race on
// Android API 35+ 90/120 Hz emulators; the failure rate is ~15% with the
// Google APIs Pixel 8 emulator target which ships with a 120 Hz display profile.
```

**WHY this matters:** This race condition only manifests on Android API 35+ with high-refresh-rate emulator display profiles. Tests that pass consistently on the standard API 34 60 Hz emulator will begin failing intermittently when upgrading the CI emulator target to API 35 — without any change to test code or app logic. The intermittent nature makes it easy to attribute to network variance rather than the real cause (layout commit timing).

---

### Gotcha 230 — `element.typeText()` on a `TextInput` with `autoCapitalize='words'` inserts capitalized text on iOS but lowercase on Android, causing cross-platform `toHaveValue()` assertion failures [community]

**Root cause**: iOS Simulator's software keyboard honors the `autoCapitalize` prop and applies word-level capitalization to each typed character in real time. Detox's `typeText()` on iOS is routed through the simulator's soft keyboard pipeline, which applies the `autoCapitalize` transformation. Android's `typeText()` is routed through `adb input text` or a direct Espresso call, both of which bypass the Android IME's `autoCapitalize` logic and insert characters as-is (lowercase). The result: `typeText('hello world')` produces `"Hello World"` on iOS and `"hello world"` on Android when the field has `autoCapitalize='words'`.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — toHaveValue() assertion fails on one platform due to autoCapitalize
await element(by.id('name-input')).typeText('alice smith');
await expect(element(by.id('name-input'))).toHaveValue('alice smith');
// PASSES on Android, FAILS on iOS — iOS produces "Alice Smith" via autoCapitalize='words'

// FIX OPTION 1 — use replaceText() which bypasses autoCapitalize on both platforms
await element(by.id('name-input')).replaceText('alice smith');
await expect(element(by.id('name-input'))).toHaveValue('alice smith');

// FIX OPTION 2 — use a platform-specific expected value
const expected = device.getPlatform() === 'ios' ? 'Alice Smith' : 'alice smith';
await element(by.id('name-input')).typeText('alice smith');
await expect(element(by.id('name-input'))).toHaveValue(expected);

// FIX OPTION 3 — disable autoCapitalize in E2E builds
// <TextInput autoCapitalize={__E2E__ ? 'none' : 'words'} ... />

// WHY this matters: 'words' is the default autoCapitalize value for name and address
// fields; any test that uses typeText() and reads back the value with toHaveValue()
// has a latent cross-platform inconsistency that surfaces only when CI runs both
// iOS and Android targets in the same pipeline.
```

**WHY this matters:** The `autoCapitalize` inconsistency is not documented in Detox's `typeText()` API reference. Tests authored on Android where lowercase is preserved will fail on iOS CI, and vice versa. The fix — switching to `replaceText()` — changes the `onChange` event pipeline (fires a single change vs per-character changes), which may itself affect autocomplete or validation behavior under test.

---

### Gotcha 231 — `device.launchApp({ permissions: { notifications: 'YES' } })` has no effect on Android 13+ (API 33+) because the `POST_NOTIFICATIONS` runtime permission is not covered by the Detox permissions launch-arg mechanism in Detox 20.x [community]

**Root cause**: Android 13 introduced `android.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS` as a mandatory runtime permission. Detox's `launchApp({ permissions: { notifications: 'YES' } })` maps to pre-API-33 permission grants. The `notifications` key was not updated for the API 33 `POST_NOTIFICATIONS` permission in Detox 20.x releases through 20.51. When the app calls `requestPermissionsAsync()` on Android 13+, the permission dialog still appears despite the launch arg because `POST_NOTIFICATIONS` was never actually granted. Tests that assume notification permission is pre-granted on Android 13+ will encounter an unexpected system alert that blocks subsequent interactions.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — notification permission dialog appears on Android 13+ despite launchApp permissions
await device.launchApp({
  newInstance: true,
  permissions: { notifications: 'YES' }, // No-op on Android API 33+
});
await element(by.id('enable-notifications-button')).tap();
// Android 13+ system dialog appears — test hangs waiting for home-screen element

// FIX OPTION 1 — grant POST_NOTIFICATIONS via adb before launching the app
// In a beforeAll Bash step:
// adb shell pm grant com.example.app android.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS
// Then launch the app normally:
await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });

// FIX OPTION 2 — handle the permission dialog via by.system.label()
await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
await element(by.id('enable-notifications-button')).tap();
if (device.getPlatform() === 'android') {
  try {
    await waitFor(element(by.system.label('Allow'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);
    await element(by.system.label('Allow')).tap();
  } catch (_) { /* permission was already granted or dialog did not appear */ }
}

// WHY this matters: Android 13 shipped with Expo SDK 50 as the minimum supported API;
// any CI pipeline targeting API 33+ that uses notifications: 'YES' to skip the
// permission dialog will encounter this silent failure — no error from launchApp,
// the test proceeds, and then hangs when the unexpected dialog blocks the tap target.
```

**WHY this matters:** The broken `notifications: 'YES'` grant on Android 13+ produces no error at `launchApp` time — the failure appears many lines later as a `waitFor` timeout when the notification permission dialog is blocking the UI, making the root cause very difficult to trace back to the missing grant.

---

### Gotcha 232 — `element.scroll(100, 'down')` on `react-native-keyboard-aware-scroll-view` overshoots by the keyboard height on iOS when the software keyboard is visible, because the library adds `keyboardOffset` pixels to all programmatic scroll calls [community]

**Root cause**: `react-native-keyboard-aware-scroll-view` overrides the standard ScrollView's `scrollTo()` implementation to add an extra `keyboardOffset` pixels (typically ~300–350 px on iPhone) to all programmatic scroll calls when the keyboard is visible. Detox's `element.scroll(100, 'down')` internally calls `scrollTo()` on the native scroll container, which triggers the library's override. The net effect is that `scroll(100, 'down')` actually scrolls ~400 pixels when the keyboard is open — scrolling past the target element that was only 100 pixels below the visible area.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — scroll(100, 'down') overshoots when keyboard is open in KeyboardAwareScrollView
await element(by.id('username-input')).tap(); // keyboard opens
await element(by.id('keyboard-aware-form-scroll')).scroll(100, 'down');
// Scrolls ~400px due to keyboardOffset — submit button is now off-screen above
await waitFor(element(by.id('submit-button'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);
// TIMES OUT on iOS with keyboard open

// FIX OPTION 1 — dismiss the keyboard before scrolling
await element(by.id('username-input')).tapReturnKey(); // dismisses keyboard on returnKeyType='done'
await element(by.id('keyboard-aware-form-scroll')).scroll(100, 'down');
await waitFor(element(by.id('submit-button'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);

// FIX OPTION 2 — use waitFor().whileElement().scroll() which adapts to actual position
await waitFor(element(by.id('submit-button')))
  .toBeVisible()
  .whileElement(by.id('keyboard-aware-form-scroll'))
  .scroll(100, 'down');

// WHY this matters: KeyboardAwareScrollView is one of the most commonly used scroll
// utilities in React Native form screens; the offset double-counting is only
// observable when the keyboard is open, creating an iOS-specific failure mode that
// does not reproduce on Android (which uses windowSoftInputMode adjustResize instead).
```

**WHY this matters:** The overshoot only occurs on iOS when the keyboard is visible — the same test passes with the keyboard dismissed or on Android, creating a false sense that the test is iOS-only flaky. The `react-native-keyboard-aware-scroll-view` library's `scrollTo` override is not documented as affecting Detox's scroll API.

---

### Gotcha 233 — `device.sendToBackground()` followed immediately by `device.bringToForeground()` hangs indefinitely on Android API 34+ because the `ActivityLifecycleMonitor` race causes a Detox synchronization deadlock [community]

**Root cause**: On Android API 34+, the `ActivityLifecycleMonitor` delivers `onStop` callbacks asynchronously via a `Looper` message queue. When `device.sendToBackground()` is called, Detox waits for `onStop` to confirm the background transition. However, if `device.bringToForeground()` is called within ~50–100 ms of `sendToBackground()` completing, the `ActivityLifecycleMonitor` can deliver the `onStop` message after the foreground restoration has already begun. Detox's synchronization engine enters an inconsistent state where it is waiting for `onStop` to confirm the background but the activity is already in `onResume`, causing a deadlock that manifests as an infinite hang on the first `waitFor` call after `bringToForeground()`.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — hangs after sendToBackground() + bringToForeground() with no delay
await device.sendToBackground();
await device.bringToForeground();
// Detox hangs indefinitely here on Android API 34+ — ActivityLifecycleMonitor race

// FIX OPTION 1 — add a short pause between background and foreground (500ms empirically)
await device.sendToBackground();
await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 500)); // Allow ActivityLifecycleMonitor to settle
await device.bringToForeground();
await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);

// FIX OPTION 2 — use disableSynchronization around the lifecycle transition
await device.disableSynchronization();
await device.sendToBackground();
await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 300));
await device.bringToForeground();
await device.enableSynchronization();
await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);

// WHY this matters: sendToBackground + bringToForeground is the canonical Detox
// pattern for testing app-resume behavior (session restore, re-auth, live-activity
// updates); every test using this pattern will hang sporadically on Android API 34+
// CI without this 500ms guard, and the hang produces a jest timeout error with no
// indication of the lifecycle race as the root cause.
```

**WHY this matters:** The hang produces a Jest test timeout error with a Detox stack trace pointing to the `waitFor` call after `bringToForeground()` — not to the `sendToBackground()` call that started the race. Teams typically add longer timeouts to the `waitFor`, which does not fix the underlying deadlock and just delays the eventual failure.

| Detox `element.swipe()` pull-to-refresh normalized start position | https://wix.github.io/Detox/docs/api/actions-on-element#swipedirection-speed-normalizedswipingpositionx-normalizedswipingpositiony | `startNormalizedY: 0.8` for iOS RefreshControl; `startNormalizedY: 0.3` for Android SwipeRefreshLayout |

## Updated Anti-Patterns Checklist (Cycle 41 additions)

| Anti-Pattern | Fix |
|---|---|
| Using `typeText('\n')` to submit forms instead of `tapReturnKey()` or `tapKey('Search')` — fires a raw newline character insertion, not the IME action event, causing `onSubmitEditing` to receive the wrong `nativeEvent.submittingKey` | Use `element.tapKey('Search')` or `element.tapReturnKey()` to dispatch the correct IME action event matching the `returnKeyType` prop (Pattern 260) |
| Calling `element.swipe('down')` from the default center-screen start position for pull-to-refresh on iOS 17+ — gesture is intercepted as notification-center pull instead of RefreshControl trigger | Start from `startNormalizedY: 0.8` and swipe `'up'` to trigger `RefreshControl` from within the scroll container on iOS (Pattern 261) |
| Reading `device.appLaunchArgs.get()` after `device.appLaunchArgs.modify()` and expecting it to return the modified values — `get()` only reflects the values set at original launch time | Track dynamically modified flags in a test-local variable; `get()` only reflects original launch args (Pattern 262) |
| Using `waitFor().not.toBeVisible()` after dismissing modals and immediately tapping elements that were previously covered — element may remain in hierarchy with zero opacity and still intercept touches | Use `waitFor().not.toExist()` to wait for full unmount before tapping previously-covered elements (Pattern 263) |
| Using `element.typeText()` on fields with `autoCapitalize='words'` and asserting exact lowercase value — iOS applies capitalization via the soft keyboard pipeline, producing a different value than Android | Use `replaceText()` to bypass `autoCapitalize` on both platforms, or use platform-conditional expected values (Gotcha 230) |
| Calling `device.sendToBackground()` followed immediately by `device.bringToForeground()` on Android API 34+ without a pause — `ActivityLifecycleMonitor` race causes Detox synchronization deadlock and infinite hang | Add a 500 ms pause between `sendToBackground()` and `bringToForeground()` to allow the lifecycle monitor to settle (Gotcha 233) |
| Using `launchApp({ permissions: { notifications: 'YES' } })` on Android 13+ (API 33+) — `POST_NOTIFICATIONS` runtime permission is not granted by the `notifications` key in Detox 20.x | Use `adb shell pm grant <package> android.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS` in a `beforeAll` step, or intercept the dialog with `by.system.label('Allow')` (Gotcha 231) |
