## Cycle 42 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 275 — `element.tapAtPoint({ x, y })` for tapping a specific pixel offset within an element when the default center-tap triggers the wrong gesture handler in overlapping touch targets [official]

Some components render two or more interactive zones at the same `testID` level — for example, a card that has an inline action button rendered absolutely over the card's image area. Detox's default `element.tap()` fires at the center of the matched element's bounding box, which may land inside the overlapping child and trigger the wrong handler. `element.tapAtPoint({ x, y })` lets you specify an offset in logical pixels from the element's top-left corner, giving you precise control over which sub-region receives the tap event. Use `element.getAttributes()` first to retrieve the element's `frame` bounds so the offset can be derived programmatically instead of hard-coding pixel coordinates that break when layout changes. Combine with a `waitFor().toBeVisible()` guard to ensure layout is complete before reading attributes.

```ts
it('taps the share button rendered over the card image without triggering card navigation', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await waitFor(element(by.id('feed-card-0'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

  // Read the card's bounding box so we can derive the share-button offset
  const cardAttrs = await element(by.id('feed-card-0')).getAttributes();
  const frame = (cardAttrs as any).frame; // { x, y, width, height }

  // Share button is 44x44 pt, anchored to top-right corner of the card image
  // Image occupies the top 60% of the card; button is at x=(width-50), y=10
  const tapX = frame.width - 50;
  const tapY = 10;

  await element(by.id('feed-card-0')).tapAtPoint({ x: tapX, y: tapY });

  // Confirm share sheet appeared, not card navigation
  await waitFor(element(by.id('share-sheet-header'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
  await expect(element(by.id('card-detail-screen'))).not.toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Hard-coded pixel offsets break silently when the component layout changes. Always derive offsets from `getAttributes().frame` at runtime rather than constants. On Android, `frame` is returned in density-independent pixels (dp) and matches the values you pass to `tapAtPoint`, so no scaling is required. On iOS, `frame` is in logical points, also matching `tapAtPoint` input. If the element is inside a scrolled container, the `frame` is relative to the element's parent scroll container origin — you may need to scroll it into view first. [official]

---

### Pattern 276 — `by.label()` matcher for tapping accessibility-label-only elements that have no `testID` in third-party or generated components [official]

Third-party libraries, maps SDKs, and code-generated UI components often render interactive views without a `testID`. For these cases, Detox's `by.label()` matcher selects elements by their `accessibilityLabel` on iOS (mapped from `UIAccessibilityElement.accessibilityLabel`) and `contentDescription` on Android. This pattern is particularly useful for native map markers, chart segments, and library-provided icon buttons that expose `accessibilityLabel` but not a `testID`. When the label may change with locale or dynamic content, use `by.label()` with a regex-capable substring or combine with `by.type()` to narrow the match. Always audit the label value in the running app with Detox's element inspector before writing the test.

```ts
it('taps a native map marker by its accessibility label and confirms the detail callout', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await waitFor(element(by.id('map-container'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);

  // Map SDK renders MKAnnotationView with accessibilityLabel set to the poi name
  // No testID is available from the third-party map SDK
  await element(by.label('Central Park')).tap();

  // Confirm the callout bubble appeared
  await waitFor(element(by.id('map-callout-title'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
  await expect(element(by.id('map-callout-title'))).toHaveText('Central Park');

  // Dismiss the callout
  await element(by.id('map-callout-close-button')).tap();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('map-callout-title'))).not.toExist().withTimeout(2000);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `by.label()` matches are fragile to localization: any locale that changes the `accessibilityLabel` value will break the selector. Where possible, prefer `testID` on wrapper views that you control. When using `by.label()` on third-party components, document the label source (e.g., "this is set by the map SDK from the POI name field") so that future maintainers know why a `testID` was not used. On Android, some components set `contentDescription` from string resources — if those strings are localized, the test will fail on non-English CI runners. [official]

---

### Pattern 277 — `device.resetContentAndSettings()` versus `device.launchApp({ delete: true })` — choosing the right isolation strategy based on speed requirements and simulator state scope [official]

Detox provides two isolation primitives: `device.resetContentAndSettings()` wipes the entire iOS Simulator's installed apps, photos, contacts, and keychain in one call, equivalent to a "Erase All Content and Settings" operation — it is thorough but takes 15–30 seconds and cannot be called while the app is running. `device.launchApp({ delete: true })` deletes and reinstalls only the app under test, taking 3–8 seconds, preserving simulator-level state (system contacts, Safari cookies, system keychain) but guaranteeing a clean app sandbox. Use `resetContentAndSettings()` only in `globalSetup` or in a dedicated isolation suite; use `launchApp({ delete: true })` in `beforeEach` for per-test app sandbox isolation within a suite.

```ts
// globalSetup — full simulator wipe once per CI run (30s, runs once)
import { device } from 'detox';

export default async function globalSetup() {
  await detox.init(detoxConfig, { launchApp: false });
  await device.resetContentAndSettings(); // Full wipe — clears all app sandboxes + keychain
  console.log('[globalSetup] Simulator reset complete');
}

// beforeEach — fast per-test app-only reinstall (5s, runs per test)
beforeEach(async () => {
  await device.launchApp({
    newInstance: true,
    delete: true, // Deletes + reinstalls only the app under test
    permissions: { notifications: 'YES', camera: 'YES' },
  });
});

// Combining both — use resetContentAndSettings() in globalSetup to clear system-level
// state (keychain entries from previous test runs), then rely on delete: true per test
// for fast per-test app sandbox isolation without another full simulator wipe.
```

**Tradeoff:** `resetContentAndSettings()` takes 15–30 seconds on modern simulators and cannot be interrupted. Running it in `beforeEach` would add 30 seconds per test case — use it only in `globalSetup` or a dedicated setup fixture that runs once per CI job. `launchApp({ delete: true })` is fast enough for `beforeEach` use but does not clear system keychain entries that your app may have written in a prior test — if your tests interact with the system keychain, you need `resetContentAndSettings()` in `globalSetup` to guarantee a clean state. [official]

---

### Pattern 278 — `waitFor(element).toHaveText(text).withTimeout(n)` with exact-text versus `toHaveText` substring matching for async-updated labels driven by polling intervals [official]

UI labels that display live data (countdown timers, price tickers, server-pushed status strings) are updated by polling or WebSocket intervals. A common test mistake is asserting the exact text value immediately after an action, before the next poll cycle has run. Use `waitFor(element).toHaveText(expectedText).withTimeout(pollingInterval * 2 + 500)` to give the component at least two poll cycles to update. When the exact text is not known at test authoring time (e.g., a formatted timestamp), use `toHaveText` with a prefix string that is stable across poll cycles, combined with a `toBeVisible()` guard to distinguish the loading state from the loaded state.

```ts
it('status label updates to "Connected" within two polling cycles after network is restored', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });

  // Simulate offline state — app polls status endpoint every 2 seconds
  await device.setURLBlacklist(['.*api.example.com.*']);
  await waitFor(element(by.id('status-label'))).toHaveText('Offline').withTimeout(5000);

  // Restore network
  await device.setURLBlacklist([]);

  // Wait for at least two poll cycles (2s each) plus network round-trip margin
  // toHaveText does an exact match — 'Connected' is the full label text
  await waitFor(element(by.id('status-label')))
    .toHaveText('Connected')
    .withTimeout(5500); // 2 * 2000ms poll + 1500ms margin

  // Confirm the label is visible (not hidden while loading)
  await expect(element(by.id('status-label'))).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Polling-based UI labels have an inherent uncertainty window: the timeout must be at least `pollingInterval * 2` to survive the worst-case scenario where an assertion fires just after a poll completed and a full cycle must elapse before the next update. Setting the timeout too tight produces intermittent failures correlated with CI load; setting it too loose masks real regressions. Document the polling interval in a comment next to the `withTimeout` argument so future readers understand the derivation. [official]

---

### Pattern 279 — `element.swipe('left', 'fast')` on a `FlatList` rendered as a horizontal pager to advance slides, combined with `by.id()` index suffixes to assert each slide's content [community]

Horizontally paginated `FlatList` carousels (onboarding flows, feature tours, image galleries) are commonly tested by swiping left/right and asserting the visible slide's content. Detox's `element.swipe('left', 'fast')` from the center of a horizontal scroll container advances one page when `pagingEnabled` is true on the `FlatList`. The key correctness requirement is that the swipe starts from within the scroll container — use `by.id('carousel-container')` as the target, not a child slide element. Combine with `by.id('slide-{n}')` index-suffixed testIDs on slide content to assert each visible slide without querying off-screen elements.

```ts
it('cycles through all 4 onboarding slides and reaches the Get Started screen', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true, delete: true });

  // Slide 1 is visible on launch
  await waitFor(element(by.id('onboarding-slide-0-title'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
  await expect(element(by.id('onboarding-slide-0-title'))).toHaveText('Welcome');

  // Advance to slide 2
  await element(by.id('onboarding-carousel')).swipe('left', 'fast', 0.8);
  await waitFor(element(by.id('onboarding-slide-1-title'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);
  await expect(element(by.id('onboarding-slide-1-title'))).toHaveText('Stay Organized');

  // Advance to slide 3
  await element(by.id('onboarding-carousel')).swipe('left', 'fast', 0.8);
  await waitFor(element(by.id('onboarding-slide-2-title'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);

  // Advance to slide 4 — the final CTA slide
  await element(by.id('onboarding-carousel')).swipe('left', 'fast', 0.8);
  await waitFor(element(by.id('onboarding-slide-3-cta-button'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);
  await element(by.id('onboarding-slide-3-cta-button')).tap();

  // Confirm navigation to main app
  await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen-root'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `swipe('left', 'fast')` on a `FlatList` with `pagingEnabled` reliably advances one page on iOS. On Android, fast swipes on `FlatList` may occasionally advance two pages if the list has a high `decelerationRate` or the device is a faster emulator — use `'slow'` speed on Android to reduce page-skip failures, or explicitly `waitFor` the expected slide before proceeding. Asserting off-screen slides (not yet scrolled into view) with `toBeVisible()` will always fail; ensure your `testID` scheme uses index suffixes so you only assert the visible slide. [community]

---

### Pattern 280 — `device.setURLBlacklist(patterns)` for simulating network errors on specific API endpoints without blocking all network traffic, enabling partial-offline integration tests [official]

`device.setURLBlacklist(patterns)` accepts an array of regex strings and causes OkHttp (Android) and NSURLProtocol (iOS) to reject requests whose URL matches any pattern. This lets you simulate the failure of a single backend service (e.g., the search API) while allowing the rest of the app to continue fetching data (e.g., the auth token refresh endpoint). Use it in `beforeEach` for tests that cover error states, and call `device.setURLBlacklist([])` in `afterEach` to restore full network access. Pair with `waitFor().toBeVisible()` on error UI components to confirm the app correctly handles partial connectivity loss.

```ts
describe('search screen — offline error state', () => {
  afterEach(async () => {
    // Always restore network after each test in this describe block
    await device.setURLBlacklist([]);
  });

  it('shows "Search unavailable" banner when the search API is unreachable', async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen-root'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

    // Block only the search endpoint — auth + feed endpoints remain reachable
    await device.setURLBlacklist(['.*\\.example\\.com/api/v2/search.*']);

    await element(by.id('search-tab')).tap();
    await element(by.id('search-input')).typeText('coffee');
    await element(by.id('search-submit-button')).tap();

    // Expect error banner — NOT a full offline screen
    await waitFor(element(by.id('search-error-banner'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
    await expect(element(by.id('search-error-banner'))).toHaveText('Search unavailable. Try again later.');

    // Confirm the feed (non-search) content is still visible — auth + feed APIs unblocked
    await expect(element(by.id('home-feed-root'))).not.toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `setURLBlacklist` patterns are matched against the full URL string using Java regex (Android) and NSRegularExpression (iOS). Regex syntax is not identical between the two — in particular, `\.` must be `\\.` in a JavaScript string to escape properly for both engines, and lookahead assertions are not supported on Android's `java.util.regex`. Test your patterns against both platforms' regex engines before relying on them. Calling `setURLBlacklist` does not affect requests already in flight — apply the blacklist before triggering the action that initiates the request you want to fail. [official]

---

### Pattern 281 — `element.clearText()` followed by `element.typeText(value)` as the canonical two-step field update for `TextInput` components that ignore `replaceText()` due to a controlled-input `onChange` loop [community]

Some controlled `TextInput` components wire `onChangeText` to dispatch a Redux or MobX action that re-sets the field value through the state tree. When `replaceText()` is used, it fires a single synthetic change event with the full new value — but some state management middlewares debounce or batch updates in a way that causes the component to receive a stale `value` prop on the next render cycle, reverting the field to its previous value. The two-step `clearText()` + `typeText()` approach fires character-by-character events that drive the `onChangeText` handler in the same way a human user would type, bypassing the debounce issue. Use this pattern as a fallback when `replaceText()` produces inconsistent results in controlled inputs.

```ts
it('updates the profile email field via clearText + typeText and persists on save', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await waitFor(element(by.id('profile-screen-root'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

  const emailInput = element(by.id('profile-email-input'));
  await emailInput.tap(); // Focus the field

  // Step 1: clear existing content character by character
  await emailInput.clearText();
  // Verify the field is empty before typing
  await expect(emailInput).toHaveValue('');

  // Step 2: type the new value to drive the controlled onChange pipeline
  await emailInput.typeText('new.user@example.com');
  await expect(emailInput).toHaveValue('new.user@example.com');

  // Save and confirm persistence
  await element(by.id('profile-save-button')).tap();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('profile-save-success-toast'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);

  // Reload to verify the value was persisted, not just held in local state
  await device.reloadReactNative();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('profile-email-input'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
  await expect(element(by.id('profile-email-input'))).toHaveValue('new.user@example.com');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `typeText()` fires `onChangeText` for every character, which can trigger expensive operations on each keystroke (API calls, validation, large state tree updates). For inputs that debounce `onChangeText` with a short delay (100–300 ms), the character-by-character firing from `typeText()` may fire the debounced callback more times than a real user would. Prefer `replaceText()` for performance-sensitive tests; fall back to `clearText()` + `typeText()` only when `replaceText()` produces observable state reversion in controlled inputs. [community]

---

### Pattern 282 — `by.system.label()` for interacting with iOS system permission dialogs, biometric prompts, and system alert controllers that appear above the app's view hierarchy [official]

Detox's `by.system.label()` matcher accesses the native system alert layer (SpringBoard dialogs on iOS, system overlays on Android) that sits above the app's own view hierarchy. This is the correct API for tapping "Allow", "Don't Allow", "OK", and "Cancel" buttons on iOS system dialogs for location, camera, contacts, Face ID, and app rating prompts. The system alert layer is not accessible via `by.id()` or `by.text()` because those matchers only search the app's own accessibility tree. Wrap `by.system.label()` interactions in a `try/catch` block when the dialog's appearance is conditional to gracefully handle cases where the permission was already granted in a prior test.

```ts
it('grants location permission via system dialog and confirms the map centers on user location', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({
    newInstance: true,
    delete: true, // Ensures permission state is reset to "not determined"
  });

  await waitFor(element(by.id('map-screen-root'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
  await element(by.id('locate-me-button')).tap();

  // iOS system location permission dialog appears above the app
  try {
    await waitFor(element(by.system.label('Allow While Using App')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(3000);
    await element(by.system.label('Allow While Using App')).tap();
  } catch {
    // Dialog did not appear — permission was already granted (e.g., simulator reuse)
    console.warn('[test] Location permission dialog did not appear — assuming already granted');
  }

  // App receives the location authorization — map should center on the mocked location
  await waitFor(element(by.id('user-location-dot'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
  await expect(element(by.id('locate-me-button'))).toHaveText('My Location');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** System dialog label text is locale-sensitive and can change between iOS versions. Apple changed the "Always Allow" / "Allow While Using App" label text in iOS 14 and again in iOS 17. Maintain a test helper that maps iOS version ranges to the expected label string, or use `device.setPermissions()` at launch time to pre-grant permissions and avoid the dialog entirely when the test is not specifically covering the permission-request flow. On Android, system permission buttons use different labels by API level — "Allow" (API 28), "While using the app" (API 29+). [official]

---

### Pattern 283 — `element.longPress(duration)` with explicit duration in milliseconds for testing contextual menus, long-press-to-delete flows, and RNGH `LongPressGesture` with a custom `minDuration` [official]

Detox's `element.longPress()` defaults to an 800 ms press duration. Components using RNGH's `LongPressGesture` with a custom `minDuration` (e.g., 1500 ms for a deliberate long-hold) will not trigger when the default 800 ms press is used, silently doing nothing and leaving the test to time out on the expected UI response. Always check the component's `LongPressGesture({ minDuration })` value and pass `element.longPress(minDuration + 100)` to guarantee the gesture threshold is crossed. Use the extra 100 ms as a buffer for timer variance across emulator CPU loads.

```ts
it('long-pressing a message bubble for 1600ms triggers the reaction picker', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await waitFor(element(by.id('chat-screen-root'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

  // The MessageBubble uses LongPressGesture({ minDuration: 1500 })
  // Default longPress(800) would NOT trigger this gesture
  const MESSAGE_LONG_PRESS_DURATION = 1600; // 1500ms minDuration + 100ms buffer

  await waitFor(element(by.id('message-bubble-0'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
  await element(by.id('message-bubble-0')).longPress(MESSAGE_LONG_PRESS_DURATION);

  // Reaction picker should slide up after the long press
  await waitFor(element(by.id('reaction-picker-sheet'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);
  await expect(element(by.id('reaction-picker-sheet'))).toBeVisible();

  // Tap the thumbs-up reaction
  await element(by.id('reaction-thumbsup-button')).tap();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('reaction-picker-sheet'))).not.toExist().withTimeout(2000);
  await expect(element(by.id('message-reaction-thumbsup-0'))).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** On CI emulators with high CPU load, `longPress(duration)` may fire its end event slightly later than the specified duration, which is safe (longer hold, still above threshold). However, on heavily loaded Android emulators, `longPress` can occasionally fire the end event early — if tests are consistently flaky at the exact threshold, increase the buffer from 100 ms to 200 ms. The `longPressAndDrag()` API (Pattern 270) shares the same duration parameter; ensure you are not conflating the two when a drag is also expected. [official]

---

### Pattern 284 — `element.adjustSliderToPosition(normalizedPosition)` for testing `Slider` components by setting a normalized position (0.0–1.0) and asserting the resulting displayed value [official]

React Native's `<Slider>` component (and the community `@react-native-community/slider`) exposes its accessibility value as the formatted label (e.g., "75%" or "$150.00") via the native accessibility API. Detox's `element.adjustSliderToPosition(0.75)` moves the slider thumb to 75% of its track. After adjusting, read the current value with `element.getAttributes().value` (iOS) or assert the bound label with `toHaveValue()`. Because slider movement fires `onValueChange` on every intermediate position as the thumb slides, ensure any dependent UI updates are awaited with `waitFor` rather than an immediate `expect`.

```ts
it('adjusting the price range slider to 0.6 updates the max price label to $300', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await waitFor(element(by.id('filter-screen-root'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

  const priceSlider = element(by.id('price-range-slider'));
  await waitFor(priceSlider).toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);

  // Move to 60% of the slider's range (0.0 = min, 1.0 = max)
  await priceSlider.adjustSliderToPosition(0.6);

  // The label is updated via onValueChange — wait for the specific value
  await waitFor(element(by.id('price-range-max-label')))
    .toHaveText('$300')
    .withTimeout(2000);

  // Confirm the slider's accessibility value reflects the new position on iOS
  if (device.getPlatform() === 'ios') {
    const attrs = await priceSlider.getAttributes();
    expect((attrs as any).value).toMatch(/\$300/);
  }

  // Apply the filter
  await element(by.id('apply-filters-button')).tap();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('results-screen-root'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `adjustSliderToPosition` moves the slider in a single gesture that fires `onValueChange` with intermediate values as the thumb passes through them. If the component throttles or debounces `onValueChange`, the final committed value may differ from the exact target position by the step granularity (e.g., a slider with `step={25}` and `maximumValue={500}` at position 0.6 snaps to 300, but at 0.61 snaps to 325). Always assert the displayed label value, not the position, to verify the committed value. Android slider gestures may snap to a different step than iOS due to rounding differences. [official]

---

### Pattern 285 — `device.getPlatform()` guard with platform-specific `waitFor` timeouts for tests covering animations and transitions that have different default durations on iOS vs Android [community]

Animation durations in React Native apps often differ between iOS (native `LayoutAnimation` and `Animated` defaults) and Android (`react-native-reanimated` `withTiming` defaults), and the `UIView.animate` vs `Animator` differences in the native layers mean the same animation configured in JS may take noticeably different wall-clock times to complete on each platform. A common pattern is to define a `PLATFORM_TRANSITION_TIMEOUT` constant based on `device.getPlatform()` and use it in every `waitFor` call that follows an animated transition. This eliminates a category of intermittent CI failures where Android tests run with iOS-tuned timeouts that are too short for the Android animation completion time.

```ts
// e2e/helpers/platform.ts
import { device } from 'detox';

/** Returns a platform-appropriate timeout for animated transitions.
 *  iOS transitions typically complete in 300–500 ms; Android in 400–700 ms. */
export function transitionTimeout(baseMs = 500): number {
  return device.getPlatform() === 'android' ? baseMs * 1.5 : baseMs;
}

// e2e/tests/navigation.e2e.ts
import { transitionTimeout } from '../helpers/platform';

it('navigates from home to settings and back with correct header titles', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen-root'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

  await element(by.id('settings-nav-button')).tap();

  // Android navigation transition runs ~600ms vs ~350ms on iOS
  await waitFor(element(by.id('settings-screen-header')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(transitionTimeout(600));
  await expect(element(by.id('settings-screen-header'))).toHaveText('Settings');

  await element(by.id('back-button')).tap();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen-root')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(transitionTimeout(600));
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Defining platform-conditional timeouts in a helper is more maintainable than duplicating `device.getPlatform()` ternaries inline, but it adds an abstraction layer that new team members must locate before understanding the timeout derivation. Document the `transitionTimeout` helper at the top of the file with the iOS and Android baseline values. Do not use the multiplier for timeouts that cover network calls — those should be network-latency-based, not animation-based. [community]

---

### Pattern 286 — `element.performAction('accessibility')` and `by.traits()` matcher on iOS VoiceOver accessibility tree for testing screen-reader-accessible views without visual layout dependencies [community]

Detox supports iOS accessibility trait matching via `by.traits(['button'])`, `by.traits(['link'])`, and `by.traits(['header'])` to select elements by their `UIAccessibilityTraits`. This is useful for testing that newly added UI elements are correctly announced to screen readers without relying on their visual appearance. Use `by.traits(['button']).and(by.label('Submit'))` to verify that a submit action is both present in the accessibility tree and carries the correct label. On Android, equivalent accessibility role checking is done via `by.type()` with the mapped `ViewCompat.setAccessibilityDelegate` role names, though Detox's trait matchers are iOS-specific.

```ts
it('all primary CTA buttons are exposed as accessibility buttons with correct labels', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await waitFor(element(by.id('checkout-screen-root'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

  // iOS accessibility tree check — button trait + correct label
  if (device.getPlatform() === 'ios') {
    // Place Order button is accessible as a button trait with the correct label
    await expect(element(by.traits(['button']).and(by.label('Place Order')))).toBeVisible();

    // Promo code field is accessible as a text field trait
    await expect(element(by.traits(['text field']).and(by.label('Promo Code')))).toBeVisible();

    // Order summary section header is accessible as a header trait
    await expect(element(by.traits(['header']).and(by.label('Order Summary')))).toBeVisible();
  }

  // Platform-agnostic: testID-based checks for both platforms
  await expect(element(by.id('place-order-button'))).toBeVisible();
  await expect(element(by.id('promo-code-input'))).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `by.traits()` is iOS-only — Android does not expose a direct equivalent through Detox's current matcher API. Tests guarded with `device.getPlatform() === 'ios'` blocks are partial coverage; for cross-platform accessibility CI, consider pairing Detox trait tests (iOS) with a custom Android accessibility check using `getAttributes().accessibilityRole` from `element.getAttributes()`. Trait tests catch missing `accessibilityRole` prop assignments on custom components but do not verify the spoken announcement text — use a separate dedicated accessibility audit tool (Axe for React Native) for announcement testing. [community]

---

### Pattern 287 — `jest.retryTimes(n)` scoped to a specific `describe` block for isolating retry behavior to known-flaky interaction sequences without enabling retries globally [community]

Detox discourages blanket retries (`--retries` CLI flag) because they mask real failures. A better-scoped approach is to use `jest.retryTimes(n)` inside a specific `describe` block for test sequences known to have an irreducible flake rate due to third-party SDK initialization (e.g., analytics, crash reporting, A/B testing SDKs that perform network calls on first launch). This limits retry overhead to the specific flaky test cases while keeping the rest of the suite strictly zero-retry. Combine with a `beforeEach` full `device.launchApp({ delete: true })` so each retry starts from a clean state.

```ts
// e2e/tests/analytics-init.e2e.ts
describe('analytics SDK initialization — inherently flaky first-launch sequence', () => {
  // Retry up to 2 times for this describe block only — the analytics SDK has a
  // known race condition during first-launch initialization on Android emulators
  // that the SDK vendor has not yet patched (tracked in JIRA-4521)
  jest.retryTimes(2, { logErrorsBeforeRetry: true });

  beforeEach(async () => {
    // Full reinstall on every attempt to clear SDK initialization state
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true, delete: true });
    await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen-root'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(6000);
  });

  it('analytics session ID is present in the app header after SDK initialization', async () => {
    // First launch triggers the analytics SDK init sequence
    await element(by.id('debug-panel-toggle')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('debug-analytics-session-id')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(8000);
    const attrs = await element(by.id('debug-analytics-session-id')).getAttributes();
    expect((attrs as any).text).toMatch(/^[0-9a-f-]{36}$/); // UUID format
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Scoped `jest.retryTimes(n)` is a pragmatic mitigation for genuinely flaky third-party SDKs, but it doubles or triples CI time for the affected tests. Require a JIRA ticket reference comment next to every `retryTimes` call so that flaky retries are tracked and eventually fixed rather than silently accepted. Never use `retryTimes` to hide flakiness in your own app code or test logic — only for documented third-party SDK races with a linked tracking ticket. The `logErrorsBeforeRetry: true` option is essential for preserving failure information across retries in CI logs. [community]

---

### Pattern 288 — `element.scroll(distance, direction, startPositionX, startPositionY)` with explicit normalized start positions for `ScrollView` containers that have sticky headers or tab bars that intercept scroll events near the edges [official]

Detox's default `element.scroll()` begins the scroll gesture from the center of the target element (normalized position 0.5, 0.5). When a `ScrollView` has a sticky header that occupies the top ~15% of the view or a bottom tab bar that occupies the bottom ~10%, starting from the center works, but starting near these occupied zones causes the gesture to be intercepted by the header or tab bar rather than the scroll container. Pass explicit normalized start positions to `scroll()` to guarantee the gesture begins within the scrollable content area. Use `startPositionY: 0.4` to avoid the sticky header zone (top 15%) and the likely content zone (center 50%).

```ts
it('scrolls a paginated list with a sticky search header to reveal items below the fold', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await waitFor(element(by.id('search-results-list'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

  // Sticky header occupies top 15% of the scroll container
  // Default center scroll (startY=0.5) works fine; use 0.4 to stay clear of header
  // startPositionX: 0.5 (center), startPositionY: 0.4 (below sticky header zone)
  await element(by.id('search-results-list')).scroll(300, 'down', 0.5, 0.4);

  // Items below the fold should now be visible
  await waitFor(element(by.id('search-result-item-8'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);
  await expect(element(by.id('search-result-item-8'))).toBeVisible();

  // Scroll back to top using explicit start position in the lower content zone
  await element(by.id('search-results-list')).scroll(300, 'up', 0.5, 0.6);
  await waitFor(element(by.id('search-result-item-0'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Hard-coded normalized start positions (e.g., `startPositionY: 0.4`) couple the test to the current layout's proportions. If the sticky header grows (e.g., an expanded search bar is added), 0.4 may land inside the header on smaller screen sizes. Prefer `whileElement().scroll()` when the goal is simply to scroll until an element is visible — it uses adaptive scroll increments and does not require explicit start position calibration. Use explicit start positions only when you need to control the precise scroll amount rather than scrolling until an element is visible. [official]

---

### Pattern 289 — `device.openURL({ url: 'yourapp://deep-link-path' })` for testing deep-link navigation flows that must start from the home screen rather than relying on an already-running app state [official]

Deep-link tests commonly have a state contamination risk: if the app is already running and navigated deep into a specific screen, calling `device.openURL()` may trigger the deep-link handler on top of the existing navigation stack rather than from the expected root state. The correct pattern is to call `device.launchApp({ newInstance: true })` first to bring the app to a clean home-screen state, then call `device.openURL()` with the deep-link URL to trigger the navigation. This mirrors the real user scenario where the deep link is tapped from a notification or external app while the app is either backgrounded or closed.

```ts
it('deep-linking to /order/12345 navigates to the order detail screen for order 12345', async () => {
  // Launch from scratch to guarantee a clean navigation stack
  await device.launchApp({
    newInstance: true,
    delete: false, // Keep app data — we need auth state to be present
    url: 'yourapp://order/12345', // Pass deep-link URL at launch for cold-start deep-link
  });

  // Cold-start deep-link: the app should open directly to the order detail screen
  await waitFor(element(by.id('order-detail-screen-root'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(6000);
  await expect(element(by.id('order-id-label'))).toHaveText('#12345');

  // Verify back-navigation returns to home (deep-link placed at root of stack)
  await element(by.id('back-button')).tap();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen-root'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
});

it('deep-linking to /order/12345 while app is in background resumes to order detail', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen-root'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

  // Send app to background, then trigger the deep link from an external source
  await device.sendToBackground();
  await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 500)); // Allow lifecycle to settle (Gotcha 233)
  await device.openURL({ url: 'yourapp://order/12345' });

  // App should come to foreground and navigate to the order detail screen
  await waitFor(element(by.id('order-detail-screen-root'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(6000);
  await expect(element(by.id('order-id-label'))).toHaveText('#12345');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Passing `url` to `launchApp()` is the cold-start deep-link path — the app receives the URL via `getInitialURL()` in the JS runtime. Calling `device.openURL()` after launch is the foreground/background deep-link path — the app receives the URL via the `Linking` `url` event listener. Both paths must be tested separately because cold-start URL parsing and live-link event handling are different code paths that can fail independently. Ensure the test for the cold-start path calls `launchApp({ newInstance: true })` without the `url` key first, then the next test uses `url` in `launchApp` — never rely on test ordering without a `beforeEach` reset. [official]

---

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 42

### Gotcha 234 — `waitFor(element).toBeVisible()` returns successfully for a `Modal` whose `visible` prop is `false` but whose exit animation has not yet completed, because Detox checks the current opacity/frame rather than the `visible` prop [community]

**Root cause**: React Native's `<Modal>` component uses a native animation to hide itself when `visible` transitions from `true` to `false`. During the exit animation (typically 250–350 ms on iOS), the modal view remains in the native view hierarchy with a declining opacity. Detox's `toBeVisible()` matcher evaluates the element's current alpha and frame at the moment the check fires. If the check fires during the exit animation window, the modal is still partially opaque and Detox correctly reports `toBeVisible()` as true — even though the JS `visible` prop is already `false`. The test proceeds to interact with UI elements behind the modal, which are still intercepted by the modal's touch handler during the animation.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — tapping a button behind the modal immediately after setting visible=false
await element(by.id('close-modal-button')).tap(); // Sets visible=false in state
// Exit animation takes 300ms — toBeVisible() fires at ~50ms into the animation
await expect(element(by.id('modal-container'))).not.toBeVisible();
// This PASSES too early — modal is still animating (opacity ~0.8)
await element(by.id('behind-modal-button')).tap();
// TAP INTERCEPTED by modal touch handler during the 300ms exit animation — test fails

// FIX OPTION 1 — use not.toExist() to wait for full hierarchy removal after animation
await element(by.id('close-modal-button')).tap();
await waitFor(element(by.id('modal-container'))).not.toExist().withTimeout(2000);
// Modal is now fully unmounted — touch events reach the element behind it
await element(by.id('behind-modal-button')).tap();

// FIX OPTION 2 — set animationType="none" in E2E builds to eliminate the animation gap
// <Modal animationType={__E2E__ ? 'none' : 'slide'} ... />

// WHY this matters: Modal exit animations are one of the most common sources of
// "tap intercepted by invisible element" failures in React Native E2E test suites;
// not.toBeVisible() is insufficient — not.toExist() is the correct guard.
```

**WHY this matters:** The `not.toBeVisible()` vs `not.toExist()` distinction is critical for animated dismissal flows. Teams that use `not.toBeVisible()` as their standard modal-close assertion will encounter intermittent touch-interception failures on faster devices and CI runners where the subsequent tap fires during the exit animation window.

---

### Gotcha 235 — `element(by.id('list')).scroll(distance, 'down')` on a `FlatList` with `removeClippedSubviews={true}` causes test elements that were scrolled off-screen to return `not.toExist()` rather than just `not.toBeVisible()`, making `not.toExist()` unsafe as a "scrolled out of view" assertion [community]

**Root cause**: `FlatList` with `removeClippedSubviews={true}` (the default on Android) unmounts native views for list items that scroll beyond the render window. When Detox's `by.id()` matcher searches the view hierarchy for a clipped item, the native view is genuinely absent from the hierarchy — not just invisible, but unmounted. This means `waitFor(element(by.id('list-item-99'))).not.toExist()` may succeed immediately after the list mounts (before item 99 is rendered) and again after item 99 is scrolled far off-screen (after it is clipped). A test that uses `not.toExist()` to confirm a delete operation cannot distinguish "item was deleted" from "item is outside the render window".

```ts
// SYMPTOM — not.toExist() passes for both "deleted" and "scrolled out of render window"
await element(by.id('item-list')).scroll(2000, 'down'); // Scroll item-0 out of window
await expect(element(by.id('list-item-0'))).not.toExist();
// PASSES — but item-0 was NOT deleted; it was just clipped by removeClippedSubviews

// FIX OPTION 1 — scroll back to the top before asserting deletion
await element(by.id('delete-item-0-button')).tap();
await element(by.id('item-list')).scrollTo('top');
// Now assert not.toExist() — item-0 is within the render window but should be gone
await waitFor(element(by.id('list-item-0'))).not.toExist().withTimeout(2000);

// FIX OPTION 2 — assert a count change or an empty-state indicator instead
await element(by.id('delete-item-0-button')).tap();
await waitFor(element(by.id('empty-list-message'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);
// OR assert that item-1 is now the first item (structural change, not existence)
await expect(element(by.id('list-item-1'))).toBeVisible();

// WHY this matters: any test that deletes items from a FlatList and uses not.toExist()
// to confirm the deletion can produce false positives if the list is long enough that
// the deleted item was scrolled out of the render window before the assertion fires.
```

**WHY this matters:** `removeClippedSubviews` is enabled by default on Android and is frequently enabled on iOS for performance in long lists. The failure is particularly insidious because the test passes even when the delete operation failed — the assertion is vacuously true due to the clipped view.

---

### Gotcha 236 — `element.tap()` on a `TouchableOpacity` nested inside a `react-native-swipeable` row fires the swipe gesture instead of the tap when the swipeable row is partially open [community]

**Root cause**: `react-native-swipeable` (and `react-native-gesture-handler`'s `Swipeable`) wraps the row content in a `PanGestureHandler` that captures horizontal touch events. When the swipeable row is in a partially-open state (e.g., swiped 30 px to reveal the delete button), the `PanGestureHandler` is still active and captures horizontal touch movement from `element.tap()`. Detox's `tap()` implementation on iOS delivers the touch via `UIApplication.sendEvent()` as a `touchesBegan/Moved/Ended` sequence. The small positional jitter in the `touchesMoved` event (a few pixels) is interpreted by the `PanGestureHandler` as a swipe continuation rather than a tap-and-release, causing the row to continue opening instead of tapping the element.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — tapping inside a partially-open Swipeable row continues the swipe instead of tapping
await element(by.id('swipeable-row-0')).swipe('left', 'slow', 0.3); // Partially open
// Row is now 30% open — action buttons are partially visible
await element(by.id('row-0-edit-button')).tap();
// TAP FIRES THE SWIPE HANDLER — row opens further instead of navigating to edit screen

// FIX OPTION 1 — swipe to fully open first, then tap the action button
await element(by.id('swipeable-row-0')).swipe('left', 'fast', 0.8); // Fully open
await waitFor(element(by.id('row-0-edit-button'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(1000);
await element(by.id('row-0-edit-button')).tap();

// FIX OPTION 2 — close the row first, then use a long-press to open the context menu
await element(by.id('swipeable-row-0')).swipe('right', 'fast', 0.8); // Close
await element(by.id('swipeable-row-0')).longPress(800); // Context menu
await waitFor(element(by.id('context-menu-edit-option'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(1000);
await element(by.id('context-menu-edit-option')).tap();

// WHY this matters: Swipeable rows are a common UI pattern for list item actions;
// tests that use partial swipe + tap will fail inconsistently across platforms
// because the PanGestureHandler jitter threshold differs between iOS and Android.
```

**WHY this matters:** The failure is non-deterministic because the `PanGestureHandler` jitter threshold is different between iOS Simulator and Android Emulator — tests may pass consistently on one platform and fail on the other. Always fully open or close a swipeable row before tapping elements within it.

---

### Gotcha 237 — `device.reloadReactNative()` does not reset in-memory async storage populated by `@react-native-async-storage/async-storage` because the storage is persisted to the device filesystem, leading to cross-test state leakage when `beforeEach` uses `reloadReactNative()` instead of `launchApp({ delete: true })` [community]

**Root cause**: `device.reloadReactNative()` restarts the JavaScript runtime and re-renders the root component, but it does not clear the native storage layer. `@react-native-async-storage/async-storage` stores key-value pairs in the app's `Documents` directory (iOS) or `SharedPreferences` / SQLite (Android). After `reloadReactNative()`, the storage is intact and the app loads its persisted state (auth tokens, user preferences, cached API responses). Tests that rely on `reloadReactNative()` for reset isolation will encounter data from previous test runs, causing "already logged in" states, stale feature-flag overrides, or cached network responses that should not exist in a fresh session.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — reloadReactNative() does not clear AsyncStorage; stale auth token persists
beforeEach(async () => {
  await device.reloadReactNative(); // Restarts JS — but AsyncStorage persists
});

it('login screen is shown for a new user', async () => {
  await waitFor(element(by.id('login-screen-root'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
  // FAILS — auth token from a previous test is still in AsyncStorage; app navigates to home
});

// FIX OPTION 1 — call launchApp({ delete: true }) instead of reloadReactNative()
beforeEach(async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true, delete: true }); // Clears app sandbox
});

// FIX OPTION 2 — call AsyncStorage.clear() via a test helper before each test
// Requires a test-only route in the app that clears storage on command:
beforeEach(async () => {
  await device.reloadReactNative();
  // Tap a hidden dev-only "clear storage" button exposed in E2E builds
  try {
    await element(by.id('e2e-clear-storage-trigger')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('e2e-storage-cleared-confirm'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);
  } catch { /* button may not be available on release builds */ }
});

// WHY this matters: reloadReactNative() is commonly used as a fast alternative to
// launchApp({ delete: true }) because it takes ~1s vs ~5s; the performance advantage
// is real, but the lack of AsyncStorage isolation causes cross-test state leakage that
// produces false positives in auth and onboarding tests.
```

**WHY this matters:** `reloadReactNative()` feels like a "reset" operation because it restarts the JS bundle, but it is explicitly documented as a JS-runtime-only restart. Any storage, keychain, or native module state that was set in a previous test persists across `reloadReactNative()` calls. Teams that discover this behavior typically retrofit `launchApp({ delete: true })` in `beforeEach` and accept the 4–5x slower per-test setup time.

---

### Gotcha 238 — `element(by.text('Submit')).tap()` matches multiple elements when more than one visible view has the text "Submit" (e.g., a form button and a dialog confirmation button), causing Detox to throw `AmbiguousError` on Android but silently tapping the first match on iOS [community]

**Root cause**: Detox's `by.text()` matcher performs a full-tree search and returns all elements whose accessibility label or display text matches the string. On Android with Espresso, if multiple matching elements are visible, Detox throws an `AmbiguousError` ("Matches more than one view"). On iOS with EarlGrey, the behavior differs: `by.text()` returns the first match in view hierarchy traversal order, silently tapping it without error. This platform divergence means that a test that accidentally matches two "Submit" elements will fail loudly on Android (with a clear error) but pass silently on iOS by tapping the wrong element (e.g., the dialog confirm button instead of the form submit button).

```ts
// SYMPTOM — two visible elements with text 'Submit': form button + dialog confirm
await element(by.id('form-panel')).tap(); // Focuses a field, opens a confirmation dialog
// Now both the form Submit button AND the dialog's Submit button are visible
await element(by.text('Submit')).tap();
// Android: throws AmbiguousError — "matches more than one view"
// iOS: silently taps the first 'Submit' in the hierarchy (may be the dialog, not the form)

// FIX OPTION 1 — always use testID for interactive elements
await element(by.id('form-submit-button')).tap(); // Unambiguous

// FIX OPTION 2 — narrow by.text() with by.id() of the containing parent
await element(by.id('form-panel')).element(by.text('Submit')).tap();
// Scoped search: only looks for 'Submit' within the form-panel subtree

// FIX OPTION 3 — use by.text() with by.not() to exclude the dialog
await element(by.text('Submit').and(by.not(by.id('dialog-confirm-button')))).tap();

// WHY this matters: by.text() without a testID is extremely common in test suites
// that were written before testID discipline was enforced; the iOS/Android ambiguity
// divergence means these tests produce platform-specific failures that are hard to
// trace back to the ambiguous selector.
```

**WHY this matters:** The iOS/Android divergence makes `by.text()` ambiguity failures appear as platform-specific bugs — Android fails loudly while iOS "works" but may be exercising the wrong code path. Any test suite that relies on `by.text()` for interactive elements should be audited with `by.text()` across concurrent-visible-element scenarios.

## Updated Anti-Patterns Checklist (Cycle 42 additions)

| Anti-Pattern | Fix |
|---|---|
| Using `element.tap()` without `tapAtPoint()` on cards with overlapping absolute-positioned child buttons — center tap lands on the overlay button instead of the card | Derive the correct sub-region offset from `element.getAttributes().frame` and use `tapAtPoint({ x, y })` to target the correct zone (Pattern 275) |
| Using `by.text('Submit')` as a selector when multiple visible elements share the text "Submit" — Android throws `AmbiguousError`, iOS silently taps the wrong element | Always use `testID` for interactive elements; narrow `by.text()` with a parent scope `element(by.id('panel')).element(by.text('Submit'))` when `testID` is unavailable (Gotcha 238) |
| Calling `device.resetContentAndSettings()` in `beforeEach` — takes 15–30 s per test, making the suite 5–10x slower without isolation benefit over `launchApp({ delete: true })` | Reserve `resetContentAndSettings()` for `globalSetup` (once per CI job) and use `launchApp({ delete: true })` for per-test app sandbox isolation (Pattern 277) |
| Using `not.toBeVisible()` after modal dismissal and immediately tapping elements previously behind the modal — tap intercepted during exit animation | Use `waitFor().not.toExist()` to wait for full hierarchy unmount before tapping covered elements; or set `animationType='none'` in E2E builds (Gotcha 234) |
| Using `device.reloadReactNative()` as a `beforeEach` isolation mechanism for tests that require a clean AsyncStorage state — storage persists across JS restarts | Use `launchApp({ delete: true })` for full isolation, or expose a test-only `AsyncStorage.clear()` trigger in E2E builds (Gotcha 237) |
| Calling `element.longPress()` with the default 800 ms duration on RNGH `LongPressGesture` components with a custom `minDuration` > 800 ms — gesture does not trigger | Pass `element.longPress(minDuration + 100)` explicitly; check the component's `LongPressGesture({ minDuration })` value before writing the test (Pattern 283) |
| Asserting `not.toExist()` on a `FlatList` item as a delete confirmation when the list is long enough for `removeClippedSubviews` to have unmounted the item's view | Scroll to the item's position first (or to the top) before asserting `not.toExist()`; alternatively assert a structural change (count, empty-state indicator) (Gotcha 235) |
| Using `element.longPress()` with a fixed `500 ms` duration across platforms — Android effective threshold is approximately 600 ms due to touch classifier debounce, causing intermittent failures | Use platform-guarded constants: `600 ms` for iOS, `800 ms` for Android, via `device.getPlatform()` (Pattern 255) |
