## Cycle 44 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 305 — `element.scroll(pixels, direction, startPositionX, startPositionY)` with explicit start-position offsets for scrolling inside nested `ScrollView` components where the default touch origin lands outside the scrollable area [official]

When a `ScrollView` is nested inside another scrollable container (e.g., a `TabView` page that itself has a vertical scroll), Detox's default `scroll()` touch origin of `(0.5, 0.5)` (normalized center of the element's frame) may land on a non-scrollable decorator — a sticky header, a floating action button, or a tab bar — rather than on the scroll track itself. Providing explicit `startPositionX` and `startPositionY` values between 0.1 and 0.9 lets you aim the scroll gesture at a region you know is scroll-track territory. The values are normalized against the element's own frame, not the screen. Always pair this with `waitFor(targetElement).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000)` after the scroll to confirm the target was actually brought into view before asserting on its content.

```ts
// Pattern 305 — nested ScrollView scroll with explicit start position
it('scrolls a nested ScrollView avoiding the sticky header', async () => {
  // The sticky header occupies the top 15% of the outer scroll view's frame
  // Default startPositionY=0.5 lands on it; we aim at 0.65 (below the header)
  await element(by.id('product-detail-scroll')).scroll(
    400,     // pixels to scroll
    'down',
    0.5,     // startPositionX — horizontal center
    0.65,    // startPositionY — below the sticky header overlay
  );

  // Wait for the target section to be visible before asserting on content
  await waitFor(element(by.id('reviews-section-header')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(5000);

  await expect(element(by.id('reviews-section-header'))).toHaveText('Customer Reviews');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Hard-coded normalized offsets are fragile — if the sticky header height changes, the offset needs to be updated. Prefer deriving the offset from the element's `getAttributes().frame` when the header size is variable; fall back to a fixed constant only when the layout is locked by design. [official]

---

### Pattern 306 — `by.label(accessibilityLabel)` matcher combined with `by.type('RCTTextInput')` for locating unlabeled `TextInput` fields in third-party components that do not forward `testID` props [community]

Some third-party form SDKs (credit-card inputs, OTP fields, search-bar libraries) render `TextInput` elements without forwarding the `testID` prop from their public API, making `by.id()` unusable. The `by.label()` matcher targets the element's `accessibilityLabel` attribute, which many libraries do set. When even `accessibilityLabel` is absent, combining `by.type('RCTTextInput')` with `withAncestor(by.id('credit-card-form'))` narrows to the specific input within a known container. Always test in `accessibilityInspector` (iOS) or `uiautomatorviewer` (Android) first to confirm which attribute is available. The `by.type()` class name differs between platforms: `RCTTextInput` on iOS, `android.widget.EditText` on Android.

```ts
// Pattern 306 — fallback matchers for third-party TextInput without testID
it('fills in the credit card number using accessibilityLabel fallback', async () => {
  // Preferred: library sets accessibilityLabel even when testID is blocked
  const cardInput = element(by.label('Card Number').withAncestor(by.id('payment-form')));
  await cardInput.tap();
  await cardInput.typeText('4111111111111111');

  // Fallback: by.type() scoped to a known container when label is also absent
  const expiryInput = element(
    by.type('RCTTextInput').withAncestor(by.id('expiry-field-wrapper'))
  );
  await expiryInput.tap();
  await expiryInput.typeText('12/28');

  // Confirm values rendered via sibling label elements
  await expect(element(by.id('card-number-display'))).toHaveText('•••• •••• •••• 1111');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `by.type()` queries are tightly coupled to the internal class name of the native view, which can change between React Native versions without notice. Treat `by.type()` as a last resort and file an issue with the library maintainer requesting `testID` forwarding as a proper fix. [community]

---

### Pattern 307 — `device.shake()` for triggering the React Native developer menu in E2E debug builds to validate in-app developer-menu shortcuts and staging-environment toggles [official]

React Native apps in debug builds respond to a physical device shake by displaying the developer menu. `device.shake()` simulates this event programmatically, allowing E2E tests to verify that developer-menu-triggered behaviours (e.g., toggling a staging flag, forcing a crash reporter boundary, or enabling layout inspection overlays) work correctly without requiring a physical gesture. The call is synchronous in Detox but the menu itself renders asynchronously; always follow `device.shake()` with a `waitFor(element(by.id('dev-menu-overlay'))).toBeVisible()` before interacting with menu items. On iOS Simulator, `device.shake()` sends the `UIApplicationShakeMotionEvent`; on Android Emulator, it triggers the `RNDevMenu` module's `show()` command directly without a physical sensor event.

```ts
// Pattern 307 — device.shake() to open the RN developer menu
it('toggles the staging environment via the dev menu', async () => {
  // Shake to open the developer menu
  await device.shake();

  // Wait for the dev-menu overlay to appear
  await waitFor(element(by.id('dev-menu-overlay')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(3000);

  // Tap the custom staging toggle added by the app
  await element(by.id('dev-menu-staging-toggle')).tap();

  // Dismiss the menu
  await element(by.id('dev-menu-done-button')).tap();

  // Confirm the staging banner is now visible in the app header
  await waitFor(element(by.id('staging-environment-banner')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(2000);

  await expect(element(by.id('staging-environment-banner'))).toHaveText('STAGING');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The developer menu is only available in debug builds. Tests using `device.shake()` must target a debug configuration and will fail against release builds. Gate these tests using a `beforeAll` guard that calls `device.getPlatform()` and checks that the build is a debug variant, or segregate them into a `dev-menu` test suite with a dedicated `release: false` build configuration. [official]

---

### Pattern 308 — `element.adjustSliderToPosition(normalizedPosition)` with a calibration step that reads the initial slider value via `getAttributes()` to compute the correct normalized target position for percentage-based slider assertions [official]

Detox's `adjustSliderToPosition(normalizedPosition)` accepts a value between 0.0 (minimum) and 1.0 (maximum) and moves a `Slider` component to the corresponding position. However, the mapping between normalized position and the rendered slider value is non-linear when the slider uses a custom `step` or a non-zero `minimumValue`. Reading the current `value` via `getAttributes()` before adjusting lets you compute the exact normalized target: `target = (desiredValue - min) / (max - min)`. Always follow the adjustment with a `getAttributes()` re-read and a numeric tolerance assertion (`Math.abs(actual - desired) < step / 2`) to account for snapping behaviour.

```ts
// Pattern 308 — calibrated adjustSliderToPosition for stepped sliders
it('sets the brightness slider to 75%', async () => {
  const sliderEl = element(by.id('brightness-slider'));

  // Read the slider's min/max/step from native attributes
  const attrs = await sliderEl.getAttributes() as Detox.ElementAttributes;
  // React Native Slider exposes value as a string in the accessibility label: "75%"
  // For precise control, rely on configured min=0, max=100, step=5 from app design

  const min = 0, max = 100, desiredValue = 75;
  const normalizedTarget = (desiredValue - min) / (max - min); // 0.75

  await sliderEl.adjustSliderToPosition(normalizedTarget);

  // Re-read and assert within half-step tolerance (±2.5)
  const afterAttrs = await sliderEl.getAttributes() as Detox.ElementAttributes;
  const actualLabel = (afterAttrs as any).label ?? '';   // "75%" on iOS
  const actualValue = parseFloat(actualLabel.replace('%', ''));
  expect(Math.abs(actualValue - desiredValue)).toBeLessThan(2.5);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `adjustSliderToPosition` on Android can drift by one `step` unit due to touch quantization in the emulator. For critical exact-value tests, follow up with a tap on the `+` / `-` nudge buttons exposed via `testID` rather than relying solely on the slider gesture. [official]

---

### Pattern 309 — `waitFor(element).toHaveValue(value).withTimeout()` for asserting that a `TextInput`'s programmatically updated value settles to a computed result after an async validation debounce [official]

When a `TextInput` runs an async debounced validator (e.g., checking username availability or formatting a phone number mask), the displayed value does not immediately match the expected result after `typeText()`. Using `waitFor(element).toHaveValue(expectedValue).withTimeout(4000)` polls the element's `value` attribute on iOS (maps to `UITextField.text`) or the `contentDescription` on Android until it matches or the timeout expires. This is more reliable than inserting a fixed `sleep()` delay or wrapping the assertion in a retry loop. The `toHaveValue()` assertion works on `TextInput`, `Switch`, and `Slider` elements — for `Switch`, the value is `'true'`/`'false'` as strings.

```ts
// Pattern 309 — waitFor.toHaveValue() for async-validated TextInput
it('formats a phone number after debounced masking resolves', async () => {
  const phoneInput = element(by.id('phone-number-input'));
  await phoneInput.tap();

  // Type the raw digits — the mask formatter debounces for 300ms
  await phoneInput.typeText('4155550101');

  // waitFor polls until the masking debounce settles (value = '(415) 555-0101')
  await waitFor(phoneInput)
    .toHaveValue('(415) 555-0101')
    .withTimeout(4000);

  // Now assert on the formatted display label as a secondary confirmation
  await expect(element(by.id('phone-formatted-display'))).toHaveText('(415) 555-0101');

  // Test the Switch using toHaveValue for boolean state
  const smsConsentSwitch = element(by.id('sms-consent-switch'));
  await smsConsentSwitch.tap();
  await waitFor(smsConsentSwitch).toHaveValue('true').withTimeout(1000);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `toHaveValue()` reads from the accessibility value attribute, which on Android requires the component to explicitly set `accessibilityValue`. Third-party masked-input libraries sometimes write the formatted value to `accessibilityLabel` instead of `accessibilityValue`; in those cases fall back to `toHaveLabel()` or use `toHaveText()` on a sibling display element. [official]

---

### Pattern 310 — `device.reverseTcpPort(remotePort)` combined with `fetch()` inside the app to connect E2E tests to a local mock server running on the host machine during Android Emulator test runs [community]

Android Emulator's virtual network interface routes `10.0.2.2` to the host machine, but for deterministic port access in CI (where multiple emulators may run in parallel), `device.reverseTcpPort(port)` creates an `adb reverse` tunnel from a fixed device port to the same host port. This allows the app under test to call `http://localhost:3000/api/mock` and reach the test's local Express/MSW mock server without hardcoding `10.0.2.2`. The reverse must be set up before `device.launchApp()` and torn down in `afterAll` via `device.unreverseTcpPort(port)`. On iOS Simulator, no tunnel is needed — `localhost` in the simulator resolves to the host machine directly.

```ts
// Pattern 310 — adb reverse tunnel for Android Emulator mock server
const MOCK_PORT = 3001;

beforeAll(async () => {
  // Set up the adb reverse tunnel before launching the app
  if (device.getPlatform() === 'android') {
    await device.reverseTcpPort(MOCK_PORT);
  }
  await device.launchApp({
    newInstance: true,
    launchArgs: { mockServerPort: MOCK_PORT },
  });
});

afterAll(async () => {
  if (device.getPlatform() === 'android') {
    await device.unreverseTcpPort(MOCK_PORT);
  }
});

it('loads products from the mock server', async () => {
  await waitFor(element(by.id('product-list-item-0')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(6000);
  await expect(element(by.id('product-list-item-0'))).toHaveText('Mock Product A');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `device.reverseTcpPort()` is Android-only. For cross-platform test suites that share the same mock server setup, wrap the tunnel calls in a `device.getPlatform() === 'android'` guard, and confirm iOS tests use the `localhost` address directly. Do not use `MOCK_PORT` values below 1024 — they require root access on the emulator. [community]

---

### Pattern 311 — `element.multiTap(taps)` for testing double-tap and triple-tap gesture handlers on custom touch components that use `onStartShouldSetResponder` instead of `TouchableOpacity` [official]

React Native's `onStartShouldSetResponder` / `onResponderRelease` gesture handler chain can implement multi-tap interactions (double-tap to like, triple-tap to zoom) without using `TouchableOpacity`. `element.multiTap(taps)` sends `taps` rapid sequential taps at the element center with the native inter-tap interval, correctly triggering the gesture recognizer's tap count check. Using `tap()` inside a loop with `await` delays between iterations introduces inter-tap gaps longer than the gesture recognizer's `maximumDoubleTapInterval` (~250 ms), causing the recognizer to reset the count. Always use `multiTap(2)` for double-tap and `multiTap(3)` for triple-tap instead of sequential `tap()` calls.

```ts
// Pattern 311 — multiTap for gesture-handler-based double-tap interactions
it('double-taps a photo to add it to favourites', async () => {
  const photoCard = element(by.id('photo-card-0'));

  // Confirm the heart icon is not filled before interaction
  await expect(element(by.id('photo-card-0-heart-icon'))).not.toBeVisible();

  // multiTap(2) fires both taps within the gesture recognizer's interval window
  await photoCard.multiTap(2);

  // Wait for the heart animation to settle then assert icon is now visible
  await waitFor(element(by.id('photo-card-0-heart-icon')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(2000);

  // Verify the favourite count incremented
  await expect(element(by.id('photo-card-0-like-count'))).toHaveText('1');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** On Android, `multiTap()` can fail on devices with non-standard gesture recognizer timeout values set via `Settings.System.LONG_PRESS_TIMEOUT`. If double-tap is registered as two separate single-taps, add `"gestureInteractionTimeout": 200` to the device config in `.detoxrc.json` to reduce the emulator's input dispatch latency. [official]

---

### Pattern 312 — `by.id().withDescendant(by.label())` relational matcher for locating a container card by the dynamic text content of a child label element when the card's own `testID` is shared across a list [community]

When a `FlatList` renders many cards that all share the same root `testID` (e.g., `notification-card`), `element(by.id('notification-card'))` returns only the first match. Appending `.withDescendant(by.label('Order Shipped'))` narrows the match to the specific card whose child `Text` element has that `accessibilityLabel`. This is more stable than using index-based matchers like `element(by.id('notification-card')).atIndex(2)` because index positions change when new notifications are inserted at the top of the list. The pattern requires that each card's dynamic content element has an accurate `accessibilityLabel` set — often satisfied automatically by React Native's label inference from `Text` content.

```ts
// Pattern 312 — withDescendant(by.label()) to target a specific list card by content
it('expands the "Order Shipped" notification card', async () => {
  // Scroll until the target card is visible (list may be long)
  await waitFor(
    element(by.id('notification-card').withDescendant(by.label('Order Shipped')))
  )
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(5000)
    .whileElement(by.id('notification-list'))
    .scroll(300, 'down');

  // Tap the specific card
  await element(
    by.id('notification-card').withDescendant(by.label('Order Shipped'))
  ).tap();

  // Assert the expanded detail panel is visible
  await waitFor(element(by.id('notification-detail-panel')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(2000);

  await expect(element(by.id('notification-detail-tracking-number'))).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The `withDescendant(by.label())` chain performs a tree walk on every poll cycle, which is slower than `by.id()` with a unique `testID`. For lists with hundreds of items, prefer adding a unique `testID` suffix (e.g., `notification-card-${item.id}`) to each card as the canonical fix, and reserve `withDescendant` for read-only third-party components where you cannot modify the `testID`. [community]

---

### Pattern 313 — `device.openURL({ url, sourceApp })` for deep-link E2E tests that verify correct navigation to specific in-app screens from a universal link or custom URI scheme [official]

`device.openURL({ url })` triggers the device's URL open handler, routing the URL through the OS to the app under test if it is registered as a handler for the scheme. On iOS this simulates a universal link or custom scheme tap from Safari/Messages; on Android it fires an `Intent.ACTION_VIEW` with the supplied URI. The `sourceApp` parameter (iOS only) sets the `UIApplication.openURL` source bundle ID, allowing tests to verify that scheme-specific permission gates (`openedFrom: 'com.apple.mobilesafari'` checks) are correctly enforced. Always launch the app with `newInstance: false` before calling `openURL` — the app must already be running to receive the link intent.

```ts
// Pattern 313 — deep-link navigation via device.openURL()
describe('deep link routing', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    // Navigate to home screen — app must be running to receive the deep link
    await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen-root'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
  });

  it('navigates to the product detail screen via custom URI scheme', async () => {
    await device.openURL({ url: 'myapp://products/42' });

    // Wait for the router to resolve and render the product detail screen
    await waitFor(element(by.id('product-detail-screen')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(4000);

    await expect(element(by.id('product-title'))).toHaveText('Widget Pro 42');
  });

  it('validates sourceApp gate on iOS (Safari-only universal link)', async () => {
    if (device.getPlatform() !== 'ios') { return; }
    await device.openURL({
      url: 'https://myapp.example.com/products/42',
      sourceApp: 'com.apple.mobilesafari',
    });
    await waitFor(element(by.id('product-detail-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `device.openURL()` on Android fires a system Intent, meaning the OS may display a disambiguation dialog if multiple apps handle the same scheme. In CI, ensure no other apps are installed that claim the same URI scheme. For universal links on Android (App Links), the `assetlinks.json` verification must pass — use a test server with a valid Digital Asset Links file or disable App Link verification in the test build. [official]

---

### Pattern 314 — `device.takeScreenshot(name)` integrated into a custom `expect`-extension wrapper that compares against a stored baseline using pixel-diff tolerance for visual regression tests without a full Storybook snapshot infrastructure [community]

Detox's `device.takeScreenshot(name)` saves a PNG to the artifact directory; combining it with a lightweight pixel-diff comparison (e.g., `pixelmatch`) in a custom Jest matcher creates a self-contained visual regression system without requiring a dedicated screenshot service. The baseline PNG is stored in `e2e/__baselines__/` and committed to git. On the first run without a baseline the test writes the screenshot as the new baseline and passes. On subsequent runs it compares pixel-by-pixel with a configurable `threshold` (0.1 = 10% pixel difference allowed). Mismatches are reported as a diff PNG in the artifact directory.

```ts
// Pattern 314 — visual regression with device.takeScreenshot + pixelmatch
// File: e2e/helpers/expectScreenshotToMatchBaseline.ts
import * as fs from 'fs';
import * as path from 'path';
import { PNG } from 'pngjs';
import pixelmatch from 'pixelmatch';

export async function expectScreenshotToMatchBaseline(
  screenshotName: string,
  threshold = 0.05
): Promise<void> {
  const artifactPath = await device.takeScreenshot(screenshotName);
  const baselinePath = path.join(__dirname, '../__baselines__', `${screenshotName}.png`);

  if (!fs.existsSync(baselinePath)) {
    // First run — write baseline
    fs.copyFileSync(artifactPath, baselinePath);
    return; // Pass on first run
  }

  const img1 = PNG.sync.read(fs.readFileSync(baselinePath));
  const img2 = PNG.sync.read(fs.readFileSync(artifactPath));
  const { width, height } = img1;
  const diff = new PNG({ width, height });

  const numDiffPixels = pixelmatch(img1.data, img2.data, diff.data, width, height, { threshold });
  const diffRatio = numDiffPixels / (width * height);

  if (diffRatio > threshold) {
    const diffPath = artifactPath.replace('.png', '-diff.png');
    fs.writeFileSync(diffPath, PNG.sync.write(diff));
    throw new Error(
      `Visual regression: ${screenshotName} differs by ${(diffRatio * 100).toFixed(1)}% ` +
      `(threshold: ${threshold * 100}%). Diff saved to ${diffPath}`
    );
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Pixel-diff baselines are sensitive to font rendering differences between OS versions and emulator API levels. Re-generate baselines whenever the CI emulator image is updated, and store separate baseline sets per `(platform, OS version)` combination. For production-grade visual testing, prefer a dedicated service (Percy, Applitools) that handles baseline management automatically. [community]

---

### Pattern 315 — `element.swipe('left', 'fast', 0.8, 0.5, 0.5)` with `waitFor().not.toExist()` to assert that a swipe-to-delete gesture fully removes a list item from the data model and the view hierarchy [official]

Swipe-to-delete in React Native is commonly implemented via `react-native-gesture-handler`'s `Swipeable` or the native `UITableView` swipe action on iOS. A single `swipe('left', 'fast')` call opens the delete affordance (red "Delete" button appears); a second swipe or a tap on the revealed button triggers the deletion. The pattern chains the two interactions and asserts using `waitFor(element).not.toExist()` (stricter than `.not.toBeVisible()`) to confirm the item was removed from both the view and the accessibility tree. Using `.not.toBeVisible()` alone can give false positives if the item fades out but remains in the DOM.

```ts
// Pattern 315 — swipe-to-delete with strict not.toExist() assertion
it('swipe-deletes a to-do item and confirms it is removed from the list', async () => {
  const todoItem = element(by.id('todo-item-grocery-shopping'));

  // Confirm item exists before deletion
  await expect(todoItem).toBeVisible();

  // First swipe opens the delete affordance (halfway across)
  await todoItem.swipe('left', 'fast', 0.6, 0.5, 0.5);

  // Wait for the "Delete" button to appear, then tap it
  await waitFor(element(by.id('todo-swipe-delete-button')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(2000);
  await element(by.id('todo-swipe-delete-button')).tap();

  // Wait for the deletion animation to complete and assert strict not.toExist()
  await waitFor(todoItem)
    .not.toExist()
    .withTimeout(3000);

  // Confirm the list count label updated
  await expect(element(by.id('todo-count-label'))).toHaveText('2 tasks');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** On Android, `Swipeable` from `react-native-gesture-handler` opens the action panel on a single swipe past a threshold rather than requiring a second full swipe. The swipe `normalizedOffset` (third parameter) may need to be tuned separately for iOS and Android: iOS typically requires 0.8+ to reveal the delete button; Android may reveal it at 0.5. Use a platform-specific constant for the offset. [official]

---

### Pattern 316 — `device.getPlatform()`-gated `by.type()` queries using platform-specific native class names (`XCUIElementTypeSwitch` on iOS, `android.widget.Switch` on Android) to interact with third-party toggle components that render native views [community]

Some React Native wrappers around native UI components (e.g., settings-screen toggles built with `NativeModules` rather than JS `Switch`) render a pure native `UISwitch` (iOS) or `android.widget.Switch` (Android) that has no React Native `testID` bridge. `by.type('XCUIElementTypeSwitch')` on iOS or `by.type('android.widget.Switch')` on Android matches the native widget directly via the accessibility type. Scope the query with `withAncestor(by.id('notifications-settings-row'))` to avoid matching other unrelated switches on the screen. Combine with `getAttributes()` to read the current `value` before tapping to implement an idempotent toggle helper.

```ts
// Pattern 316 — platform-specific by.type() for native Switch elements
async function tapNativeSwitchIfOff(containerId: string): Promise<void> {
  const platform = device.getPlatform();
  const switchType = platform === 'ios'
    ? 'XCUIElementTypeSwitch'
    : 'android.widget.Switch';

  const switchEl = element(
    by.type(switchType).withAncestor(by.id(containerId))
  );

  // Read current value before tapping — avoid double-toggling
  const attrs = await switchEl.getAttributes() as Detox.ElementAttributes;
  const currentValue = (attrs as any).value ?? (attrs as any).text ?? '';

  // iOS: value '0' = off, '1' = on. Android: value 'false'/'true' or label 'OFF'/'ON'
  const isOff = platform === 'ios'
    ? currentValue === '0'
    : currentValue.toLowerCase() === 'false' || currentValue.toLowerCase() === 'off';

  if (isOff) {
    await switchEl.tap();
    await waitFor(switchEl).toHaveValue(platform === 'ios' ? '1' : 'true').withTimeout(2000);
  }
}

it('enables push notifications via native switch', async () => {
  await tapNativeSwitchIfOff('push-notifications-row');
  await expect(element(by.id('notifications-enabled-badge'))).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Native type class names are tied to specific OS versions. `XCUIElementTypeSwitch` is stable across iOS 13+, but Android class names can vary between OEM ROMs. Always fall back to a `testID`-based approach if the app team can patch the native module, and document `by.type()` usage with a comment explaining why `testID` is unavailable. [community]

---

### Pattern 317 — `waitFor(element).toBeVisible().whileElement(by.id()).scroll()` inside a Jest `retry` wrapper to handle flaky visibility assertions in paginated `FlatList` components where the target item may not be in the initial render window [community]

`FlatList` with `initialNumToRender` set below the total item count will not render off-screen items until the list is scrolled. `waitFor(element).toBeVisible().whileElement(by.id('list')).scroll(200, 'down')` combines polling with incremental scrolling in a single Detox call, but may time out on very long lists. Wrapping the entire `waitFor().whileElement().scroll()` call in a custom `scrollUntilVisible(listId, targetId, maxScrolls)` helper that retries with increasing scroll distances provides a reliable fallback for variable-length server-driven lists. The helper caps at `maxScrolls` iterations and throws a descriptive error on timeout.

```ts
// Pattern 317 — scrollUntilVisible helper for long FlatList pagination
async function scrollUntilVisible(
  listTestId: string,
  targetTestId: string,
  maxScrolls = 10,
  pixelsPerScroll = 300
): Promise<void> {
  for (let i = 0; i < maxScrolls; i++) {
    try {
      await waitFor(element(by.id(targetTestId)))
        .toBeVisible()
        .withTimeout(1500);
      return; // Found it — exit
    } catch {
      // Not yet visible — scroll and retry
      await element(by.id(listTestId)).scroll(pixelsPerScroll, 'down');
    }
  }
  throw new Error(
    `scrollUntilVisible: element "${targetTestId}" not visible after ` +
    `${maxScrolls} scrolls of ${pixelsPerScroll}px each`
  );
}

it('scrolls to and taps the last item in a server-driven product list', async () => {
  await waitFor(element(by.id('product-list'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);

  await scrollUntilVisible('product-list', 'product-item-id-99', 15, 250);

  await element(by.id('product-item-id-99')).tap();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('product-detail-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The manual scroll-and-retry loop is not aware of the list's total item count and will scroll past the end of the list if the target item does not exist, triggering `overscroll` animations that can destabilize subsequent assertions. Always ensure the target item is seeded in the test data before calling `scrollUntilVisible`, and cap `maxScrolls` at a value that cannot exceed the total list height. [community]

---

### Pattern 318 — `element.clearText()` followed by `element.typeText()` in a `beforeEach` hook for resetting shared `TextInput` state between tests when `device.reloadReactNative()` would be too slow for a large form with many fields [official]

Calling `device.reloadReactNative()` between every test in a complex multi-step form suite can add 3-6 seconds of reload time per test. For suites where only the text field contents need to be reset, using `clearText()` + `typeText()` in `beforeEach` to restore each field to its initial state is 10-20x faster. The approach works when: (a) the form component does not have internal `useState` that persists non-text state (like `isSubmitting`), and (b) the test suite uses `beforeEach` to navigate to the form screen. If the form has derived state from the text values, a `reloadReactNative()` is safer — prefer speed only when the form's state model is fully text-driven.

```ts
// Pattern 318 — clearText + typeText in beforeEach for fast form state reset
describe('registration form — field validation', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    await element(by.id('nav-register-button')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('registration-form'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
  });

  beforeEach(async () => {
    // Reset all fields without a full reload (~200ms vs ~4000ms for reloadReactNative)
    for (const fieldId of ['email-input', 'password-input', 'confirm-password-input']) {
      const field = element(by.id(fieldId));
      await field.clearText();
    }
    // Dismiss any open keyboard
    await element(by.id('registration-form')).tap();
  });

  it('shows a validation error for an invalid email format', async () => {
    await element(by.id('email-input')).typeText('not-an-email');
    await element(by.id('register-submit-button')).tap();
    await expect(element(by.id('email-error-message'))).toHaveText('Enter a valid email address');
  });

  it('shows a mismatch error when passwords differ', async () => {
    await element(by.id('email-input')).typeText('user@example.com');
    await element(by.id('password-input')).typeText('SecurePass1!');
    await element(by.id('confirm-password-input')).typeText('DifferentPass1!');
    await element(by.id('register-submit-button')).tap();
    await expect(element(by.id('password-mismatch-error'))).toHaveText('Passwords do not match');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `clearText()` fires a native `select all + delete` action, which triggers `onChangeText` with an empty string intermediate. If the form has a validator that flags empty strings with an error banner, that banner will flash during the `beforeEach` reset and may interfere with the first assertion of the following test if the animation overlaps. Add a short `waitFor(errorBanner).not.toBeVisible()` guard after `clearText()` in forms with aggressive real-time validators. [official]

---

### Pattern 319 — `element.tapAtPoint({ x, y })` with absolute coordinates derived from `getAttributes().frame` for tapping a specific sub-region of a canvas or custom-drawn `View` that does not expose child accessibility nodes [community]

Some React Native components (charting libraries, map overlays, canvas-based drawing views) render via a single native `View` with no child accessibility nodes for individual interactive regions. `element.tapAtPoint({ x, y })` accepts absolute screen coordinates (not normalized) in device-independent pixels, allowing a test to tap an exact pixel position within the component's frame. To make the tap position relative to the component rather than hardcoded screen coordinates, read the element's `frame` via `getAttributes()` and add the desired offset: `{ x: frame.x + frame.width * 0.3, y: frame.y + frame.height * 0.6 }`. This is the only reliable method for testing tap zones in fully custom-drawn views.

```ts
// Pattern 319 — tapAtPoint with frame-relative coordinates for custom canvas views
it('taps the "Q2" bar in a custom bar chart component', async () => {
  const chartEl = element(by.id('revenue-bar-chart'));
  await waitFor(chartEl).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);

  // Read the chart's absolute frame on screen
  const attrs = await chartEl.getAttributes() as Detox.ElementAttributes;
  const frame = (attrs as any).frame as {
    x: number; y: number; width: number; height: number;
  };

  // Q2 bar is at ~37.5% across the chart width, 80% down from the top (bar midpoint)
  const tapX = Math.round(frame.x + frame.width * 0.375);
  const tapY = Math.round(frame.y + frame.height * 0.80);

  await element(by.id('revenue-bar-chart')).tapAtPoint({ x: tapX, y: tapY });

  // Assert the tooltip for Q2 appeared
  await waitFor(element(by.id('chart-tooltip')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(2000);

  await expect(element(by.id('chart-tooltip-label'))).toHaveText('Q2: $1.2M');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Frame-relative `tapAtPoint` coordinates are sensitive to screen resolution and device pixel density. Always compute tap coordinates from `getAttributes().frame` at runtime rather than hard-coding pixel values. The approach breaks if the chart library responds to touch at the JavaScript layer (using `PanResponder`) instead of at the native layer, because Detox's touch injection targets the native view tree. [community]

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 44

### Gotcha 244 — `element.typeText()` on a `TextInput` with `keyboardType='numeric'` silently drops non-numeric characters on Android because the IME strips them before delivering the input event, causing the typed string to differ from the expected value without any error [community]

**Root cause**: Android's numeric IME (`InputType.TYPE_CLASS_NUMBER`) filters input at the `InputConnection` layer before forwarding characters to the React Native `TextInput` onChange handler. When `typeText('abc123')` is called, the IME discards `a`, `b`, and `c` silently; only `123` reaches the text field. On iOS, `keyboardType='numeric'` restricts the on-screen keyboard's displayed keys but does not filter characters at the input event level — `typeText('abc123')` will insert all six characters because Detox bypasses the on-screen keyboard entirely by directly injecting keystrokes. This creates a platform divergence where the same `typeText()` call produces different field values on iOS (`abc123`) and Android (`123`), causing cross-platform assertions like `toHaveValue('abc123')` to fail only on Android.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — typeText with mixed content on numeric keyboardType
await element(by.id('quantity-input')).typeText('abc123');
// iOS result: 'abc123' (Detox bypasses on-screen keyboard filtering)
// Android result: '123'  (IME strips non-numeric characters silently)

// FIX — only type valid characters for the input's keyboardType
await element(by.id('quantity-input')).typeText('123');
// Platform-consistent result: '123' on both iOS and Android

// If you need to verify that the field REJECTS non-numeric input (Android only):
if (device.getPlatform() === 'android') {
  await element(by.id('quantity-input')).typeText('abc');
  await expect(element(by.id('quantity-input'))).toHaveValue('');
}
// iOS: test the input restriction at the unit/component level instead

// WHY: Android's IME filtering is a system-level behaviour outside Detox's control;
// it cannot be disabled per-test and affects any field with a restrictive InputType.
```

**WHY this matters:** Tests that verify form fields with `keyboardType='numeric'` and pass `typeText()` strings with mixed content will produce different field values on each platform, giving false passing results on iOS while the Android test assertion diverges. Always match `typeText()` arguments to the expected valid character set for the field's `keyboardType`.

### Gotcha 245 — `waitFor(element).toBeVisible().whileElement(by.id()).scroll()` stops scrolling and reports `"Element not found"` on iOS when the `FlatList` uses `removeClippedSubviews={true}` because off-screen cells are removed from the accessibility tree entirely, making the target element not found even before Detox can scroll it into view [community]

**Root cause**: React Native's `removeClippedSubviews` prop unmounts native views that are clipped outside the scroll container's bounds — they are removed from both the render tree and the native accessibility tree. When Detox polls the accessibility tree for the target element during a `whileElement().scroll()` cycle, it finds no match and throws `"Element not found"` rather than continuing to scroll. This is distinct from `toBeVisible()` failure (element exists but hidden) — the element is completely absent from the tree. `removeClippedSubviews` is `true` by default on Android and opt-in on iOS, but many performance-tuned apps set it explicitly to `true` on iOS for long lists, triggering this Detox limitation. The fix is to set `removeClippedSubviews={false}` in E2E builds or to use the `scrollUntilVisible` helper from Pattern 317 which catches `not.toExist()` errors and continues scrolling.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — whileElement().scroll() throws "Element not found" on FlatList
//           with removeClippedSubviews={true}
await waitFor(element(by.id('product-item-id-80')))
  .toBeVisible()
  .withTimeout(10000)
  .whileElement(by.id('product-list'))
  .scroll(300, 'down');
// iOS (removeClippedSubviews=true): throws "Element not found" instead of scrolling

// FIX OPTION 1 — disable removeClippedSubviews in E2E builds
// <FlatList removeClippedSubviews={!__E2E__} ... />

// FIX OPTION 2 — use scrollUntilVisible helper (Pattern 317) that handles missing elements
// await scrollUntilVisible('product-list', 'product-item-id-80');

// WHY: removeClippedSubviews is a performance optimization that conflicts with Detox's
// accessibility-tree-based polling; the element must exist in the tree to be found,
// but removeClippedSubviews removes it precisely when it is off-screen and needs to be
// scrolled into view.
```

**WHY this matters:** This gotcha causes a confusing error — `"Element not found"` during a scroll operation implies the element's `testID` is wrong, but the real cause is a performance flag that removes elements from the accessibility tree. Teams that add `removeClippedSubviews` as a performance optimization without updating E2E tests will see apparently unrelated test failures.

---

### Gotcha 246 — `device.launchApp({ url: 'myapp://deep-link' })` and `device.openURL({ url: 'myapp://deep-link' })` behave differently for cold-start deep links: `launchApp({ url })` sends the URL as the initial launch intent before the app's JavaScript bundle has loaded, causing deep-link navigation to fail on apps that route in a `useEffect` on the root navigator component [community]

**Root cause**: `device.launchApp({ url: 'myapp://deep-link' })` delivers the URL via `application:openURL:options:` (iOS) or `Intent.getAction()` (Android) at the earliest point in the app lifecycle, before the React Native bridge has initialised and before any navigation container has mounted. Apps that parse the deep link URL in a `useEffect(() => { /* navigate */ }, [])` on the root `NavigationContainer` will miss the URL because `useEffect` runs after the first render, by which point the OS-level URL delivery has already been consumed and cleared. `device.openURL()` — which requires the app to already be running — delivers the URL via `onURL` callbacks to registered listeners in the running app, hitting the React Navigation `linking.getInitialURL` callback at the correct time. The fix is to handle cold-start URLs via `Linking.getInitialURL()` in app startup code, not via `useEffect`.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — cold-start deep link via launchApp({ url }) does not navigate
await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true, url: 'myapp://products/42' });
await waitFor(element(by.id('product-detail-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
// FAILS: app launches to home screen; deep link URL consumed before JS bridge loaded

// FIX — use openURL() after the app is running for apps with useEffect routing
await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen-root'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
await device.openURL({ url: 'myapp://products/42' });
await waitFor(element(by.id('product-detail-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

// OR fix the app code to use Linking.getInitialURL() for cold-start deep links
// (React Navigation's linking config handles this correctly when configured)

// WHY: launchApp({ url }) and openURL() deliver URLs at different lifecycle points;
// teams that test deep links only via openURL() may ship apps that silently drop
// cold-start universal links from email marketing campaigns or push notifications.
```

**WHY this matters:** Cold-start deep links from push notifications and email links are a common user journey. If the app only handles warm-start deep links, a whole category of real-world user interactions is broken. Always test both cold-start (`launchApp({ url })` + `Linking.getInitialURL()`) and warm-start (`openURL()` + `Linking.addEventListener`) paths separately.

---

### Gotcha 247 — `element.scroll()` on a `KeyboardAwareScrollView` adjusts the scroll offset by the keyboard height after each tap, causing subsequent `scroll()` calls to over-scroll by the keyboard inset and move the target element out of the visible area [community]

**Root cause**: `react-native-keyboard-aware-scroll-view` listens to keyboard show/hide events and adds the keyboard height as a bottom content inset to keep the focused input visible. When Detox taps a `TextInput` inside the scroll view (to type text), the keyboard appears and the library adds a `contentInset.bottom` equal to the keyboard height (~300-350 dp). A subsequent `scroll(300, 'down')` call scrolls an additional 300 dp past the already-keyboard-adjusted position, often pushing the next `TextInput` above the keyboard inset into a region that is still technically within the scroll content but not visible due to the keyboard covering the bottom of the scroll view. The net effect is that the targeted input is scrolled out of view in the opposite direction from what was intended. The fix is to dismiss the keyboard before calling `scroll()`, resetting the `contentInset.bottom` to zero.

```ts
// SYMPTOM — scroll over-shoots due to keyboard inset adjustment
await element(by.id('email-input')).tap();
await element(by.id('email-input')).typeText('user@example.com');
// Keyboard is now open; scroll view has contentInset.bottom = ~330dp
await element(by.id('form-scroll-view')).scroll(300, 'down');
// Target input is now above the visible area — keyboard + scroll over-corrected

// FIX — dismiss keyboard before scrolling to reset the contentInset.bottom
await element(by.id('email-input')).typeText('user@example.com');
// Tap a non-input area of the scroll view to dismiss the keyboard
await element(by.id('form-scroll-view')).tapAtPoint({ x: 20, y: 20 });
// Wait for keyboard to fully close
await waitFor(element(by.id('keyboard-dismiss-indicator')))
  .not.toBeVisible()
  .withTimeout(2000);
// Now scroll without keyboard inset interference
await element(by.id('form-scroll-view')).scroll(300, 'down');

// WHY: KeyboardAwareScrollView dynamically adjusts scroll offsets in response to
// keyboard events; Detox's scroll() call does not know about this inset and applies
// the full scroll distance on top of the library's own adjustment.
```

**WHY this matters:** This is one of the most common causes of flaky E2E tests in apps with long registration or checkout forms. The failure mode is non-deterministic because the keyboard appearance animation timing varies; tests that pass locally on a fast simulator may fail in CI on a slower emulator where the keyboard inset is applied at a different point in the scroll sequence.

---

### Gotcha 248 — `expect(element(by.id('loading-spinner'))).not.toBeVisible()` returns immediately as `true` when the spinner is inside a `Modal` that has already been closed, because the `Modal`'s native container view is removed from the accessibility tree on close and Detox treats absent elements as "not visible" rather than throwing `"Element not found"` [community]

**Root cause**: Detox's `.not.toBeVisible()` assertion returns `true` for two distinct states: (1) the element exists in the tree but is visually hidden, and (2) the element does not exist in the tree at all. When a `Modal` closes, React Native unmounts its entire subtree including all children — the `loading-spinner` element ceases to exist. A `.not.toBeVisible()` assertion on it passes immediately, giving the false impression that the loading state resolved correctly. In reality, the Modal may have closed due to an error dismissal rather than a successful load completion. Using `.not.toExist()` would catch the absence for a different reason, but the root problem is that `.not.toBeVisible()` cannot distinguish between "successfully completed loading" and "modal closed prematurely due to an error". The correct assertion strategy is to wait for the success-state element instead of waiting for the spinner to disappear.

```ts
// ANTI-PATTERN — not.toBeVisible() on a spinner inside a Modal
await expect(element(by.id('modal-loading-spinner'))).not.toBeVisible();
// PASSES immediately if the Modal closed for ANY reason (success OR error dismissal)
// Cannot distinguish between successful completion and error-induced Modal close

// CORRECT PATTERN — assert on the positive success state instead
await waitFor(element(by.id('dashboard-welcome-message')))
  .toBeVisible()
  .withTimeout(10000);
await expect(element(by.id('dashboard-welcome-message'))).toHaveText('Welcome, Test User');

// If you MUST verify the Modal is fully gone, use not.toExist() on the modal root
await waitFor(element(by.id('login-modal-root')))
  .not.toExist()
  .withTimeout(10000);
// Only passes when the entire Modal is unmounted — more precise than spinner visibility

// WHY: asserting on the disappearance of a negative state (spinner gone) is inherently
// ambiguous; the element could be absent for multiple reasons (success, error, crash).
// Always assert on the presence of the intended positive successor state.
```

**WHY this matters:** This pattern creates tests that pass on error paths as well as success paths, giving false confidence in the E2E suite. A test that passes when the server returns a 500 error (causing the Modal to close with an error toast) and also passes on success is not testing anything meaningful. Always anchor assertions to positive success states.

## Updated Anti-Patterns Checklist (Cycle 44 additions)

| Anti-Pattern | Fix |
|---|---|
| Using `waitFor(element).not.toBeVisible()` as the sole assertion that a loading operation succeeded when the spinner lives inside a `Modal` — passes on both success and error-induced Modal close | Assert on the positive success-state element instead (e.g., `waitFor(dashboard).toBeVisible()`) to distinguish success from error paths (Gotcha 248) |
| Calling `element.scroll()` on a `KeyboardAwareScrollView` while the keyboard is open — library adds keyboard height as `contentInset.bottom`, causing `scroll()` to over-shoot by the keyboard inset | Dismiss the keyboard by tapping a non-input area of the scroll view before calling `scroll()`, then re-focus the next field (Gotcha 247) |
| Using `device.launchApp({ url: 'myapp://deep-link' })` to test cold-start deep links in apps that route via a `useEffect` on the root navigator — URL is delivered before the JS bridge initialises | Fix app code to read cold-start URLs via `Linking.getInitialURL()`, or use `launchApp()` + `waitFor(home)` + `openURL()` for the warm-start path (Gotcha 246) |
| Enabling `removeClippedSubviews={true}` on a `FlatList` in E2E builds when tests use `waitFor().whileElement().scroll()` to find off-screen items — removes cells from accessibility tree causing `"Element not found"` during scroll | Set `removeClippedSubviews={false}` in E2E builds, or use the `scrollUntilVisible` helper (Pattern 317) that handles missing elements (Gotcha 245) |
| Calling `element.typeText('abc123')` on a `TextInput` with `keyboardType='numeric'` and asserting on the full typed string — Android IME silently drops non-numeric characters | Only pass valid characters for the `keyboardType` in `typeText()` arguments; test rejection of invalid input via a platform-guarded check (Gotcha 244) |
| Hard-coding absolute `tapAtPoint({ x, y })` pixel values without reading the element's `getAttributes().frame` — breaks across device sizes and resolutions | Always derive `tapAtPoint` coordinates from `frame.x + frame.width * normalizedX` computed at runtime (Pattern 319) |
| Using `by.text()` inside a `FlatList` without `withAncestor()` scope when multiple visible items share the same text — `AmbiguousError` on Android; silent wrong-item tap on iOS | Scope the matcher: `by.text('label').withAncestor(by.id('card-N'))`, or use index-suffixed `testID` values for list items (Pattern 302) |
