## Cycle 45 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 320 — `device.appLaunchArgs.reset()` between `describe` blocks to prevent launch-arg contamination across test suites that modify feature flags [official]

`device.appLaunchArgs.modify()` accumulates changes across the process lifetime; a `describe` block that enables a feature flag with `modify({ featureFlag: '1' })` will contaminate all subsequently launched app instances in the same Jest worker unless the args are explicitly reset. Call `device.appLaunchArgs.reset()` in `afterAll` to restore the baseline arg set. This is distinct from `device.appLaunchArgs.modify({})` which merges an empty object (no-op) rather than clearing existing keys. When testing multiple feature-flag combinations in a single file, the safest pattern is to call `reset()` then `modify()` in each `beforeAll` so each suite starts from a known zero state.

```typescript
import { device, by, element, waitFor } from 'detox';

describe('Feature: experimental checkout flow (flag ON)', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    device.appLaunchArgs.reset();
    device.appLaunchArgs.modify({ enableExperimentalCheckout: '1' });
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  });

  afterAll(async () => {
    // Clear the flag so subsequent describe blocks start clean
    device.appLaunchArgs.reset();
  });

  it('shows the new checkout button', async () => {
    await waitFor(element(by.id('checkout-btn-new')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(5000);
  });
});

describe('Feature: experimental checkout flow (flag OFF)', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    // reset() ensures no residual keys from the previous describe
    device.appLaunchArgs.reset();
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  });

  it('shows the legacy checkout button', async () => {
    await waitFor(element(by.id('checkout-btn-legacy')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(5000);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `reset()` followed by `launchApp({ newInstance: true })` adds ~3–6 seconds of cold-start overhead per `describe`; if the feature flag is only read at runtime (not at startup), prefer calling `modify()` / `reset()` mid-test with `device.reloadReactNative()` to avoid the full cold-start penalty.

---

### Pattern 321 — `element(by.id('x')).scroll(100000, 'up', 0.5, 0.5)` as a scroll-to-top idiom when `element.scrollTo('top')` produces an `"Action not supported"` error on Android `NestedScrollView` components [community]

`element.scrollTo('top')` dispatches a native "scroll to edge" action that is supported on `ScrollView` and `FlatList` but not on all `NestedScrollView` or `RecyclerView` implementations on Android. A zero-pixel scroll in the 'up' direction (`scroll(0, 'up')`) is a no-op. The reliable idiom is to use `scrollTo('top')` on iOS and fall back to a large negative-pixel scroll on Android: `scroll(100000, 'up')`. Wrapping this in a `getPlatform()` guard makes the intent explicit and avoids silent failures when the app migrates between scroll implementations.

```typescript
import { device, element, by, waitFor } from 'detox';

async function scrollToTop(listTestId: string): Promise<void> {
  const list = element(by.id(listTestId));
  if (device.getPlatform() === 'ios') {
    // scrollTo('top') is reliable on iOS ScrollView and FlatList
    await list.scrollTo('top');
  } else {
    // Android NestedScrollView may reject scrollTo('top') with "Action not supported"
    // A large upward scroll distance acts as a reliable scroll-to-top substitute
    await list.scroll(100000, 'up', 0.5, 0.5);
  }
}

describe('Transaction history list', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.reloadReactNative();
    // Navigate to the screen under test
    await element(by.id('nav-history')).tap();
  });

  it('loads the oldest item after scrolling back to top', async () => {
    const list = element(by.id('history-list'));
    // Scroll to the bottom first to simulate a user who has paginated
    await list.scrollTo('bottom');
    await waitFor(element(by.id('load-more-spinner'))).not.toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
    // Now scroll back to the top using the platform-safe helper
    await scrollToTop('history-list');
    await expect(element(by.id('transaction-item-0'))).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The `scroll(100000, 'up')` idiom works but is visually noisy in recorded test videos because Detox animates the scroll in increments. Use `device.disableSynchronization()` around the scroll call if animation noise in artifacts is a concern, and re-enable it immediately after.

---

### Pattern 322 — `element.typeText()` with `\n` (newline character) to submit a `TextInput` via the keyboard's Return/Done action instead of tapping a separate submit button [official]

Many single-line `TextInput` components respond to the keyboard's Return key by submitting a form or triggering a search, but there is no dedicated Detox API to press the Return key in a single call. Appending `'\n'` to the `typeText()` argument dispatches a newline character that the RN `TextInput` translates to an `onSubmitEditing` event on both iOS and Android. This is semantically equivalent to what a real user does when pressing Return, and is more robust than `tapKey('Return')` which requires the software keyboard to be fully visible. Reserve `tapKey('Return')` for cases where the `returnKeyType` prop does something other than submit (e.g., `'next'` to advance to the next field).

```typescript
import { element, by, waitFor } from 'detox';

describe('Product search', () => {
  it('submits a search query via the Return key', async () => {
    // Tap the search bar to focus it
    await element(by.id('search-input')).tap();

    // Append '\n' to simulate pressing the keyboard Return/Search button
    // This triggers onSubmitEditing on both iOS and Android
    await element(by.id('search-input')).typeText('running shoes\n');

    // The search results list should appear without needing to tap a button
    await waitFor(element(by.id('search-results-list')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(8000);

    // Verify at least the first result card is visible
    await expect(element(by.id('search-result-0'))).toBeVisible();
  });

  it('advances focus to the next field with returnKeyType="next" using tapKey', async () => {
    await element(by.id('first-name-input')).tap();
    await element(by.id('first-name-input')).typeText('Alice');
    // returnKeyType="next" moves focus — use tapKey so we don't type a literal newline
    await element(by.id('first-name-input')).tapKey('Return');
    // Focus should now be on the last-name field
    await expect(element(by.id('last-name-input'))).toBeFocused();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Appending `'\n'` works reliably when `blurOnSubmit` is `false` (default for multi-line inputs). For `multiline={true}` inputs, `'\n'` inserts an actual newline character instead of submitting — use `tapKey('Return')` or tap the submit button explicitly for multiline fields.

---

### Pattern 323 — `waitFor(element(by.id('x'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(n)` chained with `element(by.id('x')).getAttributes()` to read a dynamically-computed label value after async resolution [official]

When an element's text content is computed asynchronously (e.g., a running total updated after an API call), `getAttributes()` called before the element is visible may return stale data or fail with `"Element not found"`. The safe idiom is to first `waitFor` the element to be visible, which ensures Detox's synchronization mechanism has settled the async update, and then read `getAttributes().text` for further assertion logic. This two-step pattern is required when the assertion logic needs the raw string value for a regex match, numeric parse, or comparison that exceeds what `toHaveText()` can express directly.

```typescript
import { element, by, waitFor, jestExpect } from 'detox';

describe('Order confirmation', () => {
  it('displays a correctly formatted order total after checkout', async () => {
    // Tap place order — the total is computed server-side and returned async
    await element(by.id('place-order-btn')).tap();

    // Step 1: wait for the total label to appear (Detox synchronization settles)
    await waitFor(element(by.id('order-total-label')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(12000);

    // Step 2: read the settled value for custom assertion logic
    const attrs = await element(by.id('order-total-label')).getAttributes();
    const totalText = (attrs as { text: string }).text;

    // Verify currency formatting: must start with "$" and have 2 decimal places
    jestExpect(totalText).toMatch(/^\$\d+\.\d{2}$/);

    // Verify the total is within a plausible range for the test fixture
    const numericTotal = parseFloat(totalText.replace('$', ''));
    jestExpect(numericTotal).toBeGreaterThan(0);
    jestExpect(numericTotal).toBeLessThan(10000);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `getAttributes()` issues a synchronous read of the element's current native state — it does not poll. If the element's text continues to update after becoming visible (e.g., a live counter), add a secondary `waitFor(element).toHaveText(expectedFinalValue)` after `toBeVisible()` before calling `getAttributes()`, so the read captures the final settled value rather than an intermediate one.

---

### Pattern 324 — `by.id('x').atIndex(n)` for selecting the nth element when multiple siblings share the same `testID` and restructuring the component tree to add unique IDs is not immediately feasible [official]

Detox's `atIndex(n)` selector resolves ambiguity when the same `testID` appears multiple times in the view hierarchy, returning the nth match in document order (zero-indexed). This is a pragmatic escape hatch for legacy components or third-party libraries that reuse `testID` internally. The correct long-term fix is always to add unique, index-suffixed `testID` values to list items; `atIndex` is an interim tool. On Android, "document order" follows the view traversal order of the accessibility tree, which may differ from visual top-to-bottom order when the component uses absolute positioning or `z-index` layering.

```typescript
import { element, by, expect as detoxExpect, waitFor } from 'detox';

describe('Notification tray', () => {
  it('marks the second notification as read', async () => {
    await waitFor(element(by.id('notification-item')).atIndex(0))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(5000);

    // atIndex(1) selects the second notification (zero-indexed)
    const secondNotification = element(by.id('notification-item')).atIndex(1);

    // Verify it is currently unread
    await detoxExpect(secondNotification).toHaveText(expect.stringContaining('Unread'));

    // Tap to mark as read
    await secondNotification.tap();

    // Verify the "Unread" indicator is gone from the second item
    await waitFor(element(by.id('notification-unread-badge')).atIndex(1))
      .not.toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(3000);
  });

  it('dismisses the first item via swipe', async () => {
    const firstItem = element(by.id('notification-item')).atIndex(0);
    await firstItem.swipe('left', 'fast', 0.75);
    // After dismissal the original index 0 is occupied by the former index 1
    await waitFor(element(by.id('notification-item')).atIndex(0))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(3000);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Index-based selection is order-sensitive: inserting a new item above the target shifts all subsequent indices, silently breaking tests. Introduce index-suffixed `testID` values (e.g., `notification-item-0`, `notification-item-1`) as soon as the component can be modified, and migrate tests away from `atIndex` as part of the same commit.

---

### Pattern 325 — `device.launchApp({ permissions: { notifications: 'YES' } })` combined with `device.sendUserNotification(payload)` for testing the foreground notification banner and its tap-to-navigate behavior [official]

Testing in-app notification handling requires two setup steps: granting the `notifications` permission via `launchApp` so the OS delivers banners, and then using `device.sendUserNotification(payload)` to inject a simulated push notification while the app is in the foreground. The payload shape mirrors Apple's `UILocalNotification` dictionary for iOS; on Android, pass an `intent` bundle to `device.sendUserNotification()`. The foreground banner appears only if the app's `UNUserNotificationCenter` delegate implements `willPresent` and returns `.banner`; tests that expect the banner but see nothing should first verify the delegate implementation rather than the Detox call.

```typescript
import { device, element, by, waitFor } from 'detox';

describe('Foreground push notification', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({
      newInstance: true,
      permissions: { notifications: 'YES' },
    });
  });

  it('shows a banner and navigates to the correct screen on tap', async () => {
    // Ensure we start from the home screen
    await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);

    // Inject a simulated foreground push notification
    await device.sendUserNotification({
      trigger: { type: 'push' },
      title: 'New message',
      body: 'Alice sent you a message',
      payload: {
        screen: 'ChatScreen',
        conversationId: 'conv-abc-123',
      },
    });

    // The app's UNUserNotificationCenter willPresent delegate must return .banner
    // for the banner to appear — verify the banner element is visible
    await waitFor(element(by.id('notification-banner')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(4000);

    // Tap the banner to trigger navigation
    await element(by.id('notification-banner')).tap();

    // Verify the app navigated to the correct chat conversation
    await waitFor(element(by.id('chat-screen-conv-abc-123')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(5000);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `device.sendUserNotification()` is iOS-only in the current Detox API; Android background/foreground push testing requires either a real Firebase test-message endpoint or a custom native module that calls `NotificationManagerCompat.notify()` from within the app's test helper code. Wrap the entire test in `if (device.getPlatform() === 'ios')` until Android parity is implemented.

---

### Pattern 326 — `jestExpect.extend()` with a `toBeAccessible()` custom matcher that reads `getAttributes().accessibilityLabel`, `.accessibilityRole`, and `.accessibilityState` in a single assertion for auditing screen-reader correctness [community]

Auditing accessibility in Detox tests typically requires three separate `expect()` calls: one for the label, one for the role, and one for the state. A custom `toBeAccessible(spec)` matcher consolidates these into a single, self-documenting assertion that reads all three attributes in one `getAttributes()` call, reducing test verbosity and making accessibility regressions immediately visible in diff output. The matcher returns a structured failure message that names exactly which attribute violated the spec.

```typescript
import { jestExpect, element, by, waitFor } from 'detox';

// In e2e/helpers/accessibility-matcher.ts
jestExpect.extend({
  async toBeAccessible(
    received: Detox.IndexableNativeElement,
    spec: { label?: string; role?: string; disabled?: boolean }
  ) {
    const attrs = await received.getAttributes() as {
      accessibilityLabel?: string;
      accessibilityRole?: string;
      accessibilityState?: { disabled?: boolean };
    };

    const failures: string[] = [];

    if (spec.label !== undefined && attrs.accessibilityLabel !== spec.label) {
      failures.push(
        `accessibilityLabel: expected "${spec.label}", got "${attrs.accessibilityLabel}"`
      );
    }
    if (spec.role !== undefined && attrs.accessibilityRole !== spec.role) {
      failures.push(
        `accessibilityRole: expected "${spec.role}", got "${attrs.accessibilityRole}"`
      );
    }
    if (spec.disabled !== undefined) {
      const isDisabled = attrs.accessibilityState?.disabled ?? false;
      if (isDisabled !== spec.disabled) {
        failures.push(
          `accessibilityState.disabled: expected ${spec.disabled}, got ${isDisabled}`
        );
      }
    }

    return failures.length === 0
      ? { pass: true, message: () => 'Element meets accessibility spec' }
      : { pass: false, message: () => failures.join('\n') };
  },
});

// Usage in a test
it('submit button has correct accessibility attributes', async () => {
  await waitFor(element(by.id('submit-btn'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
  await jestExpect(element(by.id('submit-btn'))).toBeAccessible({
    label: 'Submit order',
    role: 'button',
    disabled: false,
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `getAttributes()` is an async RPC call; running `toBeAccessible()` on every interactive element in a large test suite adds measurable overhead. Reserve the custom matcher for a dedicated accessibility smoke test suite rather than embedding it in every functional test.

---

### Pattern 327 — `element.swipe('up', 'slow', 0.3)` on a `BottomSheetModal` from `@gorhom/bottom-sheet` v5 to snap it to a lower snap point without dismissing it, combined with scroll-position awareness of the embedded `ScrollView` [community]

`@gorhom/bottom-sheet` v5 uses a `GestureDetector` that competes with its embedded `ScrollView` for vertical gesture ownership. When the `ScrollView` content is scrolled to its topmost position, a slow upward swipe on the sheet handle snaps the sheet to a lower snap point. If the `ScrollView` is not at the top, the gesture is consumed by the scroll instead, and the sheet does not move. The test must first scroll the inner content to the top before attempting to snap the sheet. Use `swipe('up', 'slow', 0.3)` rather than `'fast'` because a fast swipe dismisses the sheet entirely.

```typescript
import { device, element, by, waitFor } from 'detox';

describe('Product detail bottom sheet', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.reloadReactNative();
    await element(by.id('product-card-0')).tap();
    // Wait for the sheet to animate open at the full snap point
    await waitFor(element(by.id('product-detail-sheet')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(4000);
  });

  it('snaps the sheet to the half-height snap point', async () => {
    // Step 1: ensure the sheet's inner ScrollView is scrolled to the top
    // so the gesture propagates to the sheet's GestureDetector, not the ScrollView
    if (device.getPlatform() === 'android') {
      await element(by.id('product-detail-scroll')).scroll(100000, 'up', 0.5, 0.5);
    } else {
      await element(by.id('product-detail-scroll')).scrollTo('top');
    }

    // Step 2: swipe up slowly on the sheet handle to snap to the lower snap point
    // 'fast' would dismiss the sheet; 'slow' with normalizedOffset 0.3 snaps it
    await element(by.id('product-detail-sheet-handle')).swipe('up', 'slow', 0.3);

    // Step 3: assert the sheet is at the half-height snap point by checking
    // that a below-fold element is no longer visible
    await expect(element(by.id('product-detail-reviews-section'))).not.toBeVisible();

    // The sheet header should still be visible at the lower snap point
    await expect(element(by.id('product-detail-title'))).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Bottom sheet snap behavior is highly sensitive to the `normalizedOffset` parameter — the correct value depends on the configured `snapPoints` array. Test this interactively in the simulator first, then hard-code the working value with an explanatory comment. A change to `snapPoints` in production code will silently break the test without a type error.

---

### Pattern 328 — `device.disableSynchronization()` scoped around a `Lottie` animation that loops indefinitely, paired with a generous explicit `withTimeout` for the CTA that appears after the first animation cycle [community]

Lottie animations configured with `loop={true}` keep the RN JS thread continuously busy dispatching animation frame events, causing Detox's idle detector to never settle and the test to hang indefinitely. The standard mitigation is to wrap the interaction in `device.disableSynchronization()` / `device.enableSynchronization()`. The key discipline is to re-enable synchronization before any tap actions so that post-tap navigation assertions benefit from normal idle detection again. Always pair the two calls in a `try/finally` block to prevent permanent synchronization disablement if an assertion throws.

```typescript
import { device, element, by, waitFor } from 'detox';

describe('Onboarding animation screen', () => {
  it('completes the intro Lottie animation and shows the CTA button', async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });

    // The Lottie animation loops and blocks Detox idle detection
    // Disable synchronization while the animation plays
    await device.disableSynchronization();

    try {
      // Wait for the CTA button which appears after the first animation cycle (4 s)
      // We cannot use Detox idle detection here — use a generous explicit timeout
      await waitFor(element(by.id('onboarding-cta-btn')))
        .toBeVisible()
        .withTimeout(8000);
    } finally {
      // Re-enable synchronization before any tap actions so subsequent
      // idle detection resumes for the post-tap navigation assertions
      await device.enableSynchronization();
    }

    await element(by.id('onboarding-cta-btn')).tap();

    // Verify navigation to the next screen after the CTA tap
    await waitFor(element(by.id('signup-screen')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(5000);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `disableSynchronization()` is a global switch — all Detox idle waiting is suppressed until `enableSynchronization()` is called. Any test that forgets `enableSynchronization()` before the next assertion will produce non-deterministic results across the remainder of the suite. The `try/finally` pattern shown above is mandatory; without it, a failing `waitFor` will leave synchronization permanently disabled for the rest of the Jest worker's lifetime.

---

### Pattern 329 — `element(by.id('input')).replaceText(value)` for `TextInput` components where `clearText()` + `typeText()` triggers an `onChange` event with an empty string that resets controlled-input state back to its initial value [official]

`element.replaceText(value)` atomically replaces the entire field content in a single native call, bypassing the intermediate empty-string `onChange` event that `clearText()` produces. This is essential for controlled `TextInput` components whose `onChangeText` handler resets dependent state (e.g., form validation, autocomplete suggestions) when it receives an empty string. `replaceText()` dispatches only one `onChange` event with the final value, so dependent state transitions happen exactly once. Note that `replaceText()` does not trigger `onSubmitEditing` — add `tapKey('Return')` or tap the submit button if form submission is also required.

```typescript
import { element, by, waitFor, expect as detoxExpect } from 'detox';

describe('Email address field', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await element(by.id('email-input')).tap();
    // Seed the field with an initial valid value
    await element(by.id('email-input')).typeText('old@example.com');
    await waitFor(element(by.id('email-valid-icon'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
  });

  it('replaces the email address without triggering an intermediate empty-string reset', async () => {
    // replaceText() sends a single onChange with 'new@example.com'
    // clearText() + typeText() would first send onChange(''), resetting validation state
    await element(by.id('email-input')).replaceText('new@example.com');

    // Validation icon should update to reflect the new address without a
    // transient "invalid" flash caused by the empty-string intermediate state
    await waitFor(element(by.id('email-valid-icon'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
    await detoxExpect(element(by.id('email-input'))).toHaveText('new@example.com');
  });

  it('shows a validation error for an invalid email replacement', async () => {
    await element(by.id('email-input')).replaceText('not-an-email');
    await waitFor(element(by.id('email-error-label')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(3000);
    await detoxExpect(element(by.id('email-error-label'))).toHaveText(
      'Please enter a valid email address'
    );
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `replaceText()` is not supported on all Android `TextInput` variants — specifically, inputs that use a custom `InputConnection` implementation (common in some rich-text editors) may ignore the native `setText()` call that `replaceText()` maps to. Fall back to `clearText()` + `typeText()` with a `disableSynchronization()` bracket around the intermediate empty-string state for those components.

---

### Pattern 330 — `device.takeScreenshot(name)` called inside a custom Jest `testEnvironment` `handleTestEvent('test_fn_failure')` hook for automatic failure screenshots without per-test boilerplate [community]

Adding `device.takeScreenshot()` to `afterEach` captures screenshots for all tests, but attaches them even to passing tests, inflating artifact storage. A more targeted approach is to subclass `DetoxCircusEnvironment` and override `handleTestEvent` to call `takeScreenshot()` only when `event.name === 'test_fn_failure'`. This fires exactly once per failing test, immediately after the failure, capturing the screen state at the exact moment of the assertion failure before any cleanup runs. The screenshot name is derived from the test's full path, producing deterministic filenames suitable for CI artifact links.

```typescript
// e2e/environment/detox-failure-screenshot.ts
import { DetoxCircusEnvironment } from 'detox/runners/jest';
import { device } from 'detox';

export default class DetoxFailureScreenshotEnvironment extends DetoxCircusEnvironment {
  async handleTestEvent(event: Circus.Event, state: Circus.State): Promise<void> {
    await super.handleTestEvent(event, state);

    if (event.name === 'test_fn_failure') {
      // Derive a filename from the full test title path
      const suiteName = state.currentDescribeBlock.name.replace(/\s+/g, '_');
      const testName = event.test.name.replace(/\s+/g, '_');
      const timestamp = Date.now();
      const screenshotName = `FAIL__${suiteName}__${testName}__${timestamp}`;

      try {
        await device.takeScreenshot(screenshotName);
      } catch {
        // takeScreenshot can throw if the device is in a bad state; swallow to
        // avoid masking the original test failure with a secondary error
      }
    }
  }
}

// detox.config.ts — register the custom environment:
// testRunner: { jest: { testEnvironment: './e2e/environment/detox-failure-screenshot.ts' } }
```

**Tradeoff.** `handleTestEvent('test_fn_failure')` fires after the assertion error but before `afterEach` cleanup; the screenshot reflects the UI state at failure time, which is exactly what debugging requires. However, if `afterEach` calls `device.reloadReactNative()` on failure, the screen may change before the screenshot is written — confirm that Circus awaits the `handleTestEvent` promise (it does in Jest 27+) before relying on the capture order.

---

### Pattern 331 — `element(by.id('date-picker')).setColumnToValue(0, 'May')` with explicit column indices derived from locale-aware `Intl.DateTimeFormat` output for cross-locale `DateTimePicker` testing [official]

`setColumnToValue(column, value)` sets a wheel-picker column by zero-based column index and exact string value. For `DateTimePicker` components, the column order (month/day/year vs day/month/year) depends on the device locale, making hard-coded column indices `0`, `1`, `2` locale-specific. The robust pattern computes the expected column assignment by querying `Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-US').formatToParts(date)` at test time and mapping part `'month'`, `'day'`, `'year'` to their ordinal positions in the resolved format. This makes the test locale-aware without requiring a separate test configuration per region.

```typescript
import { element, by, waitFor, device } from 'detox';

/** Returns { month, day, year } mapped to column indices for the current locale */
function getDatePickerColumnIndices(locale: string): Record<string, number> {
  const parts = new Intl.DateTimeFormat(locale, {
    month: 'long',
    day: 'numeric',
    year: 'numeric',
  })
    .formatToParts(new Date('2000-01-01'))
    .filter((p) => p.type !== 'literal');

  const indices: Record<string, number> = {};
  parts.forEach((part, index) => {
    indices[part.type] = index;
  });
  return indices;
}

describe('Event scheduling — date picker', () => {
  it('selects a specific date in the wheel picker', async () => {
    await element(by.id('schedule-event-btn')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('date-picker'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

    const locale = 'en-US';
    const cols = getDatePickerColumnIndices(locale);

    // Set month, day, year using locale-derived column indices
    await element(by.id('date-picker')).setColumnToValue(cols['month'], 'December');
    await element(by.id('date-picker')).setColumnToValue(cols['day'], '25');
    await element(by.id('date-picker')).setColumnToValue(cols['year'], '2026');

    await element(by.id('confirm-date-btn')).tap();

    await waitFor(element(by.id('selected-date-label')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(3000);
    await expect(element(by.id('selected-date-label'))).toHaveText('December 25, 2026');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `setColumnToValue()` requires that the string value exactly matches the picker's rendered cell text, including locale-specific month names and separator styles. Pre-warm the simulator with the target locale using `launchApp({ languageAndLocale: { language: 'en-US', locale: 'en_US' } })` to eliminate locale variability across CI runners.

---

### Pattern 332 — `waitFor(element(by.id('x'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(n)` inside a `for…of` retry loop with `device.reloadReactNative()` between attempts for tests that are flaky due to a known race between React Navigation initial route resolution and the first render [community]

React Navigation's initial route is resolved asynchronously during the JS bundle hydration phase, and on slow CI Android emulators the first navigation render can lag behind Detox's initial `waitFor` timeout. Rather than increasing the timeout globally, a targeted retry loop with `reloadReactNative()` between attempts provides bounded recovery without inflating the suite's total wall-clock time. The loop should be capped at 2–3 attempts; more than 3 retries indicates a structural timing issue that requires a code fix rather than a test workaround.

```typescript
import { device, element, by, waitFor } from 'detox';

const MAX_NAVIGATION_RETRIES = 3;
const NAVIGATION_TIMEOUT_MS = 6000;

async function waitForInitialScreen(screenTestId: string): Promise<void> {
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= MAX_NAVIGATION_RETRIES; attempt++) {
    try {
      await waitFor(element(by.id(screenTestId)))
        .toBeVisible()
        .withTimeout(NAVIGATION_TIMEOUT_MS);
      return; // success — exit the loop
    } catch {
      if (attempt === MAX_NAVIGATION_RETRIES) throw; // exhausted retries — rethrow
      // Reload the React Native bundle and try again
      await device.reloadReactNative();
    }
  }
}

describe('Dashboard screen', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.reloadReactNative();
    await waitForInitialScreen('dashboard-screen');
  });

  it('shows the welcome message on first load', async () => {
    await expect(element(by.id('dashboard-welcome-message'))).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Each `reloadReactNative()` adds ~2–4 seconds of reload overhead. The loop is appropriate only when the flakiness rate is known to be < 30% (i.e., passes on the second attempt most of the time). If the screen fails to appear on 50%+ of first loads, the app has a structural navigation timing bug that must be fixed rather than masked by retries.

---

### Pattern 333 — `device.setNetworkConditions({ downloadSpeed, uploadSpeed, latency })` combined with `waitFor` assertions to verify that skeleton loading screens and error states are correctly rendered under degraded network conditions [official]

`device.setNetworkConditions()` (Detox 20.49+) configures the emulator's network link conditioner to simulate specific throughput and latency scenarios without an external proxy. This enables tests that verify: (1) skeleton/shimmer loading states appear immediately on slow connections, (2) retry buttons appear when requests time out, and (3) cached data is shown correctly when the connection drops entirely. Restore default conditions with `device.resetNetworkConditions()` after the test to avoid leaking degraded conditions into subsequent tests.

```typescript
import { device, element, by, waitFor } from 'detox';

describe('Network degradation UX', () => {
  afterEach(async () => {
    // Always restore network conditions to avoid leaking into other tests
    await device.resetNetworkConditions();
  });

  it('shows the skeleton loader on a 3G connection', async () => {
    // Simulate a 3G network: ~750 kbps download, 250 kbps upload, 100ms latency
    await device.setNetworkConditions({
      downloadSpeed: 750 * 1024,
      uploadSpeed: 250 * 1024,
      latency: 100,
    });

    await device.reloadReactNative();
    await element(by.id('nav-feed')).tap();

    // The skeleton screen should appear immediately because the API is slow
    await waitFor(element(by.id('feed-skeleton-loader')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(2000);

    // Eventually the real content should load
    await waitFor(element(by.id('feed-post-0')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(30000);

    // Skeleton should be gone once content loads
    await expect(element(by.id('feed-skeleton-loader'))).not.toBeVisible();
  });

  it('shows the retry button when the network is completely unavailable', async () => {
    // Use setURLBlacklist to block app API traffic without risking the Detox channel
    await device.setURLBlacklist(['.*api\\.yourapp\\.com.*']);

    await device.reloadReactNative();
    await element(by.id('nav-feed')).tap();

    // The request should fail and show a retry CTA
    await waitFor(element(by.id('feed-error-retry-btn')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(20000);

    // Restore the URL blacklist
    await device.setURLBlacklist([]);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `device.setNetworkConditions()` is Android emulator-only (Detox 20.49+); on iOS simulators, network link conditioning must be configured via the Network Link Conditioner profile or `simctl` before launching. Wrap these tests in `if (device.getPlatform() === 'android')` until iOS parity is available. For complete network-loss simulation on Android, prefer `setURLBlacklist()` over setting speed to zero to avoid killing the Detox control channel (see Gotcha 251).

---

### Pattern 334 — `element(by.id('x')).swipe('down', 'slow', 0.6, 0.5, 0.1)` on a `RefreshControl`-backed `ScrollView` with a pre-scroll to the top to reliably trigger pull-to-refresh without the swipe being absorbed by the `ScrollView`'s bounce physics [official]

Pull-to-refresh (`RefreshControl`) requires the scroll view to be at its topmost position before the downward swipe gesture begins; if there is any residual scroll offset, the swipe scrolls the content upward instead of triggering the refresh. The safe sequence is: (1) scroll to the top, (2) wait for the bounce animation to settle, (3) execute the downward swipe. The `normalizedOffset` of `0.6` is the minimum needed to cross the iOS `refreshTriggerOffset` threshold on a standard display; use `0.75` on compact devices (iPhone SE) where the trigger threshold is a larger fraction of the screen height. Setting `startNormalizedY: 0.1` places the swipe origin near the top edge so the `UIRefreshControl` gesture recognizer takes precedence.

```typescript
import { device, element, by, waitFor } from 'detox';

async function triggerPullToRefresh(scrollViewTestId: string): Promise<void> {
  const scrollView = element(by.id(scrollViewTestId));

  // Step 1: Ensure the list is at the top before swiping
  if (device.getPlatform() === 'ios') {
    await scrollView.scrollTo('top');
  } else {
    await scrollView.scroll(100000, 'up', 0.5, 0.5);
  }

  // Step 2: Wait briefly for the bounce animation to fully settle
  await waitFor(element(by.id(scrollViewTestId))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(1000);

  // Step 3: Slow downward swipe originating near the top edge (startNormalizedY: 0.1)
  // normalizedOffset 0.6 crosses the refresh trigger; increase to 0.75 for compact devices
  await scrollView.swipe('down', 'slow', 0.6, 0.5, 0.1);
}

describe('Feed refresh', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.reloadReactNative();
    await element(by.id('nav-feed')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('feed-list'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
  });

  it('refreshes the feed content via pull-to-refresh', async () => {
    await triggerPullToRefresh('feed-list');

    // The refresh spinner should appear briefly
    await waitFor(element(by.id('feed-refresh-indicator')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(2000);

    // After refresh the spinner should disappear
    await waitFor(element(by.id('feed-refresh-indicator')))
      .not.toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(10000);

    // Content should be refreshed
    await expect(element(by.id('feed-post-0'))).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** On Android, `RefreshControl` wraps `SwipeRefreshLayout`, which has its own threshold. `normalizedOffset: 0.6` is typically sufficient, but if the refresh indicator never appears on a specific Android API level, increase to `0.8`. The `startNormalizedY: 0.1` placement is iOS-critical; on Android it has no effect on `SwipeRefreshLayout` trigger detection but does no harm.

---

### Gotcha 249 — `device.appLaunchArgs.modify()` accumulates keys across the process lifetime so a test that adds `{ featureFlag: '1' }` in `beforeAll` will expose that flag to every subsequent `launchApp()` call in the same Jest worker unless `device.appLaunchArgs.reset()` is called explicitly [official]

**Root cause**: `appLaunchArgs` is a stateful object whose `modify()` method merges the provided object into its internal map using `Object.assign`. There is no automatic rollback at test boundaries. A `describe` block that enables an experimental feature flag with `modify({ experimental: '1' })` and launches the app will leave `experimental: '1'` in the launch args for every subsequent `launchApp()` in the same worker process — including tests in other files when Jest reuses the worker. The failure mode is a test that passes in isolation (where the flag is off by default) but fails in the full suite (where a previous test left the flag on). Call `device.appLaunchArgs.reset()` in `afterAll` after every feature-flag `describe`, and defensively call `reset()` at the start of `beforeAll` before applying new flags.

```ts
// ANTI-PATTERN — modify without reset leaks args to subsequent describe blocks
beforeAll(async () => {
  device.appLaunchArgs.modify({ enableNewDashboard: '1' });
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
});
// Missing: afterAll(() => device.appLaunchArgs.reset())
// Every subsequent launchApp() in this worker sees enableNewDashboard: '1'

// CORRECT PATTERN — always reset before modifying and again in afterAll
beforeAll(async () => {
  device.appLaunchArgs.reset(); // clear any residual flags from previous describe blocks
  device.appLaunchArgs.modify({ enableNewDashboard: '1' });
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
});

afterAll(async () => {
  device.appLaunchArgs.reset(); // restore baseline for subsequent describe blocks
});
```

**WHY this matters:** The bug is particularly insidious in parallel test runs because `--workers N` assigns files to worker processes non-deterministically; the leaked flag may or may not be present depending on file execution order, making the failure appear randomly across CI runs with no clear reproduction path.

---

### Gotcha 250 — `element.replaceText(value)` silently succeeds on iOS but has no effect on Android `TextInput` components that use a custom `InputConnection` (e.g., emoji keyboards, rich-text editors, autofill-enabled fields) because the underlying `setText()` call bypasses the `InputConnection` pipeline [official]

**Root cause**: On Android, `replaceText()` dispatches a native `setText()` call on the `EditText` view. For standard React Native `TextInput` components, this triggers the `TextWatcher` that RN registers, which fires `onChange`. However, when an app uses a custom `InputConnection` (e.g., via `setEditableFactory()` or through `react-native-rich-text-editor`), the `setText()` bypass skips the `InputConnection` entirely, so no `onTextChanged` callback fires and the field appears unchanged to the JS side. The text may visually update in the native view but the React state never receives the new value, causing subsequent `toHaveText()` assertions to fail.

```ts
// SYMPTOM: replaceText() appears to do nothing on Android with custom InputConnection
await element(by.id('rich-editor')).replaceText('hello world');
// Assertion fails — React state still shows old value
await expect(element(by.id('rich-editor'))).toHaveText('hello world'); // FAILS on Android

// WORKAROUND: use clearText() + typeText() for custom InputConnection inputs
// wrap in disableSynchronization if the empty-string intermediate state causes issues
await device.disableSynchronization();
await element(by.id('rich-editor')).clearText();
await element(by.id('rich-editor')).typeText('hello world');
await device.enableSynchronization();
await expect(element(by.id('rich-editor'))).toHaveText('hello world'); // PASSES
```

**WHY this matters:** A test written against a standard `TextInput` with `replaceText()` may pass in development, then silently fail after a library upgrade that changes the `InputConnection` implementation, with no obvious connection between the library change and the Detox test failure. The test appears to succeed (no exception thrown) while the assertion reports the old value, which is a particularly deceptive failure mode.

---

### Gotcha 251 — `device.setNetworkConditions({ downloadSpeed: 0, uploadSpeed: 0 })` may block the Detox WebSocket synchronization channel in addition to app traffic, causing `"Detox connection closed unexpectedly"` instead of the expected app network-error state [community]

**Root cause**: Detox communicates with the device over a WebSocket connection established before the test runs. `device.setNetworkConditions()` applies traffic shaping at the emulator's network interface level via `tc qdisc` on Android emulator, which affects all traffic on the interface including the Detox control channel. When download speed is set to zero, the Detox WebSocket keep-alive fails, and the test runner reports `"Detox connection closed unexpectedly"` and terminates the test. The app never reaches the network-error state that the test was designed to assert. Use `device.setURLBlacklist()` to block specific API endpoints instead of throttling the entire interface, as URL blacklisting operates at the app's `URLSession`/`OkHttp` layer and does not affect the Detox WebSocket.

```ts
// ANTI-PATTERN — speed 0 may kill the Detox control channel on Android emulator
await device.setNetworkConditions({ downloadSpeed: 0, uploadSpeed: 0, latency: 99999 });
// May produce: "Error: Detox connection closed unexpectedly" — test aborts

// CORRECT PATTERN — block specific app API endpoints; Detox channel is unaffected
await device.setURLBlacklist([
  '.*api\\.yourapp\\.com.*',   // blocks all app API calls
  '.*cdn\\.yourapp\\.com.*',   // blocks CDN asset loads
]);

// Assert app error state
await waitFor(element(by.id('error-retry-btn'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(15000);

// Restore in afterEach
await device.setURLBlacklist([]);
```

**WHY this matters:** Debugging a `"Detox connection closed"` error when you believe the test should show a network-error UI is extremely time-consuming. The root cause is not a bug in the app or in Detox — it is a misuse of `setNetworkConditions` at the OS level rather than at the application layer. Understanding the difference between interface-level throttling and application-layer URL blocking is essential for reliable network-state testing.

---

### Gotcha 252 — `element.longPressAndDrag()` on Android produces a `"No view found"` error intermittently when the drag source is inside a `RecyclerView` that has `setHasStableIds(false)`, because the view can be recycled and its accessibility node ID remapped between the long-press-hold phase and the drag-move phase [community]

**Root cause**: `longPressAndDrag()` is a multi-phase gesture: the first phase long-presses and holds the source view, and the second phase dispatches move events toward the target. On Android, `RecyclerView` may recycle the source view between these two phases if a layout change is triggered by the long-press (e.g., a drag-handle overlay becoming visible inflates a new child view). When the view is recycled, its accessibility node ID changes. Detox's second-phase targeting still references the old node ID, producing `"No view found"`. The fix is to ensure `setHasStableIds(true)` in the `RecyclerView.Adapter` and that item IDs are derived from stable data model keys rather than list positions.

```ts
// SYMPTOM: longPressAndDrag fails intermittently with "No view found" on Android
await element(by.id('list-item-3')).longPressAndDrag(
  1000, 0.5, 0.5, element(by.id('list-item-6')), 0.5, 0.5, 'fast', 0
);
// Intermittent: Error: No view found with id 'list-item-3' during drag phase

// FIX A: use stable data-model-based testIDs and configure adapter setHasStableIds(true)
// In RN component: testID={`list-item-${item.id}`} (item.id is a stable UUID, not index)

// FIX B: disable synchronization during the drag to prevent layout-triggered recycling
await device.disableSynchronization();
await element(by.id(`list-item-${item.id}`)).longPressAndDrag(
  800, 0.5, 0.5,
  element(by.id(`target-item-${targetItem.id}`)),
  0.5, 0.5, 'slow', 0
);
await device.enableSynchronization();
```

**WHY this matters:** Drag-and-drop reordering tests are among the most structurally sensitive in a Detox suite. Using list-position-based `testID` values (e.g., `list-item-0`, `list-item-1`) is a root cause of both this recycling gotcha and a broad class of index-shift bugs where inserting an item above the target silently changes which item a test interacts with. Always anchor `testID` to stable data model IDs for any list that supports reordering.

---

### Gotcha 253 — `waitFor(element(by.id('x'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(n)` does not restart its internal countdown when `device.reloadReactNative()` is called during the wait period, so a timeout that starts before a reload may expire during the reload itself, producing a spurious timeout failure [community]

**Root cause**: `waitFor().toBeVisible().withTimeout(n)` begins a polling loop immediately when called. The timeout countdown is wall-clock-based and does not pause or reset when `device.reloadReactNative()` is called. If `reloadReactNative()` is called while the `waitFor` promise is active (e.g., in a shared `beforeEach` that has both a reload and a waitFor in sequence but an intermediate step throws and the error propagates unexpectedly), the reload takes 2–4 seconds, consuming that proportion of the `withTimeout` budget. On slow CI emulators where the element also takes 2–3 seconds to render post-reload, the combined latency exceeds the timeout and the test fails even though the app is in the correct state. Always `await device.reloadReactNative()` to full completion before starting a new `waitFor()`.

```ts
// ANTI-PATTERN — waitFor started before reloadReactNative; timer runs during reload
const waitPromise = waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen')))
  .toBeVisible()
  .withTimeout(5000);

await device.reloadReactNative(); // reload takes 3 s; timer has been counting for 3 s

await waitPromise;
// Only 2 s remain of the original 5 s; may timeout before the element renders

// CORRECT PATTERN — fully await the reload first, then start the waitFor timer
await device.reloadReactNative(); // timer has NOT started yet

await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen')))
  .toBeVisible()
  .withTimeout(8000); // full 8 s budget starts AFTER reload completes
```

**WHY this matters:** This pattern produces flaky timeout failures that only manifest on slow CI runners where reload + render latency > timeout budget. The failure is indistinguishable from genuine navigation bugs, leading teams to increase `withTimeout` budgets globally rather than fixing the sequencing. Always treat `reloadReactNative()` as a synchronous barrier: start no `waitFor` timers until the reload `await` has resolved.

## Updated Anti-Patterns Checklist (Cycle 45 additions)

| Anti-Pattern | Fix |
|---|---|
| Calling `device.appLaunchArgs.modify({ flag: '1' })` in `beforeAll` without a matching `device.appLaunchArgs.reset()` in `afterAll` — flag persists in the Jest worker for all subsequent `launchApp()` calls, causing order-dependent test failures | Always call `reset()` in `afterAll` after feature-flag tests; also call `reset()` at the start of `beforeAll` as a defensive guard (Gotcha 249, Pattern 320) |
| Using `element.replaceText(value)` on an Android `TextInput` backed by a custom `InputConnection` — `setText()` bypasses the pipeline so React state never receives the new value, but no exception is thrown | Detect the component type and fall back to `clearText()` + `typeText()` wrapped in `disableSynchronization()` for rich-text and autofill-enabled inputs (Gotcha 250, Pattern 329) |
| Setting `device.setNetworkConditions({ downloadSpeed: 0 })` to simulate complete network loss — may block the Detox WebSocket control channel, producing `"Detox connection closed"` instead of the app error state | Use `device.setURLBlacklist(['.*api\\.yourapp\\.com.*'])` to block specific app API endpoints while leaving the Detox control channel intact (Gotcha 251, Pattern 333) |
| Using `element.longPressAndDrag()` on Android `RecyclerView` items identified by list-position `testID` values when the adapter has `setHasStableIds(false)` — view recycling during the gesture causes `"No view found"` | Assign `testID` from stable data model IDs and configure the adapter with `setHasStableIds(true)` (Gotcha 252, Pattern 303) |
| Starting a `waitFor().withTimeout(n)` promise and then calling `device.reloadReactNative()` while the timer is counting down — timer does not pause during reload and may expire before the element renders | Always `await device.reloadReactNative()` to full completion before starting a new `waitFor()`; never interleave the two (Gotcha 253, Pattern 332) |
| Using `element.scrollTo('top')` on an Android `NestedScrollView` — throws `"Action not supported"` at runtime | Guard with `device.getPlatform()`: `scrollTo('top')` on iOS, `scroll(100000, 'up', 0.5, 0.5)` on Android (Pattern 321) |
| Swiping down for pull-to-refresh without first scrolling the `ScrollView` to the top — swipe is consumed by scroll physics and `RefreshControl` never fires | Call `scrollTo('top')` (iOS) or `scroll(100000, 'up')` (Android) before `swipe('down', 'slow', 0.6, 0.5, 0.1)` (Pattern 334) |
