## Cycle 46 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 335 — `device.adjustDateToMock(isoDate)` for freezing device clock state in date-sensitive flows such as free-trial countdowns, calendar event creation, and age-gate validations [official]

`device.adjustDateToMock(isoDate)` sets the iOS Simulator or Android Emulator system clock to an arbitrary ISO 8601 timestamp for the duration of the test. Unlike OS-level time-change tricks (setting `SIMCTL_CHILD_TZ` or the emulator's `-timezone` flag), this method is scoped to the Detox session and is reset when the app is killed or the device session ends. Call `device.adjustDateToMock(null)` in an `afterEach` or `afterAll` hook to restore the real clock; failing to do so leaves the simulator on the mocked date for all subsequent tests in the same Jest worker process. This method is iOS only as of Detox 20.x; Android date mocking requires a custom `nativeModules` bridge or a build-time flag.

```typescript
import { device, element, by, waitFor } from 'detox';

describe('Free trial expiry gate', () => {
  const TRIAL_END_DATE = '2026-06-01T00:00:00.000Z';

  beforeEach(async () => {
    // Freeze the clock 1 second before trial expiry
    await device.adjustDateToMock(TRIAL_END_DATE);
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  });

  afterEach(async () => {
    // Restore real clock so subsequent tests are not affected
    await device.adjustDateToMock(null);
    await device.terminateApp();
  });

  it('shows upgrade prompt when trial expires', async () => {
    await waitFor(element(by.id('upgrade-prompt-banner')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(6000);

    await expect(element(by.id('days-remaining-label')))
      .toHaveText('0 days remaining');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `adjustDateToMock` sets the entire OS clock, not just a JavaScript `Date.now()` stub. Any timer running in a native module (e.g., a background location polling timer) will also fire as if the date changed, which can produce unexpected side-effects if those timers interact with the UI. For pure JS date logic, a lighter approach is to inject the mock date via a launch argument (`device.appLaunchArgs.modify({ mockDate: TRIAL_END_DATE })`) and consume it in the app with `global.__e2eMockDate` instead of calling the OS-level API.

---

### Pattern 336 — `device.setOrientation('landscape')` / `device.setOrientation('portrait')` with explicit layout assertions for testing responsive layouts, split-view components, and orientation-locked screens [official]

`device.setOrientation()` changes the physical device orientation and triggers the app's `onLayout` and `useWindowDimensions` hooks. Always follow a call to `setOrientation` with a `waitFor` assertion that verifies a layout landmark specific to the new orientation (e.g., a sidebar that only appears in landscape), because the layout pass is asynchronous and querying element positions immediately after `setOrientation` can return stale frame data. Reset to `portrait` in `afterEach` to prevent orientation state from leaking to subsequent tests; orientation state is not automatically restored between tests even after `reloadReactNative()`.

```typescript
describe('Responsive layout — landscape', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: false });
    await device.setOrientation('portrait'); // ensure known start state
  });

  afterEach(async () => {
    await device.setOrientation('portrait'); // restore for sibling tests
  });

  it('shows the sidebar navigation in landscape mode', async () => {
    await device.setOrientation('landscape');

    // Wait for the layout-driven sidebar to appear before asserting
    await waitFor(element(by.id('sidebar-nav')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(3000);

    await expect(element(by.id('main-content-area'))).toBeVisible();
    // Sidebar should be hidden in portrait — no need to scroll to find it
    await device.setOrientation('portrait');
    await expect(element(by.id('sidebar-nav'))).not.toBeVisible();
  });

  it('reflows form fields to two-column layout in landscape', async () => {
    await element(by.id('open-form-btn')).tap();
    await device.setOrientation('landscape');
    await waitFor(element(by.id('form-field-col-2-first-name')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(3000);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** On Android Emulator, `setOrientation` takes 500–800 ms to complete the sensor simulation and native layout pass. Using a hard `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 1000))` sleep to wait for layout is a common workaround, but it is fragile on slow CI runners. The correct approach is always the `waitFor` + layout-landmark pattern shown above, which self-adjusts to the actual layout completion time.

---

### Pattern 337 — Expo Router v3 screen-level `testID` convention and `device.openURL` deep-link testing for file-system-based routing [community]

Expo Router v3 generates screen components from the `app/` file-system tree. Because screen components are auto-generated, they do not have user-authored `testID` props by default. The recommended convention is to wrap the root `<View>` of each screen with `testID="screen-{route-name}"` (e.g., `testID="screen-home"`, `testID="screen-profile-[id]"`) so that E2E tests can assert which screen is active without parsing the URL. Combine this with `device.openURL({ url: 'exp://localhost:8081/--/profile/42' })` (or your custom scheme) to land directly on a parameterized route and then assert the screen-level `testID` before proceeding.

```typescript
describe('Expo Router — deep link to profile screen', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    // Wait for the Expo Router shell to hydrate
    await waitFor(element(by.id('screen-home')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(10000);
  });

  it('navigates to profile screen via deep link and renders user name', async () => {
    // Trigger the deep link while the app is foregrounded
    await device.openURL({ url: 'myapp://profile/42' });

    // Assert the correct screen is active
    await waitFor(element(by.id('screen-profile-42')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(6000);

    // Assert the parameterized content rendered correctly
    await expect(element(by.id('profile-username-label')))
      .toHaveText('Alice');
  });

  it('handles unknown route with 404 screen', async () => {
    await device.openURL({ url: 'myapp://does-not-exist/999' });
    await waitFor(element(by.id('screen-not-found')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(6000);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Expo Router's `<Slot />` and layout groups (`(tabs)`, `(stack)`) render multiple screen-level wrappers in the accessibility tree simultaneously. Using `screen-{route}` testIDs on the innermost content view rather than the layout wrapper avoids false positives where a background screen's `testID` is technically present in the hierarchy even though it is visually behind the foreground screen.

---

### Pattern 338 — `device.pressBack()` for testing Android hardware Back button behavior in navigation stacks, `Dialog` dismissal, and `BackHandler` custom listeners [official]

`device.pressBack()` simulates a press of the Android hardware Back button and triggers the same `BackHandler` event chain as a physical button press. Use it to test that `Dialog` components are correctly dismissed, that navigation stacks pop to the previous screen, and that custom `BackHandler` listeners registered with `BackHandler.addEventListener('hardwareBackPress', handler)` are invoked and return `true` (indicating they handled the event). This method has no iOS equivalent — on iOS, use `element.swipe('right', 'slow', 0.5, 0.05, 0.5)` from the left screen edge to simulate the interactive pop gesture.

```typescript
describe('Android Back button — dialog dismissal and navigation', () => {
  it('dismisses an alert dialog with the hardware Back button', async () => {
    await element(by.id('show-alert-btn')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('alert-dialog'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);

    await device.pressBack(); // Hardware Back press

    await waitFor(element(by.id('alert-dialog')))
      .not.toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(3000);
    // Underlying screen should still be visible
    await expect(element(by.id('home-screen'))).toBeVisible();
  });

  it('pops navigation stack to parent screen', async () => {
    await element(by.id('open-detail-btn')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('screen-detail'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

    await device.pressBack();

    await waitFor(element(by.id('screen-list'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
  });

  it('custom BackHandler blocks Back press while media is playing', async () => {
    await element(by.id('play-fullscreen-btn')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('fullscreen-player'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

    await device.pressBack(); // Custom BackHandler returns true — should not pop

    await expect(element(by.id('fullscreen-player'))).toBeVisible();
    // Now stop media and Back should work
    await element(by.id('stop-btn')).tap();
    await device.pressBack();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('screen-home'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `device.pressBack()` fires the native `onBackPressed` cycle, which calls `BackHandler` listeners in LIFO order before triggering the default navigation pop. If a third-party library registers its own `BackHandler` listener (e.g., `react-native-screens`, `@react-navigation/stack`) and that listener consumes the event, your test's intended Back-press effect may be swallowed silently. Always assert the post-Back-press screen state rather than assuming the navigation happened.

---

### Pattern 339 — `element(by.type('android.widget.Switch')).tap()` and `element(by.type('XCUIElementTypeSwitch')).tap()` for interacting with native `Switch` widgets in third-party SDK screens that do not expose `testID` [community]

Some third-party screens (settings SDKs, consent managers, analytics dashboards) render native `Switch` widgets without forwarding `testID` or `accessibilityLabel` from the React Native component. In these cases, `by.type()` with the platform-specific native class name is the only reliable matcher. On iOS the class is `XCUIElementTypeSwitch`; on Android it is `android.widget.Switch`. Combine `by.type()` with `.withAncestor(by.id('settings-row-notifications'))` to scope the match when multiple switches are on the screen. Never use bare `by.type('android.widget.Switch')` without an ancestor scope in a screen with more than one switch, as Detox will throw `AmbiguousError`.

```typescript
const PLATFORM = device.getPlatform();
const SWITCH_TYPE = PLATFORM === 'ios'
  ? 'XCUIElementTypeSwitch'
  : 'android.widget.Switch';

describe('Third-party consent SDK — toggle interactions', () => {
  it('enables analytics consent via native Switch', async () => {
    await element(by.id('open-consent-settings-btn')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('consent-screen-root'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(6000);

    const analyticsSwitch = element(
      by.type(SWITCH_TYPE).withAncestor(by.id('analytics-consent-row'))
    );

    // Read current state before tapping
    const attrs = await analyticsSwitch.getAttributes();
    if (PLATFORM === 'ios') {
      // XCUIElementTypeSwitch exposes value '0' (off) / '1' (on)
      if (attrs.value === '0') {
        await analyticsSwitch.tap();
      }
    } else {
      if (!attrs.checked) {
        await analyticsSwitch.tap();
      }
    }

    // Confirm the switch is now on
    const updatedAttrs = await analyticsSwitch.getAttributes();
    const isOn = PLATFORM === 'ios' ? updatedAttrs.value === '1' : updatedAttrs.checked;
    expect(isOn).toBe(true);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `by.type()` queries depend on the native rendering class name, which can change between OS versions. Android renamed `android.widget.ToggleButton` to `android.widget.Switch` in API 14 and the class path can diverge in OEM-skinned ROMs (Samsung OneUI, MIUI). Always add a fallback matcher using `by.label()` if the consent screen provides accessibility labels, and document the SDK version this test targets.

---

### Pattern 340 — `device.matchFace()` / `device.unmatchFace()` and `device.matchFinger()` / `device.unmatchFinger()` for testing biometric authentication flows end-to-end on iOS Simulator and Android Emulator [official]

Detox provides `device.matchFace()` and `device.matchFinger()` to simulate successful biometric authentication, and `device.unmatchFace()` / `device.unmatchFinger()` to simulate failed biometric attempts. These calls must be preceded by `device.launchApp({ permissions: { faceid: 'YES' } })` (iOS) or the equivalent Android biometric permission grant. The calls are timing-sensitive: they must be issued while the biometric prompt is visible on screen, which requires a `waitFor` assertion first or a very short `await` pause before the call. Wrap both in `try/finally` so that a biometric failure never leaves the simulator in a permanently-enrolled or permanently-failed state.

```typescript
describe('Biometric authentication', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({
      newInstance: true,
      permissions: { faceid: 'YES' },
    });
  });

  it('unlocks the app with a successful Face ID match', async () => {
    await element(by.id('use-biometrics-btn')).tap();

    // Biometric sheet appears asynchronously — wait before simulating
    await waitFor(element(by.id('biometric-prompt-overlay')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(5000);

    await device.matchFace(); // Simulate successful Face ID scan

    await waitFor(element(by.id('authenticated-home-screen')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(5000);
  });

  it('shows error state after two consecutive Face ID failures', async () => {
    await element(by.id('use-biometrics-btn')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('biometric-prompt-overlay')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(5000);

    await device.unmatchFace(); // First failure
    await waitFor(element(by.id('biometric-prompt-overlay')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(5000);
    await device.unmatchFace(); // Second failure

    await waitFor(element(by.id('biometric-too-many-attempts-error')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(5000);
    await expect(element(by.id('enter-passcode-fallback-btn'))).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `device.matchFace()` and `device.matchFinger()` only work on iOS Simulator (Xcode Simulator's enrolled biometric state) and Android Emulator (API 28+). They do not work on physical devices because real biometric hardware cannot be spoofed programmatically. Keep biometric tests in a separate configuration file (`detox.biometric.config.js`) with `type: 'ios.simulator'` or `type: 'android.emulator'` and exclude them from physical-device test plans.

---

### Pattern 341 — `waitFor(element).toBeVisible().whileElement(by.id('outer-list')).scroll(200, 'down')` inside a `RecyclerView`-within-`ScrollView` nested structure by scoping the scroll to the correct parent element [official]

Detox's `whileElement().scroll()` clause scrolls a specific container element while polling for visibility of the target. In nested scroll layouts (e.g., a `ScrollView` containing a `FlatList` which itself contains a `ScrollView`), the wrong scroll target is the most common source of `"Element not found while scrolling"` failures. The rule is: always scope `.whileElement()` to the innermost scrollable that contains the target element, not the outermost. Determine the correct container by reading the element tree with `device.captureViewHierarchy()` and identifying which `ScrollView` has the target as a direct or near-direct descendant.

```typescript
describe('Nested scroll — find item in inner FlatList', () => {
  it('scrolls the inner list to find a recently added item', async () => {
    // Navigate to a screen that has: page ScrollView > category FlatList > item FlatList
    await element(by.id('category-electronics')).tap();

    // WRONG: scrolling outerPageScroll won't move the inner item list
    // await waitFor(element(by.id('product-item-42')))
    //   .toBeVisible()
    //   .withTimeout(8000)
    //   .whileElement(by.id('outer-page-scroll'))
    //   .scroll(200, 'down');

    // CORRECT: scroll the inner product list that contains the item
    await waitFor(element(by.id('product-item-42')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(10000)
      .whileElement(by.id('product-list-electronics'))
      .scroll(200, 'down');

    await element(by.id('product-item-42')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('screen-product-detail')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(5000);
  });

  it('uses view hierarchy capture to identify the correct scroll container', async () => {
    // Use captureViewHierarchy in a throw-away debug test to identify containers
    await device.captureViewHierarchy('debug-nested-scroll');
    // Inspect the .viewhierarchy artifact in Xcode to find the testID of
    // the innermost ScrollView that wraps the target item
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `whileElement().scroll()` dispatches scroll events up to a maximum of 50 iterations before giving up. If the target item is deep in a 10,000-item virtualized list, the scroll step size (200 pts per step) may require more than 50 iterations to reach it. In that case, use a server-side data fixture that places the target item within the first visible window, or use `element.scroll(distance, direction)` with a large distance value first to fast-forward to the approximate area before handing off to `whileElement`.

---

### Pattern 342 — React Native Gesture Handler v2 `GestureDetector` + Detox `disableSynchronization()` bracket for testing composed gesture sequences (pan + pinch, swipe + long-press) that use the new composition API [community]

RNGH v2's `Gesture.Simultaneous()` and `Gesture.Exclusive()` composition API registers compound gesture recognizers that hold the UI in a non-idle "gesture active" state for the duration of the gesture. Detox's synchronization mechanism treats any active gesture recognizer as "UI not idle" and will hang indefinitely waiting for the gesture to complete before evaluating `waitFor` assertions. The fix is to bracket the entire composed gesture sequence in `disableSynchronization()` / `enableSynchronization()`, issue the gesture calls, and then re-enable synchronization before asserting the post-gesture state. Always use `try/finally` to guarantee re-enabling.

```typescript
describe('Map view — pan and pinch compose simultaneously', () => {
  it('zooms into a region by pinching on the map', async () => {
    await waitFor(element(by.id('map-view'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(6000);

    // RNGH v2 Simultaneous composition holds gesture-active indefinitely
    await device.disableSynchronization();
    try {
      // First pan to center the target region
      await element(by.id('map-view')).swipe('left', 'slow', 0.3, 0.5, 0.5);
      // Then pinch to zoom in (scale > 1 = zoom in)
      await element(by.id('map-view')).pinch(1.8, 'slow', 0);
    } finally {
      await device.enableSynchronization();
    }

    // Now safe to use waitFor — synchronization is re-enabled
    await waitFor(element(by.id('map-zoom-label')))
      .toHaveText('Zoom: 14')
      .withTimeout(4000);
  });

  it('rejects a swipe-then-long-press on a locked item', async () => {
    await device.disableSynchronization();
    try {
      await element(by.id('locked-item')).swipe('right', 'slow', 0.2, 0.1, 0.5);
      await element(by.id('locked-item')).longPress(600);
    } finally {
      await device.enableSynchronization();
    }

    await expect(element(by.id('locked-context-menu'))).not.toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Disabling synchronization removes Detox's idle-waiting safety net for the bracketed section. Any `waitFor` calls inside the `disableSynchronization` bracket will time out immediately if the element is not already visible because there is no idle polling. Only issue `element.action()` calls (not `waitFor`) inside the bracket, then re-enable synchronization before evaluating post-gesture state.

---

### Pattern 343 — `device.launchApp({ languageAndLocale: { language: 'ar', locale: 'ar_SA' } })` for RTL layout testing including element visibility verification in right-to-left mirrored navigation stacks [official]

Detox's `languageAndLocale` launch argument configures the iOS Simulator or Android Emulator to use a specific locale and language, causing React Native's `I18nManager.isRTL` to return `true` for right-to-left languages. This triggers layout mirroring: `flexDirection: 'row'` becomes visually right-to-left, and the navigation back button moves to the right side of the header. Test RTL layouts by asserting that primary action elements (CTAs, navigation arrows) are on the correct side using `getAttributes().frame` coordinates: in RTL the primary CTA should have a lower `x` origin than the secondary action. Always launch with `newInstance: true` when changing locale to avoid stale `I18nManager` state from a previous test session.

```typescript
describe('RTL layout — Arabic locale', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({
      newInstance: true,
      languageAndLocale: {
        language: 'ar',
        locale: 'ar_SA',
      },
    });
    await waitFor(element(by.id('screen-home'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(10000);
  });

  afterAll(async () => {
    // Restore default locale for subsequent test suites
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  });

  it('renders the primary CTA on the left edge in RTL (visually right side)', async () => {
    await element(by.id('open-checkout-btn')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('checkout-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);

    const primaryAttr = await element(by.id('checkout-confirm-btn')).getAttributes();
    const secondaryAttr = await element(by.id('checkout-cancel-btn')).getAttributes();

    // In RTL, primary action (confirm) should be on the right side (lower x in LTR)
    // After mirroring, confirm.frame.x < cancel.frame.x
    expect(primaryAttr.frame.x).toBeLessThan(secondaryAttr.frame.x);
  });

  it('displays Arabic numerals in price labels', async () => {
    await waitFor(element(by.id('product-price-label'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
    const attrs = await element(by.id('product-price-label')).getAttributes();
    // Arabic-Indic numerals: ٠١٢٣٤٥٦٧٨٩
    expect(attrs.text).toMatch(/[٠-٩]/);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `languageAndLocale` affects the entire simulator session. If a test file that uses `ar_SA` runs in the same Jest worker as a test that uses `en_US` layout assumptions (e.g., `frame.x` comparisons expecting LTR), the LTR test will fail. Use separate Detox configurations for RTL and LTR test suites (`detox.ltr.config.js`, `detox.rtl.config.js`) and run them in separate CI jobs rather than mixing locale-sensitive and locale-neutral tests in the same worker.

---

### Pattern 344 — `device.launchApp({ permissions: { camera: 'YES', photos: 'YES' } })` with `element(by.system.label('Choose Library'))` for testing `react-native-image-picker` and `expo-image-picker` photo library selection flows [community]

Testing photo library selection requires granting the `photos` permission at launch time and then interacting with the system photo picker sheet that appears above the app's view hierarchy. The system picker uses `by.system.label()` matchers (iOS) to locate buttons on the native `PHPickerViewController` or `UIImagePickerController`. Tap `Choose Library` to open the picker, then tap the first available photo cell (identified by `by.system.label('Photo')` or an index-qualified `by.system.label().atIndex(0)`), and then assert that the selected image preview renders in your app's `Image` component. On Android, use `by.type('android.widget.ImageView')` scoped to the system gallery intent activity.

```typescript
describe('Profile photo selection', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({
      newInstance: true,
      permissions: {
        camera: 'YES',
        photos: 'YES',
        medialibrary: 'YES',
      },
    });
    await waitFor(element(by.id('screen-profile-edit')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(8000);
  });

  it('selects a photo from the library and shows the preview', async () => {
    await element(by.id('change-avatar-btn')).tap();

    // iOS system action sheet — tap "Choose from Library"
    await waitFor(element(by.system.label('Choose Library')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(5000);
    await element(by.system.label('Choose Library')).tap();

    // PHPickerViewController — select the first available photo
    await waitFor(element(by.system.label('Photo')).atIndex(0))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(6000);
    await element(by.system.label('Photo')).atIndex(0).tap();

    // Confirm the picker (PHPicker uses "Add" button, legacy picker uses "Choose")
    if (await element(by.system.label('Add')).exists()) {
      await element(by.system.label('Add')).tap();
    }

    // Assert the preview rendered in the app
    await waitFor(element(by.id('avatar-preview-image')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(6000);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The iOS `PHPickerViewController` introduced in iOS 14 changed the system picker UI compared to the legacy `UIImagePickerController`. The `by.system.label()` strings differ between iOS versions: `'Choose'` (legacy) vs `'Add'` (PHPicker). Add a conditional existence check (`element(by.system.label('Add')).exists()`) to handle both picker variants within the same test without branching on the OS version number, which is brittle across Simulator configurations.

---

### Pattern 345 — `jest.retryTimes(n, { logErrorsBeforeRetry: true })` scoped per `describe` block with Detox `afterEach` cleanup to prevent leaked state from causing silent retry masking [community]

Jest's `retryTimes` option can be set inside a `beforeAll` or at the top of a describe block using `jest.retryTimes(2, { logErrorsBeforeRetry: true })`. The `logErrorsBeforeRetry: true` option (added in Jest 29.7) logs the failure reason before retrying, which prevents the retry from silently masking flaky infrastructure errors that should be investigated. Pair `retryTimes` with a thorough `afterEach` cleanup (app state reset or `reloadReactNative()`) to ensure each retry starts from a clean state. Without cleanup, a retry may start from a screen that the previous attempt left in a partially-completed state, causing the retry to fail at a different assertion than the original failure.

```typescript
describe('Checkout flow — retry on infrastructure flakiness only', () => {
  // Limit retries to 2; log first error before retrying
  jest.retryTimes(2, { logErrorsBeforeRetry: true });

  afterEach(async () => {
    // Full app reset between retries to prevent partial checkout state
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: false });
    await element(by.id('cancel-order-btn')).tap().catch(() => {
      // Ignore if cancel btn not visible (clean state already)
    });
  });

  it('completes checkout and shows order confirmation', async () => {
    await element(by.id('product-item-0')).tap();
    await element(by.id('add-to-cart-btn')).tap();
    await element(by.id('go-to-cart-btn')).tap();
    await element(by.id('checkout-btn')).tap();
    await element(by.id('confirm-order-btn')).tap();

    await waitFor(element(by.id('order-confirmation-screen')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(12000);

    const attrs = await element(by.id('order-number-label')).getAttributes();
    expect(attrs.text).toMatch(/^ORD-\d{6}$/);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `jest.retryTimes` is a coarse instrument — it retries the entire test on any failure, including genuine app regression failures. Set `logErrorsBeforeRetry: true` as a mandatory practice and review retry-triggered CI run logs weekly. Establish a policy: if a test retries more than 5% of the time over a two-week window, it is required to be fixed rather than retained with retries.

---

### Pattern 346 — `element(by.id('webview')).tap({ x, y })` with `by.web()` hybrid approach for testing React Native screens that embed a `WebView` with a partially-interactable web UI alongside native elements [community]

Detox 20.x's `by.web()` API targets DOM elements inside a `WebView` using CSS selectors or XPath, but it requires the `WebView` to be fully loaded and its `id` prop to match the Detox WebView registration. When the `WebView` embeds a third-party web app that cannot be modified to add test hooks, combine `element.tap({ x, y })` with known pixel offsets derived from the web layout to trigger clicks, and use `element.getAttributes()` on the native `WebView` wrapper to read load progress. Reserve `by.web()` for first-party web UIs where you can add `data-testid` attributes to DOM elements.

```typescript
describe('Hybrid screen — native + embedded WebView', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: false });
    await element(by.id('open-help-center-btn')).tap();
    // Wait for the WebView to finish loading (native progress indicator)
    await waitFor(element(by.id('webview-load-progress')))
      .not.toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(15000);
  });

  it('interacts with a native header button above the WebView', async () => {
    await expect(element(by.id('help-close-btn'))).toBeVisible();
    await element(by.id('help-close-btn')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('screen-home'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
  });

  it('taps a known DOM element via by.web() on a first-party WebView', async () => {
    // by.web() targets DOM elements — requires data-testid in the web app
    await element(by.id('faq-webview'))
      .web.element(by.web.cssSelector('[data-testid="faq-category-billing"]'))
      .tap();

    await waitFor(
      element(by.id('faq-webview'))
        .web.element(by.web.cssSelector('[data-testid="billing-articles-list"]'))
    ).toExist().withTimeout(5000);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `by.web()` queries traverse the DOM via the `WKWebView` (iOS) or `WebView` (Android) JavaScript bridge. Bridge round-trips add 50–200 ms per query, making deep DOM traversals slow in tight assertion loops. For asserting that a web page loaded to a specific route, reading the native URL bar via `getAttributes().value` on the `WebView` element (if exposed) is faster than a `by.web` DOM query. Reserve `by.web` for interaction flows, not just existence checks.

---

### Pattern 347 — `device.launchApp({ userDefaults: { 'onboarding_completed': true } })` for skipping multi-screen onboarding flows in E2E tests that target authenticated post-onboarding screens [official]

iOS `userDefaults` injection via `launchApp` sets values in `NSUserDefaults` before the app's JavaScript bundle loads. This is the fastest and most reliable way to skip UI flows (onboarding, permissions prompts, tutorial overlays) that are gated on a persisted boolean. On Android, use `launchApp({ launchArgs: { onboarding_completed: '1' } })` and read the value via `NativeModules.LaunchArgs` in your app code. Always pair `userDefaults` injection with a `device.clearUserNotifications()` and `device.launchApp({ delete: false })` strategy: only inject flags, do not combine with `delete: true` which wipes all app data and would make the `userDefaults` injection redundant.

```typescript
describe('Home feed — post-onboarding user', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({
      newInstance: true,
      userDefaults: {
        onboarding_completed: true,
        push_permission_prompt_shown: true,
        app_review_prompt_shown: true, // suppress review prompt during tests
      },
    });
    await waitFor(element(by.id('screen-home-feed')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(10000);
  });

  it('shows the personalized feed without any onboarding overlay', async () => {
    await expect(element(by.id('onboarding-overlay'))).not.toBeVisible();
    await expect(element(by.id('home-feed-list'))).toBeVisible();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('feed-item-0'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(6000);
  });

  it('tapping a feed item navigates to the article screen', async () => {
    await element(by.id('feed-item-0')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('screen-article'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
    await expect(element(by.id('article-title-heading'))).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `userDefaults` injection bypasses the onboarding flow entirely, so it cannot catch regression bugs in the onboarding-to-home-feed transition itself. Maintain one dedicated onboarding E2E test suite that does NOT use `userDefaults` injection and runs the full onboarding flow, even if it is slower. Reserve `userDefaults` injection for all other suites that are testing post-onboarding product behavior.

---

### Pattern 348 — Custom `DetoxCircusEnvironment` `setup()` override for seeding global test data via an authenticated REST call before the first test in a suite, avoiding per-test `beforeEach` overhead for static fixture data [community]

`DetoxCircusEnvironment.setup()` is called once per worker before any test runs. Override it to perform async setup that would otherwise require a slow per-test `beforeEach`: authenticate with your staging API, seed required fixture data (user accounts, product catalogue, feature flags), and store the result in environment variables for consumption by test helpers. This pattern is especially useful for CI pipelines where an API seeding call takes 500–2000 ms — running it once per worker instead of once per test saves significant CI time on suites with many tests.

```typescript
// e2e/environment.ts
import { DetoxCircusEnvironment } from 'detox/runners/jest';

export default class CustomEnvironment extends DetoxCircusEnvironment {
  async setup(): Promise<void> {
    await super.setup();

    // Seed fixture user once per worker — persists for all tests in the worker
    const resp = await fetch('https://staging-api.yourapp.com/test/seed-user', {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', 'x-test-token': process.env.E2E_SEED_TOKEN! },
      body: JSON.stringify({ role: 'premium', planExpiry: '2027-01-01' }),
    });
    const { userId, authToken } = await resp.json();

    // Store in process.env so test helpers can read them via device.appLaunchArgs.modify()
    process.env.E2E_USER_ID = userId;
    process.env.E2E_AUTH_TOKEN = authToken;
  }

  async teardown(): Promise<void> {
    // Clean up seeded data after all tests in this worker finish
    if (process.env.E2E_USER_ID) {
      await fetch(`https://staging-api.yourapp.com/test/cleanup-user/${process.env.E2E_USER_ID}`, {
        method: 'DELETE',
        headers: { 'x-test-token': process.env.E2E_SEED_TOKEN! },
      }).catch(() => { /* best-effort cleanup */ });
    }
    await super.teardown();
  }
}
```

```typescript
// detox.config.js
module.exports = {
  testRunner: {
    $0: 'jest',
    args: { config: 'e2e/jest.config.js' },
  },
};

// e2e/jest.config.js
module.exports = {
  testEnvironment: './environment.ts',
  // ... other jest config
};
```

**Tradeoff.** Because `setup()` runs once per Jest worker and Detox can spin up multiple workers for parallel execution, each worker independently seeds its own test user. Ensure your staging API generates unique user IDs per seed call (do not use a fixed `test-user@example.com` email) to avoid inter-worker state collision when parallel workers try to modify the same seeded user concurrently.

---

### Pattern 349 — `device.captureViewHierarchy(name)` called proactively on `element-not-found` failures via `handleTestEvent('test_fn_failure')` to produce a `.viewhierarchy` artifact that can be opened in Xcode for visual debugging of accessibility tree gaps [official]

`device.captureViewHierarchy()` saves the complete native accessibility tree as an Xcode `.viewhierarchy` file. Combined with the `handleTestEvent` override in `DetoxCircusEnvironment`, you can trigger a capture automatically whenever any test fails with an `"Element not found"` error, before the failure is reported to Jest. Xcode's View Hierarchy Debugger opens the `.viewhierarchy` file and allows three-dimensional inspection of the layer stack, which is the fastest way to determine whether a missing element is hidden by an overlay, clipped by a container, or genuinely absent from the tree. This is more actionable than a screenshot for `element-not-found` failures because screenshots do not show invisible or off-screen elements.

```typescript
// e2e/environment.ts
import { DetoxCircusEnvironment } from 'detox/runners/jest';
import { device } from 'detox';

export default class CustomEnvironment extends DetoxCircusEnvironment {
  async handleTestEvent(event: any, state: any): Promise<void> {
    if (event.name === 'test_fn_failure') {
      const testName = state.currentlyRunningTest?.name
        ?? 'unknown-test';
      const safeName = testName.replace(/[^a-z0-9_-]/gi, '_').slice(0, 60);
      const errorMsg: string = event.error?.message ?? '';

      // Only capture hierarchy on element-not-found; screenshots on other failures
      if (errorMsg.includes('Element not found') || errorMsg.includes('No view found')) {
        try {
          await device.captureViewHierarchy(`failure-hierarchy-${safeName}`);
        } catch {
          // captureViewHierarchy may itself fail (e.g., app crashed) — don't mask original
        }
      } else {
        try {
          await device.takeScreenshot(`failure-screenshot-${safeName}`);
        } catch {
          // ignore secondary screenshot failure
        }
      }
    }

    await super.handleTestEvent(event, state);
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `.viewhierarchy` files are iOS Simulator only — Android does not have a Detox-level equivalent. For Android `"No view found"` failures, `device.takeScreenshot()` plus `adb shell uiautomator dump` (via a `Bash` call) produces a similar diagnostic artifact. On iOS, `.viewhierarchy` files can be 2–10 MB each; add a CI artifact size cap or a 30-day retention policy to prevent storage costs from accumulating on suites with frequent failures.

---

### Gotcha 254 — `device.adjustDateToMock(isoDate)` does not affect the JavaScript `Date` object's return value on Android because Android lacks an equivalent of the iOS Simulator `simctl` clock override, meaning `new Date().toISOString()` in JS still returns the real system time even after the call [community]

**Root cause**: On iOS Simulator, `device.adjustDateToMock()` calls `xcrun simctl` under the hood, which overrides the Mach kernel's clock source. On Android Emulator, Detox has no equivalent low-level clock override available via the ADB or Emulator control protocol. The call is documented as iOS-only in the Detox source, but the TypeScript type definitions do not emit a compile-time error if you call it on Android, making it silently a no-op. Any test that calls `device.adjustDateToMock()` without a `device.getPlatform() === 'ios'` guard will report a false pass on iOS CI and a false fail on Android CI because the app will receive different date values on each platform.

```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN — calling adjustDateToMock on Android is a no-op; no error thrown
await device.adjustDateToMock('2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z');
await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
// On Android: new Date() in JS still returns today's real date
// Test may pass or fail depending on whether today happens to satisfy the assertion

// CORRECT — platform-guard the call
if (device.getPlatform() === 'ios') {
  await device.adjustDateToMock('2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z');
} else {
  // Android: inject the mock date via a launchArg and consume it in JS with
  // global.__e2eMockDate = new Date(NativeModules.LaunchArgs.mockDate ?? Date.now())
  await device.appLaunchArgs.modify({ mockDate: '2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z' });
}
await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
```

**WHY this matters:** Tests that silently pass on iOS CI and fail on Android CI (or vice versa) create the dangerous perception that the tested feature works on one platform and is broken on the other. The actual root cause — a missing platform guard around a no-op API call — is not visible in the test output because no exception is thrown. Always consult the Detox API documentation note on platform support before using `device.*` methods in cross-platform test suites, and add a platform guard as the first line of any test that calls a platform-exclusive Detox API.

---

### Gotcha 255 — `device.pressBack()` fires the Android `BackHandler` listeners registered via `BackHandler.addEventListener` in LIFO order, so a third-party SDK listener registered after your app's listener receives the event first and may consume it, preventing the app's listener from running and causing `pressBack()` to appear to have no effect [community]

**Root cause**: React Native's `BackHandler` uses a last-in-first-out listener stack. If a third-party navigation SDK (e.g., `react-navigation/native`, a deep-link library, or an in-app browser) registers its own `hardwareBackPress` listener after your app code does, that SDK listener runs first on `device.pressBack()`. If the SDK listener returns `true` (meaning it consumed the event), your app's listener never runs. In tests, this manifests as `device.pressBack()` appearing to do nothing — the `BackHandler` stack ran, but the "wrong" listener handled it. Debugging requires logging all registered listeners, which React Native does not expose natively. The workaround is to call `device.pressBack()` twice in sequence: once to trigger the SDK-level listener and once to trigger your app-level listener, or to ensure your app registers its listener after the SDK does (LIFO order).

```typescript
// SYMPTOM: pressBack() has no effect on the "Exit confirmation" dialog
await element(by.id('start-sensitive-flow-btn')).tap();
await waitFor(element(by.id('exit-confirmation-dialog'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

await device.pressBack(); // This fires the SDK's listener, which closes an internal overlay
// The exit dialog is still visible — SDK consumed the Back press

// FIX: press Back a second time after the SDK has processed its event
await device.pressBack();
await waitFor(element(by.id('exit-confirmation-dialog')))
  .not.toBeVisible()
  .withTimeout(3000);

// BETTER FIX: add an explicit waitFor between the two presses to ensure
// the SDK overlay closes before the second Back press
await device.pressBack(); // First: SDK listener
await waitFor(element(by.id('sdk-internal-overlay')))
  .not.toBeVisible()
  .withTimeout(2000)
  .catch(() => {}); // SDK overlay may not always be present
await device.pressBack(); // Second: app listener
```

**WHY this matters:** Silent consumption of `device.pressBack()` by a third-party SDK is one of the hardest Detox failures to diagnose because the test sees no error — the `pressBack()` call succeeds without throwing, but the expected UI transition does not occur. The failure is indistinguishable from a genuine bug in the app's `BackHandler` logic. Always add a `waitFor` assertion immediately after `pressBack()` to verify the expected state change, rather than relying on the absence of an error from the `pressBack()` call itself.

---

### Gotcha 256 — `device.setOrientation('landscape')` does not trigger `useWindowDimensions` re-renders in components that read dimensions only in a `useMemo` with an empty dependency array `[]` because the `Dimensions` event listener is never subscribed, causing the component to render with stale portrait dimensions after the orientation change [community]

**Root cause**: React Native's `Dimensions.addEventListener('change', handler)` is the mechanism by which `useWindowDimensions` notifies subscribers of orientation changes. Components that cache dimension values in `useMemo([])` or in module-scope constants (`const { width, height } = Dimensions.get('window')` at the top of a file) are initialized once and never re-read from the `Dimensions` event. After `device.setOrientation('landscape')`, these components still render using portrait dimensions, producing layout bugs that are invisible in the Detox test because the test asserts on `testID` visibility rather than pixel-accurate frame sizes. The bug is only caught if the test reads `getAttributes().frame.width` and asserts against the expected landscape width.

```typescript
// COMPONENT BUG: stale dimension value in useMemo([])
// const { width } = useMemo(() => Dimensions.get('window'), []); // Never re-runs!

// COMPONENT FIX: use useWindowDimensions hook — subscribes to Dimensions events
// const { width } = useWindowDimensions(); // Correct

// TEST — catch the stale-dimensions bug
it('re-renders with landscape dimensions after orientation change', async () => {
  await device.setOrientation('landscape');
  await waitFor(element(by.id('responsive-card'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);

  const attrs = await element(by.id('responsive-card')).getAttributes();
  const { width: screenWidth } = await device.getUIDeviceWindowSize?.() ?? { width: 844 };

  // In landscape, card should span most of the screen width
  // A stale useMemo([]) will give portrait width (~390) in a landscape test
  expect(attrs.frame.width).toBeGreaterThan(screenWidth * 0.8);
});
```

**WHY this matters:** Layout bugs caused by stale `Dimensions` values only appear in E2E tests if the test explicitly asserts on frame sizes. Most Detox tests check visibility and text content, not pixel dimensions. This gotcha explains why a feature can pass all Detox tests and still display broken layout in QA or production when a user rotates their device — the Detox tests never exercised the `Dimensions` update path. Always include at least one orientation-change test per screen that has responsive layout logic, and assert `frame.width` against an expected landscape value.

---

### Gotcha 257 — `element(by.id('webview')).web.element(by.web.cssSelector('...')).tap()` throws `"WebView is still loading"` when called immediately after a navigation that causes the `WebView` to start a new page load, because Detox does not automatically wait for `WebView` load completion the way it waits for RN navigation transitions [community]

**Root cause**: Detox's idle synchronization mechanism tracks RN bridge activity (JS Promise queues, `setTimeout`, `setInterval`) and native animation frames. It does not track `WKWebView` or `WebView` page-load states — these are external async operations that complete independently of the RN bridge idle state. When a test taps a link that causes the `WebView` to navigate to a new URL, Detox's synchronization considers the RN bridge idle as soon as the tap event is dispatched, and proceeds to the next `by.web()` call while the `WebView` is still loading the new page. The fix is to wait for a DOM element that only appears after the page has fully loaded, using `waitFor(element(by.id('webview')).web.element(by.web.cssSelector('[data-testid="page-loaded"]'))).toExist().withTimeout(10000)` as a loading sentinel before interacting with the new page's DOM.

```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN — by.web() query immediately after navigation tap
await element(by.id('faq-webview'))
  .web.element(by.web.cssSelector('[data-testid="category-billing"]'))
  .tap(); // Causes WebView to navigate to /billing page

// Error: WebView is still loading — called too soon after navigation
await element(by.id('faq-webview'))
  .web.element(by.web.cssSelector('[data-testid="billing-article-0"]'))
  .tap();

// CORRECT — wait for a DOM sentinel that confirms the new page has loaded
await element(by.id('faq-webview'))
  .web.element(by.web.cssSelector('[data-testid="category-billing"]'))
  .tap();

await waitFor(
  element(by.id('faq-webview'))
    .web.element(by.web.cssSelector('[data-testid="billing-page-ready"]'))
).toExist().withTimeout(10000); // Wait for new page's sentinel element

await element(by.id('faq-webview'))
  .web.element(by.web.cssSelector('[data-testid="billing-article-0"]'))
  .tap(); // Now safe — page is loaded
```

**WHY this matters:** `"WebView is still loading"` errors appear intermittently because network speed varies: on fast CI runners the new page loads before Detox issues the next query; on slow runners or degraded network conditions it does not. Without a `waitFor` sentinel, these failures are categorized as network flakiness and masked with `jest.retryTimes()` rather than fixed at the root cause. Add a `data-testid="page-ready"` marker to every first-party `WebView`-embedded page that the E2E suite targets, and always use it as the loading gate.

---

### Gotcha 258 — `device.launchApp({ languageAndLocale: { language: 'ar' } })` on Android Emulator does not change `I18nManager.isRTL` to `true` in the app's JavaScript layer when the React Native app was built with `forceRTL: false` hardcoded in the app's root component or `react-native.config.js`, because the hardcoded flag overrides the system locale [community]

**Root cause**: React Native reads `I18nManager.isRTL` from the system locale at app startup, but this value can be overridden by calling `I18nManager.forceRTL(false)` in the app's root `index.js` or `App.tsx` initialization block. Some apps do this to suppress RTL during early development or to maintain LTR layout for specific product reasons. When `forceRTL(false)` is present, launching the app with `languageAndLocale: { language: 'ar' }` sets the system locale to Arabic but `I18nManager.isRTL` remains `false` in JS, so RTL layout styles are never applied. The test will observe that layout did not mirror and may incorrectly conclude that the Android RTL feature is broken when it is actually disabled by the app's own code.

```typescript
// SYMPTOM: launching with Arabic locale does not trigger RTL layout
await device.launchApp({
  newInstance: true,
  languageAndLocale: { language: 'ar', locale: 'ar_SA' },
});
// I18nManager.isRTL === false in the app — forceRTL(false) overrides the locale
// RTL assertions fail, but it's not a Detox bug

// DIAGNOSTIC PATTERN — read the actual RTL state via a testID-exposed element
// In the app: <View testID={`rtl-state-${I18nManager.isRTL}`} />
await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
await waitFor(element(by.id('rtl-state-true')))
  .toExist()
  .withTimeout(5000)
  .catch(async () => {
    const rtlFalseExists = await element(by.id('rtl-state-false')).exists();
    if (rtlFalseExists) {
      throw new Error('RTL was not enabled despite Arabic locale — check forceRTL() call in app root');
    }
  });
```

**WHY this matters:** The disconnect between the system locale (Arabic, RTL) and the app's JS `I18nManager.isRTL` value produces tests that pass on one CI configuration (where the app was built without `forceRTL` override) and fail on another (where a different build variant has it). Rather than debugging `setOrientation` or `languageAndLocale` calls, the root cause investigation should start with the app code. Add a diagnostic `testID` that exposes the current `I18nManager.isRTL` value so that E2E tests can assert the RTL state before testing layout behavior, rather than inferring it from frame coordinates.

## Updated Anti-Patterns Checklist (Cycle 46 additions)

| Anti-Pattern | Fix |
|---|---|
| Calling `device.adjustDateToMock(isoDate)` in an Android test without a `device.getPlatform() === 'ios'` guard — silently a no-op on Android, causing the test to pass or fail based on the real system date | Platform-guard the call; inject mock date via `device.appLaunchArgs.modify({ mockDate: isoDate })` on Android and consume via `NativeModules.LaunchArgs` (Gotcha 254, Pattern 335) |
| Omitting `afterEach(() => device.setOrientation('portrait'))` after orientation-change tests — subsequent tests in the same worker run in landscape mode and fail on layout-sensitive assertions | Always reset orientation in `afterEach`; orientation state is not restored by `reloadReactNative()` (Pattern 336) |
| Calling `device.pressBack()` once and expecting it to dismiss an app-level dialog when a third-party SDK has registered a `BackHandler` listener after the app — SDK consumes the Back press silently | Add a `waitFor` assertion after each `pressBack()` to verify state change; issue a second `pressBack()` if the SDK overlay must be dismissed first (Gotcha 255, Pattern 338) |
| Using `by.web()` immediately after a `WebView` navigation tap — throws `"WebView is still loading"` intermittently because WebView page-load is not tracked by Detox idle synchronization | Add a `waitFor` DOM sentinel (`data-testid="page-ready"`) to every first-party WebView page and gate all post-navigation `by.web()` queries on it (Gotcha 257, Pattern 346) |
| Hard-coding `useMemo([])` to cache `Dimensions.get('window')` in a responsive component — cached value never updates after `device.setOrientation()`, causing stale portrait dimensions in landscape tests | Replace `useMemo(() => Dimensions.get('window'), [])` with `useWindowDimensions()` hook; add an orientation-change E2E test that asserts `frame.width > screenWidth * 0.8` (Gotcha 256) |
| Launching with `languageAndLocale: { language: 'ar' }` and asserting RTL layout without verifying `I18nManager.isRTL` is actually `true` in JS — `forceRTL(false)` in app root silently overrides the locale | Expose `I18nManager.isRTL` via a diagnostic `testID` and assert it before RTL layout assertions; investigate app root for `forceRTL(false)` calls if RTL is not enabled (Gotcha 258, Pattern 343) |
