## Cycle 47 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 350 — `element(by.id('input')).tapReturnKey()` for submitting forms via the keyboard's Return/Done action and asserting the resulting navigation or validation state without tapping a separate submit button [official]

`tapReturnKey()` simulates the keyboard Return key press on a focused `TextInput`, triggering `onSubmitEditing` handlers and keyboard-return-based form submission. It is the correct action to use when the submit button only becomes enabled after all fields are valid — tapping the button directly before field completion would test the wrong path. After calling `tapReturnKey()`, the keyboard is dismissed and the app transitions to the post-submission state; always follow with a `waitFor` assertion on the outcome element rather than relying on a fixed `sleep`. On iOS, `tapReturnKey()` triggers both `onSubmitEditing` and the `blurOnSubmit` blur event; on Android it matches the IME action defined by `returnKeyType`.

```typescript
// Pattern: tapReturnKey() for form submission via keyboard
it('submits login form via keyboard Return key', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });

  await element(by.id('email-input')).tap();
  await element(by.id('email-input')).typeText('user@example.com');
  await element(by.id('email-input')).tapReturnKey(); // advances focus to password field

  await element(by.id('password-input')).typeText('s3cr3t!');
  await element(by.id('password-input')).tapReturnKey(); // submits the form

  // Keyboard is now dismissed; wait for the success screen
  await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(6000);

  // Assert the keyboard is gone (no keyboard-overlap element visible)
  await expect(element(by.id('keyboard-avoid-placeholder'))).not.toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `tapReturnKey()` only works on a focused `TextInput`. If the field is not already focused, the call is silently ignored on iOS and throws on Android. Always call `.tap()` first to ensure focus, or chain fields via `tapReturnKey()` on an earlier field that has `returnKeyType="next"`. Do not use for multi-line `TextInput` with `blurOnSubmit={false}`, where Return inserts a newline instead of submitting.

---

### Pattern 351 — `device.appLaunchArgs.modify({ featureFlag: '1' })` between `describe` blocks for toggling runtime feature flags without re-launching the app from a cold start, reducing suite time for feature-flag-gated UI branches [official]

`device.appLaunchArgs.modify()` merges new key/value pairs into the existing launch argument bag. When called between `describe` blocks in the same Detox session (without `newInstance: true`), the changes take effect on the next `device.launchApp()` or `device.reloadReactNative()` call within that `beforeAll`/`beforeEach`. This is significantly faster than a full cold-start launch (~3–5 s) versus `reloadReactNative()` (~0.8–1.5 s). The pattern enables a single test file to cover both `featureFlag=0` and `featureFlag=1` branches. Always call `device.appLaunchArgs.reset()` in an `afterAll` to prevent flag contamination from leaking into subsequent spec files loaded by the same Jest worker.

```typescript
// Pattern: feature-flag toggling with appLaunchArgs.modify() across describe blocks
describe('Checkout flow — legacy UI', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    device.appLaunchArgs.modify({ USE_NEW_CHECKOUT: '0' });
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  });

  afterAll(async () => {
    device.appLaunchArgs.reset(); // prevent leak into next describe
  });

  it('shows legacy payment summary card', async () => {
    await waitFor(element(by.id('legacy-payment-summary'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
  });
});

describe('Checkout flow — new UI', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    device.appLaunchArgs.modify({ USE_NEW_CHECKOUT: '1' });
    await device.reloadReactNative(); // hot-reload is enough — no cold start
  });

  afterAll(async () => {
    device.appLaunchArgs.reset();
  });

  it('shows redesigned checkout stepper', async () => {
    await waitFor(element(by.id('checkout-stepper'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `reloadReactNative()` does not reset native module state (Keychain, SharedPreferences, MMKV). If the feature flag is read by a native module at startup, use `device.launchApp({ newInstance: true })` instead. Also note that `appLaunchArgs.modify()` accumulates — calling it twice without `reset()` in between keeps both sets of args. Use `appLaunchArgs.reset()` + `appLaunchArgs.modify()` in sequence when you need a clean slate rather than a merge.

---

### Pattern 352 — `by.web.cssSelector()` vs `by.web.xpath()` selection strategy in `element(by.id('webview')).web` queries, with a fallback decision tree for when each locator is appropriate [official]

Detox's `by.web` API exposes `cssSelector`, `xpath`, `name`, `id`, `className`, `tag`, and `href` locators. `cssSelector` should be the default choice: it is fast, readable, and maps directly to `data-testid` attributes applied by the web team. `xpath` is a last resort for legacy web content where CSS selectors cannot uniquely identify elements — it is 3–8× slower than CSS on large DOMs and brittle when markup changes. The `by.web.id(id)` locator targets the HTML `id` attribute (not `testID`), which is faster than `cssSelector('#id')` because it uses the browser's `getElementById` fast path. Always assert that the `WebView` is loaded before issuing any `by.web` query, and scope queries to the smallest unambiguous selector to minimize DOM-traversal cost.

```typescript
// Pattern: by.web locator selection strategy
const webview = element(by.id('content-webview'));

// Tier 1 — Prefer: CSS data-testid (fastest + most stable)
await webview.web.element(by.web.cssSelector('[data-testid="submit-btn"]')).tap();

// Tier 2 — Use when CSS is ambiguous: HTML id (uses getElementById fast path)
await webview.web.element(by.web.id('main-heading')).tap();

// Tier 3 — Fallback for legacy content without data-testid or stable id
const legacySelector = '//form[@class="legacy-form"]/button[contains(text(),"Submit")]';
await webview.web.element(by.web.xpath(legacySelector)).tap();

// Always gate on a load sentinel before any by.web query
await waitFor(
  webview.web.element(by.web.cssSelector('[data-testid="page-ready"]'))
).toExist().withTimeout(8000);

// Reading text content from a web element
const heading = await webview.web.element(by.web.cssSelector('h1')).getText();
expect(heading).toBe('Welcome');
```

**Tradeoff.** `by.web.xpath()` traverses the full DOM tree and re-parses the XPath expression on every call — in pages with 1,000+ nodes this can add 200–800 ms per query. Avoid using XPath in loops or for multiple queries in the same test. `by.web.cssSelector('[data-testid]')` requires the web team to add `data-testid` attributes, which creates a coordination dependency. Establish a shared `data-testid` naming convention across the mobile and web codebases early in the project rather than retrofitting.

---

### Pattern 353 — `element(by.id('map-view')).pinch(scale, speed, angle)` for testing pinch-to-zoom on `react-native-maps` and other gesture-enabled views that use `PinchGestureHandler` from RNGH [official]

`pinch(scale, speed, angle)` synthesizes a two-finger pinch gesture with a normalized scale factor (`> 1.0` zooms in, `< 1.0` zooms out), a speed string (`'slow'` | `'fast'`), and an optional angle in degrees. On iOS it translates to a `UIPinchGestureRecognizer` simulation; on Android it injects two pointer events via `MotionEvent.ACTION_POINTER_DOWN`. The `angle` parameter rotates the pinch axis — `0` is horizontal, `90` is vertical — which matters for testing rotation-aware views. After a pinch, always assert the zoom level via a `testID`-exposed label or a coordinate-based frame measurement rather than trusting a fixed `sleep` for the animation to settle.

```typescript
// Pattern: pinch-to-zoom on a map view with zoom-level assertion
it('zooms into the map on pinch-in gesture', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });

  // Ensure the map is loaded and idle before gesturing
  await waitFor(element(by.id('map-ready-indicator')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(8000);

  // Read initial zoom label before pinch
  const beforeAttrs = await element(by.id('zoom-level-label')).getAttributes();
  const initialZoom = parseFloat((beforeAttrs as ElementAttributes).text ?? '0');

  // Pinch in — scale > 1.0 zooms in; use 'slow' to prevent gesture drop
  await element(by.id('map-view')).pinch(2.0, 'slow', 0);

  // Wait for zoom animation to settle (map tile re-fetch may add latency)
  await waitFor(element(by.id('zoom-level-label')))
    .toHaveText(String(initialZoom + 2))
    .withTimeout(5000);

  // Pinch out back to original zoom
  await element(by.id('map-view')).pinch(0.5, 'slow', 0);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `pinch()` on Android requires API level 24+ for reliable two-pointer injection. On API 23 and below, the emulator may drop one of the two pointers, making the gesture behave as a single tap. Add an API-level guard (`if (device.getPlatform() === 'android' && (await device.getAPILevel()) < 24) return;`). Also, RNGH `PinchGestureHandler` may conflict with a parent `ScrollView` scroll handler — enable `disableSynchronization()` around the pinch call if the gesture causes Detox's synchronization to time out waiting for the gesture-active state to clear.

---

### Pattern 354 — `device.setNetworkConditions(null)` as an explicit network-condition reset idiom in `afterEach` to prevent degraded-network settings from leaking into subsequent tests [official]

`device.setNetworkConditions({ downloadSpeed, uploadSpeed, latency })` applies simulated network throttling via the iOS Simulator's network link conditioner. Passing `null` as the argument resets the conditions to full-speed unthrottled networking. Without an explicit reset, a test that sets degraded conditions and then fails before completing its `afterEach` cleanup leaves the simulator in a throttled state for all subsequent tests in the same worker, causing spurious `withTimeout` failures that look like app bugs rather than test infrastructure issues. Always wrap both the `setNetworkConditions` call and its `null` reset in a `try/finally` block.

```typescript
// Pattern: network condition reset in afterEach with try/finally guard
describe('Offline and degraded network states', () => {
  afterEach(async () => {
    // Always reset — even if the test failed mid-way through
    if (device.getPlatform() === 'ios') {
      await device.setNetworkConditions(null);
    }
  });

  it('shows skeleton loader under 3G network conditions', async () => {
    if (device.getPlatform() !== 'ios') {
      return; // setNetworkConditions is iOS Simulator only
    }
    try {
      await device.setNetworkConditions({
        downloadSpeed: 400_000,  // 400 Kbps — EDGE
        uploadSpeed: 100_000,
        latency: 400,
      });
      await device.reloadReactNative();

      await waitFor(element(by.id('skeleton-loader')))
        .toBeVisible()
        .withTimeout(3000);
    } finally {
      await device.setNetworkConditions(null); // belt-and-suspenders reset
    }
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `device.setNetworkConditions()` is only available on iOS Simulator (uses the Network Link Conditioner infrastructure). On Android Emulator the API is silently ignored — use `adb shell tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 400ms` via `execSync` as an alternative, but note that this requires root access on the emulator and must be reverted explicitly. For cross-platform network degradation testing, a test-mode mock server with configurable response delay is more portable.

---

### Pattern 355 — `waitFor(element(by.id('modal'))).not.toBeVisible().withTimeout(n)` as the canonical pattern for asserting modal and bottom-sheet dismissal, with platform-specific timeout calibration [official]

Asserting that an overlay has dismissed correctly requires a `waitFor(...).not.toBeVisible()` check rather than immediately asserting on the content behind the overlay. On iOS, modals use `UIViewControllerTransitioningDelegate` dismiss animations that run for 300–400 ms; on Android, `Dialog` close animations run for 200–300 ms. Without a `waitFor` wait, the test proceeds while the overlay's dismissal animation is still in-flight and the element below it is still obscured, causing the next tap or visibility assertion to fail intermittently. The platform-calibrated timeout should be at least `600` ms to handle slow CI runners with software rendering.

```typescript
// Pattern: canonical modal-dismissal assertion
async function dismissAndWait(modalTestId: string, timeoutMs = 3000): Promise<void> {
  // Trigger dismissal
  await element(by.id('modal-close-btn')).tap();

  // Wait for the dismiss animation to complete
  await waitFor(element(by.id(modalTestId)))
    .not.toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(timeoutMs);
}

it('dismisses the share sheet and returns to the content screen', async () => {
  await waitFor(element(by.id('share-btn'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
  await element(by.id('share-btn')).tap();

  // Wait for the share sheet to appear
  await waitFor(element(by.id('share-sheet-modal'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

  // Dismiss and confirm it is gone
  await dismissAndWait('share-sheet-modal');

  // Now safe to interact with the content below
  await waitFor(element(by.id('content-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);
  await element(by.id('content-action-btn')).tap();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `not.toBeVisible()` passes as soon as the element's `isVisible` flag returns `false`, which can happen before the element is fully removed from the view hierarchy (e.g., during a fade-out animation where opacity reaches zero before the view unmounts). If a subsequent test asserts `not.toExist()` on the same element, add a second `waitFor(...).not.toExist().withTimeout(n)` call. For `@gorhom/bottom-sheet`, `not.toBeVisible()` resolves when the sheet snaps to its collapsed state (height 0), not when it is detached from the layout tree — prefer `not.toExist()` for full removal assurance.

---

### Pattern 356 — `DetoxCircusEnvironment` `teardown()` override for cleaning up server-side test data created during `setup()`, with a dedicated REST DELETE call using the seed IDs stored in `this.testSessionData` [community]

When `DetoxCircusEnvironment.setup()` seeds test data (users, orders, inventory records) via REST API calls, the corresponding `teardown()` must delete that data to prevent test pollution across suite runs. The seed IDs should be stored on `this` (or in a module-level `Map` keyed by worker ID) during `setup()` and read back in `teardown()`. Omitting `teardown()` data cleanup causes the backend database to accumulate stale E2E test records, which eventually causes unique-constraint violations on seeded email addresses or slugs in subsequent runs. Always call `await super.teardown()` last to allow Detox's native layer to close gracefully after your REST cleanup completes.

```typescript
// custom-environment.ts
import { DetoxCircusEnvironment } from 'detox/runners/jest';

interface TestSessionData {
  userId: string;
  orderId: string;
  authToken: string;
}

export default class CustomEnvironment extends DetoxCircusEnvironment {
  private testSessionData: TestSessionData | null = null;

  override async setup(): Promise<void> {
    await super.setup(); // Detox native setup first

    // Seed a fresh user and order for this worker
    const resp = await fetch(`${process.env.API_BASE_URL}/e2e/seed`, {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify({ workerIndex: process.env.JEST_WORKER_ID }),
    });
    this.testSessionData = await resp.json();
  }

  override async teardown(): Promise<void> {
    // Clean up seeded data before Detox native teardown
    if (this.testSessionData) {
      await fetch(`${process.env.API_BASE_URL}/e2e/seed/${this.testSessionData.userId}`, {
        method: 'DELETE',
        headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${this.testSessionData.authToken}` },
      });
      this.testSessionData = null;
    }

    await super.teardown(); // Detox native teardown last
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** If the REST DELETE call in `teardown()` fails (network error, server 500), `super.teardown()` is not reached, which can leave the Detox native session open and cause the next test run to fail with `"Detox session already in progress"`. Wrap the REST call in a `try/catch` that logs the error but does not rethrow, ensuring `super.teardown()` always executes. Use a dedicated E2E service account with broad delete permissions rather than the seeded user's token, which may expire before teardown.

---

### Pattern 357 — `device.sendUserNotification(payload)` with `badge` and `shouldBeSilent` fields for testing notification badge count display and silent background refresh notification handling [official]

`device.sendUserNotification()` on iOS accepts a payload object whose `badge` field sets the app's home screen badge count. Sending a notification with `badge: 3` while the app is foregrounded then backgrounding the app and returning to the home screen allows the E2E test to assert the badge number via `by.type('XCUIElementTypeStaticText')` inside the SpringBoard app context — or, more practically, to assert that the in-app notification badge UI updates correctly. The `shouldBeSilent: true` flag sends a background-refresh notification without displaying a banner or sound, which triggers the app's `UIApplicationDelegate.didReceiveRemoteNotification(_:fetchCompletionHandler:)` — useful for testing background data sync without user-visible notification side effects.

```typescript
// Pattern: badge count and silent notification testing
it('updates the inbox badge count when a silent notification arrives', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });

  // Wait for initial state — inbox badge shows 0
  await waitFor(element(by.id('inbox-badge'))).not.toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

  // Send a regular notification to increment badge to 1
  await device.sendUserNotification({
    trigger: { type: 'push' },
    title: 'New message',
    body: 'You have a new message',
    badge: 1,
    payload: { messageId: 'msg-001', type: 'INBOX' },
  });

  await waitFor(element(by.id('inbox-badge')))
    .toHaveText('1')
    .withTimeout(3000);

  // Send a silent notification (background data refresh) — badge stays 1
  await device.sendUserNotification({
    trigger: { type: 'push' },
    shouldBeSilent: true,
    payload: { type: 'DATA_REFRESH' },
  });

  // Silent notifications don't change badge — confirm it remains 1
  await expect(element(by.id('inbox-badge'))).toHaveText('1');
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `shouldBeSilent` notifications require the app to have `remote-notification` listed in its `UIBackgroundModes` plist entry; if it is absent, iOS ignores the notification silently and the test passes without exercising the background handler. Verify this plist key exists before adding silent-notification tests to the suite. On Android, `shouldBeSilent` has no equivalent — use a broadcast intent via `device.sendBroadcast()` or a `NativeModules`-bridged event to simulate background data refresh instead.

---

### Pattern 358 — `element(by.id('feed-list')).scrollTo('bottom')` combined with `waitFor` on an `onEndReached` loading indicator for testing paginated `FlatList` infinite scroll behavior end-to-end [official]

`scrollTo('bottom')` on a `FlatList` triggers a single large scroll to the bottom of the currently-rendered content, which fires `onEndReached` when the `onEndReachedThreshold` is crossed. The `onEndReached` callback typically dispatches an API call that appends the next page to the list's data array. After `scrollTo('bottom')`, always wait for the loading spinner that appears at the bottom of the list, then wait for it to disappear (page fetched and rendered), then assert the new content. Calling `scrollTo('bottom')` again after the new page renders scrolls to the new bottom, enabling multi-page traversal in a loop.

```typescript
// Pattern: paginated FlatList infinite scroll testing
async function loadNextPage(listId: string): Promise<void> {
  await element(by.id(listId)).scrollTo('bottom');

  // Wait for the end-of-list loading spinner to appear (onEndReached fired)
  await waitFor(element(by.id('feed-loading-more')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(3000);

  // Wait for spinner to disappear (page loaded and appended)
  await waitFor(element(by.id('feed-loading-more')))
    .not.toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(8000);
}

it('loads three pages of the activity feed', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await waitFor(element(by.id('activity-feed-list'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);

  await loadNextPage('activity-feed-list'); // page 2
  await loadNextPage('activity-feed-list'); // page 3

  // Assert that a known item from page 3 is now visible after scrolling
  await waitFor(element(by.id('feed-item-page3-first')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(5000);
  await expect(element(by.id('feed-item-page3-first'))).toHaveText('Older activity');
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `scrollTo('bottom')` targets the end of the currently-rendered window, not the logical end of the infinite list. On a `FlatList` with `windowSize` set below the default of 21, items near the top may be unmounted before `scrollTo('bottom')` completes, causing the scroll offset to land at a point that no longer corresponds to the end of visible content. Increase `windowSize` in test builds or prefer `element.scroll(pixels, 'down', 0.5, 0.5)` with a large pixel value to ensure `onEndReachedThreshold` is crossed without relying on content-end semantics.

---

### Pattern 359 — `by.id('x').and(by.type('RCTTextInput'))` compound matcher for disambiguating `TextInput` elements from `Text` labels that share the same `testID` due to a third-party component's internal implementation detail [official]

The `.and()` matcher combines two matchers with logical AND, requiring an element to satisfy both conditions simultaneously. It is essential when a third-party component renders both a native `TextInput` and a `Text` label with the same `testID` (for accessibility mirroring), causing `element(by.id('search-input'))` to match two elements and throw `"Multiple elements matched"`. Adding `.and(by.type('RCTTextInput'))` constrains the match to the editable input. On Android, the equivalent type for the standard React Native `TextInput` is `android.widget.EditText`. The `by.type()` class name must be determined by inspecting the view hierarchy via `device.captureViewHierarchy()`.

```typescript
// Pattern: .and() compound matcher to resolve duplicate testID ambiguity
async function typeIntoSearchField(text: string): Promise<void> {
  // Without .and() — throws "Multiple elements matched" if label shares the ID
  // await element(by.id('search-input')).typeText(text); // ANTI-PATTERN

  const nativeClass = device.getPlatform() === 'ios'
    ? 'RCTTextInput'
    : 'android.widget.EditText';

  const inputMatcher = by.id('search-input').and(by.type(nativeClass));

  await element(inputMatcher).tap();
  await element(inputMatcher).clearText();
  await element(inputMatcher).typeText(text);
  await element(inputMatcher).tapReturnKey();
}

it('searches the product catalog by keyword', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await waitFor(element(by.id('search-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

  await typeIntoSearchField('wireless headphones');

  await waitFor(element(by.id('search-results-list')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(6000);

  await expect(element(by.id('search-result-count-label'))).not.toHaveText('0 results');
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Using `by.type()` in `.and()` creates a dependency on the native class name, which can change across React Native versions (e.g., `RCTTextInput` vs `RCTBaseTextInputView` in RN 0.76+ New Architecture). Prefer resolving the root cause — give the label a distinct `testID` such as `search-input-label` — over relying on a type-based disambiguation that couples the test to the internal rendering implementation. Use `.and(by.type())` as a short-term fix while the component fix is in progress.

---

### Pattern 360 — `device.launchApp({ url: 'https://app.example.com/product/123' })` for cold-start universal link testing that verifies the correct deep-link screen is shown before any user interaction occurs [official]

Passing a `url` to `launchApp()` simulates the OS opening the app via a Universal Link (iOS) or App Link (Android) and navigating to the corresponding in-app route. This tests the full cold-start deep-link path: app launch, JS bundle load, navigation initialization, and route resolution — a path that cannot be tested by `device.openURL()` alone when the app is already foregrounded. The `url` must match an associated domain (iOS) or intent filter (Android) configured in the app's native project; if the domain is not configured, the OS opens the URL in Safari/Chrome instead of the app and the test will time out waiting for the in-app screen.

```typescript
// Pattern: cold-start Universal Link testing
it('opens the product detail screen from a Universal Link cold start', async () => {
  // Kill any existing instance before the cold-start test
  await device.terminateApp();

  // Launch via Universal Link — app starts cold and navigates to /product/123
  await device.launchApp({
    url: 'https://app.example.com/product/123',
    newInstance: true,
  });

  // Wait for the JS bundle to load and navigation to resolve
  await waitFor(element(by.id('product-detail-screen')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(8000);

  // Assert the correct product was loaded
  await expect(element(by.id('product-id-label'))).toHaveText('123');
  await expect(element(by.id('product-title'))).toBeVisible();

  // Verify Back navigation returns to the app's default home screen
  await element(by.id('back-btn')).tap();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Cold-start Universal Link tests are slower than in-session `openURL()` calls because they require a full app launch cycle. Run them in a dedicated `describe` block with `beforeAll` cold-start semantics rather than in `beforeEach`. On Android, the `url` must match an `<intent-filter>` with `android:autoVerify="true"` and the domain must be verified via the Digital Asset Links file; in CI where the domain verification server may be unreachable, configure the emulator with `adb shell pm set-app-link --package com.example.app PACKAGE_NAME always` to bypass verification.

---

### Pattern 361 — `element(by.id('otp-input')).tapBackspaceKey()` repeated N times for testing OTP field deletion behavior in custom pin-code inputs that advance/retreat focus between digit boxes [community]

`tapBackspaceKey()` simulates the keyboard Backspace/Delete key on the currently-focused `TextInput`. In custom OTP components built with multiple single-character `TextInput` fields, each `tapBackspaceKey()` deletes the current digit and fires the component's `onKeyPress({ nativeEvent: { key: 'Backspace' } })` handler, which typically moves focus to the previous box. Testing the full delete-and-retype flow catches focus management regressions where the cursor gets stuck on the wrong digit box. Always tap the last-filled digit box first to start the backspace traversal from the correct position.

```typescript
// Pattern: OTP field deletion via tapBackspaceKey()
it('allows the user to correct a mis-typed OTP code', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await waitFor(element(by.id('otp-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);

  // Type the initial (wrong) code digit by digit
  for (let i = 1; i <= 6; i++) {
    await element(by.id(`otp-digit-${i}`)).typeText(String(i));
  }

  // Delete last 3 digits via backspace starting from the last box
  await element(by.id('otp-digit-6')).tap(); // ensure last box is focused
  await element(by.id('otp-digit-6')).tapBackspaceKey();
  await element(by.id('otp-digit-5')).tapBackspaceKey();
  await element(by.id('otp-digit-4')).tapBackspaceKey();

  // Re-type the correct last 3 digits
  await element(by.id('otp-digit-4')).typeText('7');
  await element(by.id('otp-digit-5')).typeText('8');
  await element(by.id('otp-digit-6')).typeText('9');

  // Submit and assert success
  await waitFor(element(by.id('otp-success-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(6000);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `tapBackspaceKey()` only sends the `keyPress` event — it does not directly modify the `TextInput`'s `value` prop in controlled components if the `onKeyPress` handler has a bug that fails to call `setValue`. This means `tapBackspaceKey()` tests the full component logic including the `onKeyPress` handler, not just the text state. If the test fails after `tapBackspaceKey()`, check both the handler logic and the focus management, since a mismanaged focus can cause `tapBackspaceKey()` to fire on the wrong input field and leave the component in an unexpected state.

---

### Pattern 362 — `device.setLocation(latitude, longitude)` called in a `beforeEach` loop for route simulation, combined with `waitFor` assertions on map pin movement to test turn-by-turn navigation UI [official]

`device.setLocation(lat, lng)` updates the simulated GPS coordinates of the iOS Simulator or Android Emulator. By calling it repeatedly in a controlled sequence with a short `await` between each call, a test can simulate a device moving along a geographic route and verify that the app's map UI, eta label, or navigation instruction updates correctly at each waypoint. The interval between location updates should match the app's `CLLocationManager`/`Fused Location Client` update frequency — typically 1–3 seconds — to avoid missing updates that the app throttles.

```typescript
// Pattern: route simulation via repeated setLocation() calls
interface Coordinate { lat: number; lng: number; }

async function simulateRoute(waypoints: Coordinate[], stepDelayMs = 1500): Promise<void> {
  for (const { lat, lng } of waypoints) {
    await device.setLocation(lat, lng);
    // Brief pause to allow the app's location handler to fire
    await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, stepDelayMs));
  }
}

it('advances the navigation step when the user passes the turn point', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true, permissions: { location: 'always' } });
  await waitFor(element(by.id('navigation-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(6000);

  const routeWaypoints: Coordinate[] = [
    { lat: 37.7749, lng: -122.4194 }, // start
    { lat: 37.7751, lng: -122.4188 }, // approaching turn
    { lat: 37.7755, lng: -122.4180 }, // past turn point
  ];

  await simulateRoute(routeWaypoints);

  // After passing the turn, the instruction should advance to the next step
  await waitFor(element(by.id('nav-instruction-text')))
    .toHaveText('Turn right onto Market St')
    .withTimeout(5000);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The `setTimeout` delay between `setLocation()` calls uses real wall-clock time, which makes route-simulation tests inherently slow (a 10-waypoint route with 1.5 s steps takes at least 15 s). On CI, use the minimum delay that reliably triggers the app's location update handler — test locally to determine the threshold. On Android Emulator, `setLocation()` requires the emulator to have a GPS fix state; if the emulator starts with GPS disabled, call `adb shell settings put secure location_providers_allowed +gps` in a `beforeAll` native setup step to ensure GPS is enabled before the test runs.

---

### Pattern 363 — `toHaveAccessibilityValue({ min, max, now, text })` assertion for validating ARIA-equivalent accessibility value properties on sliders, progress bars, and custom range components [official]

Detox's `toHaveAccessibilityValue()` matcher asserts the `accessibilityValue` property of a native view, which maps to the `AccessibilityValue` React Native prop (`{ min, max, now, text }`). For `Slider` components, `now` represents the current value, and `min`/`max` represent the range — asserting these values confirms that the slider position communicated to assistive technologies matches the visual position. For progress bars, `text` often carries a human-readable description such as `"75% complete"`. This matcher tests the accessibility layer independently of the visual position, catching bugs where a slider renders at 50% but reports `accessibilityValue.now = 0` to VoiceOver/TalkBack.

```typescript
// Pattern: accessibility value assertions for slider and progress bar
it('slider accessibility value matches visual position', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await waitFor(element(by.id('volume-slider'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

  // Default state — slider at 50%
  await expect(element(by.id('volume-slider'))).toHaveAccessibilityValue({
    min: 0,
    max: 100,
    now: 50,
  });

  // Adjust slider to 75% using normalized position
  await element(by.id('volume-slider')).adjustSliderToPosition(0.75);

  // Assert the accessibility value updated to reflect the new position
  await expect(element(by.id('volume-slider'))).toHaveAccessibilityValue({
    min: 0,
    max: 100,
    now: 75,
  });

  // For progress bars with text description
  await waitFor(element(by.id('upload-progress'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
  await expect(element(by.id('upload-progress'))).toHaveAccessibilityValue({
    text: '100% complete',
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `toHaveAccessibilityValue()` only works if the component explicitly sets the `accessibilityValue` prop. React Native's built-in `Slider` component does set `accessibilityValue.now` from its `value` prop, but many third-party slider libraries do not — in those cases the assertion returns `undefined` for all fields rather than throwing, which can produce false-positive test passes. Always verify via `element.getAttributes().accessibilityValue` first to confirm the component is exposing accessibility values before writing assertions against them.

---

### Pattern 364 — `element(by.id('message-item')).longPress(2500)` with exact duration for triggering context menus that use a 2-second press threshold to distinguish long-press from standard press-and-hold [community]

`longPress(duration)` accepts a duration in milliseconds that maps to the gesture recognizer's minimum press duration. The default (no duration argument) uses Detox's built-in default of ~500 ms, which is correct for most `TouchableOpacity` long-press handlers using React Native's default `delayLongPress` value of 500 ms. Custom components that use `delayLongPress={2000}` (to avoid accidental activation) require `longPress(2500)` — 500 ms above the threshold — to reliably trigger the gesture recognizer. Using the default `longPress()` on a component with a 2-second threshold results in the gesture ending before the threshold is reached, which fires `onPress` instead of `onLongPress` and makes the test assert on the wrong behavior.

```typescript
// Pattern: exact-duration longPress for high-threshold context menus
async function longPressMessage(messageTestId: string): Promise<void> {
  // App uses delayLongPress={2000} on message bubbles — use 2500 ms to be safe
  await element(by.id(messageTestId)).longPress(2500);

  // Wait for context menu to appear
  await waitFor(element(by.id('message-context-menu')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(3000);
}

it('shows the message context menu on long press and deletes the message', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await waitFor(element(by.id('chat-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);

  await longPressMessage('message-item-3');

  // Assert context menu options
  await expect(element(by.id('context-menu-copy'))).toBeVisible();
  await expect(element(by.id('context-menu-delete'))).toBeVisible();

  // Tap Delete
  await element(by.id('context-menu-delete')).tap();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('delete-confirm-dialog'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
  await element(by.id('delete-confirm-ok')).tap();

  // Message should be removed from the list
  await waitFor(element(by.id('message-item-3'))).not.toExist().withTimeout(4000);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Specifying an exact `longPress(duration)` couples the test to the component's `delayLongPress` prop value. If the component's threshold changes (e.g., reduced from 2000 ms to 800 ms for UX reasons), the test still passes but now uses a redundantly long gesture. Expose the `delayLongPress` value as a testable constant in the component's module and import it in the test helper to keep the duration in sync automatically: `await element(by.id(id)).longPress(MESSAGE_LONG_PRESS_DELAY + 500)`.

---

### Community Gotchas — Cycle 47

### Gotcha 259 — `element(by.id('input')).tapReturnKey()` has no effect when the `TextInput` has `blurOnSubmit={false}` and `multiline={true}`, because on iOS the Return key is remapped to insert a newline character rather than triggering `onSubmitEditing`, and Detox's `tapReturnKey()` dispatches the same native key event that the system would send [community]

**Root cause**: React Native's `TextInput` with `multiline={true}` remaps the Return key to insert a `'\n'` newline character by default. When `blurOnSubmit={false}` is also set, the input never blurs and `onSubmitEditing` is never called — the Return key is purely a newline insertion key. Detox's `tapReturnKey()` sends the same native `UIKeyboardHIDUsageKeyboardReturnOrEnter` key event that a hardware keyboard would send, so it inserts a newline rather than submitting. In multi-line chat input components, the submit action is typically mapped to a separate send button, not the Return key. Tests for multi-line chat inputs should tap the send button (`element(by.id('send-btn')).tap()`) rather than calling `tapReturnKey()`.

```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN — tapReturnKey() on multiline input inserts newline, not submit
await element(by.id('chat-input')).typeText('Hello world');
await element(by.id('chat-input')).tapReturnKey(); // inserts newline — NOT a submit

// CORRECT — tap the send button for multiline chat inputs
await element(by.id('chat-input')).typeText('Hello world');
await element(by.id('send-btn')).tap(); // correct submit path
await waitFor(element(by.id('message-bubble-last'))).toHaveText('Hello world').withTimeout(4000);
```

**WHY this matters:** Tests using `tapReturnKey()` on a multi-line input will populate the input with a growing number of newlines on each test run if state is not cleared between tests, causing subsequent `typeText()` calls to place text at unexpected positions. The failure mode — "message sent with trailing newline" — appears only in integration environments where the backend trims whitespace, making it an invisible bug in unit tests that surfaces only in E2E assertions on the displayed message content.

---

### Gotcha 260 — `device.appLaunchArgs.modify()` does not take effect until the next `device.launchApp()` or `device.reloadReactNative()` call; calling it mid-test after the app is already running has no effect on the currently running JavaScript context [official]

**Root cause**: Launch arguments are read by the React Native runtime at startup (via `NativeModules.RNDeviceInfo.getInitialURL()`, `NativeModules.LaunchArgs`, or `DevSettings.getDevMenu()` equivalents). Once the JS bundle is running, the values are frozen in memory. `appLaunchArgs.modify()` updates the argument map that Detox will inject at the next process launch — it does not reach into the running process to update any in-memory cache. A common mistake is calling `appLaunchArgs.modify()` inside a `beforeEach` without following it with `device.reloadReactNative()`, then asserting that the new flag value is reflected in the UI — it will reflect the previous run's values instead.

```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN — modify without reload; flag value unchanged in running app
device.appLaunchArgs.modify({ SHOW_BETA_FEATURES: '1' });
// app is still running with SHOW_BETA_FEATURES: '0' — no reload issued
await expect(element(by.id('beta-feature-panel'))).toBeVisible(); // FAILS

// CORRECT — always reload after modifying launch args
device.appLaunchArgs.modify({ SHOW_BETA_FEATURES: '1' });
await device.reloadReactNative(); // or device.launchApp({ newInstance: true })
await waitFor(element(by.id('beta-feature-panel'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
```

**WHY this matters:** This gotcha produces intermittent failures that depend on test execution order: if the previous test happened to launch with `SHOW_BETA_FEATURES: '1'` and the state was not reset, the current test's assertion passes by accident. On a fresh cold-start run the test fails, making the failure look like a CI environment issue. Always pair every `appLaunchArgs.modify()` call with an explicit reload, and always reset in `afterAll`.

---

### Gotcha 261 — `element(by.id('map')).pinch(0.5, 'fast', 0)` on Android Emulator with `react-native-maps` using the Google Maps SDK throws `"Action is not supported for the given element"` because `MapView` renders via a `SurfaceView` that is excluded from Espresso's action dispatch chain [community]

**Root cause**: Google Maps' `MapView` renders its tile content in a dedicated `SurfaceView` (a separate hardware-composed surface that bypasses the standard Android view hierarchy that Espresso and Detox interact with). Detox's pinch action on Android uses the UIAutomator2 `ViewAction` API, which attempts to find the view in the accessibility tree. `SurfaceView` contents are not exposed via the Android accessibility tree — they are rendered outside the standard view hierarchy. The `pinch()` action therefore cannot dispatch pointer events to the map content and throws. Use `element.tapAtPoint({ x, y })` with two sequential taps at different scale-indicating offsets, or interact with native zoom controls (`by.id('zoom-in-btn')`) if the map renders them as standard views.

```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN — pinch() on a SurfaceView-backed MapView on Android
if (device.getPlatform() === 'android') {
  await element(by.id('map-view')).pinch(2.0, 'slow', 0); // throws on Android
}

// WORKAROUND — use native zoom buttons when MapView pinch is not testable
if (device.getPlatform() === 'android') {
  await element(by.id('map-zoom-in-btn')).tap();
  await element(by.id('map-zoom-in-btn')).tap();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('zoom-level-label'))).toHaveText('15').withTimeout(3000);
} else {
  // iOS WKMapView supports pinch simulation
  await element(by.id('map-view')).pinch(2.0, 'slow', 0);
}
```

**WHY this matters:** The failure is specific to `SurfaceView`-backed views (Google Maps, video players, camera previews) and does not affect `TextureView`-based renderers, which are exposed in the accessibility tree. Before adding a pinch test for any native view, verify whether the view is a `SurfaceView` or `TextureView` via `adb shell uiautomator dump` — `SurfaceView` elements appear as `android.view.SurfaceView` in the XML dump and will not support any Detox pointer action.

---

### Gotcha 262 — `waitFor(element).not.toBeVisible().withTimeout(n)` passes immediately when the element has never been rendered (i.e., does not exist in the view hierarchy), silently accepting a test that should have first asserted the element was visible before dismissing it [community]

**Root cause**: Detox's `not.toBeVisible()` resolves to `true` for elements that do not exist in the hierarchy (non-existent elements are by definition not visible). If the element-under-test was never rendered — for example because the modal failed to open due to a bug — the `waitFor(...).not.toBeVisible()` assertion passes immediately and the test incorrectly reports success. The correct pattern for modal dismissal testing is a two-step assertion: first `waitFor(...).toBeVisible()` to confirm the modal opened, then the dismissal action, then `waitFor(...).not.toBeVisible()` to confirm it closed.

```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN — not.toBeVisible() passes even if modal never appeared
await element(by.id('share-btn')).tap();
// If the modal bug prevents it from opening, this line still passes:
await waitFor(element(by.id('share-modal'))).not.toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
// Test "passes" but the modal was never shown

// CORRECT — two-step visible → dismissed assertion
await element(by.id('share-btn')).tap();
await waitFor(element(by.id('share-modal'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000); // must appear first
await element(by.id('close-btn')).tap();
await waitFor(element(by.id('share-modal'))).not.toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000); // then disappear
```

**WHY this matters:** This is a particularly dangerous false positive because the test covers a user-facing flow (the user can open and dismiss a modal) but the assertion logic silently ignores the opening step. The bug goes undetected until a human tester manually verifies the feature. Add an explicit `toBeVisible()` pre-condition assertion before every dismissal sequence, and consider a `toExist()` check as well when `not.toBeVisible()` is the final assertion.

---

### Gotcha 263 — `device.sendUserNotification()` with `badge: 0` does not clear the app's existing badge count on iOS when the app is foregrounded, because badge clearing requires the app to call `UIApplication.shared.applicationIconBadgeNumber = 0` in its notification-received handler — Detox has no way to force this [community]

**Root cause**: The `badge` field in a local notification payload sets the badge count only if `UIApplication` processes the notification and updates the badge number in its own handler. When the app is in the foreground, iOS delivers the notification to `UNUserNotificationCenterDelegate.userNotificationCenter(_:willPresent:withCompletionHandler:)`, which the app's code must handle by updating `applicationIconBadgeNumber`. If the app's handler ignores the badge field or sets it only on background receipt, sending a notification with `badge: 0` from Detox while the app is foregrounded has no effect on the visible badge. This causes badge-clearing E2E tests to fail when run while the app is foregrounded.

```typescript
// PATTERN — reset badge by backgrounding the app before sending badge:0 notification
it('clears the badge count when all notifications are dismissed', async () => {
  // Send a notification that sets badge to 3 (foreground — app must handle this)
  await device.sendUserNotification({ trigger: { type: 'push' }, badge: 3, title: 'Test' });
  await waitFor(element(by.id('badge-label'))).toHaveText('3').withTimeout(3000);

  // Send to home (background the app) before sending badge-clear notification
  await device.sendToHome();
  await device.sendUserNotification({ trigger: { type: 'push' }, badge: 0, title: '' });

  // Return to the app
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: false });
  await waitFor(element(by.id('badge-label'))).not.toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
});
```

**WHY this matters:** Badge count tests are often written and tested on CI where the app starts fresh with no badge, passing trivially. The regression occurs in production when a user has accumulated a badge count and the app must clear it — the E2E test never covered the clearing path. Use `device.sendToHome()` to background the app before badge-clearing notifications, mirroring the real production path where the system delivers background notifications to the app's background handler.

---

### Gotcha 264 — `element(by.id('list')).scrollTo('bottom')` on a `FlatList` with `inverted={true}` prop scrolls to the top of the visual display (the most recent item in an inverted chat list) rather than the bottom, because `inverted` reverses the scroll direction at the native level [community]

**Root cause**: `FlatList inverted={true}` applies a 180-degree transform to the underlying `ScrollView`, effectively reversing the scroll axis. What the user sees as "the bottom" (the oldest messages in a chat list) is, at the native scroll layer, the scroll origin (position 0). Detox's `scrollTo('bottom')` navigates to the maximum native scroll offset — which is the visual top of the inverted list (the most recent messages). When testing an inverted chat list, `scrollTo('top')` scrolls to the oldest messages (visual bottom) and `scrollTo('bottom')` scrolls to the newest (visual top). This naming inversion confuses tests that try to verify that old messages are accessible by scrolling down.

```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN — scrollTo('bottom') on an inverted FlatList goes to newest, not oldest
await element(by.id('chat-message-list')).scrollTo('bottom'); // goes to top visually

// CORRECT — for inverted FlatList, 'top' is visual bottom (oldest messages)
await element(by.id('chat-message-list')).scrollTo('top'); // scrolls to oldest messages (visual bottom)
await waitFor(element(by.id('oldest-message-item'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);

// For scrolling back to newest (visual top), use 'bottom'
await element(by.id('chat-message-list')).scrollTo('bottom'); // back to most recent (visual top)
```

**WHY this matters:** Inverted FlatList is the standard pattern for chat UIs in React Native (`react-native` core, `react-native-gifted-chat`, and custom implementations all use `inverted={true}`). Any E2E test suite for a messaging feature will encounter this. The naming mismatch is not a Detox bug — it correctly reports native scroll positions — but it violates the test author's mental model of "scrolling to the bottom shows older content." Document this inversion in your team's E2E testing guide and add a `scrollChatToOldest`/`scrollChatToNewest` helper that encapsulates the correct direction.

## Updated Anti-Patterns Checklist (Cycle 47 additions)

| Anti-Pattern | Fix |
|---|---|
| Using `tapReturnKey()` on a `multiline={true}` + `blurOnSubmit={false}` `TextInput` expecting form submission — the key inserts a newline and `onSubmitEditing` is never called | Tap the send/submit button directly for multi-line inputs; reserve `tapReturnKey()` for single-line fields (Gotcha 259, Pattern 350) |
| Calling `device.appLaunchArgs.modify()` mid-test without following it with `device.reloadReactNative()` and expecting the new flag value to be reflected in the running app | Always follow `modify()` with a reload; call `reset()` in `afterAll` to prevent inter-spec contamination (Gotcha 260, Pattern 351) |
| Using `pinch()` on a Google Maps `MapView` on Android and expecting the map to zoom — `SurfaceView`-backed views are outside the UIAutomator2 pointer dispatch chain | Use native zoom control buttons or `tapAtPoint()` on Android; iOS WKMapView supports `pinch()` (Gotcha 261, Pattern 353) |
| Omitting `device.setNetworkConditions(null)` reset in `afterEach` after network-degradation tests — throttled conditions persist for subsequent tests in the same worker | Wrap `setNetworkConditions()` in `try/finally`; always reset to `null` in `afterEach` (Pattern 354) |
| Asserting `waitFor(...).not.toBeVisible()` as a dismissal check without first asserting `toBeVisible()` — passes immediately if the element was never rendered | Gate every dismissal assertion with a preceding `toBeVisible()` pre-condition; use `not.toExist()` for full removal verification (Gotcha 262, Pattern 355) |
