### Gotcha 271 — `waitFor(element).toBeVisible().whileScrollingTo()` silently exhausts the scroll limit and resolves without throwing when the element does not exist in the list, causing the next assertion to fail with a confusing "element not visible" error instead of "element not found" [community]

**Root cause**: `whileScrollingTo()` performs incremental scrolls and checks visibility after each scroll. When the scroll reaches the end of the list (either `scrollTo('bottom')` or the maximum scroll offset), the loop exits. If the target element was never found, Detox resolves the `waitFor()` promise without throwing — it simply never matched the condition. The assertion technically fails at this point, but the error is reported as a timeout or as `"expected element to be visible but it was not"` rather than `"element does not exist in the hierarchy"`. This makes it hard to distinguish between "element exists but is scrolled off-screen" and "element does not exist at all".

```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN — no existence check before whileScrollingTo()
await waitFor(element(by.id('item-that-might-not-exist')))
  .toBeVisible()
  .whileScrollingTo('down', element(by.id('list'))); // silently scrolls to end then times out

// CORRECT — verify existence first, then scroll to reveal
await waitFor(element(by.id('item-that-might-not-exist')))
  .toExist()
  .withTimeout(3000); // fast-fail with "element not found" if not in the tree at all

// Only scroll if the element exists
await waitFor(element(by.id('item-that-might-not-exist')))
  .toBeVisible()
  .whileScrollingTo('down', element(by.id('list')));
```

**WHY this matters:** The confusing error message causes developers to waste time debugging scroll logic and element selectors when the real problem is that the element was never rendered. Adding a `toExist()` pre-check separates the two failure modes: "element is in the tree but off-screen" (scroll to reveal) vs. "element is not in the tree" (data or navigation bug). The `toExist()` check is cheap (no scrolling) and fails immediately with a clear message, dramatically reducing time-to-root-cause for "missing element" regressions.

---

### Gotcha 272 — `device.launchApp({ permissions: { notifications: 'YES' } })` pre-grants permissions only at the app launch boundary; calling it after the app is already running has no effect on iOS, causing permission tests to fail if the launch order is incorrect [community]

**Root cause**: iOS permission grants via Detox are implemented by writing to the `SpringBoard` permissions database via `AppleSimUtils` before the app process starts. The permission state is read by the app's process at startup. If `launchApp({ permissions: ... })` is called when the app is already running (i.e., `newInstance: false` is used or the app was not terminated before the call), `AppleSimUtils` updates the database, but the running process has already read its permissions and cached them. The permission change will not take effect until the app is relaunched. This means that a test which calls `device.launchApp({ permissions: { camera: 'YES' } })` in `beforeEach` without explicitly terminating the previous app instance may see stale `'unset'` or `'NO'` camera permission in the running process.

```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN — launchApp with permissions on already-running app (no-op on iOS)
beforeEach(async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ permissions: { camera: 'YES' } }); // newInstance defaults to false
  // Camera permission may still be 'unset' in the running process
});

// CORRECT — terminate the app first to ensure a clean permission grant
beforeEach(async () => {
  await device.terminateApp();
  await device.launchApp({
    newInstance: true,
    permissions: { camera: 'YES', microphone: 'YES' },
  });
});

afterAll(async () => {
  // Reset permissions to avoid contaminating other test suites
  await device.terminateApp();
  await device.launchApp({
    newInstance: true,
    permissions: { camera: 'unset', microphone: 'unset' },
  });
});
```

**WHY this matters:** Permission tests that do not enforce a clean app launch are among the most common sources of "works locally, fails in CI" bugs in Detox suites. Local development environments often have permissions pre-granted from previous manual testing sessions; CI starts with a fresh Simulator that has no pre-granted permissions. Always pair permission grants with `newInstance: true` and follow up with an `afterAll` that resets permissions to `'unset'` to prevent test-order contamination in suites that mix permission-granted and permission-denied test cases.

---

### Gotcha 273 — `element.swipe('right')` on an iOS navigation controller's root view controller does not trigger the interactivePopGestureRecognizer, so swipe-back-to-navigate tests always fail on screens that are the first in the navigation stack [community]

**Root cause**: React Navigation's iOS stack navigator installs `UIScreenEdgePanGestureRecognizer` (the `interactivePopGestureRecognizer`) only when there is a previous screen in the navigation stack. When the test navigates directly to a screen via deep link or `device.openURL()` — bypassing the navigation stack push — the screen is technically the root view controller and no `interactivePopGestureRecognizer` is active. Calling `element.swipe('right', 'slow', 0.75, 0.02, 0.5)` (the swipe-from-left-edge pattern) does nothing and the screen does not dismiss. This causes swipe-back navigation tests to time out waiting for the previous screen to appear.

```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN — swipe-back on a screen that is the navigation root (e.g., seeded via deep link)
await device.openURL({ url: 'myapp://profile/123' }); // makes profile the root VC
await element(by.id('profile-screen')).swipe('right', 'slow', 0.75, 0.02, 0.5);
// interactivePopGestureRecognizer is inactive — swipe does nothing

// CORRECT — navigate by tapping through the stack so the screen has a back entry
await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
await element(by.id('user-avatar')).tap(); // navigate via the UI to build the back stack
await waitFor(element(by.id('profile-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
// Now swipe-back will work because the home screen is behind it in the stack
await element(by.id('profile-screen')).swipe('right', 'slow', 0.75, 0.02, 0.5);
await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
```

**WHY this matters:** Tests that use deep-link seeding for speed inadvertently bypass the navigation stack, making swipe-back gesture tests structurally impossible. The fix — navigating through the UI to reach the screen — conflicts with the deep-link optimization philosophy. The correct resolution is to split screen-feature tests (which may use deep links) from navigation-gesture tests (which must build the navigation stack via UI interactions). Keep swipe-back tests in a dedicated navigation spec file that navigates through the full UI path.

---

### Gotcha 274 — `device.reloadReactNative()` resets `AsyncStorage` on Android (when using JSI-based storage in some bridge configurations), but does NOT reset it on iOS, creating cross-platform test contamination patterns that are invisible in single-platform CI [community]

**Root cause**: On Android, certain React Native builds (particularly those using `react-native-mmkv` or early versions of the new architecture with JSI-based storage) bind the storage module to the JS runtime instance. When `reloadReactNative()` reinitializes the JS runtime (as opposed to just re-rendering the tree), a new JSI binding is created and the old storage is orphaned. The app re-initializes with empty storage on the next read. On iOS, the JS runtime is not reinitialized by `reloadReactNative()` — the same JSI instance persists and storage remains populated. This means a test that writes to `AsyncStorage` in one test and reads it in a subsequent test will see the written value on iOS (contamination) but an empty value on Android (false isolation).

```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN — relying on reloadReactNative() for AsyncStorage isolation
beforeEach(async () => {
  await device.reloadReactNative();
  // iOS: AsyncStorage may retain previous test's data
  // Android (MMKV/JSI): storage may be cleared unexpectedly
});

// CORRECT — explicitly clear storage via a test-only launch arg before each test
beforeEach(async () => {
  // App checks this flag in its AppDelegate/MainApplication and calls AsyncStorage.clear()
  await device.launchApp({
    newInstance: true,
    launchArgs: { CLEAR_STORAGE_ON_LAUNCH: '1' },
  });
});
```

**WHY this matters:** Cross-platform storage isolation divergence is particularly dangerous because it means each platform's CI run tests different behaviors — iOS tests contamination resilience while Android tests cold-start storage behavior. A bug that causes incorrect storage reads will be detected on one platform but not the other depending on which direction the contamination flows. The fix requires a deterministic storage-clear mechanism at test setup time, not reliance on runtime re-initialization behavior which differs by platform, storage library, and RN architecture (bridge vs. new architecture).

### Pattern 395 — `element.adjustSliderToPosition(normalizedPosition)` for Slider and RangeSlider value testing [official]

`adjustSliderToPosition` moves a native `Slider` component to a normalized position between `0.0` (minimum) and `1.0` (maximum). It is the only reliable way to set a slider value in Detox — `typeText`, `replaceText`, and tap-based approaches do not work on native slider controls. On iOS the mapping is direct; on Android the slider thumb is dragged proportionally across the track.

```typescript
// helpers/sliderHelpers.ts
import { expect as detoxExpect } from 'detox'; // type import only

/** Move a Slider to a target value within [min, max].
 *  Returns the normalized position actually applied (useful for assertion logging).
 */
export async function setSliderValue(
  testID: string,
  targetValue: number,
  min: number,
  max: number,
): Promise<void> {
  const normalized = Math.max(0, Math.min(1, (targetValue - min) / (max - min)));
  await element(by.id(testID)).adjustSliderToPosition(normalized);
}

/** Assert a slider is within ±tolerance of expectedValue.
 *  getAttributes().value returns a string representation of the current value.
 */
export async function assertSliderNear(
  testID: string,
  expectedValue: number,
  tolerance = 1,
): Promise<void> {
  const attrs = await element(by.id(testID)).getAttributes();
  // attrs.value is a locale-formatted string (e.g., "50%" or "50")
  const actual = parseFloat((attrs as any).value ?? '0');
  if (Math.abs(actual - expectedValue) > tolerance) {
    throw new Error(
      `Slider "${testID}" expected ~${expectedValue}, got ${actual} (tolerance ±${tolerance})`,
    );
  }
}

// e2e/settings/volume.test.ts
describe('Volume control', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    await element(by.id('settings-tab')).tap();
  });

  it('sets volume to 75%', async () => {
    await setSliderValue('volume-slider', 75, 0, 100);
    await assertSliderNear('volume-slider', 75, 2);
    // Confirm UI label reflects new value
    await expect(element(by.id('volume-label'))).toHaveText('75%');
  });

  it('sets minimum volume', async () => {
    await element(by.id('volume-slider')).adjustSliderToPosition(0);
    await expect(element(by.id('mute-icon'))).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `adjustSliderToPosition` accepts normalized 0–1 values, not raw component values (e.g., 0–100 for a volume slider). Always write a helper that converts from domain values to normalized positions. Also note that due to native rounding, `adjustSliderToPosition(0.5)` may not land precisely at `50` — assert within a tolerance range rather than for exact equality. On Android, the drag simulation can miss the target by 1–2 step increments for sliders with small step values (e.g., `step={1}` over 0–100).

---

### Pattern 396 — Multi-step `device.setLocation()` route simulation for GPS-dependent feature testing [official]

`device.setLocation(lat, lon)` instantly moves the simulated GPS position. For features that respond to movement (routing, geofencing, step counters), use a timed sequence of `setLocation` calls to simulate a route. iOS Simulator supports arbitrary coordinate injection; Android Emulator requires the app to have `ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION` permission and `LocationManager.GPS_PROVIDER` to be the active provider.

```typescript
// helpers/locationHelpers.ts
interface Waypoint {
  lat: number;
  lon: number;
}

/** Walk a route by visiting each waypoint with a pause between steps. */
export async function simulateRoute(
  waypoints: Waypoint[],
  intervalMs = 500,
): Promise<void> {
  for (const wp of waypoints) {
    await device.setLocation(wp.lat, wp.lon);
    // Detox does not inject a sleep helper — use a minimal waitFor idiom
    // to allow the app's location handler to process each coordinate update.
    await new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, intervalMs));
  }
}

// e2e/maps/routing.test.ts
const ROUTE_SF_TO_FERRY: Waypoint[] = [
  { lat: 37.7749, lon: -122.4194 }, // Market St
  { lat: 37.7751, lon: -122.4141 }, // 5th St
  { lat: 37.7756, lon: -122.4075 }, // 3rd St
  { lat: 37.7955, lon: -122.3937 }, // Embarcadero
  { lat: 37.7955, lon: -122.3935 }, // Ferry Building
];

describe('Navigation routing', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({
      newInstance: true,
      permissions: { location: 'always' },
    });
  });

  it('shows ETA progress as the user moves along the route', async () => {
    // Start the navigation
    await device.setLocation(37.7749, -122.4194);
    await element(by.id('start-navigation-btn')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('eta-banner'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

    // Walk the route
    await simulateRoute(ROUTE_SF_TO_FERRY, 400);

    // Assert arrival screen
    await waitFor(element(by.id('arrival-screen')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(6000);
    await expect(element(by.id('arrival-message'))).toHaveText('You have arrived');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `simulateRoute` uses `setTimeout` (which breaks Detox's automatic synchronization because it creates a pending timer). Wrap the entire route simulation in `device.disableSynchronization()` / `device.enableSynchronization()` if the app has an idle-based synchronization hook, or add `launchArgs: { DISABLE_LOCATION_ANIMATION: '1' }` to eliminate animation-based idle delays. On Android physical devices, `setLocation` is not supported at all — guard the test with `if (device.getPlatform() === 'android') { return; }` when running against physical device farms.

---

### Pattern 397 — `expect(element).toHaveId(testID)` for dynamic testID verification after conditional rendering [official]

`toHaveId` asserts that an element's `testID` attribute matches a specific string. This is most useful when a component changes its `testID` based on state (e.g., `testID={isActive ? 'toggle-on' : 'toggle-off'}`). It avoids the anti-pattern of selecting an element by one testID and then asserting a side effect — instead, the testID itself encodes the state.

```typescript
// Component:
// <Pressable testID={`filter-chip-${isSelected ? 'selected' : 'default'}-${label}`}>

// e2e/search/filters.test.ts
describe('Search filter chips', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    await element(by.id('search-tab')).tap();
  });

  it('toggles the category filter chip and reflects state in testID', async () => {
    // Initially unselected
    const chip = element(by.id('filter-chip-default-Electronics'));
    await expect(chip).toBeVisible();

    // Tap to select
    await chip.tap();

    // testID changes to selected variant — assert by new testID
    const selectedChip = element(by.id('filter-chip-selected-Electronics'));
    await expect(selectedChip).toBeVisible();

    // Tapping again deselects
    await selectedChip.tap();
    await expect(element(by.id('filter-chip-default-Electronics'))).toBeVisible();
  });

  it('verifies mutually exclusive single-select filter group', async () => {
    await element(by.id('filter-chip-default-Books')).tap();
    await element(by.id('filter-chip-default-Music')).tap();

    // Only Music should be selected; Books should have reverted
    await expect(element(by.id('filter-chip-selected-Music'))).toBeVisible();
    await expect(element(by.id('filter-chip-default-Books'))).toBeVisible();
  });

  it('directly reads testID via getAttributes to verify dynamic state encoding', async () => {
    const attrs = await element(by.id('filter-chip-selected-Music')).getAttributes();
    expect((attrs as any).identifier ?? (attrs as any).testID).toBe(
      'filter-chip-selected-Music',
    );
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Using testID to encode state makes the component's testID scheme a first-class API contract. Any rename of the state suffix (`'selected'` → `'active'`) is a breaking change that silently breaks all Detox tests referencing the old suffix. Document the testID convention in `CONTRIBUTING.md` and enforce it with a custom ESLint rule (e.g., ban bare string testIDs that do not follow `<component>-<state>-<identifier>` naming).

---

### Pattern 398 — `by.label().withAncestor(by.id())` scoped accessibility label matching for cards with repeated labels [official]

When multiple list cards each contain an "Add to cart" button, `element(by.label('Add to cart'))` throws `"Multiple elements found"`. Scoping the label search to a specific card via `withAncestor(by.id('product-card-<id>'))` unambiguously targets the correct button without requiring unique testIDs on every button instance.

```typescript
// Component tree:
// <View testID="product-card-42">
//   <Text>Widget Pro</Text>
//   <Pressable accessibilityLabel="Add to cart" testID="add-to-cart-btn">
//     <Text>Add to cart</Text>
//   </Pressable>
// </View>

// helpers/productHelpers.ts
/** Tap "Add to cart" for a specific product card by product ID. */
export async function addProductToCart(productId: string): Promise<void> {
  const cardMatcher = by.id(`product-card-${productId}`);
  const btnMatcher = by.label('Add to cart').withAncestor(cardMatcher);
  await element(btnMatcher).tap();
}

// e2e/shop/cart.test.ts
describe('Shopping cart — add items', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    await element(by.id('shop-tab')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('product-list'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
  });

  it('adds two specific products to the cart', async () => {
    await addProductToCart('42');
    await addProductToCart('107');

    await element(by.id('cart-tab')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('cart-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);

    // Assert both items are in the cart
    await expect(element(by.id('cart-item-42'))).toBeVisible();
    await expect(element(by.id('cart-item-107'))).toBeVisible();
    await expect(element(by.id('cart-count-badge'))).toHaveText('2');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `withAncestor` requires the ancestor element to be present in the view hierarchy at the time of the query. If the list virtualizes (e.g., `FlatList`) and the target card is off-screen, the ancestor element is not in the hierarchy and the query fails. Always scroll the target card into view before using `withAncestor`. In virtualized lists, prefer adding a unique testID to every action button via `testID={\`add-to-cart-${item.id}\`}` to avoid the scroll dependency entirely.

---

### Pattern 399 — `device.installApp()` and `device.uninstallApp()` for multi-app handoff and deep link origin testing [official]

`device.installApp()` installs the app binary (`.app` on iOS, `.apk` on Android) from an absolute path. `device.uninstallApp()` removes it. This pair enables testing flows where the app being tested is freshly installed mid-suite (onboarding), or where a secondary helper app must be installed to trigger a deep link or share-sheet interaction.

```typescript
// .detoxrc.ts — add secondaryApp configuration
const config: Detox.DetoxConfig = {
  apps: {
    'ios.release': {
      type: 'ios.app',
      binaryPath: 'ios/build/Build/Products/Release-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app',
      bundleId: 'com.example.myapp',
    },
    'ios.sender': {
      type: 'ios.app',
      binaryPath: 'e2e/fixtures/SenderApp.app',
      bundleId: 'com.example.senderapp',
    },
  },
};

// e2e/sharing/deeplink.test.ts
describe('Deep link from external app', () => {
  const SENDER_BINARY = path.resolve(__dirname, '..', 'fixtures', 'SenderApp.app');
  const SENDER_BUNDLE = 'com.example.senderapp';

  beforeAll(async () => {
    // Install the sender helper app
    await device.installApp(SENDER_BINARY);
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true }); // Launch main app first
  });

  afterAll(async () => {
    await device.uninstallApp(SENDER_BUNDLE);
  });

  it('opens the product detail screen from a shared deep link', async () => {
    // Launch sender app and trigger the share action
    await device.launchApp({ bundleId: SENDER_BUNDLE, newInstance: true });
    await element(by.id('share-product-42-btn')).tap();

    // Switch back to main app (Detox maintains control over both)
    await device.launchApp({
      bundleId: 'com.example.myapp',
      newInstance: false,
      url: 'myapp://product/42',
    });

    await waitFor(element(by.id('product-detail-screen')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(6000);
    await expect(element(by.id('product-title'))).toHaveText('Widget Pro');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The binary path passed to `installApp` must be an absolute path pointing to a pre-built binary. In CI, ensure the binary is built before the test suite starts and that the path is consistent across build machines. The `device.installApp()` / `device.uninstallApp()` API does not support installing from a URL or a relative path — use `path.resolve(__dirname, '..', 'fixtures', 'SenderApp.app')` to compute the absolute path reliably from any working directory.

---

### Pattern 400 — `globalSetup` and `globalTeardown` with Detox worker pool lifecycle management [official]

Detox's recommended CI configuration uses Jest's `globalSetup` and `globalTeardown` to start and stop the Detox infrastructure (simulator/emulator, app install) once per test run, while individual test workers handle `beforeAll/afterAll` for per-worker app lifecycle. This avoids reinstalling the app binary N times (once per shard) and reduces total CI time by 30–60% on large suites.

```typescript
// e2e/jest.config.ts
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  globalSetup: 'detox/runners/jest/globalSetup',
  globalTeardown: 'detox/runners/jest/globalTeardown',
  testEnvironment: 'detox/runners/jest/testEnvironment',
  testRunner: 'jest-circus/runner',
  testTimeout: 120000,
  maxWorkers: process.env.CI ? 2 : 1,
  testMatch: ['<rootDir>/e2e/**/*.test.ts'],
  transform: {
    '^.+\\.(ts|tsx)$': ['babel-jest', { configFile: './babel.config.js' }],
  },
  reporters: [
    'default',
    ['jest-junit', {
      outputDirectory: 'e2e/reports',
      outputName: `junit-${process.env.DETOX_WORKER_ID ?? 'main'}.xml`,
    }],
  ],
};
export default config;

// e2e/setup/workerSetup.ts — per-worker beforeAll (in jest.setup.ts or directly in tests)
beforeAll(async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
});

afterAll(async () => {
  await device.terminateApp();
});
```

```bash
# CI invocation — runs the global setup once, then N shards via workers
npx detox test \
  --configuration ios.sim.release \
  --maxWorkers 2 \
  --record-logs all \
  --record-videos failing \
  --jestRootDir e2e
```

**Tradeoff:** `globalSetup` and `globalTeardown` run in the Node.js main process before any workers spawn. They have no access to the `device` global — attempting to call `device.launchApp()` inside `globalSetup` throws `"device is not defined"`. Worker-level app lifecycle (launch, terminate, reload) must live in `beforeAll`/`afterAll` inside test files or a shared `workerSetup.ts` referenced via Jest's `setupFilesAfterFramework`. Mixing `globalSetup` device calls with per-worker device calls is the most common Detox CI architecture mistake.

---

### Pattern 401 — Nested horizontal scroll inside vertical `ScrollView` using composed `whileElement().scroll()` [community]

When a horizontal carousel (`ScrollView horizontal`) is nested inside a vertical `ScrollView`, calling `scroll()` on the outer container scrolls vertically even when the target is inside the carousel. To scroll the carousel horizontally, always target the carousel's own `testID` and scroll horizontally on that element.

```typescript
// e2e/home/carousel.test.ts

/** Scroll horizontally inside a named carousel to reveal a card. */
async function scrollCarouselToCard(
  carouselTestID: string,
  cardTestID: string,
): Promise<void> {
  await waitFor(element(by.id(cardTestID)))
    .toBeVisible()
    .whileElement(by.id(carouselTestID))
    .scroll(300, 'right');
}

describe('Featured carousel', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
  });

  it('reveals the 4th card in the featured carousel', async () => {
    // The carousel may need multiple scrolls; whileElement retries automatically
    await scrollCarouselToCard('featured-carousel', 'featured-card-4');
    await element(by.id('featured-card-4')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('article-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
  });

  it('scrolls the page vertically to reveal a second carousel and scrolls it', async () => {
    await element(by.id('home-scroll-view')).scrollTo('bottom');
    await waitFor(element(by.id('trending-carousel'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
    await scrollCarouselToCard('trending-carousel', 'trending-card-6');
    await expect(element(by.id('trending-card-6'))).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `whileElement().scroll()` retries the scroll-and-check loop up to a maximum attempt count (default 10). If the carousel is infinite (wrapping) or very long, the loop may exhaust retries before reaching the target. For infinite carousels, add a testID to each card that includes its position and assert a reasonable position (e.g., the first 8 cards) rather than trying to scroll to an arbitrarily distant position. Also note that nested scroll views on Android have different event dispatch semantics — test both platforms separately.

---

### Pattern 402 — `DetoxCircusEnvironment` `onTestStart` hook for per-test device log capture [community]

Overriding `handleTestEvent` in a custom `DetoxCircusEnvironment` subclass allows you to start a device log capture at the beginning of every test and then flush/save it in `onTestFailed`. This produces a focused log file per failed test rather than a single massive log for the entire suite, dramatically reducing triage time in CI.

```typescript
// e2e/environment/DetoxEnv.ts
import { DetoxCircusEnvironment } from 'detox/runners/jest/testEnvironment';
import type { Circus } from '@jest/types';
import * as fs from 'fs';
import * as path from 'path';

export default class DetoxEnv extends DetoxCircusEnvironment {
  private currentTestName = '';

  async handleTestEvent(event: Circus.Event, state: Circus.State): Promise<void> {
    // CRITICAL: always call super first
    await super.handleTestEvent(event, state);

    if (event.name === 'test_start') {
      this.currentTestName = event.test.name;
      // Capture hierarchy at test start for comparison on failure
      await device.captureViewHierarchy(
        `e2e/artifacts/hierarchy-${this.sanitize(this.currentTestName)}-start`,
      ).catch(() => {/* non-fatal */});
    }

    if (event.name === 'test_fn_failure') {
      const safeTitle = this.sanitize(this.currentTestName);
      const artifactDir = path.resolve('e2e/artifacts');
      fs.mkdirSync(artifactDir, { recursive: true });
      // Take a screenshot at the exact moment of failure
      await device.takeScreenshot(`${safeTitle}-FAILED`);
    }
  }

  private sanitize(name: string): string {
    return name.replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9-_]/g, '_').slice(0, 80);
  }
}

// jest.config.ts — register the custom environment
// testEnvironment: './e2e/environment/DetoxEnv.ts'
```

**Tradeoff:** Overriding `handleTestEvent` without calling `super.handleTestEvent(event, state)` first breaks Detox's own lifecycle hooks (app launch/terminate timing, artifact collection). Always `await super.handleTestEvent()` before your custom logic, never after. Also be aware that `captureViewHierarchy()` is asynchronous and can take 200–500 ms — calling it in `test_start` adds overhead to every test. Gate it behind an environment variable (`process.env.CAPTURE_HIERARCHY_ON_START`) so it only runs on CI.

---

### Pattern 403 — `device.setNetworkConditions()` throttling tiers with a preset helper for offline/2G/3G/4G simulation [official]

`device.setNetworkConditions()` accepts a `NetworkConditions` object specifying `downloadKbps`, `uploadKbps`, `latencyMs`, and `packetLoss`. Defining named presets ensures consistent throttling across tests and CI, and makes the intent of each test self-documenting.

```typescript
// helpers/networkHelpers.ts

type NetworkPreset = 'offline' | '2g' | '3g' | '4g' | 'perfect';

interface NetworkConditions {
  downloadKbps: number;
  uploadKbps: number;
  latencyMs: number;
  packetLoss: number; // 0–100
}

const NETWORK_PRESETS: Record<NetworkPreset, NetworkConditions> = {
  offline:  { downloadKbps: 0,      uploadKbps: 0,     latencyMs: 0,   packetLoss: 100 },
  '2g':     { downloadKbps: 50,     uploadKbps: 30,    latencyMs: 400, packetLoss: 5   },
  '3g':     { downloadKbps: 750,    uploadKbps: 250,   latencyMs: 100, packetLoss: 1   },
  '4g':     { downloadKbps: 4000,   uploadKbps: 3000,  latencyMs: 20,  packetLoss: 0   },
  perfect:  { downloadKbps: 100000, uploadKbps: 100000, latencyMs: 0,  packetLoss: 0   },
};

export async function setNetwork(preset: NetworkPreset): Promise<void> {
  if (device.getPlatform() !== 'ios') {
    // setNetworkConditions is iOS Simulator only — skip silently on Android
    return;
  }
  await device.setNetworkConditions(NETWORK_PRESETS[preset]);
}

export async function resetNetwork(): Promise<void> {
  await setNetwork('perfect');
}

// e2e/network/offline.test.ts
describe('Offline banner — iOS Simulator only', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  });

  afterEach(async () => {
    await resetNetwork();
  });

  it('shows offline banner when network is unavailable', async () => {
    await setNetwork('offline');
    // Trigger a network request
    await element(by.id('refresh-feed-btn')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('offline-banner')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(5000);
    await expect(element(by.id('offline-banner-text'))).toHaveText('No connection');
  });

  it('shows slow network warning on 2G', async () => {
    await setNetwork('2g');
    await element(by.id('load-images-btn')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('slow-network-warning')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(8000);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `setNetworkConditions` only works on iOS Simulator. On Android Emulator, the equivalent `device.setNetworkConditions()` call is silently ignored (see Gotcha 120 from earlier cycles). For Android network simulation, use a mock server approach (Pattern 51) or Android's built-in emulator network throttling via `adb emu network speed <preset>`. Always reset to `perfect` in `afterEach` — forgetting to reset will throttle all subsequent tests in the session.

---

### Pattern 404 — Layered `waitFor().withTimeout()` + `retryTimes` strategy for network-dependent content [community]

For tests that depend on real or mock network responses, combine jest-circus's `retryTimes` with a generous `withTimeout` to absorb transient CI network delays without introducing brittle arbitrary sleeps.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts — enable per-test retry at the runner level
// testRunner: 'jest-circus/runner'
// Use jest.retryTimes(2) inside the describe block, not globally

// e2e/feed/loading.test.ts
describe('News feed loading', () => {
  // Retry up to 2 times on transient network timeouts in CI
  // Note: retryTimes only retries on assertion failures, not on thrown errors
  jest.retryTimes(2, { logErrorsBeforeRetry: true });

  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  });

  it('loads the news feed within 8 seconds on a fresh launch', async () => {
    // Wait for the loading skeleton to appear first (confirms network request started)
    await waitFor(element(by.id('feed-skeleton')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(3000);

    // Wait for the skeleton to be replaced by real content
    await waitFor(element(by.id('feed-skeleton')))
      .not.toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(8000);

    // Assert at least one feed item is visible
    await waitFor(element(by.id('feed-item-0')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(2000);
  });

  it('shows an error state after 30 seconds with no response', async () => {
    // Use launchArgs to activate the mock slow-network mode in the app
    await device.launchApp({
      newInstance: true,
      launchArgs: { MOCK_NETWORK_DELAY_MS: '31000' },
    });

    await waitFor(element(by.id('feed-error-state')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(35000);
    await expect(element(by.id('retry-button'))).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `retryTimes` reruns the entire test, not just the failing assertion. If the test has side effects (e.g., it taps "Add to cart"), those side effects execute on every retry, potentially leaving the app in a different state than the first run. Always use `beforeEach` with `newInstance: true` so retries start from a clean app state. Also note that `retryTimes` interacts badly with Detox's artifact collection: screenshots and logs are generated per retry, leading to multiple artifacts with the same test name. Use the `DETOX_WORKER_ID` environment variable in the artifact filename to distinguish retry artifacts.

---

### Pattern 405 — `element.replaceText()` followed by `element.tapReturnKey()` for reliable cross-platform form submission [official]

`replaceText` atomically replaces the entire text field value without firing intermediate `onChangeText` events (unlike `typeText` which fires a callback per character). Pairing it with `tapReturnKey` submits the form via the keyboard's return/done action rather than tapping a submit button, which is more realistic for single-field forms and search bars.

```typescript
// helpers/formHelpers.ts

/** Fill a TextInput and submit via the return key.
 *  Prefer over typeText when the field has onChangeText validation that fires on every keystroke.
 */
export async function fillAndSubmit(
  fieldTestID: string,
  value: string,
): Promise<void> {
  await element(by.id(fieldTestID)).tap(); // Ensure focus
  await element(by.id(fieldTestID)).replaceText(value);
  await element(by.id(fieldTestID)).tapReturnKey();
}

/** Fill multiple fields without submitting (for multi-field forms). */
export async function fillField(
  fieldTestID: string,
  value: string,
): Promise<void> {
  await element(by.id(fieldTestID)).tap();
  await element(by.id(fieldTestID)).replaceText(value);
}

// e2e/auth/login.test.ts
describe('Login form', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.reloadReactNative();
    await element(by.id('login-nav-link')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('login-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
  });

  it('logs in via replaceText + tapReturnKey on the password field', async () => {
    await fillField('email-input', 'user@example.com');
    await fillAndSubmit('password-input', 'securePassword123');

    await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(6000);
  });

  it('shows validation error on empty email', async () => {
    await fillAndSubmit('email-input', '');
    await expect(element(by.id('email-error-message'))).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `replaceText` does not simulate realistic user input — it atomically sets the field value without triggering key-by-key `onChangeText` events. Components that validate or transform input on each keystroke (e.g., an autocomplete that fires an API call on every character) will not see intermediate states. For those components, use `typeText` with `clearText()` first. Additionally, `tapReturnKey` depends on the `returnKeyType` prop being set correctly on the `TextInput` — if `returnKeyType` is not set, the return key behavior is platform-dependent and may insert a newline rather than submit.

---

### Pattern 406 — `device.matchFace()` / `device.setEnrolledToBiometrics()` biometric enrollment and match flow for iOS 26+ (Detox 20.51+) [official]

Detox 20.51+ replaced the deprecated `--matchFace` / `--matchFinger` AppleSimUtils flags with `device.matchFace()`, `device.unmatchFace()`, `device.matchFinger()`, and `device.setEnrolledToBiometrics(enrolled)`. The new APIs require the `--booted` flag to be omitted (Detox handles simulator targeting internally). This pattern covers the full enrollment-and-match lifecycle for Face ID testing.

```typescript
// e2e/auth/biometric.test.ts

describe('Face ID authentication (iOS only)', () => {
  const isIOS = device.getPlatform() === 'ios';

  // Skip entire suite on Android where Face ID is unavailable
  if (!isIOS) {
    it.skip('Face ID tests skipped on Android', () => {});
    return;
  }

  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({
      newInstance: true,
      permissions: { faceid: 'YES' },
    });
  });

  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.reloadReactNative();
    // Ensure biometrics are enrolled before each test
    await device.setEnrolledToBiometrics(true);
  });

  afterAll(async () => {
    // Clean up — reset biometric enrollment state
    await device.setEnrolledToBiometrics(false);
  });

  it('unlocks the app with a successful Face ID match', async () => {
    await element(by.id('biometric-login-btn')).tap();
    // The Face ID prompt sheet appears — match it
    await device.matchFace();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('protected-screen')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(5000);
  });

  it('shows error when Face ID does not match', async () => {
    await element(by.id('biometric-login-btn')).tap();
    await device.unmatchFace();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('biometric-error-banner')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(4000);
    await expect(element(by.id('biometric-error-banner'))).toHaveText(
      'Face ID not recognized',
    );
  });

  it('falls back to passcode when biometrics are not enrolled', async () => {
    await device.setEnrolledToBiometrics(false);
    await element(by.id('biometric-login-btn')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('passcode-screen')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(4000);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `device.matchFace()` requires the Face ID permission to be granted (`permissions: { faceid: 'YES' }`) and biometrics to be enrolled (`setEnrolledToBiometrics(true)`) before the biometric prompt appears. If either precondition is missing, `matchFace()` throws or silently fails. Always structure biometric tests as: (1) launch with `faceid: 'YES'`, (2) call `setEnrolledToBiometrics(true)`, (3) trigger the prompt, (4) call `matchFace()` or `unmatchFace()`. Note that these APIs are iOS Simulator only — Touch ID uses `matchFinger()` / `unmatchFinger()`.

---

### Pattern 407 — `by.type()` platform-native semantic element type matching for cross-platform assertions [official]

`by.type()` matches elements by their native view class name: `RCTSwitch` on iOS vs `android.widget.Switch` on Android, or their React Native component class. It is best used when `testID` is not available (third-party components) and the accessibility label is locale-dependent. Wrap platform divergence in a helper.

```typescript
// helpers/semanticMatchers.ts

/** Returns the correct by.type() matcher for a native Switch across platforms. */
export function nativeSwitch() {
  return device.getPlatform() === 'ios'
    ? by.type('RCTSwitch')
    : by.type('android.widget.CompoundButton');
}

/** Returns the correct by.type() matcher for a native Slider. */
export function nativeSlider() {
  return device.getPlatform() === 'ios'
    ? by.type('RCTSlider')
    : by.type('android.widget.SeekBar');
}

/** Returns the correct by.type() matcher for a native TextInput. */
export function nativeTextInput() {
  return device.getPlatform() === 'ios'
    ? by.type('RCTTextInput')
    : by.type('android.widget.EditText');
}

// e2e/settings/toggles.test.ts
describe('Settings toggles — type-based matching', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    await element(by.id('settings-screen')).tap();
  });

  it('finds the first switch regardless of testID', async () => {
    const switchEl = element(nativeSwitch()).atIndex(0);
    await expect(switchEl).toBeVisible();
    const attrs = await switchEl.getAttributes();
    // Assert it is a boolean-valued toggle
    expect(typeof (attrs as any).value).toBe('string'); // 'true' or 'false'
  });

  it('verifies all TextInput fields are enabled on the profile form', async () => {
    await element(by.id('edit-profile-btn')).tap();
    // Count enabled inputs via atIndex loop
    let i = 0;
    while (true) {
      try {
        const el = element(nativeTextInput()).atIndex(i);
        await expect(el).toBeVisible();
        i++;
      } catch {
        break;
      }
    }
    expect(i).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `by.type()` strings are tightly coupled to React Native's internal native view class names, which can change across RN major versions (e.g., Fabric components have different class names than bridge components). Prefer `testID`-based selectors for all app-owned components and reserve `by.type()` for third-party library components where `testID` is unavailable. When RN updates cause `by.type()` selectors to break, update the class name string and document the RN version that changed it.

---

### Pattern 408 — Detox configuration inheritance with TypeScript spread for shared base config across iOS/Android/tablet profiles [official]

Using a TypeScript base config object spread across all device configurations in `.detoxrc.ts` eliminates duplication of `testRunner`, `artifacts`, `behavior`, and `server` settings. This makes it easy to apply a global `testTimeout` change or `--record-videos` setting in a single place.

```typescript
// .detoxrc.ts
import type { Detox } from 'detox';

// Shared base config — all device configs extend this via spread
const baseConfig = {
  testRunner: {
    args: {
      '$0': 'jest',
      config: 'e2e/jest.config.ts',
      testTimeout: 120000,
    },
    jest: { setupTimeout: 120000 },
  },
  artifacts: {
    rootDir: '.detox-artifacts',
    plugins: {
      screenshot: {
        enabled: true,
        shouldTakeAutomaticSnapshots: true,
        keepOnlyFailingTestArtifacts: true,
      },
      video: {
        enabled: process.env.CI === 'true',
        keepOnlyFailingTestArtifacts: true,
      },
      log: { enabled: true, keepOnlyFailingTestArtifacts: false },
    },
  },
  behavior: {
    init: { reinstallApp: false },
    launchApp: 'auto' as const,
  },
} satisfies Partial<Detox.DetoxConfig>;

const config: Detox.DetoxConfig = {
  apps: {
    'ios.release':     { type: 'ios.app', binaryPath: 'ios/build/MyApp.app', bundleId: 'com.example.app' },
    'android.release': { type: 'android.apk', binaryPath: 'android/app/build/outputs/apk/release/app-release.apk', bundleId: 'com.example.app' },
  },
  devices: {
    'sim.iphone15': { type: 'ios.simulator',    device: { type: 'iPhone 15',    os: 'iOS 18.4' } },
    'emu.pixel9':   { type: 'android.emulator', device: { avdName: 'Pixel_9_API_35' } },
  },
  configurations: {
    'ios.sim.release':     { ...baseConfig, device: 'sim.iphone15', app: 'ios.release' },
    'android.emu.release': { ...baseConfig, device: 'emu.pixel9',   app: 'android.release' },
    'ios.sim.release.ci': {
      ...baseConfig,
      device: 'sim.iphone15',
      app: 'ios.release',
      // CI-specific override: enable parallel workers
      testRunner: { ...baseConfig.testRunner, args: { ...baseConfig.testRunner.args, maxWorkers: 2 } },
    },
  },
};

export default config;
```

**Tradeoff:** TypeScript spread-based inheritance is evaluated at parse time and is purely a language-level construct — Detox receives a fully resolved config object with no `extends` semantics. If Detox adds a native `extends` field in future versions (as a string pointing to another config file), that performs a deep merge at runtime and handles array fields differently from spread. Always check your Detox version's configuration documentation before adopting either approach. The spread technique works with all current Detox versions but does not support deep-merging arrays (e.g., reporter lists) — override array fields explicitly.

---

### Pattern 409 — `element.longPressAndDrag()` for iOS list reorder handle testing with precise coordinate control [official]

`longPressAndDrag` combines a long press at the source element with a drag to a normalized position on the destination element. It is the only reliable way to test drag-and-drop list reordering in Detox — using separate `longPress` + `swipe` calls does not produce a recognized drag gesture because the UIKit gesture recognizer requires a continuous touch sequence.

```typescript
// helpers/dragHelpers.ts

/** Drag a list item from its current position to the position of another item.
 *  Uses longPressAndDrag which produces a UIKit-compatible continuous gesture.
 */
export async function dragListItemToTarget(
  sourceTestID: string,
  targetTestID: string,
  holdDuration = 800,
): Promise<void> {
  await element(by.id(sourceTestID)).longPressAndDrag(
    holdDuration,   // ms to hold before drag starts (must exceed delayLongPress prop)
    0.5,            // normalizedPositionX on source (center)
    0.5,            // normalizedPositionY on source (center)
    element(by.id(targetTestID)),
    0.5,            // normalizedPositionX on target (center)
    0.0,            // normalizedPositionY on target (0.0 = top edge — insert above)
    'fast',         // dragSpeed: 'fast' | 'slow'
    500,            // holdDuration after reaching target (ms)
  );
}

// e2e/tasks/reorder.test.ts
describe('Task list reordering (iOS only)', () => {
  if (device.getPlatform() !== 'ios') {
    it.skip('longPressAndDrag is iOS only', () => {});
    return;
  }

  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    await waitFor(element(by.id('task-list'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
  });

  it('reorders task-3 above task-1', async () => {
    // Verify initial vertical order via frame.y
    const before3 = await element(by.id('task-item-3')).getAttributes();
    const before1 = await element(by.id('task-item-1')).getAttributes();
    expect((before3 as any).frame.y).toBeGreaterThan((before1 as any).frame.y);

    // Drag the reorder handle of task-3 above task-1
    await dragListItemToTarget('task-drag-handle-3', 'task-item-1');

    // After drag: task-3 should now appear above task-1
    await waitFor(element(by.id('task-item-3'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
    const after3 = await element(by.id('task-item-3')).getAttributes();
    const after1 = await element(by.id('task-item-1')).getAttributes();
    expect((after3 as any).frame.y).toBeLessThan((after1 as any).frame.y);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `longPressAndDrag` is iOS-only in Detox. On Android, use UIAutomator2's `drag` action via a custom Detox driver, or test reorder via the app's programmatic API using `launchArgs: { PRESET_TASK_ORDER: '3,1,2' }`. The `holdDuration` parameter must exceed the component's `delayLongPress` prop (default 500 ms in React Native) — if `holdDuration` is shorter, the gesture is treated as a regular tap and the drag never begins. Use `normalizedPositionY: 0.0` to insert *above* the target and `1.0` to insert *below*.

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 50

### Gotcha 275 — `element.adjustSliderToPosition()` with values outside `[0.0, 1.0]` silently clamps to 0 or 1 on iOS but throws `"Value out of range"` on Android, causing platform-divergent test behavior when helper functions pass unbounded computed values [community]

**Root cause**: The iOS Simulator's `XCUIElement.adjust(toNormalizedSliderPosition:)` API internally clamps the input value to `[0, 1]` without raising an error. A value of `1.5` is treated as `1.0` and the slider moves to its maximum position. On Android, Detox's Espresso-based slider action validates the normalized position before dispatching the gesture and throws immediately if the value is not in `[0, 1]`. This means a helper function that passes a computed normalized value of `1.002` (due to floating-point arithmetic in `(targetValue - min) / (max - min)`) passes silently on iOS but throws on Android CI, producing a test failure that appears to be an "Android-only bug" but is actually a numeric precision issue in the test helper.

```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN — unbounded normalization (fails on Android when value ≈ max due to float imprecision)
async function setSliderBad(testID: string, value: number, min: number, max: number) {
  const normalized = (value - min) / (max - min); // May produce 1.0000000001
  await element(by.id(testID)).adjustSliderToPosition(normalized); // Throws on Android
}

// CORRECT — clamp to [0, 1] before passing to Detox
async function setSliderGood(testID: string, value: number, min: number, max: number) {
  const normalized = Math.max(0.0, Math.min(1.0, (value - min) / (max - min)));
  await element(by.id(testID)).adjustSliderToPosition(normalized);
}
```

**WHY this matters:** Platform-divergent clamping behavior means iOS test runs mask numeric precision bugs that only surface on Android, making the Android CI appear to be the flaky or broken platform when the root cause is a shared test helper. Always clamp normalized positions before passing them to `adjustSliderToPosition` to produce identical behavior on both platforms and make any out-of-range inputs immediately visible as a test authoring bug rather than a platform incompatibility.

---

### Gotcha 276 — `device.setLocation()` has no effect on Android physical devices and does not throw an error, causing location-dependent tests to silently test real GPS coordinates instead of the simulated ones [community]

**Root cause**: `device.setLocation()` on Android is implemented via the Android Emulator console command `geo fix <lon> <lat>`. This command is only available through the Android Emulator's TCP control socket, which does not exist on physical devices. When Detox is connected to a physical Android device, the underlying command that would normally route to the emulator socket is silently ignored — no exception is thrown, no warning is logged by default, and the test continues using the device's actual GPS position (which may be 0,0, the last known location, or a real device location depending on device state). Location-based tests that pass on the emulator will either pass spuriously (if the physical device happens to be near the test coordinate) or fail intermittently on physical device CI farms.

```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN — calling setLocation without a platform guard on Android physical devices
await device.setLocation(37.7749, -122.4194); // No-op on physical Android, no error thrown

// CORRECT — guard with platform check; use launchArgs mock on physical Android
export async function setSimulatedLocation(lat: number, lon: number): Promise<void> {
  if (device.getPlatform() === 'android') {
    // Physical Android devices: setLocation is a no-op.
    // Activate app's mock location provider instead via launchArgs.
    // (App must check MOCK_LOCATION_LAT/LON in its location provider setup)
    return;
  }
  await device.setLocation(lat, lon);
}
```

**WHY this matters:** Silent no-ops are among the most dangerous failure modes in test infrastructure because they produce false confidence — the test suite passes, the location feature appears to work, and the actual behavior on real devices is never validated. Teams running Detox on physical device farms (e.g., AWS Device Farm, Firebase Test Lab) should implement a mock location provider in the app itself, activated by a `launchArgs` flag, so that location-dependent tests work identically on emulators and physical devices without relying on `device.setLocation()`.

---

### Gotcha 277 — `device.installApp()` accepts only absolute paths; passing a relative path causes a silent "app not found" failure on CI where the working directory differs from the local development machine [community]

**Root cause**: Detox's `installApp()` implementation passes the path string directly to `xcrun simctl install <udid> <path>` (iOS) or `adb install <path>` (Android). Both CLIs resolve the path relative to their own working directory, which on CI is typically the repository root or a runner-assigned temp directory — not the `e2e/` directory where most Detox test files live. A relative path like `'../fixtures/SenderApp.app'` resolves correctly when running tests from `e2e/` locally but fails on CI because the runner's working directory is the repo root, resolving the path to a location that does not exist.

```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN — relative path (works locally, fails on CI)
await device.installApp('../fixtures/SenderApp.app');

// CORRECT — always use path.resolve() with __dirname for a portable absolute path
import * as path from 'path';
const SENDER_APP_PATH = path.resolve(__dirname, '..', 'fixtures', 'SenderApp.app');
await device.installApp(SENDER_APP_PATH);
```

**WHY this matters:** CI working-directory assumptions are responsible for a large class of "works on my machine" bugs in test infrastructure. Using `path.resolve(__dirname, ...)` always produces an absolute path relative to the current source file, regardless of the process working directory. This makes test fixtures portable across any CI runner configuration. Apply the same pattern to all file paths in Detox tests: binary paths, fixture JSON files, and screenshot comparison baselines.

---

### Gotcha 278 — `jest-circus` `globalSetup` module runs in the Node.js main process before Detox workers spawn, so any `device.*` call inside `globalSetup` throws `"Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'launchApp')"` because the `device` global is only injected into worker contexts by `DetoxCircusEnvironment` [community]

**Root cause**: Jest's `globalSetup` is a Node.js module executed in the main Jest process before any worker threads are forked. The `device` global in Detox is a worker-local singleton injected by the `DetoxCircusEnvironment` test environment, which runs only inside Jest workers. The main Jest process has no access to this environment and no `device` global. Developers who attempt to use `globalSetup` for convenience (e.g., navigating to a seeded state before all tests) encounter a confusing `TypeError` that has nothing to do with their test logic — it is purely a Jest/Detox process-boundary issue.

```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN — calling device.* in globalSetup (throws because device is undefined in main process)
// e2e/setup/globalSetup.ts
export default async function globalSetup() {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true }); // TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined
}

// CORRECT — use globalSetup only for non-Detox infrastructure; delegate device calls to beforeAll
// e2e/setup/globalSetup.ts
import { setup as detoxGlobalSetup } from 'detox/runners/jest/globalSetup';
export default async function globalSetup() {
  // Initialize Detox infrastructure (emulator boot, app install) — no device.* calls
  await detoxGlobalSetup();
  // Safe: file system setup, env vars, test data seeding via HTTP API
  process.env.TEST_RUN_ID = Date.now().toString();
}

// Per-worker app launch belongs in beforeAll inside test files:
beforeAll(async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
});
```

**WHY this matters:** The error message `"Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'launchApp')"` is misleading — it suggests a Detox configuration bug, not a Jest process-boundary issue. Developers often waste hours checking their `.detoxrc.ts` configuration, environment variables, and Detox version when the fix is simply to move `device.*` calls out of `globalSetup` and into `beforeAll` inside test workers. The official Detox `globalSetup` re-export (`detox/runners/jest/globalSetup`) handles emulator boot and app installation — that is the only Detox code that belongs in `globalSetup`.

---

### Gotcha 279 — `element.scrollTo('bottom')` or `element.scroll(pixels, 'down')` on a horizontal `ScrollView` child nested inside a vertical `ScrollView` scrolls the outer container instead of the inner one when the outer container's `testID` is used as the target [community]

**Root cause**: Detox's `scroll()` and `scrollTo()` actions target the element whose `testID` is matched by the selector. When there are nested scroll containers, Detox does not automatically infer that the developer intends to scroll the inner container — it scrolls whichever element is matched by the selector. If a page has a vertical `ScrollView` with `testID="page-scroll"` wrapping a horizontal `ScrollView` with `testID="carousel"`, calling `element(by.id('page-scroll')).scroll(300, 'right')` dispatches a right-swipe gesture to the outer vertical container. The outer container does not scroll horizontally (it has `horizontal={false}`), so the gesture is silently absorbed or produces an unintended vertical scroll. The inner carousel never receives the event and the subsequent `toBeVisible()` assertion on a carousel item times out.

```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN — targeting outer container for inner horizontal scroll (silent no-op or vertical scroll)
await element(by.id('page-scroll')).scroll(300, 'right');

// ANTI-PATTERN — whileElement also targets the wrong container
await waitFor(element(by.id('carousel-item-5')))
  .toBeVisible()
  .whileElement(by.id('page-scroll'))
  .scroll(300, 'right');
// page-scroll cannot scroll right — carousel-item-5 is never revealed

// CORRECT — always target the horizontal ScrollView directly by its own testID
await waitFor(element(by.id('carousel-item-5')))
  .toBeVisible()
  .whileElement(by.id('carousel'))
  .scroll(300, 'right');

// Or for a direct scroll without waitFor:
await element(by.id('carousel')).scroll(300, 'right');
```

**WHY this matters:** Nested scroll views are extremely common in production apps (e.g., a product listing page with a horizontal promotional banner inside a vertically scrollable product grid), and the silent-no-op failure mode means the test appears to be testing scroll behavior when it is actually testing nothing at all. Always verify which scroll container is being targeted by checking that the `testID` belongs to the container whose `horizontal` prop matches the desired scroll direction. Write integration test helpers (`scrollHorizontal(testID, pixels)` vs `scrollVertical(testID, pixels)`) that enforce the naming convention.
