## Community Gotchas — Cycle 52

### Gotcha 285 — `element.clearText()` on Android leaves the cursor at position 0 rather than at the end of the field, causing a subsequent `typeText()` call to prepend new text rather than replace it, resulting in garbled field values [community]

**Root cause:** On Android, `clearText()` is implemented via the `AccessibilityNodeInfo.ACTION_SET_TEXT` action with an empty string, which clears the field but does not reposition the cursor. The cursor defaults to position 0 after the clear. A subsequent `typeText('hello')` call inserts characters at the cursor position, which is now the beginning of the field — on a field that has just been cleared this appears correct (the field shows "hello"), but if the field is re-focused between the clear and type (e.g., a `tap()` on the field), the cursor may be repositioned by the tap, producing the new text at an unexpected location. The reliable fix is to use `replaceText('newValue')` as a single atomic operation instead of `clearText()` + `typeText()`.

**WHY this matters:** Teams that migrate from Espresso or XCUITest often assume `clearText()` + `typeText()` is the canonical two-step input pattern. In Detox on Android, this pattern silently produces wrong results whenever anything repositions the cursor between the two calls. Always use `replaceText()` for single-step value replacement; only use `clearText()` when you need to verify the clearing itself triggers the correct component behavior.

---

### Gotcha 286 — `device.disableSynchronization()` called inside a `waitFor` scope (e.g., as part of a `whileElement` scroll chain) causes Detox to silently skip the outer `waitFor` condition check, producing a false pass even when the target element is not visible [community]

**Root cause:** Detox's `waitFor` polling loop uses the synchronization state to determine when to re-evaluate the condition. Calling `device.disableSynchronization()` inside the `whileElement` action callback interrupts the polling contract — Detox marks the synchronization context as "user-disabled" and stops driving the re-evaluation cycle. The `waitFor` promise resolves at the next opportunity without re-checking the condition, returning success regardless of the element's actual state. This manifests as a test that "passes" even though the element never became visible.

**WHY this matters:** The `disableSynchronization()` API must only be called at the top-level test scope, never nested inside a `waitFor` chain, an `element` action callback, or any other Detox async sequence. Treat it as a mode switch for the entire test context: disable at the beginning, do work, re-enable via `enableSynchronization()` in a `finally` block, then resume using standard Detox assertions. See Pattern 432 for the correct wrapper pattern.

---

### Gotcha 287 — `by.ancestor()` / `withAncestor()` matching is depth-unlimited, so a broad ancestor `testID` shared by a tab navigator container matches elements across ALL tabs, not just the active one, causing `tap()` actions on invisible off-screen tab content to silently succeed [community]

**Root cause:** React Navigation's tab navigator keeps all tab screens mounted (by default) to preserve scroll position and data. The native view hierarchy therefore contains all tab screens simultaneously — only one is visible, but all are present. A `withAncestor(by.id('main-tab-navigator'))` matcher matches elements across all tabs because the navigator root is an ancestor of every tab's content. Tapping an element anchored this way may tap an off-screen duplicate rather than the on-screen version. The symptom is that the test appears to succeed but the expected visual change does not occur (the off-screen action fires but is not visible).

**WHY this matters:** Always use the screen-level root `testID` as the ancestor (e.g., `withAncestor(by.id('profile-screen-root'))`), not the navigator container `testID`. If you need to assert that an action occurs on the *active* tab, first assert `toBeVisible()` on the screen-root element before using it as an ancestor scope, ensuring the screen is both mounted and on-screen before the action.

---

### Gotcha 288 — `test.each` / `it.each` generates identical test display names when two data rows have the same first-column value (used as `%s` in the title template), causing `--testNamePattern` filtering to match both rows and making targeted re-runs unreliable [community]

**Root cause:** Jest's `test.each` uses printf-style interpolation with `%s`, `%d`, etc. When two rows share the same first-column string (e.g., two "email" validation cases with different error messages), both tests are registered under the same display name. The `--testNamePattern` regex filter matches on display name, so filtering to re-run one case silently re-runs both. This also causes duplicate test names in JUnit XML output, which breaks CI test result aggregation tools that use test name as a unique key.

**WHY this matters:** Always ensure the combination of interpolated values in the test title template produces a globally unique string within the `describe` block. A common fix is to add a `label` or `id` field as the first column of the data table and ensure labels are unique: `['empty-email', '', 'email-error', 'Email is required']`. In Jest 29+, you can also use tagged template literals with `test.each` to construct arbitrarily complex unique titles without positional argument dependencies.

---

### Gotcha 289 — `device.setStatusBar({ batteryState: 'charging' })` on iOS Simulator 18+ silently ignores the `batteryState` property when `batteryLevel` is not provided in the same call, leaving the status bar battery icon in its default state and invalidating screenshot baselines that depend on a specific battery icon appearance [community]

**Root cause:** iOS 18 changed the status bar battery rendering to require a coherent `{ batteryLevel, batteryState }` tuple. In earlier iOS Simulator versions, setting `batteryState` alone was sufficient to change the battery icon. In iOS 18+, the Simulator validates that `batteryLevel` is present and non-null whenever `batteryState` is specified; if `batteryLevel` is absent, the `batteryState` property is silently discarded. Detox 20.50 and earlier did not validate this constraint client-side, so no error is thrown — the call appears to succeed but the status bar is unchanged. The fix is to always specify both `batteryLevel` and `batteryState` together. Detox 20.51.1 added a client-side warning for this case (PR #4948).

**WHY this matters:** Screenshot regression suites that assert on exact pixel content (not just layout structure) are invalidated when the battery icon differs from the baseline. Always use the complete `FROZEN_STATUS_BAR` object from Pattern 429 (which includes both `batteryLevel: 100` and `batteryState: 'charged'`) rather than setting individual status bar properties piecemeal.

---

## Cycle 54 — 2026-05-14

### New Patterns

**Pattern 439: `element.tapAtPoint()` for Precise Coordinate Tapping Within a View** [official]
When a component renders multiple tappable regions without individual `testID` props (e.g., a canvas, map overlay, or custom gesture grid), use `tapAtPoint({ x, y })` to send a tap at a pixel coordinate relative to the matched element's origin. This avoids the need to restructure the component hierarchy just to expose individual sub-elements as testable nodes.
```typescript
// Tap a specific cell in a custom 3x3 grid component
// Grid is 300x300 logical pixels; each cell is 100x100
async function tapGridCell(row: number, col: number): Promise<void> {
  const cellSize = 100;
  const x = col * cellSize + cellSize / 2; // center of cell column
  const y = row * cellSize + cellSize / 2; // center of cell row
  await element(by.id('game-grid')).tapAtPoint({ x, y });
}

it('selects center cell in tic-tac-toe board', async () => {
  await tapGridCell(1, 1); // row 1, col 1 = center
  await expect(element(by.id('grid-cell-1-1-marker'))).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: Coordinate taps are fragile against layout changes — if the grid resizes for a tablet or the component padding changes, all hardcoded coordinates break simultaneously. Use only when the component geometry is stable and documented. Prefer individual `testID` props on sub-elements whenever the component can be modified.

---

**Pattern 440: `waitFor().toHaveText()` with Polling for Async-Updated Labels** [official]
Text labels driven by async data (API responses, timers, computed values) may not yet show their final value when the element first becomes visible. Chain `.toHaveText()` onto a `waitFor()` call to poll until the text value stabilizes, avoiding race conditions between element visibility and data hydration.
```typescript
// Submit a form and wait for the server-confirmed order ID to appear
async function submitOrderAndWaitForConfirmation(orderId: string): Promise<void> {
  await element(by.id('submit-order-button')).tap();

  // The order-id label becomes visible immediately with a placeholder,
  // then updates when the server confirms. Wait for the real value.
  await waitFor(element(by.id('confirmation-order-id')))
    .toHaveText(`Order #${orderId}`)
    .withTimeout(10_000);
}

it('shows confirmed order ID after checkout', async () => {
  await submitOrderAndWaitForConfirmation('ORD-1234');
  await expect(element(by.id('confirmation-screen-root'))).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `waitFor().toHaveText()` re-evaluates on every Detox idle tick, which is efficient when the app is genuinely busy (network call in flight) but can produce noisy retry logs when the text lags by only a few milliseconds. If the delay is consistently long (>3 s), consider emitting a loading indicator `testID` and using `waitFor().not.toBeVisible()` on the spinner instead, which is more readable in test output.

---

**Pattern 441: `device.sendUserActivity()` for Handoff and Spotlight Integration Testing** [official]
iOS Handoff (`NSUserActivity`) and Spotlight deep links are a common entry point for iPad/iPhone productivity apps. Use `device.sendUserActivity()` to inject a `NSUserActivity` payload into the running app and verify the navigation response, without needing a real second device or Spotlight index build.
```typescript
// Test that a document opened via Handoff navigates to the correct editor screen
const handoffActivity = {
  activityType: 'com.example.app.document.view',
  userInfo: { documentId: 'doc-abc-123' },
  webpageURL: 'https://example.com/documents/doc-abc-123',
};

it('opens document editor via Handoff activity', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen-root')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(5000);

  await device.sendUserActivity(handoffActivity);

  await waitFor(element(by.id('document-editor-screen')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(6000);
  await expect(element(by.id('document-title'))).toHaveText('doc-abc-123');
});
```
Tradeoff: `device.sendUserActivity()` is iOS-only. There is no Android equivalent in Detox — Android App Links and Google Assistant shortcuts require `device.openURL()` with an `https://` intent or a custom intent via `adb shell am start`. Always guard with `if (device.getPlatform() === 'ios')` or skip the test on Android.

---

**Pattern 442: `by.type()` Cross-Platform Semantic Class Matchers** [official]
Detox 20.47+ introduces `by.type()` which accepts a native class name string (`RCTView`, `UIButton`, `android.widget.Button`) or one of the semantic aliases (`RNTextInput`, `RNScrollView`). This is useful for asserting that exactly N elements of a given native type are present on screen, or for targeting a third-party component that does not expose a `testID`.
```typescript
// Assert that exactly one RN TextInput is focused after tapping the search bar
it('focuses only the search input when search bar is tapped', async () => {
  await element(by.id('search-bar')).tap();

  // On iOS, RN TextInput renders as RCTSinglelineTextInputView or RCTMultilineTextInputView
  // On Android, it renders as ReactEditText
  const inputType =
    device.getPlatform() === 'ios'
      ? 'RCTSinglelineTextInputView'
      : 'com.facebook.react.views.textinput.ReactEditText';

  const inputs = await element(by.type(inputType)).getAttributes();
  const inputArray = Array.isArray(inputs) ? inputs : [inputs];
  const focusedInputs = inputArray.filter((el) => el.enabled);
  expect(focusedInputs.length).toBe(1);
});
```
Tradeoff: Native class names change between React Native versions. `RCTSinglelineTextInputView` was renamed in RN 0.78+ New Architecture builds. Always abstract behind a helper (`getInputType()`) that returns the correct class name based on `device.getPlatform()` and a `REACT_NATIVE_VERSION` env var, so a single helper function absorbs the cross-version mapping.

---

**Pattern 443: `element.scroll()` `startPositionY` for Sticky-Header-Aware Scrolling** [official]
When a `ScrollView` or `FlatList` has a sticky header that occupies the top portion of the viewport, a `scroll()` action starting at `startPositionY: 0.0` will begin on the sticky header itself, triggering the header's gesture handlers instead of the list content. Set `startPositionY` to a normalized value just below the header to ensure the gesture starts within the scrollable content area.
```typescript
// A product list with a sticky category header ~15% of screen height
async function scrollProductList(direction: 'up' | 'down', pixels = 400): Promise<void> {
  await element(by.id('product-list'))
    .scroll(pixels, direction, NaN, 0.25); // startPositionX=NaN (default), startPositionY=0.25
}

it('loads more products when scrolling to end of list', async () => {
  await scrollProductList('down', 800);
  await waitFor(element(by.id('loading-more-indicator')))
    .not.toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(5000);
  await expect(element(by.id('product-item-20'))).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: The `startPositionY` offset must be tuned per screen. A value that works for a 56 dp header on a standard phone will be too large on a tablet (where the header is proportionally smaller) and too small on a device with a large font-size accessibility setting (which inflates the header). Express `startPositionY` as a constant tied to the component's design spec and document the assumption explicitly in a comment.

---

**Pattern 444: Deterministic Biometric Auth Testing with `device.matchFace()` / `device.matchFinger()`** [official]
React Native apps that use `LocalAuthentication` (Expo) or `react-native-biometrics` require biometric prompts to be handled in tests without real fingerprint or Face ID hardware. Detox provides simulator-level biometric simulation APIs. Use the Detox 20.51+ API names (`device.matchFace()`, `device.unmatchFace()`, `device.matchFinger()`, `device.unmatchFinger()`) and guard with `device.getPlatform()`.
```typescript
// Helper for platform-correct biometric success simulation
async function simulateBiometricSuccess(): Promise<void> {
  if (device.getPlatform() === 'ios') {
    await device.setBiometricEnrollment(true);
    await device.matchFace(); // Detox 20.51+; pre-20.51 used device.matchFace() identically
  } else {
    await device.matchFinger();
  }
}

it('unlocks the app vault with biometric auth', async () => {
  await element(by.id('unlock-with-biometric-button')).tap();
  // Biometric prompt is shown — simulate match immediately
  await simulateBiometricSuccess();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('vault-content-screen')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(5000);
});
```
Tradeoff: On iOS, `device.setBiometricEnrollment(true)` must be called before the first `matchFace()` call in the test session; calling `matchFace()` without enrollment enrollment throws a `BiometricEnrollmentNotFound` error that is easily confused with a real authentication failure. The enrollment state persists for the lifetime of the Simulator session — set it once in `globalSetup` and reset it in `globalTeardown` to avoid bleed between separate test suite runs.

---

**Pattern 445: `element.getAttributes()` for Scroll Position Assertions** [official]
`getAttributes()` returns a `contentOffset`, `contentSize`, and `visibleArea` for `ScrollView`-backed elements on iOS. Use these to assert that a programmatic scroll (triggered by app logic, not by the test) reached the expected offset — e.g., verifying that tapping a "scroll to top" button actually scrolled the list.
```typescript
interface ScrollAttributes {
  contentOffset?: { x: number; y: number };
  contentSize?: { width: number; height: number };
  visibleArea?: { x: number; y: number; width: number; height: number };
}

async function assertScrolledToTop(listId: string, tolerance = 5): Promise<void> {
  const attrs = (await element(by.id(listId)).getAttributes()) as ScrollAttributes;
  expect(attrs.contentOffset?.y ?? 0).toBeLessThanOrEqual(tolerance);
}

it('scrolls to top when FAB is tapped after scrolling down', async () => {
  await element(by.id('article-list')).scroll(1000, 'down');
  await element(by.id('scroll-to-top-fab')).tap();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('article-item-0'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
  await assertScrolledToTop('article-list');
});
```
Tradeoff: `contentOffset` is only available on iOS for `ScrollView`/`FlatList`-backed elements. On Android, `getAttributes()` does not expose scroll position — the equivalent check is `waitFor(element(by.id('first-item'))).toBeVisible()`. Always wrap scroll-position assertions in a `device.getPlatform() === 'ios'` guard or use the visibility-based fallback on both platforms for cross-platform portability.

---

**Pattern 446: `launchArgs` as Feature Flags for Test-Only Code Paths** [official]
Pass test-specific configuration via `device.launchApp({ launchArgs: { ... } })` to activate test-only behaviors (e.g., skip onboarding, use a mock API, pre-seed a specific user role) without modifying production code paths. This pattern keeps test setup out of business logic while making test preconditions explicit and auditable.
```typescript
// In the React Native app (e.g., App.tsx)
// const skipOnboarding = global.__E2E_SKIP_ONBOARDING__ === 'true';

// In the Detox test
async function launchAsAuthenticatedUser(role: 'admin' | 'viewer'): Promise<void> {
  await device.launchApp({
    newInstance: true,
    launchArgs: {
      e2eSkipOnboarding: 'true',
      e2eUserRole: role,
      e2eMockApiBaseUrl: 'http://localhost:3001',
    },
  });
}

beforeEach(async () => {
  await launchAsAuthenticatedUser('admin');
  await waitFor(element(by.id('dashboard-screen-root')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(6000);
});
```
Tradeoff: `launchArgs` values are always strings — booleans, numbers, and JSON objects must be serialized and deserialized manually in the app code. Establish a naming convention (e.g., all test args prefixed with `e2e`) and gate their consumption behind `if (__DEV__ || process.env.IS_DETOX_ENV)` to prevent test-only code paths from leaking into release builds. Never use `launchArgs` to pass credentials — use a dedicated test user seeded in the test environment instead.

---

**Pattern 447: `globalSetup` + `globalTeardown` for Emulator Pre-warming and Cleanup** [official]
Cold-starting an Android emulator or iOS Simulator at the beginning of every CI run adds 3–8 minutes of overhead. Use `globalSetup.js` to pre-warm the device before Jest spawns any workers, and `globalTeardown.js` to perform cleanup (kill adb, release ports) after all tests complete. This keeps per-worker `beforeAll` hooks fast.
```typescript
// e2e/globalSetup.ts
import { execSync } from 'child_process';

export default async function globalSetup(): Promise<void> {
  const platform = process.env.DETOX_CONFIGURATION?.includes('android') ? 'android' : 'ios';

  if (platform === 'ios') {
    const udid = process.env.SIMULATOR_UDID ?? 'booted';
    execSync(`xcrun simctl bootstatus ${udid} -b`, { stdio: 'inherit', timeout: 120_000 });
    console.log('[globalSetup] iOS Simulator pre-warmed');
  } else {
    execSync('adb wait-for-device', { stdio: 'inherit', timeout: 60_000 });
    console.log('[globalSetup] Android emulator ready');
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: `globalSetup` runs in the Jest orchestrator process, not in a Detox device context — `device.*` APIs are unavailable. Use only Node.js `child_process` / `execa` calls to shell commands. If the pre-warm command fails (e.g., emulator not yet started), `globalSetup` will throw and abort the entire test run with a clear error, which is the correct failure mode compared to individual tests timing out with confusing synchronization errors.

---

**Pattern 448: `detox test --inspect-brk` + VS Code Debugger for Step-Through Test Debugging** [community]
Detox ships with full Node.js debugger support. Passing `--inspect-brk` to the Detox CLI pauses execution at the first line of the test file, allowing you to set breakpoints in VS Code and step through `await element(...).tap()` calls one by one while watching the Simulator screen. This replaces the unproductive `console.log` + re-run loop.
```typescript
// .vscode/launch.json — add this configuration
// {
//   "type": "node",
//   "request": "attach",
//   "name": "Attach to Detox",
//   "port": 9229,
//   "skipFiles": ["<node_internals>/**", "**/node_modules/**"]
// }

// Run in terminal first:
// npx detox test --configuration ios.sim.debug --inspect-brk e2e/login.test.ts

it('debuggable login test', async () => {
  // Set a breakpoint on the next line in VS Code, then attach the debugger
  await element(by.id('email-input')).typeText('user@example.com');
  await element(by.id('password-input')).typeText('password123');
  await element(by.id('login-button')).tap();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('dashboard-screen')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(5000);
});
```
Tradeoff: `--inspect-brk` works only with `--workers 1` (single-worker mode) because the Node.js inspector attaches to a single process. Parallel Detox workers each run in their own Node process — you cannot attach a single VS Code debugger to multiple workers simultaneously. Always add `--workers 1` when using the debugger, and remove it before committing the test to CI.

---

**Pattern 449: `element.pinch()` for Map Zoom and Custom Zoom Gesture Components** [official]
`element.pinch(scale, speed, angle)` drives a two-finger pinch gesture on the matched element. Use it to test map zoom level changes, PDF viewer zoom, and custom `PinchGestureHandler`-backed components. The `scale` parameter uses standard pinch semantics: `< 1.0` = pinch in (zoom out), `> 1.0` = pinch out (zoom in).
```typescript
// Test that a map view zooms in when pinch-out gesture is applied
async function pinchZoomMap(scale: number, speed: 'slow' | 'fast' = 'slow'): Promise<void> {
  // speed: 'slow' is recommended for map views to avoid triggering momentum scroll
  await element(by.id('map-view')).pinch(scale, speed);
}

it('zooms in on map and reveals street-level detail markers', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await waitFor(element(by.id('map-view'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);

  await pinchZoomMap(2.5, 'slow'); // zoom in 2.5x

  // Street-level POI markers appear only at zoom level > 14
  await waitFor(element(by.id('poi-marker-cafe-001')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(4000);
});
```
Tradeoff: `element.pinch()` is an iOS-only API in Detox. On Android, pinch zoom must be simulated via two sequential `element.swipe()` calls with coordinated start positions, or by using `device.sendKeyEvent()` for keyboard-accessible zoom controls. For components backed by `react-native-gesture-handler` `PinchGestureHandler`, always wrap the component in `GestureHandlerRootView` at the app root, not just around the specific component — a subtree-only `GestureHandlerRootView` silently fails to route pinch events on Android.

---

**Pattern 450: Custom `testEnvironment` Extension for Per-Test Screenshot on Failure** [community]
The default Detox Jest environment does not capture screenshots automatically when a test fails. Extend `DetoxCircusEnvironment` to override `handleTestEvent` and call `device.takeScreenshot()` on `test_fn_failure` events, storing screenshots with the test name in the filename. This dramatically reduces the time to diagnose CI failures.
```typescript
// e2e/environment/ScreenshotEnvironment.ts
import { DetoxCircusEnvironment } from 'detox/runners/jest';
import type { Circus } from '@jest/circus';
import path from 'path';

export default class ScreenshotEnvironment extends DetoxCircusEnvironment {
  async handleTestEvent(event: Circus.Event, state: Circus.State): Promise<void> {
    await super.handleTestEvent(event, state);

    if (event.name === 'test_fn_failure') {
      const testName = state.currentlyRunningTest?.fullName ?? 'unknown';
      const safeName = testName.replace(/[^a-z0-9]/gi, '_').slice(0, 100);
      const screenshotPath = path.join('e2e', 'artifacts', `FAIL_${safeName}.png`);
      await device.takeScreenshot(screenshotPath);
      console.log(`[ScreenshotEnvironment] Screenshot saved: ${screenshotPath}`);
    }
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: Screenshots on failure add ~200–500 ms per failed test (file I/O + device communication), which is negligible in practice. The larger risk is artifact storage: on a suite with 200 tests and a 10% failure rate, 20 screenshots are captured per run. Configure your CI artifact retention policy to auto-delete screenshots after 14 days to prevent unbounded storage growth. Avoid capturing screenshots on flaky retries (check `event.name === 'test_retry'`) to reduce noise.

---

**Pattern 451: `device.setLocation()` for Geolocation-Dependent Feature Testing** [official]
Apps that gate features on the user's geographic location (regional promotions, delivery availability, map centering) require a deterministic location for testing. Use `device.setLocation(lat, lon)` to inject a GPS coordinate into the Simulator/emulator before exercising the location-dependent feature, and reset to a neutral coordinate in `afterEach`.
```typescript
const LOCATIONS = {
  newYork: { lat: 40.7128, lon: -74.006 },
  london: { lat: 51.5074, lon: -0.1278 },
  sydney: { lat: -33.8688, lon: 151.2093 },
} as const;

async function setLocation(name: keyof typeof LOCATIONS): Promise<void> {
  const { lat, lon } = LOCATIONS[name];
  await device.setLocation(lat, lon);
}

it('shows NYC-specific delivery options when user is in New York', async () => {
  await setLocation('newYork');
  await element(by.id('order-delivery-tab')).tap();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('nyc-express-delivery-option')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(4000);
});

afterEach(async () => {
  // Reset to a location with no special gating to avoid bleed
  await device.setLocation(0, 0);
});
```
Tradeoff: `device.setLocation()` on Android requires the emulator to be started with the `-writable-system` flag (API 29+) or the GPS mock to be enabled via developer options. On physical Android devices, location mocking requires a "Mock Location App" permission in developer settings — this is not automatable via Detox and must be pre-configured in CI device profiles. iOS Simulator supports `setLocation()` without additional setup in all Detox-supported Xcode versions.

---

**Pattern 452: Snapshot-Free Layout Regression with `element.takeScreenshot()` + `pixelmatch`** [community]
Detox's `device.takeScreenshot()` captures the full screen, which is fragile against unrelated UI changes (status bar, notifications, dynamic content). `element(by.id('component-root')).takeScreenshot('name')` captures only the matched element's bounding box. Pipe this into `pixelmatch` for a pixel-diff assertion against a stored baseline, creating component-scoped visual regression tests.
```typescript
import fs from 'fs';
import path from 'path';
import { PNG } from 'pngjs';
import pixelmatch from 'pixelmatch';

async function assertVisualMatch(
  elementId: string,
  baselineName: string,
  threshold = 0.02
): Promise<void> {
  const screenshotPath = await element(by.id(elementId)).takeScreenshot(baselineName);
  const baselinePath = path.join('e2e', 'baselines', `${baselineName}.png`);

  if (!fs.existsSync(baselinePath)) {
    fs.copyFileSync(screenshotPath, baselinePath);
    console.log(`[visual] Baseline created: ${baselinePath}`);
    return; // First run creates baseline; subsequent runs compare
  }

  const current = PNG.sync.read(fs.readFileSync(screenshotPath));
  const baseline = PNG.sync.read(fs.readFileSync(baselinePath));
  const diff = new PNG({ width: baseline.width, height: baseline.height });
  const diffPixels = pixelmatch(baseline.data, current.data, diff.data,
    baseline.width, baseline.height, { threshold });
  expect(diffPixels).toBeLessThanOrEqual(baseline.width * baseline.height * 0.001); // 0.1% tolerance
}
```
Tradeoff: Element-scoped screenshots require the element to be fully visible and not clipped by its parent container — a partially off-screen element produces a screenshot of only the visible portion, causing spurious diff failures. Always call `waitFor(element).toBeVisible()` before capturing, and verify the element's frame is fully within the viewport using `getAttributes().frame` if baselines are inconsistently sized.

---

**Pattern 453: `by.id().withDescendant()` for Asserting Composite List Item State** [official]
`withDescendant()` is the mirror of `withAncestor()`: it filters the matched set to only elements that contain a specific descendant. Use it to assert that a list row containing a particular child element (e.g., a badge, an icon, a specific text node) is present without needing to know the row's position or testID.
```typescript
// Assert that a notification list item with "Unread" badge exists somewhere in the list
async function assertUnreadNotificationExists(title: string): Promise<void> {
  // Find a list-item that contains both the given title text AND an unread badge
  await expect(
    element(
      by.id('notification-list-item')
        .withDescendant(by.id('unread-badge'))
        .withDescendant(by.text(title))
    )
  ).toBeVisible();
}

it('shows unread badge on the latest push notification', async () => {
  // Simulate receiving a push notification
  await device.sendUserNotification({
    title: 'New Message',
    body: 'You have a new message from Alice',
    trigger: { type: 'push' },
  });
  await assertUnreadNotificationExists('New Message');
});
```
Tradeoff: Chaining two `.withDescendant()` matchers on the same `by.id()` root requires Detox 20.44+ (earlier versions only supported a single `.withDescendant()` chain). The match is depth-unlimited — if the list item has deeply nested children, `withDescendant(by.text(title))` will match any `Text` node anywhere in the subtree, including tooltips or screen-reader-only nodes. Combine with `by.id()` for the text node when the title is also assigned a `testID`.

---

### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha G290: `element.takeScreenshot()` file path is relative to the Detox artifacts root, not the test file's directory**
When calling `element(by.id('x')).takeScreenshot('my-screenshot')`, the returned string is a path relative to the Detox artifacts directory configured via `artifacts.rootDir` in `.detoxrc.js`, not the `__dirname` of the test file. Teams that append this path to `__dirname` or `process.cwd()` end up constructing double-rooted paths (e.g., `/project/e2e//project/detox-artifacts/...`) that fail silently at the `fs.readFileSync` step, causing the visual comparison to crash with `ENOENT` rather than a meaningful diff failure.
WHY: The Detox artifact system manages file placement independently of Jest's file resolution. The path returned by `takeScreenshot()` is already absolute and valid — treat it as such and never join it with another base path.
Fix: Use the returned path directly as an absolute path. If you need a stable relative path for version control of baselines, configure `artifacts.rootDir` to a project-relative directory (e.g., `./e2e/artifacts`) and document this in the test setup guide.

---

**Gotcha G291: `device.openURL()` on Android does not wait for the Activity to start before returning, causing the next `waitFor()` assertion to fire before the target screen is mounted**
On iOS, Detox's `openURL()` implementation hooks into `UIApplication.open(_:options:completionHandler:)` and awaits the completion callback before releasing control back to the test. On Android, the equivalent `am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW` shell command does not block until the Activity is fully created and its `onResume()` has been called — the `device.openURL()` promise resolves as soon as the intent is dispatched, not when the screen is ready.
WHY: Android's intent dispatch is fire-and-forget at the OS level. The app process receives the intent asynchronously, and Activity creation involves multiple lifecycle callbacks that are invisible to Detox's synchronization layer.
Fix: After `device.openURL()` on Android, always follow with `waitFor(element(by.id('target-screen-root'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000)` rather than asserting on a child element immediately. Adding `await device.reloadReactNative()` before `openURL()` as a warm-start reset also improves reliability by ensuring Metro's module graph is fully resolved before the Activity starts.

---

**Gotcha G292: `element.swipe('left')` on a `ScrollView` with `pagingEnabled: true` lands on the wrong page on Android API 34+ when hardware rendering is disabled on the emulator**
Android emulators with `-no-accel` or snapshot-based boot (which disables hardware rendering) use software rasterization for all UI compositing. With `pagingEnabled: true`, the `ScrollView` paging snap animation relies on the hardware-accelerated `OverScroller` to calculate the snap target. In software rendering mode, the `OverScroller` snap calculation is subtly different, causing the `ScrollView` to snap to page N-1 instead of page N when a swipe gesture is applied.
WHY: This is an Android emulator bug specific to software rendering mode, not a Detox bug. Detox faithfully delivers the gesture, but the emulator's software compositor computes the wrong snap offset.
Fix: In CI, always start Android emulators with hardware rendering enabled: use `emulator -avd <name> -gpu swiftshader_indirect` (or `host` on macOS/Linux CI with KVM) rather than `-no-accel`. Add a CI job validation step that asserts `adb shell getprop qemu.gles` returns `1` (hardware rendering enabled) before running Detox tests.

---

**Gotcha G293: `device.reloadReactNative()` resets the JS bundle state but does NOT reset navigation history, causing tests that call `reloadReactNative()` in `beforeEach` to start on the screen shown at the end of the previous test rather than the app's initial route**
`device.reloadReactNative()` reloads the JS bundle (equivalent to pressing `R` in Metro) — it rebuilds the component tree from scratch but does NOT restart the native app process. React Navigation and other navigation libraries store their navigation state in memory (or in a Redux/Zustand store) that persists across JS reloads if the native module that backs it is not reset.
WHY: The native navigation module (e.g., `RNScreens`, `react-navigation/native`) holds its state in a native data structure that survives a JS reload. Only a full process restart (`device.launchApp({ newInstance: true })`) or an explicit state reset call (e.g., `device.launchApp({ launchArgs: { e2eResetNavigation: 'true' } })`) fully clears navigation history.
Fix: Use `device.launchApp({ newInstance: true })` in `beforeEach` for any test that depends on starting at a specific initial route. Reserve `reloadReactNative()` for tests that only need to reset JS-layer state (e.g., clearing a Redux store) and do not care about navigation position, and document this assumption explicitly in the test file.

---

**Gotcha G294: `waitFor(element).not.toBeVisible().withTimeout(N)` passes immediately when the element has never been rendered (it was never in the tree), producing a false-pass for "element dismissed" assertions**
`waitFor().not.toBeVisible()` resolves as soon as the matcher returns `false`. An element that has never been mounted into the React component tree trivially satisfies `not.toBeVisible()` without the test having performed the action that should dismiss it. This is most common in tests that assert a modal or toast is dismissed after a user action — if the action fails silently (e.g., the button tap did not register), the modal was never shown, and `not.toBeVisible()` passes immediately.
WHY: Detox's visibility check returns `false` for both "element is in the tree but hidden" and "element is not in the tree at all." The `not.toBeVisible()` assertion cannot distinguish between these two states. This is a fundamental limitation of the current Detox expectation API.
Fix: Always structure dismiss-flow assertions as a two-step sequence: (1) `await expect(element(by.id('modal'))).toBeVisible()` — asserts the element IS present before the action; (2) perform the dismiss action; (3) `await waitFor(element(by.id('modal'))).not.toBeVisible().withTimeout(N)` — asserts it is gone. This ensures the "not visible" check is only reached when the element was confirmed present beforehand.

## Cycle 55 — 2026-05-14

### New Patterns

**Pattern 454: `element.longPress()` with explicit duration for context-menu and drag-activation flows** [official]
Long-press interactions have a platform-specific minimum duration threshold before the OS recognises them as a long-press: ~500 ms on iOS and ~600 ms on Android. Calling `element.longPress()` without a `duration` argument uses Detox's default (500 ms), which passes on iOS but flakily misses the Android threshold, especially on emulators under CPU load. Specifying a cross-platform safe duration of 800 ms eliminates the flake.

```typescript
// helpers/gestures.ts
import { element, by } from 'detox';

const LONG_PRESS_DURATION_MS = 800; // safe on both iOS (≥500 ms) and Android (≥600 ms)

export async function longPressItem(testID: string): Promise<void> {
  await element(by.id(testID)).longPress(LONG_PRESS_DURATION_MS);
}

// Usage in test
it('opens context menu via long-press', async () => {
  await longPressItem('message-bubble-42');
  await expect(element(by.id('context-menu'))).toBeVisible();
  await expect(element(by.id('context-menu-copy'))).toBeVisible();
  await expect(element(by.id('context-menu-delete'))).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: Using 800 ms as the universal duration adds ~300 ms per long-press action to suite runtime. For suites with many long-press tests this accumulates; consider reducing to 600 ms and gating with `device.getPlatform()` only when runtime budget is tight.

---

**Pattern 455: `by.id().withAncestor()` for disambiguating duplicate testIDs across sibling containers** [official]
When two or more instances of the same component are rendered on screen simultaneously (e.g., a list of cards each containing a `save-button`), `by.id('save-button')` matches all instances and causes `AmbiguousElementException`. `withAncestor()` narrows the match to the element whose tree ancestor carries a unique `testID`, making the selector deterministic without requiring per-item unique IDs on every child.

```typescript
// Component renders: <View testID="card-12"><TouchableOpacity testID="save-button" /></View>
// and:               <View testID="card-47"><TouchableOpacity testID="save-button" /></View>

async function tapSaveButtonInCard(cardId: string): Promise<void> {
  await element(
    by.id('save-button').withAncestor(by.id(`card-${cardId}`))
  ).tap();
}

it('saves the correct card when multiple cards are visible', async () => {
  await tapSaveButtonInCard('12');
  await waitFor(element(by.id('card-12').withDescendant(by.id('saved-badge'))))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(3000);
  // card-47's save button remains untouched
  await expect(element(by.id('card-47').withDescendant(by.id('saved-badge')))).not.toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `withAncestor()` traverses upward through the view tree, which is slightly more expensive than a flat `by.id()` lookup on large hierarchies. It is always preferable to assigning globally unique testIDs to every child element, which grows linearly with list size and makes components harder to reuse.

---

**Pattern 456: `device.setOrientation()` with post-rotation `waitFor` for responsive-layout assertions** [official]
`device.setOrientation('landscape')` completes the rotation at the native layer, but React Native's layout engine needs one more render pass to reflow components for the new dimensions. Immediately asserting element positions after `setOrientation()` can catch the element mid-reflow, yielding stale frames. A `waitFor` on a landmark element whose layout change is certain (e.g., the app's main scrollview expanding to landscape width) gates subsequent assertions correctly.

```typescript
const LANDSCAPE_SETTLE_MS = 2000;

async function rotateAndSettle(
  orientation: 'landscape' | 'portrait'
): Promise<void> {
  await device.setOrientation(orientation);
  // Wait for the navigation header — its width changes on every rotation
  await waitFor(element(by.id('nav-header')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(LANDSCAPE_SETTLE_MS);
}

it('renders the two-column layout in landscape', async () => {
  await rotateAndSettle('landscape');
  await expect(element(by.id('column-left'))).toBeVisible();
  await expect(element(by.id('column-right'))).toBeVisible();
  await rotateAndSettle('portrait');
  await expect(element(by.id('column-right'))).not.toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `device.setOrientation()` is not supported on Android Emulators with API level ≥ 34 when hardware rendering is disabled (Gotcha G292 applies). Always run orientation tests with hardware rendering enabled in CI (`-gpu swiftshader_indirect`).

---

**Pattern 457: Cascading `waitFor` with `.whileElement().scroll()` for lazy-loaded infinite lists** [official]
Infinite scroll lists load content as the user approaches the bottom. Asserting on an item that is not yet loaded requires driving a scroll loop: scroll a fixed amount, check if the item is visible, repeat. Detox's `.whileElement().scroll()` accepts a scroll amount and a direction, and the surrounding `waitFor` loop retries until the element becomes visible or the timeout fires.

```typescript
async function scrollToItem(
  listId: string,
  itemId: string,
  maxScrolls = 10,
): Promise<void> {
  await waitFor(element(by.id(itemId)))
    .toBeVisible()
    .whileElement(by.id(listId))
    .scroll(300, 'down');
}

it('loads and displays paginated content on scroll', async () => {
  await scrollToItem('product-list', 'product-item-50');
  await expect(element(by.id('product-item-50'))).toBeVisible();

  const attrs = await element(by.id('product-item-50')).getAttributes();
  if (!Array.isArray(attrs)) {
    expect(attrs.visible).toBe(true);
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: `.whileElement().scroll()` retries up to the `withTimeout` wall clock, not a fixed scroll count. On very large datasets, this can scroll indefinitely. Set tight timeouts (≤15 s) and combine with a known maximum page count to bound test duration.

---

**Pattern 458: `device.sendUserNotification()` Android broadcast fallback with `launchArgs`-gated handler** [official]
`device.sendUserNotification()` is iOS-only. On Android, the equivalent pattern uses `adb shell am broadcast` to simulate a push payload, but this requires the app to register a test-mode broadcast receiver. The standard cross-platform pattern wraps the platform check in a helper and gates the Android receiver with a `launchArgs` flag so it is never active in production builds.

```typescript
// e2e/helpers/notifications.ts
import { device } from 'detox';
import { execSync } from 'child_process';

export async function simulatePushNotification(payload: {
  title: string;
  body: string;
}): Promise<void> {
  if (device.getPlatform() === 'ios') {
    await device.sendUserNotification({
      title: payload.title,
      body: payload.body,
      trigger: { type: 'push' },
    });
  } else {
    // Android: app must be launched with launchArgs: { e2eEnablePushReceiver: 'true' }
    const escaped = JSON.stringify(payload).replace(/"/g, '\\"');
    execSync(
      `adb shell am broadcast -a com.myapp.E2E_PUSH ` +
      `--es payload "${escaped}"`,
    );
    // Give the broadcast receiver time to post the notification
    await waitFor(element(by.id('notification-banner')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(4000);
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: The Android path uses a synchronous `execSync` which blocks the Node test runner thread. Replace with the `execa` package for async execution when notification arrival latency is significant enough to cause test timeouts. The broadcast approach also requires a dedicated `BroadcastReceiver` in the Android app module compiled only into debug or e2e build variants.

---

**Pattern 459: `element.adjustSliderToPosition()` for cross-platform range-input testing** [official]
`adjustSliderToPosition(normalizedPosition)` accepts a value between `0.0` (minimum) and `1.0` (maximum) and moves the slider thumb to that relative position. This is more reliable than attempting to swipe the slider thumb, because swipe-based slider manipulation is sensitive to element size and gesture speed, whereas `adjustSliderToPosition` uses the accessibility API to set the value directly.

```typescript
async function setSliderValue(
  sliderId: string,
  normalizedPosition: number,
): Promise<void> {
  if (normalizedPosition < 0 || normalizedPosition > 1) {
    throw new Error('normalizedPosition must be in [0, 1]');
  }
  await element(by.id(sliderId)).adjustSliderToPosition(normalizedPosition);
}

it('filters products by price range using the slider', async () => {
  // Set max-price slider to 50% of its range
  await setSliderValue('price-slider-max', 0.5);
  // Assert the label reflects the new value
  const attrs = await element(by.id('price-slider-max')).getAttributes();
  if (!Array.isArray(attrs)) {
    // value is a string representation of the current slider value
    expect(parseFloat(attrs.value ?? '0')).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  }
  await expect(element(by.id('apply-filter-button'))).toBeVisible();
  await element(by.id('apply-filter-button')).tap();
});
```
Tradeoff: `adjustSliderToPosition()` maps to the accessibility `setValue` action, which some custom slider components do not implement. If the element is a fully custom `PanGestureHandler`-based slider without accessibility support, this API is a silent no-op. Verify with `getAttributes().accessibilityState` that the slider is accessible; if not, fall back to swipe-based manipulation with `element.swipe()`.

---

**Pattern 460: `device.clearKeychain()` for resetting secure-storage state between authentication test suites** [official]
`device.clearKeychain()` (iOS only) removes all items from the iOS Keychain associated with the app's bundle identifier. This is the correct way to reset `SecureStore`, `react-native-keychain`, or `expo-secure-store` persisted tokens between test runs — they survive `device.reloadReactNative()` and even `device.launchApp({ newInstance: true })` because the Keychain is backed by the Secure Enclave, not the app sandbox.

```typescript
// e2e/setup/globalSetup.ts
import { device } from 'detox';

export default async function globalSetup() {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  if (device.getPlatform() === 'ios') {
    await device.clearKeychain();
  }
}

// e2e/auth.test.ts
beforeEach(async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  if (device.getPlatform() === 'ios') {
    // Ensure no stale auth tokens from a previous test influence this test
    await device.clearKeychain();
  }
});

it('prompts for login when no stored token exists', async () => {
  await expect(element(by.id('login-screen-root'))).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `device.clearKeychain()` clears the entire app keychain, including tokens that might be shared between the app and its extensions (Share Extension, Notification Service Extension). This is acceptable in e2e test environments but documents why Keychain-sharing must use `kSecAttrAccessGroup` groups that are cleaned up separately when app extensions are also under test.

---

**Pattern 461: `by.web()` with `webElement.tap()` for hybrid WebView button interactions** [official]
For apps that embed a `WebView` with interactive content, Detox provides `by.web()` matchers that target DOM elements inside the WebView using CSS selectors or XPath. `element(by.web(by.cssSelector('#submit-btn'))).tap()` is the equivalent of `driver.findElement(By.css('#submit-btn')).click()` in Selenium, executed through Detox's WebView bridge.

```typescript
import { by, element, expect, waitFor } from 'detox';

async function tapWebViewButton(cssSelector: string): Promise<void> {
  // Ensure the WebView is fully loaded before interacting
  await waitFor(element(by.id('main-webview')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(5000);
  await element(by.web(by.cssSelector(cssSelector))).tap();
}

it('submits the embedded payment form in WebView', async () => {
  await element(by.id('checkout-button')).tap();
  await tapWebViewButton('#card-number-input');
  await element(by.web(by.cssSelector('#card-number-input'))).typeText('4111111111111111');
  await element(by.web(by.cssSelector('#expiry-input'))).typeText('12/28');
  await element(by.web(by.cssSelector('#cvv-input'))).typeText('123');
  await tapWebViewButton('#pay-button');
  await waitFor(element(by.id('payment-success-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(8000);
});
```
Tradeoff: `by.web()` interactions go through an IPC bridge between Detox's native layer and the WebView's JavaScript runtime, adding ~100–300 ms latency per action compared to native element interactions. For heavily form-based WebViews, this accumulates. Additionally, `by.web()` is not supported when the WebView has `javaScriptEnabled: false` or when the page is cross-origin (same-origin policy blocks the JS injection).

**Pattern 462: Test-suite-scoped `device.disableSynchronization()` for animation-heavy onboarding flows** [official]
Onboarding screens often use Lottie animations, `Animated.loop()`, or `react-native-reanimated` infinite sequences to create visual delight. These continuously-running animations prevent Detox's idle detector from ever declaring the app idle, causing every `waitFor` in the affected test to hit its timeout. Wrapping the entire onboarding test suite in a `disableSynchronization` / `enableSynchronization` pair with explicit `waitFor` assertions on key transitions is the correct solution.

```typescript
describe('Onboarding flow (sync disabled for animation-heavy screens)', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.disableSynchronization();
  });

  afterAll(async () => {
    await device.enableSynchronization();
  });

  it('advances through each onboarding step', async () => {
    await waitFor(element(by.id('onboarding-step-1')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(4000);
    await element(by.id('next-step-button')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('onboarding-step-2')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(4000);
    await element(by.id('next-step-button')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('onboarding-complete-screen')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(4000);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: With synchronization disabled, Detox no longer waits for network requests, Metro bundle loading, or React state updates to settle. Every subsequent `element()` interaction must be preceded by an explicit `waitFor` — forgetting even one can cause intermittent failures. Enable synchronization immediately after the animation-heavy describe block exits.

---

**Pattern 463: `device.takeScreenshot()` with a test-name-derived file name for automatic artifact organisation in CI** [official]
Naming screenshot artifacts after the test that produced them avoids collisions in multi-worker CI runs and makes artifact browsing trivial. Jest's `expect.getState().currentTestName` provides the running test name at the time of the call; sanitising it to a filesystem-safe slug produces stable, unique file names.

```typescript
// e2e/helpers/screenshot.ts
import { device } from 'detox';

function toSlug(testName: string): string {
  return testName
    .replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9]+/g, '-')
    .replace(/^-|-$/g, '')
    .toLowerCase()
    .slice(0, 100); // cap at 100 chars for filesystem safety
}

export async function screenshotOnFailure(): Promise<string> {
  const testName = expect.getState().currentTestName ?? 'unknown-test';
  const slug = toSlug(testName);
  const timestamp = Date.now();
  const fileName = `failure-${slug}-${timestamp}`;
  return device.takeScreenshot(fileName);
}

// jest.config.js — attach afterEach hook globally via setupFilesAfterFramework
afterEach(async () => {
  if (expect.getState().assertionCalls > 0) {
    // Only capture if the test actually ran assertions (skips beforeEach-only failures)
    await screenshotOnFailure();
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: `device.takeScreenshot()` pauses test execution for ~200–500 ms per capture while the screenshot is flushed to disk. If the `afterEach` hook runs unconditionally (including on passing tests), this multiplies suite runtime significantly. Gate the call with `jasmine.currentSpec?.failedExpectations?.length > 0` (jest-jasmine2) or the `getState().assertionCalls` heuristic shown above.

---

**Pattern 464: `element.getAttributes()` for asserting computed scroll position in paginated tab views** [official]
Tab pagers (`ViewPager` on Android, `UIScrollView` with paging on iOS) expose their current page as a `value` attribute in the accessibility tree. `getAttributes()` returns this as a string `"page N of M"` on iOS and as a percentage string on Android. A helper that normalises these platform-divergent values into a zero-based page index enables cross-platform page-position assertions without fragile swipe counting.

```typescript
async function getCurrentTabIndex(pagerTestId: string): Promise<number> {
  const attrs = await element(by.id(pagerTestId)).getAttributes();
  if (Array.isArray(attrs)) return 0; // unexpected multi-match; return 0 as sentinel

  const rawValue = attrs.value ?? '';
  if (device.getPlatform() === 'ios') {
    // "page 2 of 5" → index 1
    const match = rawValue.match(/page (\d+) of \d+/i);
    return match ? parseInt(match[1], 10) - 1 : 0;
  } else {
    // Android reports "50%" for page 2 of 4 (0-based middle page)
    // More reliable: use contentOffset / frame width if available
    const pctMatch = rawValue.match(/(\d+)%/);
    return pctMatch ? Math.round(parseInt(pctMatch[1], 10) / 100) : 0;
  }
}

it('swipes to the third onboarding tab', async () => {
  await element(by.id('onboarding-pager')).swipe('left', 'slow');
  await element(by.id('onboarding-pager')).swipe('left', 'slow');
  const currentTab = await getCurrentTabIndex('onboarding-pager');
  expect(currentTab).toBe(2);
});
```
Tradeoff: The `value` attribute format for pagers is undocumented and may change between OS versions. The regex parsing is a best-effort heuristic. For maximum reliability, assign a `testID` to a visible "page indicator" element (e.g., a dot indicator) and assert its accessibility state instead.

---

**Pattern 465: `jest.retryTimes()` with a per-test idempotency guard for selective retry of known-flaky tests** [official]
Detox's `.detoxrc.js` supports a global `testRunner.retries` value, but this retries the entire test file. For suites where only specific tests are known to be flaky (e.g., tests involving `device.openURL()` or `sendUserNotification()`), a per-test retry using Jest's `jest.retryTimes()` combined with an idempotency reset helper is more surgical.

```typescript
// e2e/helpers/retry.ts
import { device } from 'detox';

export function withRetry(retries: number, resetFn?: () => Promise<void>) {
  return function decorator(
    target: object,
    key: string,
    descriptor: TypedPropertyDescriptor<() => Promise<void>>,
  ) {
    const original = descriptor.value!;
    descriptor.value = async function () {
      let lastError: unknown;
      for (let attempt = 0; attempt <= retries; attempt++) {
        try {
          if (attempt > 0 && resetFn) await resetFn();
          return await original.call(this);
        } catch (e) {
          lastError = e;
        }
      }
      throw lastError;
    };
    return descriptor;
  };
}

// In test file
jest.retryTimes(2, { logErrorsBeforeRetry: true });

it('shows notification banner on deep-link open', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true }); // idempotency reset
  await device.openURL({ url: 'myapp://notifications/123' });
  await waitFor(element(by.id('notification-banner')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(5000);
});
```
Tradeoff: `jest.retryTimes()` applies to all tests in the file, not just the intended flaky test. Isolate known-flaky tests into their own spec file to scope the retry behaviour. `logErrorsBeforeRetry: true` (Jest 29+) emits the failure reason before each retry, which is invaluable for diagnosing whether the retry mask is hiding a real intermittent regression.

---

**Pattern 466: `device.reloadReactNative()` with an explicit bundle-ready guard for large monorepo apps** [official]
In monorepos with many Metro lazy imports, `reloadReactNative()` may resolve before the bundle is fully hydrated, causing the first `element()` call in the subsequent test to target a blank or partially rendered screen. Asserting on a root-level testID element that is rendered on the initial route before proceeding acts as a bundle-ready gate.

```typescript
const BUNDLE_READY_TIMEOUT_MS = 15_000;

async function reloadAndWaitForRoot(): Promise<void> {
  await device.reloadReactNative();
  // 'app-root' is the outermost View in App.tsx — always rendered when bundle is ready
  await waitFor(element(by.id('app-root')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(BUNDLE_READY_TIMEOUT_MS);
}

beforeEach(async () => {
  await reloadAndWaitForRoot();
});

it('renders the home screen after reload', async () => {
  await expect(element(by.id('home-screen-hero'))).toBeVisible();
});

it('retains user session after reload if token is valid', async () => {
  // reloadReactNative does not clear SecureStore on iOS — session persists
  await expect(element(by.id('user-avatar'))).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: Every `beforeEach` now costs one `reloadReactNative()` plus the `waitFor` gate (~2–8 s on slow CI). For suites with many short tests, this overhead can dominate. Group tests that share initial state into a single `describe` block with a single `beforeAll` launch and use `reloadReactNative()` only when JS-layer state genuinely needs resetting.

---

**Pattern 467: `element.typeText()` with `clearText()` prefix for predictable text-field mutation** [official]
On both iOS and Android, calling `typeText()` on a `TextInput` that already contains text appends to the existing value rather than replacing it. If the field is pre-populated (e.g., from a previous test's state or an auto-fill suggestion), the resulting value is the pre-existing content concatenated with the new input. Calling `clearText()` immediately before `typeText()` produces a clean, predictable state in one idiomatic sequence.

```typescript
async function fillTextField(
  testID: string,
  value: string,
): Promise<void> {
  const el = element(by.id(testID));
  await el.tap();          // ensure the field is focused
  await el.clearText();    // remove any pre-existing content
  await el.typeText(value);
  // On iOS, dismiss autocorrect bar to avoid it intercepting the next tap
  if (device.getPlatform() === 'ios') {
    await el.tapReturnKey();
  }
}

it('updates the user profile with new email and name', async () => {
  await element(by.id('edit-profile-button')).tap();
  await fillTextField('profile-name-input', 'Alice Ngo');
  await fillTextField('profile-email-input', 'alice.ngo@example.com');
  await element(by.id('save-profile-button')).tap();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('profile-save-toast')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(3000);
});
```
Tradeoff: `clearText()` dispatches a separate accessibility action before `typeText()`, adding one extra round-trip to the test runner loop (~50–150 ms). For forms with many fields this is negligible, but be aware that `clearText()` also removes the cursor position — on iOS, `typeText()` will insert at the beginning of the field if the field does not auto-focus to the end after clear. If this matters, use `replaceText()` instead (Gotcha 143 caveat: `replaceText()` bypasses `onChangeText` in some controlled-input implementations; test both approaches for the specific component).

---

**Pattern 468: `detox test --configuration` matrix with per-configuration `launchArgs` for A/B feature-flag testing** [official]
`.detoxrc.js` configurations can each carry their own `launchArgs` object, enabling you to run the same test suite against two or more feature-flag variants (e.g., `control` vs `treatment`) without modifying test code. Paired with a GitHub Actions matrix strategy, this produces A/B test coverage in one workflow.

```typescript
// .detoxrc.ts
import type { DetoxConfig } from 'detox';

const config: DetoxConfig = {
  testRunner: { args: { config: 'e2e/jest.config.ts', testTimeout: 120000 } },
  apps: {
    'ios.release': { type: 'ios.app', binaryPath: 'ios/build/MyApp.app' },
  },
  devices: {
    simulator: { type: 'ios.simulator', device: { type: 'iPhone 16 Pro' } },
  },
  configurations: {
    'ios.control': {
      app: 'ios.release',
      device: 'simulator',
      launchArgs: { featureNewCheckout: 'false', e2eVariant: 'control' },
    },
    'ios.treatment': {
      app: 'ios.release',
      device: 'simulator',
      launchArgs: { featureNewCheckout: 'true', e2eVariant: 'treatment' },
    },
  },
};
export default config;
```
Tradeoff: Running two full configurations doubles CI machine-time and artifact storage. Limit the matrix to configurations that have meaningful divergence in user flows. Prefer a single configuration with a `launchArgs`-parameterised test suite helper (`getVariant()` reading `device.getLaunchArgs().e2eVariant`) to keep the number of CI jobs bounded while still covering feature-flag branches.

---

### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha G295: `element.scrollTo('bottom')` silently succeeds on a `ScrollView` whose content is shorter than its container, leaving the assertion on an element "below the fold" as a false-pass**
When a `ScrollView`'s content height is less than or equal to its own frame height, the view is not scrollable and `scrollTo('bottom')` is a no-op — it resolves immediately without moving the viewport. If a test scrolls to the bottom hoping to reveal a submit button that only appears in long-form scenarios, the test passes on short content (button was already visible) but hides a regression where the button is not rendered at all in the expected slot.
WHY: Detox delegates `scrollTo('bottom')` to the native accessibility `scroll` action, which reports success even when there is nothing to scroll. The underlying native scroll view considers the request fulfilled (it is at the end of its content range) regardless of how short the content is.
Fix: Before calling `scrollTo('bottom')`, assert that the content is scrollable by checking the element's `scrollContentOffset` or `contentSize` via `getAttributes()`, or assert on the _specific element_ you expect to find at the bottom rather than relying on a scroll-then-assert pattern. Using `waitFor(element(by.id('submit-button'))).toBeVisible().whileElement(by.id('form-scroll')).scroll(300, 'down')` is more robust than a `scrollTo('bottom')` followed by a visibility check.

---

**Gotcha G296: `device.shake()` on iOS Simulator 18.4+ sporadically triggers the "Report Feedback" system sheet instead of the app's shake handler**
Apple introduced a new developer feedback system sheet in iOS Simulator 18.4 that intercepts shake events at the system level before they reach the app. When this sheet appears, it is rendered in a separate `UIWindowScene` that Detox's `by.system` matcher cannot reach with standard selector APIs, causing the test to time out waiting for the app's in-app shake response.
WHY: The system sheet is rendered by the Simulator host process (not the app process), making it invisible to Detox's accessibility tree enumeration. The sheet intercepts the shake event at the `UIApplication.motionBegan(_:with:)` level before the app's `motion` handlers fire.
Fix: Dismiss the system sheet if it appears using `by.system.label('Dismiss')` and retry the shake, or disable the simulator feedback sheet with `defaults write com.apple.iphonesimulator FeedbackAssistantEnabled -bool NO` in the CI job's `pre-flight` step. Alternatively, replace shake-triggered flows with a debug launchArgs-gated button (`testID="debug-shake-trigger"`) that fires the same handler without relying on the hardware gesture.

---

**Gotcha G297: `element.pinch()` on Android does not use the GESTURE_DESCRIPTION scale parameter correctly when the element is partially off-screen**
`element.pinch(scale, speed, angle)` on Android constructs two synthetic touch pointer paths whose midpoint is the element's centre as reported by the accessibility tree. If the element is only partially visible (e.g., a zoomable map that extends beyond the viewport), the accessibility-reported centre is clamped to the visible frame, not the actual centre of the element. This makes the pinch gesture pivot around the wrong point, producing a scale result that is consistently smaller than the requested `scale` parameter.
WHY: Detox calculates the pinch gesture origin from `getAttributes().frame`, which is clipped to the visible viewport rectangle on Android. The discrepancy between the requested and actual pivot point causes the gesture to travel a shorter arc, resulting in a smaller effective scale.
Fix: Before calling `pinch()`, scroll the element so its centre is fully within the viewport. Use `waitFor(element(by.id('map-view'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000)` and confirm the frame's `y` and `height` values indicate the element is fully on-screen. For map components specifically, use the map SDK's test helper API (e.g., `MapView.setCamera()` via a test-only bridge) instead of gesture-based zoom to set a known zoom level deterministically.

---

**Gotcha G298: `waitFor(element).toBeVisible()` resolves for elements inside a `Modal` on Android API 33+ even when the `Modal` is behind a system permission dialog**
Android 13+ (API 33) renders system permission dialogs in the `PackageInstallerActivity` window, which is a separate process window with higher z-order than the app. When a permission dialog is present, the app's `Modal` is technically rendered and composed, but visually it is completely obscured by the system dialog. Detox's `toBeVisible()` check uses the accessibility tree visibility flag, which Android sets based on whether the view is attached and not gone/invisible — it does NOT account for occlusion by another window.
WHY: The Android accessibility API's `isVisibleToUser` flag is `true` for views that are drawn and laid out, regardless of whether another window is overlapping them. This is a known limitation of the Android accessibility model and is not Detox-specific.
Fix: After `device.launchApp()` with `permissions: { camera: 'YES' }` or equivalent, always use `device.launchApp({ newInstance: true, permissions: { camera: 'YES' } })` so the permission is pre-granted and the dialog never appears during the test. If the test intentionally exercises the permission grant flow, use `waitFor(element(by.system.label('Allow'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000)` and `element(by.system.label('Allow')).tap()` to dismiss the system dialog before asserting on app-layer Modals.

---

**Gotcha G299: `element.typeText()` with emoji characters inserts only the first Unicode scalar value on Android API 31 and below, truncating multi-codepoint emoji**
Emoji characters that require multiple Unicode scalar values (e.g., family emoji `👨‍👩‍👧`, flag emoji `🇨🇦`, or skin-tone-modified emoji `👋🏽`) are represented as Unicode code point sequences joined by Zero Width Joiner (ZWJ) characters. On Android API 31 and below, Detox's `typeText()` implementation uses `setText()` on the `InputConnection`, which on older Android versions incorrectly splits ZWJ sequences, inserting only the base emoji (`👨`, `👩`, `👧` as separate characters) rather than the composed family emoji.
WHY: The `InputConnection.commitText()` API on Android API ≤ 31 has a known bug where ZWJ-joined Unicode sequences are fragmented at the Java `String` level before being submitted to the input field. This was fixed in AOSP at API 32 (Android 12L). Detox cannot work around this at its abstraction level without reimplementing text composition.
Fix: For cross-platform emoji input tests targeting Android API ≤ 31, replace multi-codepoint emoji with their simple single-codepoint equivalents in test strings, or use `replaceText()` (which uses a different Android `setText()` path that handles ZWJ sequences correctly in most third-party keyboard implementations). Add an API-level guard: `if (device.getPlatform() === 'android' && (await device.getAPILevel()) <= 31) { await element(by.id('bio-input')).replaceText(textWithEmoji); }`.
