**Pattern 530** — `element.rotate()` for Rotation Gesture Testing (Dial, Knob, and Compass Controls)

```typescript
// e2e/compassControl.test.ts
import { device, element, by, expect, waitFor } from 'detox';

/**
 * Rotates an element by the given angle in radians.
 * Positive angle = clockwise (iOS UIRotationGestureRecognizer convention).
 */
async function rotateElement(testID: string, radians: number): Promise<void> {
  await element(by.id(testID)).rotate(radians);
}

describe('Compass Dial Rotation', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    await waitFor(element(by.id('compass-dial'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
  });

  it('rotates compass 90° clockwise to point East', async () => {
    await rotateElement('compass-dial', Math.PI / 2);
    await expect(element(by.id('compass-direction-label'))).toHaveText('E');
  });

  it('rotates compass 180° to point South', async () => {
    await rotateElement('compass-dial', Math.PI);
    await expect(element(by.id('compass-direction-label'))).toHaveText('S');
  });

  it('returns compass to North with a counter-clockwise rotation', async () => {
    await rotateElement('compass-dial', -Math.PI);
    await waitFor(element(by.id('compass-direction-label')))
      .toHaveText('N')
      .withTimeout(2000);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `element.rotate()` is iOS Simulator–only — `UIRotationGestureRecognizer` is simulated via two-finger touch injection, which the iOS Simulator supports but Android Emulator's `UiAutomator2` does not. For Android, file a separate test that drives the same state by calling a debug launch arg (`COMPASS_HEADING=90`) rather than gesturing. Radians are measured from the initial touch vector, not from the element's current orientation — if the dial has a stored heading from a previous test, the resulting heading is relative to the current position, so reset heading state in `beforeEach` via `device.launchApp({ newInstance: true })` or a mock API call.

**Pattern 531** — `device.setStatusBar()` + `device.resetStatusBar()` for Deterministic Screenshot Baselines

```typescript
// helpers/statusBarHelper.ts
import { device } from 'detox';

const CANONICAL_STATUS_BAR = {
  time: '9:41',
  batteryLevel: 100,
  batteryState: 'charged',
  wifiBars: 3,
  wifiMode: 'active',
  cellularBars: 4,
  cellularMode: 'active',
  dataNetwork: '5G',
} as const;

export async function freezeStatusBar(): Promise<void> {
  if (device.getPlatform() !== 'ios') return; // Android uses adb separately
  await device.setStatusBar(CANONICAL_STATUS_BAR);
}

export async function thawStatusBar(): Promise<void> {
  if (device.getPlatform() !== 'ios') return;
  await device.resetStatusBar();
}

// e2e/onboarding.test.ts
it('onboarding step 1 matches visual baseline', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await freezeStatusBar();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('onboarding-step-1'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
  const screenshotPath = await device.takeScreenshot('onboarding-step-1');
  await thawStatusBar();
  // Feed screenshotPath to your visual comparator
  expect(screenshotPath).toBeTruthy();
});
```
Tradeoff: `device.setStatusBar()` is iOS Simulator–only and does not affect real iPhones — the simctl `status_bar` command is only available for Simulator targets. On Android, freeze the status bar by launching the emulator with `-status-bar-disabled` or by calling `adb shell settings put global policy_control immersive.full=*` via a `beforeAll` Bash hook. Failing to reset the status bar with `resetStatusBar()` in `afterAll` leaves the frozen status bar for subsequent test suites run in the same simulator session, causing real-time clock and signal-strength changes to be suppressed in non-visual tests that rely on those labels.

**Pattern 532** — `device.setOrientation()` for Portrait/Landscape Layout Testing

```typescript
// e2e/orientationLayout.test.ts
import { device, element, by, expect, waitFor } from 'detox';

async function setPortrait(): Promise<void> {
  await device.setOrientation('portrait');
  await waitFor(element(by.id('app-root'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
}

async function setLandscape(): Promise<void> {
  await device.setOrientation('landscape');
  await waitFor(element(by.id('app-root'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
}

describe('Orientation-Responsive Layout', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    await setPortrait(); // always start in portrait
  });

  afterEach(async () => {
    await setPortrait(); // restore portrait for next suite
  });

  it('shows bottom tab bar in portrait mode', async () => {
    await expect(element(by.id('bottom-tab-bar'))).toBeVisible();
    await expect(element(by.id('side-drawer'))).not.toBeVisible();
  });

  it('switches to side drawer navigation in landscape mode', async () => {
    await setLandscape();
    await expect(element(by.id('side-drawer'))).toBeVisible();
    await expect(element(by.id('bottom-tab-bar'))).not.toBeVisible();
  });

  it('video player renders in fullscreen landscape without controls clipping', async () => {
    await element(by.id('video-card-0')).tap();
    await setLandscape();
    await expect(element(by.id('fullscreen-controls-bar'))).toBeVisible();
    const attrs = await element(by.id('fullscreen-controls-bar')).getAttributes();
    const frame = (attrs as { frame: { width: number } }).frame;
    expect(frame.width).toBeGreaterThan(500); // wider than portrait viewport
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `device.setOrientation()` triggers the same safe-area inset recalculation as a physical rotation, but on Android Emulator it can cause a brief re-layout flash (~100–200 ms) before the React Native `useWindowDimensions()` hook fires its update. Insert a `waitFor(element(by.id('layout-sentinel'))).toBeVisible()` after `setOrientation()` to confirm the layout has stabilised before asserting frame widths. On iOS Simulator, the orientation change is synchronous from Detox's perspective but the accessibility tree update lags by one render cycle — always `waitFor` a landmark element after rotation before using `getAttributes().frame`.

---

**Pattern 533** — `by.web()` Matchers for WebView Assertion: `toHaveText`, `scrollTo`, and `element.tap()`

```typescript
// e2e/webview.test.ts
import { device, by, expect, waitFor, web } from 'detox';

describe('In-App WebView — Terms of Service', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    await element(by.id('terms-btn')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('tos-webview-container'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
  });

  it('renders the Terms heading', async () => {
    await expect(
      web(by.id('tos-webview-container')).element(by.web.tag('h1')),
    ).toHaveText('Terms of Service');
  });

  it('scrolls to the bottom and reveals the Accept button', async () => {
    await web(by.id('tos-webview-container'))
      .element(by.web.tag('body'))
      .scrollTo('bottom');
    await expect(
      web(by.id('tos-webview-container')).element(by.web.id('accept-tos-btn')),
    ).toExist();
  });

  it('taps the Accept button and dismisses the WebView', async () => {
    await web(by.id('tos-webview-container'))
      .element(by.web.id('accept-tos-btn'))
      .tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('tos-accepted-banner')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(3000);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `web(by.id())` scopes the WebView context to a specific native WebView container by `testID` — this is required when the screen contains more than one WebView (e.g., an ad banner + a content WebView). `by.web.tag()` selects by HTML tag name within the WebView DOM; `by.web.id()` selects by `id` attribute. WebView web matchers execute JavaScript in the WebView's JS context via `evaluateJavaScript` — on iOS this requires `WKWebView` with `allowsContentJavaScript` enabled (the default). On Android, the `WebView.setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled(true)` flag must be set in the debug build variant for Detox's ChromeDriver bridge to reach the DOM.

**Pattern 534** — `device.captureViewHierarchy()` for DOM-Level Debugging of Invisible Element Failures

```typescript
// helpers/debugHelper.ts
import { device } from 'detox';
import * as path from 'path';

/**
 * Captures the native view hierarchy to a .viewhierarchy file for debugging.
 * Call when a `waitFor().toBeVisible()` failure needs to be diagnosed without
 * a visual screenshot (e.g. element is in the tree but out of viewport).
 */
export async function captureHierarchyOnFailure(label: string): Promise<string> {
  const artifactPath = await device.captureViewHierarchy(label);
  console.log(`[debug] View hierarchy saved: ${artifactPath}`);
  return artifactPath;
}

// e2e/checkout.test.ts
afterEach(async () => {
  // Only capture hierarchy when the test failed
  const testName = expect.getState().currentTestName ?? 'unknown';
  const testPassed = expect.getState().assertionCalls > 0;
  if (!testPassed) {
    await captureHierarchyOnFailure(
      `${testName.replace(/\s+/g, '-').toLowerCase()}-hierarchy`,
    );
  }
});

it('shows order summary before payment', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await element(by.id('cart-tab')).tap();
  await element(by.id('checkout-btn')).tap();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('order-summary-section')))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(5000);
  await expect(element(by.id('order-total-label'))).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `device.captureViewHierarchy()` produces a `.viewhierarchy` file (on iOS: Xcode-compatible accessibility snapshot; on Android: `uiautomatorviewer`-compatible XML). It is a synchronous point-in-time snapshot — it captures the tree at the moment of the call, not at the moment of the assertion failure. For failure diagnosis, call it immediately in `afterEach` before `device.reloadReactNative()` resets the tree. The file can be large (5–20 MB) on screens with deep component trees; avoid calling `captureViewHierarchy` on every test — gate it on failure only to prevent artifact storage costs in CI.

---

**Pattern 535** — `element.typeText()` vs `element.replaceText()` for Pre-Filled Input Field Updates

```typescript
// e2e/editProfile.test.ts
import { device, element, by, expect, waitFor } from 'detox';

describe('Edit Profile — Pre-filled Fields', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    // App auto-fills profile fields from stored data
    await waitFor(element(by.id('edit-profile-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
  });

  it('updates display name without appending to existing value', async () => {
    // replaceText clears the field first, then types — avoids "John DoeJane Doe" bug
    await element(by.id('display-name-input')).replaceText('Jane Doe');
    await element(by.id('save-profile-btn')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('profile-saved-toast'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
    await expect(element(by.id('display-name-label'))).toHaveText('Jane Doe');
  });

  it('clears bio field entirely using replaceText with empty string', async () => {
    await element(by.id('bio-input')).replaceText('');
    await expect(element(by.id('bio-input'))).toHaveText('');
    await element(by.id('save-profile-btn')).tap();
    await expect(element(by.id('bio-label'))).not.toBeVisible();
  });

  it('appends text using typeText after focusing the field', async () => {
    await element(by.id('bio-input')).tap();
    // Move caret to end, then append
    await element(by.id('bio-input')).tapReturnKey();
    await element(by.id('bio-input')).typeText(' — Updated bio');
    await expect(element(by.id('bio-input'))).toHaveText(
      expect.stringContaining('— Updated bio'),
    );
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `typeText()` appends to the current cursor position (wherever focus lands, which is often the beginning of a pre-filled field on Android), producing duplicate-prefix values like `"Jane DoeJohn Doe"`. `replaceText()` clears the native input and sets the value atomically — it bypasses React's `onChange` event chain on some controlled input implementations, so `onChangeText` may not fire, leaving the React state stale while the native view shows the new value. Always follow `replaceText()` with a `tap()` or `tapReturnKey()` to trigger a focus/blur cycle that syncs React's controlled value state with the native field.

**Pattern 536** — `element.tapReturnKey()` for Keyboard Submission and Multi-Field Form Navigation

```typescript
// e2e/loginForm.test.ts
import { device, element, by, expect, waitFor } from 'detox';

describe('Login Form — Keyboard Navigation', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    await waitFor(element(by.id('login-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
  });

  it('navigates email → password → submit via Return key', async () => {
    await element(by.id('email-input')).tap();
    await element(by.id('email-input')).typeText('user@example.com');
    // returnKeyType="next" on email field — Return advances focus to password
    await element(by.id('email-input')).tapReturnKey();
    await expect(element(by.id('password-input'))).toBeFocused();
    await element(by.id('password-input')).typeText('P@ssw0rd!');
    // returnKeyType="done" on password field — Return submits the form
    await element(by.id('password-input')).tapReturnKey();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen-root')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(5000);
  });

  it('shows inline validation error when email is blank and Return is pressed', async () => {
    await element(by.id('email-input')).tap();
    await element(by.id('email-input')).tapReturnKey();
    await expect(element(by.id('email-error-label'))).toBeVisible();
    await expect(element(by.id('email-error-label'))).toHaveText('Email is required');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `tapReturnKey()` fires the native Return key action, which respects the `returnKeyType` prop (`'next'`, `'done'`, `'go'`, `'search'`, `'send'`). If the `TextInput` does not have `returnKeyType` set, it defaults to `'done'` on iOS (dismisses the keyboard) and `'default'` on Android (inserts a newline for single-line fields). A mismatch between the test's assumption of `'next'` behaviour and the field's actual `returnKeyType` will cause the test to pass locally (where the keyboard visually advances focus) but fail on CI when the field does not have `onSubmitEditing` wired to `focus()` the next field. Always verify both the `returnKeyType` prop and the `onSubmitEditing` handler are present before writing keyboard-navigation tests.

---

**Pattern 537** — `device.pressBack()` for Android Hardware Back Button Testing

```typescript
// e2e/navigation.test.ts
import { device, element, by, expect, waitFor } from 'detox';

describe('Android Back Button Navigation', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);
  });

  it('navigates back from product detail to list', async () => {
    await element(by.id('product-card-0')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('product-detail-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
    if (device.getPlatform() === 'android') {
      await device.pressBack();
    } else {
      await element(by.id('back-btn')).tap();
    }
    await waitFor(element(by.id('product-list-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
  });

  it('exits the app when back is pressed from the root screen', async () => {
    if (device.getPlatform() !== 'android') return;
    await device.pressBack();
    // App should go to background — home screen is no longer visible
    await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen')))
      .not.toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(2000);
  });

  it('back button dismisses a modal without closing the underlying screen', async () => {
    if (device.getPlatform() !== 'android') return;
    await element(by.id('open-filter-modal-btn')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('filter-modal'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
    await device.pressBack();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('filter-modal'))).not.toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);
    await expect(element(by.id('product-list-screen'))).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `device.pressBack()` is Android-only — calling it on iOS throws a Detox runtime error. Always guard with `if (device.getPlatform() === 'android')` or write a cross-platform wrapper that calls `element(by.id('back-btn')).tap()` on iOS. `pressBack()` dispatches the native hardware back event, which triggers `BackHandler` listeners in React Navigation before popping the stack — this is the correct way to test custom `BackHandler.addEventListener('hardwareBackPress', ...)` overrides, such as preventing back on unsaved-form screens. Do not confuse with the Android system back gesture (swipe from edge), which is separate and not currently testable via Detox.

---

**Pattern 538** — `device.terminateApp()` + `device.launchApp({ newInstance: false })` for Background-Resume State Persistence Testing

```typescript
// e2e/statePersistence.test.ts
import { device, element, by, expect, waitFor } from 'detox';

describe('App State Persistence Across Background/Resume Cycle', () => {
  it('preserves shopping cart contents after app is backgrounded and resumed', async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });

    // Add item to cart
    await element(by.id('product-card-0')).tap();
    await element(by.id('add-to-cart-btn')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('cart-count-badge'))).toHaveText('1').withTimeout(3000);

    // Background the app (simulates user pressing Home button)
    await device.sendToHome();

    // Resume the app (brings it to foreground without killing the process)
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: false });
    await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(4000);

    // Cart should still have the item
    await element(by.id('cart-tab')).tap();
    await expect(element(by.id('cart-item-0'))).toBeVisible();
    await expect(element(by.id('cart-count-badge'))).toHaveText('1');
  });

  it('resets cart on full process kill and relaunch', async () => {
    await device.terminateApp();
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true }); // fresh process
    await element(by.id('cart-tab')).tap();
    await expect(element(by.id('empty-cart-label'))).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `device.launchApp({ newInstance: false })` resumes the existing process — it does NOT restart the JS bundle — whereas `newInstance: true` kills the process and starts fresh. Background-resume tests are particularly important for React Navigation's persistence layer (`@react-navigation/native`'s `persistNavigationState`) and for Redux Persist / MMKV stores that hydrate asynchronously on foreground. On Android, `newInstance: false` maps to `am start` without `--force-stop`, which preserves the Activity stack; on iOS it calls `activateApp()` which brings the Simulator app to foreground without relaunching. Never use `newInstance: false` as the first call in a suite — the app process may not be running yet, causing a silent no-op.

---

**Pattern 539** — `waitFor(element).toHaveValue()` for `TextInput`, `Switch`, and `Picker` State Assertions

```typescript
// e2e/formState.test.ts
import { device, element, by, expect, waitFor } from 'detox';

describe('Form Control Value Assertions', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    await waitFor(element(by.id('settings-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
  });

  it('TextInput reflects typed value via toHaveValue', async () => {
    await element(by.id('username-input')).typeText('alice');
    await expect(element(by.id('username-input'))).toHaveValue('alice');
  });

  it('Switch reflects on/off state via toHaveValue', async () => {
    // Default is off
    await expect(element(by.id('notifications-switch'))).toHaveValue('0');
    await element(by.id('notifications-switch')).tap();
    await expect(element(by.id('notifications-switch'))).toHaveValue('1');
  });

  it('Picker reflects selected option via toHaveValue', async () => {
    await element(by.id('country-picker')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('picker-option-DE'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);
    await element(by.id('picker-option-DE')).tap();
    await expect(element(by.id('country-picker'))).toHaveValue('DE');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `toHaveValue()` asserts the element's `accessibilityValue` (iOS) or `stateDescription` / `contentDescription value part` (Android). For `TextInput`, this maps to the actual text content. For `Switch`, React Native sets the accessibility value to `'1'` (on) or `'0'` (off) — not `'true'`/`'false'`. For `Picker`, the value maps to the selected option's `value` prop, not its display label. On Android API < 30, `stateDescription` is not available and `toHaveValue()` may return `undefined` for `Switch` — use `getAttributes().value` with an explicit null-check and fall back to `toHaveText()` on a sibling label element for pre-API-30 compatibility.

**Pattern 540** — Detox `globalSetup` / `globalTeardown` Hooks for WireMock / MSW Mock Server Lifecycle Management

```typescript
// e2e/setup/globalSetup.ts
import { execSync } from 'child_process';
import * as http from 'http';

const MOCK_PORT = 3001;
let mockServer: http.Server | null = null;

export default async function globalSetup(): Promise<void> {
  // Start a lightweight JSON mock server for all Detox workers
  const express = require('express');
  const app = express();
  app.use(express.json());

  app.get('/api/products', (_req: unknown, res: { json: Function }) => {
    res.json([{ id: 1, name: 'Widget Pro', inStock: true }]);
  });
  app.post('/api/orders', (_req: unknown, res: { status: Function }) => {
    res.status(201).json({ orderId: 'ORD-001' });
  });

  await new Promise<void>((resolve) => {
    mockServer = app.listen(MOCK_PORT, resolve);
  });

  console.log(`[globalSetup] Mock server started on port ${MOCK_PORT}`);
}

// e2e/setup/globalTeardown.ts
export default async function globalTeardown(): Promise<void> {
  if (mockServer) {
    await new Promise<void>((resolve) => mockServer!.close(resolve));
    console.log('[globalTeardown] Mock server stopped');
  }
}

// detox.config.ts (relevant snippet)
// testRunner: { args: { $0: 'jest', config: 'e2e/jest.config.ts' } }
// jest.config.ts:
// globalSetup: './e2e/setup/globalSetup.ts',
// globalTeardown: './e2e/setup/globalTeardown.ts',
```
Tradeoff: `globalSetup` / `globalTeardown` run in the Jest main process, outside of any Detox worker — the `device` object is not available there. All Detox-level setup (app launch, permission grants) must remain in `beforeAll`/`beforeEach`. The mock server started in `globalSetup` is shared across all parallel worker processes, so route handlers must be stateless or use worker-scoped state (e.g., a per-request header `X-Worker-ID`) to avoid cross-worker response contamination. On Windows CI, `execSync` in `globalTeardown` to kill the server by port is unreliable — use `mockServer.close()` from the module reference instead.

**Pattern 541** — `detox test --inspect-brk` + Node Inspector for Debugging Flaky Tests Interactively

```typescript
// e2e/debug/flakyTest.test.ts
// Usage: detox test --inspect-brk -c ios.sim.debug e2e/debug/flakyTest.test.ts
// Then open chrome://inspect and attach to the Node process
import { device, element, by, waitFor } from 'detox';

describe('Debugging Flaky Assertion', () => {
  it('reproduces the intermittent waitFor timeout', async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });

    // Set a breakpoint here in the Chrome DevTools to inspect app state
    // before the assertion fires — use the "Paused in debugger" overlay
    // to manually trigger the network mock response that makes the element appear
    debugger; // eslint-disable-line no-debugger

    await waitFor(element(by.id('async-loaded-section')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(10000);

    // After resuming from the breakpoint, verify the element state
    const attrs = await element(by.id('async-loaded-section')).getAttributes();
    console.log('[debug] element attrs:', JSON.stringify(attrs, null, 2));
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `--inspect-brk` pauses the Jest worker at the first line of the test file — the Detox test runner is single-threaded per worker when debugging, so parallel workers are effectively serialised. With `debugger` statements in the test body, the timeout for any `waitFor()` call continues to tick while the debugger is paused; always increase `withTimeout()` to a large value (e.g., 60000 ms) when debugging to avoid timeout failures during inspection pauses. `--inspect-brk` is incompatible with `--runInBand` on some Jest versions — use `--workers=1` instead to force single-worker execution without the `--runInBand` flag that Jest 29 changed to be process-isolating.

**Pattern 542** — `element.getAttributes()` `frame` Property for Overlap and Z-Order Assertion

```typescript
// helpers/overlapHelper.ts
import { element, by } from 'detox';

interface Frame { x: number; y: number; width: number; height: number }

async function getFrame(testID: string): Promise<Frame> {
  const attrs = await element(by.id(testID)).getAttributes();
  return (attrs as { frame: Frame }).frame;
}

function framesOverlap(a: Frame, b: Frame): boolean {
  return (
    a.x < b.x + b.width &&
    a.x + a.width > b.x &&
    a.y < b.y + b.height &&
    a.y + a.height > b.y
  );
}

// e2e/tooltipOverlap.test.ts
it('tooltip does not overlap the bottom navigation bar', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await element(by.id('info-icon-btn')).tap();
  await waitFor(element(by.id('tooltip-bubble'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);
  const tooltip = await getFrame('tooltip-bubble');
  const tabBar = await getFrame('bottom-tab-bar');
  expect(framesOverlap(tooltip, tabBar)).toBe(false);
});

it('floating action button does not overlap the last list item', async () => {
  await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  await element(by.id('items-list')).scrollTo('bottom');
  const fab = await getFrame('floating-action-btn');
  const lastItem = await getFrame('list-item-last');
  expect(framesOverlap(fab, lastItem)).toBe(false);
});
```
Tradeoff: `getAttributes().frame` returns coordinates in the logical point space of the device (not raw pixels) — on Retina/high-DPI devices, multiply by `displayScale` only when comparing with pixel-level screenshot masks. Frame coordinates are measured from the screen's top-left origin, so elements off the top of the viewport have negative `y` values. The overlap check is purely geometric — it does not account for `zIndex` or native layer elevation, so an element with a higher `elevation` (Android) may visually appear on top even if `framesOverlap` returns `true`. Use this pattern for layout regression (e.g., FAB obscures a form field after a keyboard resizes the screen) rather than for render-order assertions.

**Pattern 543** — `detox.init()` / `detox.cleanup()` in Custom Jest Environment for Shared Setup Across Multiple Config Files

```typescript
// e2e/environment/DetoxEnvironment.ts
import { DetoxCircusEnvironment } from 'detox/runners/jest/testEnvironment';

export default class CustomDetoxEnvironment extends DetoxCircusEnvironment {
  constructor(config: unknown, context: unknown) {
    super(config as never, context as never);

    // Register a custom reporter that writes structured JSON test results
    // to a per-worker output file for downstream CI aggregation
    this.registerListeners({
      onTestStart: async ({ title }: { title: string }) => {
        console.log(`[env] starting: ${title}`);
      },
      onTestFinish: async ({
        title,
        passed,
      }: {
        title: string;
        passed: boolean;
      }) => {
        const result = { title, passed, timestamp: Date.now() };
        const fs = await import('fs/promises');
        const workerId = process.env.JEST_WORKER_ID ?? '0';
        await fs.appendFile(
          `./artifacts/results-worker-${workerId}.jsonl`,
          JSON.stringify(result) + '\n',
        );
      },
    });
  }
}

// jest.config.ts
// testEnvironment: './e2e/environment/DetoxEnvironment.ts',
```
Tradeoff: Extending `DetoxCircusEnvironment` is the officially supported way to customise the Jest test environment in Detox 20.x — do not use `DetoxTestEnvironment` (removed in Detox 20). The `registerListeners` API is Circus-specific (Jest 27+); if your project still uses Jest 26 with the legacy `jasmine2` runner, use `setupFilesAfterFramework` instead. Custom environment files must be CommonJS-compatible (or use `require()` interop) because Jest loads them in a Node.js context before any TypeScript transpilation is applied — ensure your `tsconfig` targets `CommonJS` or use `ts-jest` with `isolatedModules: true` in the environment config.

### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha G320: `element.pinch()` on Android throws `"UiDevice.performMultiPointerGesture is not supported"` with UiAutomator2 driver — silent no-op on older Detox versions**
Detox's `element.pinch()` action is wired exclusively to the iOS `XCUIElement.pinch(withScale:velocity:)` API. On Android, UiAutomator2 does not expose a two-finger pinch action via its public `InteractionController` API. In Detox versions prior to 20.14, calling `element.pinch()` on Android silently returned without throwing, making tests appear to pass (the gesture was never performed). From Detox 20.14 onwards, it throws `ActionNotSupportedError` on Android.
Why this matters: A cross-platform test suite that calls `element.pinch()` without a platform guard will pass silently on Android in older Detox versions, giving false confidence that zoom behaviour was tested on Android. The code path that handles pinch events never executes on Android emulators. Teams that upgrade Detox discover these tests now throw on Android CI jobs, and the underlying Android zoom behaviour was never actually covered.
Fix: Wrap every `pinch()` call with `if (device.getPlatform() === 'ios')`. For Android zoom coverage, test via an alternative: set a `zoomLevel` via `launchArgs` in a debug build variant, or interact with the zoom-in button if the component exposes one. Document the Android gap in the test file with a `// TODO: Android pinch not supported in Detox — covered by unit test in ZoomableView.test.tsx` comment.

---

**Gotcha G321: `device.setOrientation('landscape')` on Android Emulator with `screenOrientation: sensorLandscape` ignores the API and keeps portrait — the emulator's auto-rotate lock must be disabled first**
On Android Emulator, `device.setOrientation('landscape')` calls `adb shell settings put system accelerometer_rotation 0` followed by an accelerometer injection. If the emulator was launched with the `-screen-orientation landscape` flag or if the app's `AndroidManifest.xml` declares `android:screenOrientation="sensorLandscape"` for the `MainActivity`, the emulator may be locked to a specific orientation by the sensor policy, and the `setOrientation()` call has no effect — the app stays in portrait.
Why this matters: Orientation-responsive layout tests pass locally (where the developer manually rotates the emulator) but fail in CI (where the emulator starts in the default orientation and the API call is silently ignored). The test asserts that a side drawer is visible in landscape mode, but since the orientation never changed, the bottom tab bar is visible instead — the assertion fails with a confusing "element not found" error rather than an orientation error.
Fix: Before calling `device.setOrientation()`, run `adb shell settings put system accelerometer_rotation 0` (disable auto-rotate lock) and `adb shell settings put system user_rotation 0` (reset rotation) via a `beforeAll` shell hook. Then call `device.setOrientation('landscape')`. Alternatively, configure the emulator without `-screen-orientation` flags and ensure `android:screenOrientation` is not set in `AndroidManifest.xml` for the debug build variant.

---

**Gotcha G322: `device.captureViewHierarchy()` on iOS produces an empty `.viewhierarchy` file when the app is in a background state or after `device.sendToHome()` — the accessibility tree is suspended**
When `device.sendToHome()` is called to background the app, iOS suspends the app process and the accessibility service stops updating the view hierarchy. If `device.captureViewHierarchy()` is called while the app is backgrounded (e.g., in an `afterEach` that runs after a `sendToHome()` call), the resulting `.viewhierarchy` file is created but contains only the root `UIWindow` with no children — it does not reflect the pre-background state.
Why this matters: Developers who add `captureViewHierarchy()` to their `afterEach` failure handler do not notice that the hierarchy file is empty when the failing test happens to background the app as part of its flow. They open the `.viewhierarchy` file in Xcode and see a blank canvas, concluding that the feature is broken, when in fact the capture simply ran too late.
Fix: Call `device.captureViewHierarchy()` immediately after the failing `waitFor()` throws, before any app lifecycle changes. Use a try/catch around the assertion and capture the hierarchy in the `catch` block: `try { await waitFor(...) } catch (e) { await device.captureViewHierarchy('failure'); throw e; }`. This ensures the capture runs while the app is still in the foreground with a live accessibility tree.

---

**Gotcha G323: `element.replaceText('')` on Android leaves the field in a focused-but-empty state that still shows the placeholder — `toHaveText('')` passes but `toHaveValue()` returns the previous value until a `tapReturnKey()` syncs native state**
On Android, `replaceText('')` calls `UiObject2.setText('')`, which clears the native `EditText` content. However, the React Native `TextInput` component maintains its own JS-side controlled value — `onChangeText` fires with the empty string, but the synthetic event may not trigger `onChange` in libraries like `react-hook-form` that subscribe to the native `onChange` event (not `onChangeText`). As a result, the form library's internal state retains the previous value while the visual field appears empty.
Why this matters: Tests that use `replaceText('')` to clear a form field and then `tapReturnKey()` to submit observe the form submit with the old value (the form library's state), not the empty string. This causes validation logic to accept the previous value as non-empty, and the test receives a success toast even though the business rule requires the field to be cleared. The test passes, but the actual bug (form library not responding to `replaceText`) is missed.
Fix: After `replaceText('')`, fire a `typeText(' ')` followed by `tapBackspaceKey()` to simulate a real user clearing the field — this generates both `onChangeText` and the native `onChange` event that form libraries listen to. Alternatively, check that your form library uses `onChangeText` (not just `onChange`) in the `TextInput` component, which is required for correct Detox compatibility.

---

**Gotcha G324: `by.web.xpath()` expressions that traverse shadow DOM boundaries in WebViews return zero results on Android but work on iOS — Chrome's `evaluateJavaScript` treats shadow roots differently from WebKit**
Detox's `by.web.xpath()` matcher executes an XPath query against the WebView DOM using the browser's `document.evaluate()`. On iOS (WKWebView backed by WebKit), XPath queries can traverse into open shadow DOM trees because WebKit's `document.evaluate()` includes shadow-host subtrees in its traversal. On Android (WebView backed by Chromium), XPath queries are scoped to the light DOM only — shadow DOM children are not included in `document.evaluate()` results, returning an empty `XPathResult`.
Why this matters: Web Component–based UI libraries (Lit, FAST, Shoelace) render their internal structure inside shadow roots. A WebView that embeds such a component library will have form inputs, buttons, and labels inside shadow roots. Tests that use `by.web.xpath()` to find these elements will appear to work during iOS runs but produce "element not found" errors on Android CI — often only discovered when the CI Android job is added to the pipeline.
Fix: Replace `by.web.xpath()` with `by.web.cssSelector()` for elements that may be inside shadow roots, and pierce the shadow DOM explicitly with `>>>` combinators (e.g., `my-component >>> input[type="text"]`) — Chromium supports the `>>>` shadow-piercing combinator in `querySelectorAll` (Detox's `cssSelector` implementation). Verify each selector works on both platforms in a dedicated `by.web.cssSelector()` smoke test before adopting `xpath()` queries in WebView test suites.

## Cycle 61 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 544** — `device.setNetworkConditions()` for Simulated Offline and Degraded-Network Testing on iOS Simulator
```typescript
// detox-network-conditions.ts
import { device, element, by, waitFor } from 'detox';

describe('Offline / Degraded-Network Behaviour', () => {
  afterEach(async () => {
    // Always restore full connectivity so subsequent tests are not affected
    await device.setNetworkConditions('off');
    await device.setNetworkConditions('on');
  });

  it('shows the offline banner when the network is fully disconnected', async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    await device.setNetworkConditions('off'); // iOS Simulator only — no-op on physical device
    // The app's network-state listener typically fires within 500 ms
    await waitFor(element(by.id('offline-banner')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(4000);
    await expect(element(by.id('offline-banner'))).toHaveText('No connection');
  });

  it('shows the retry button after a failed API call under 2G conditions', async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    // Preset: 250 Kbps down, 50 Kbps up, 300 ms latency, 5 % packet loss
    await device.setNetworkConditions({
      downloadSpeed: 250,
      uploadSpeed: 50,
      latency: 300,
      lossRatio: 0.05,
    });
    await element(by.id('refresh-btn')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('retry-btn'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(15000);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `device.setNetworkConditions()` is implemented only for iOS Simulator via the Network Link Conditioner API; calling it on Android emulators or any physical device is a documented no-op (Detox 20.49+), so you must gate every call with `if (device.getPlatform() === 'ios')` in cross-platform suites, and provide a separate `adb shell` tc-netem command path for Android emulator degraded-network tests.

---

**Pattern 545** — `element.tapAtPoint()` for Pixel-Precise Tap on Non-Accessible Canvas and Chart Elements
```typescript
// chart-tap.e2e.ts
import { element, by, waitFor, expect } from 'detox';

describe('Line Chart Data-Point Tap', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    await element(by.id('nav-analytics')).tap();
  });

  it('shows a tooltip when the user taps the March data point', async () => {
    // The chart canvas is a single native view — no child testIDs
    // Use getAttributes() to get its absolute frame, then calculate
    // the fractional position of the March bar (column 3 of 12)
    const chart = element(by.id('revenue-chart'));
    const { frame } = await chart.getAttributes() as { frame: { x: number; y: number; width: number; height: number } };

    // March = index 2 (0-based), evenly-spaced columns
    const marchX = frame.width * (2.5 / 12); // centre of column 3
    const midY = frame.height * 0.5;

    await chart.tapAtPoint({ x: marchX, y: midY });

    await waitFor(element(by.id('chart-tooltip')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(2000);
    await expect(element(by.id('chart-tooltip-label'))).toHaveText('March');
    await expect(element(by.id('chart-tooltip-value'))).toHaveText('$42,300');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `tapAtPoint()` coordinates are relative to the element's own bounding box (not the screen origin), so you must retrieve `frame` fresh each time the test runs on a different device size — hardcoding pixel values makes the test fragile across iPhone SE vs Pro Max screen widths; always derive coordinates as fractional multiples of the frame's `width` and `height`.

**Pattern 546** — `device.sendToHome()` + `device.launchApp({ newInstance: false })` for Push-Notification-While-Backgrounded Testing
```typescript
// background-notification.e2e.ts
import { device, element, by, waitFor } from 'detox';

const iosPushPayload = {
  trigger: { type: 'push' },
  title: 'New message',
  body: 'Alice sent you a photo',
  badge: 1,
  payload: {
    notificationType: 'chat',
    conversationId: 'conv-42',
  },
};

describe('Push notification while backgrounded', () => {
  it('resumes to the correct conversation when notification is tapped', async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    // Navigate to home screen — app is now backgrounded
    await device.sendToHome();
    // Deliver the push while backgrounded, then tap it to foreground
    await device.sendUserNotification(iosPushPayload);
    // The system banner appears; Detox auto-taps default action on iOS Simulator
    await device.launchApp({
      newInstance: false,
      userNotification: iosPushPayload,
    });
    await waitFor(element(by.id(`conversation-${iosPushPayload.payload.conversationId}`)))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(5000);
    await expect(element(by.id('conversation-header-title'))).toHaveText('Alice');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `device.sendUserNotification()` only works on iOS Simulator — on Android you must use `device.sendBroadcast()` with the app's notification-receiver intent or trigger a Firebase-emulator HTTP call; the payload shape differs between platforms, so maintain separate `iosPayload` and `androidPayload` fixtures and a platform switch in `beforeAll`.

**Pattern 547** — `device.clearKeychain()` + `device.launchApp({ permissions: { biometricID: 'YES' } })` for Biometric Enrolment Reset
```typescript
// biometric-enrolment.e2e.ts
import { device, element, by, waitFor, expect } from 'detox';

describe('Biometric setup — first-time enrolment', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    // Clear any previously enrolled credentials from prior test runs
    await device.clearKeychain();
    await device.launchApp({
      newInstance: true,
      permissions: { biometricID: 'YES' },
    });
  });

  it('shows the biometric enrolment prompt on first login', async () => {
    await element(by.id('email-input')).typeText('user@example.com');
    await element(by.id('password-input')).typeText('P@ss1234');
    await element(by.id('login-btn')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('biometric-enrolment-sheet')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(4000);
    await expect(element(by.id('biometric-enrolment-sheet-title')))
      .toHaveText('Enable Face ID?');
  });

  it('enables biometric login and skips password on subsequent launch', async () => {
    await element(by.id('enable-biometric-btn')).tap();
    await device.matchFace(); // simulate successful Face ID enrolment
    await waitFor(element(by.id('dashboard-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
    // Re-launch without credentials — app should auto-authenticate
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true, permissions: { biometricID: 'YES' } });
    await device.matchFace();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('dashboard-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `device.clearKeychain()` is iOS-only; on Android you must call `device.launchApp({ delete: true })` to wipe app data (including SharedPreferences/EncryptedSharedPreferences) before re-testing enrolment flow, and `device.matchFinger()` replaces `device.matchFace()` as the simulated biometric action.

**Pattern 548** — `element.swipe('left', 'slow', 0.9)` for iOS Delete-on-Swipe List Row Without Triggering Navigation Drawer
```typescript
// list-swipe-delete.e2e.ts
import { device, element, by, waitFor, expect } from 'detox';

const ITEM_TEST_ID = 'notification-item-7';

describe('Notification list — swipe to delete', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    await element(by.id('nav-notifications')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id(ITEM_TEST_ID))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
  });

  it('reveals the Delete button on slow left swipe', async () => {
    // speed: 'slow' keeps the gesture sub-threshold for the navigation drawer
    // normalizedSwipeDistance 0.9 ensures the "Delete" action button is fully revealed
    await element(by.id(ITEM_TEST_ID)).swipe('left', 'slow', 0.9);
    await waitFor(element(by.id(`delete-action-${ITEM_TEST_ID}`)))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(1500);
    await element(by.id(`delete-action-${ITEM_TEST_ID}`)).tap();
    await expect(element(by.id(ITEM_TEST_ID))).not.toBeVisible();
    await expect(element(by.id('empty-notifications-label'))).not.toBeVisible();
  });

  it('does not remove the item on a fast short swipe (gesture cancel)', async () => {
    await element(by.id('notification-item-8')).swipe('left', 'fast', 0.2);
    // A fast short swipe should spring back without revealing the action
    await expect(element(by.id('delete-action-notification-item-8'))).not.toBeVisible();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: The `normalizedSwipeDistance` parameter (0.0–1.0) controls how far the swipe travels relative to the element width — a value above 0.95 on short list rows can overshoot past the action button bounds and trigger a full-row delete without showing the confirmation button; calibrate with 0.85–0.90 for typical `UITableView` trailing action rows.

**Pattern 549** — `device.reverseTcp()` + WireMock `__admin/mappings` Hot-Reload for In-Test Stub Switching
```typescript
// stub-switching.e2e.ts
import { device, element, by, waitFor } from 'detox';
import axios from 'axios';

const WIREMOCK_PORT = 8080;
const WIREMOCK_ADMIN = `http://localhost:${WIREMOCK_PORT}/__admin`;

async function setStub(scenarioName: string, stubBody: object) {
  await axios.post(`${WIREMOCK_ADMIN}/mappings`, {
    ...stubBody,
    scenarioName,
  });
}

describe('Payment result screen — server response variants', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    // Forward Android emulator port to host WireMock
    if (device.getPlatform() === 'android') {
      await device.reverseTcp(WIREMOCK_PORT, WIREMOCK_PORT);
    }
    await device.launchApp({
      newInstance: true,
      launchArgs: { mockServerPort: String(WIREMOCK_PORT) },
    });
  });

  it('shows success screen when payment stub returns 200', async () => {
    await setStub('payment', {
      request: { method: 'POST', url: '/api/payment' },
      response: { status: 200, jsonBody: { status: 'SUCCESS' } },
    });
    await element(by.id('pay-btn')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('payment-success-screen')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(5000);
  });

  it('shows decline screen when payment stub returns 402', async () => {
    await setStub('payment', {
      request: { method: 'POST', url: '/api/payment' },
      response: { status: 402, jsonBody: { status: 'DECLINED', reason: 'INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS' } },
    });
    await element(by.id('pay-btn')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('payment-declined-screen')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(5000);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `device.reverseTcp()` is Android-only and sets up an adb reverse tunnel that lives for the duration of the device session; on iOS Simulator the host `localhost` is already reachable from the simulated network, so no tunnel is needed — but the WireMock process must be started in `jest globalSetup` before any test worker tries to connect, otherwise the first stub registration call fails with `ECONNREFUSED`.

**Pattern 550** — `device.setURLBlacklist()` for Suppressing Analytics and Crash-Reporter Traffic During Tests
```typescript
// url-blacklist-setup.e2e.ts
import { device } from 'detox';

// Put in a global beforeAll (e.g., jest globalSetup or the first describe block)
const ANALYTICS_ORIGINS = [
  '.*\\.amplitude\\.com.*',
  '.*\\.segment\\.io.*',
  '.*\\.sentry\\.io.*',
  '.*\\.firebaseapp\\.com.*',
  '.*crashlytics.*',
  '.*\\.datadog-browser-agent.*',
];

beforeAll(async () => {
  // Blacklisted URLs are excluded from Detox's idle-synchronisation wait.
  // Without this, Detox waits for long-polling analytics connections to settle
  // before every waitFor(), adding 1–3 s of artificial latency to each step.
  await device.setURLBlacklist(ANALYTICS_ORIGINS);
});

afterAll(async () => {
  // Reset to empty blacklist so the next test file gets a clean state
  await device.setURLBlacklist([]);
});
```
Tradeoff: `setURLBlacklist()` uses regex patterns matched against the full request URL — overly broad patterns (e.g., `.*google.*`) can accidentally suppress legitimate API calls your app makes to Firebase Realtime Database or Google Maps, causing test failures where the app hangs waiting for data that Detox's synchronisation mechanism already considers "settled"; always anchor patterns to the analytics subdomain (`.*\\.amplitude\\.com.*`) rather than the parent domain.

**Pattern 551** — `element.getAttributes()` `enabled` and `focused` Properties for Button-State and Focus-Ring Assertions
```typescript
// form-validation-state.e2e.ts
import { element, by, waitFor, expect } from 'detox';

describe('Checkout form — submit button state transitions', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    await element(by.id('nav-checkout')).tap();
  });

  it('submit button is disabled before all required fields are filled', async () => {
    const attrs = await element(by.id('submit-btn')).getAttributes();
    // getAttributes() returns { enabled: boolean } on both platforms
    expect((attrs as any).enabled).toBe(false);
  });

  it('submit button is enabled after all required fields are filled', async () => {
    await element(by.id('card-number-input')).typeText('4242424242424242');
    await element(by.id('expiry-input')).typeText('12/28');
    await element(by.id('cvv-input')).typeText('123');
    const attrs = await element(by.id('submit-btn')).getAttributes();
    expect((attrs as any).enabled).toBe(true);
  });

  it('first field receives focus after the form screen mounts', async () => {
    await device.reloadReactNative();
    await element(by.id('nav-checkout')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('card-number-input'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);
    const attrs = await element(by.id('card-number-input')).getAttributes();
    // `focused` is iOS-only; on Android use `toHaveValue('')` + keyboard visible check
    if (device.getPlatform() === 'ios') {
      expect((attrs as any).focused).toBe(true);
    }
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `getAttributes().enabled` maps to `UIView.isUserInteractionEnabled && UIControl.isEnabled` on iOS and `View.isEnabled()` on Android — however on Android, a custom `Pressable` that renders as a `View` with an `onPress` handler always reports `enabled: true` even when its `disabled` prop is `true`, because the underlying native view does not propagate the React `disabled` prop to the accessibility `enabled` flag; use `toHaveText()` on a companion status label instead for Android disabled-state assertions.

**Pattern 552** — `expect(element).toHaveLabel()` Cross-Platform Accessibility Label Assertion for Screen-Reader Compliance Testing
```typescript
// accessibility-labels.e2e.ts
import { element, by, expect as detoxExpect } from 'detox';

describe('Accessibility labels — WCAG 2.1 Level AA', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    await element(by.id('nav-product-list')).tap();
  });

  it('product card image has a descriptive accessibility label', async () => {
    // toHaveLabel() maps to accessibilityLabel (iOS) / contentDescription (Android)
    await detoxExpect(element(by.id('product-image-0')))
      .toHaveLabel('Blue running shoes, size range 6–14, $89.99');
  });

  it('favourite button label reflects current state', async () => {
    await detoxExpect(element(by.id('favourite-btn-0')))
      .toHaveLabel('Add to favourites');
    await element(by.id('favourite-btn-0')).tap();
    await detoxExpect(element(by.id('favourite-btn-0')))
      .toHaveLabel('Remove from favourites');
  });

  it('loading spinner announces "Loading" to screen readers', async () => {
    await element(by.id('refresh-btn')).tap();
    // Spinner is visible during fetch — check its label before it disappears
    await detoxExpect(element(by.id('loading-spinner'))).toHaveLabel('Loading');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `toHaveLabel()` performs an exact string match — if the label is assembled programmatically (e.g., interpolating a product name and price), a locale formatting change (comma vs period as decimal separator) will break the assertion; prefer testing that the label `toHaveLabel(new RegExp('running shoes'))` when exact text is locale-sensitive, noting that Detox's `toHaveLabel` does not accept a `RegExp` directly — use `getAttributes().label` and `expect(label).toMatch(/pattern/)` in that case.

**Pattern 553** — `device.reloadReactNative()` with Post-Reload `waitFor` Gate to Prevent Race with Large Hermes Bundle
```typescript
// safe-reload.ts — shared test helper
import { device, element, by, waitFor } from 'detox';

/**
 * Reloads the RN bundle and waits for the root navigator to be ready
 * before yielding. Safe for Hermes bundles > 8 MB where the default
 * Detox sync heuristic (idle network + idle JS queue) resolves before
 * the navigator registers its screens.
 */
export async function safeReloadRN(rootScreenTestId = 'home-screen', timeout = 10000) {
  await device.reloadReactNative();
  // Hermes pre-compilation is async — the root screen mounts only after
  // the navigator is hydrated from AsyncStorage (persisted nav state).
  await waitFor(element(by.id(rootScreenTestId)))
    .toBeVisible()
    .withTimeout(timeout);
}

// usage in test file:
// import { safeReloadRN } from '../helpers/safe-reload';
// beforeEach(async () => { await safeReloadRN('dashboard-screen'); });
```
Tradeoff: Adding a `waitFor` gate after `reloadReactNative()` adds ~200–400 ms per test in fast suites with in-memory state, but it is essential for large apps using `react-navigation` with `persistNavigationState` — without the gate, subsequent `element.tap()` calls hit the navigator before it has reconstructed its screen registry from AsyncStorage, causing "element not found" errors that are non-deterministic and disappear on retry, making them impossible to reproduce in isolation.

**Pattern 554** — `by.id()` + `by.type()` Compound Matcher Using `.and()` for Unambiguous Native Component Targeting
```typescript
// compound-matcher.e2e.ts
import { element, by, expect as detoxExpect } from 'detox';

describe('Compound matchers for ambiguous view hierarchies', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    await element(by.id('nav-settings')).tap();
  });

  it('toggles the correct Switch when two Switches share the same parent testID', async () => {
    // Both switches are inside a section with testID="notifications-section"
    // but the individual switches lack unique testIDs in the current codebase
    // Use .and() to narrow by RN component type (platform-specific class name)
    const notifSwitchMatcher =
      device.getPlatform() === 'ios'
        ? by.id('notifications-section').and(by.type('RCTSwitch'))
        : by.id('notifications-section').and(by.type('android.widget.Switch'));

    // atIndex(0) = push notifications, atIndex(1) = email notifications
    await element(notifSwitchMatcher).atIndex(0).tap();
    await detoxExpect(element(notifSwitchMatcher).atIndex(0)).toHaveToggleValue(false);
    await detoxExpect(element(notifSwitchMatcher).atIndex(1)).toHaveToggleValue(true);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Using `by.type()` with platform-specific class names (`RCTSwitch` vs `android.widget.Switch`) couples the test to React Native's internal view mapping — these class names changed when the New Architecture (Fabric) replaced `RCTView` with `RCTViewComponentView` in React Native 0.74+; always verify class names with `device.captureViewHierarchy()` after any major RN upgrade rather than relying on hardcoded type strings.

**Pattern 555** — `device.getPlatform()` + `device.getRuntimeDevice()` for Emulator vs Physical Device Guard in Performance-Sensitive Assertions
```typescript
// runtime-device-guard.e2e.ts
import { device, element, by, waitFor } from 'detox';

type DetoxRuntimeDevice = {
  type: string; // e.g., 'ios.simulator', 'android.emulator', 'ios.device', 'android.attached'
  name: string;
};

async function isEmulator(): Promise<boolean> {
  const rd = device.getRuntimeDevice() as DetoxRuntimeDevice;
  return rd.type.includes('simulator') || rd.type.includes('emulator');
}

describe('Dashboard initial load time', () => {
  it('loads the dashboard within the performance budget', async () => {
    const onEmulator = await isEmulator();
    // Emulators are ~2× slower than physical devices for JS execution
    const timeoutMs = onEmulator ? 6000 : 3000;
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    const start = Date.now();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('dashboard-screen')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(timeoutMs);
    const elapsed = Date.now() - start;
    console.log(`Dashboard load: ${elapsed} ms on ${onEmulator ? 'emulator' : 'device'}`);
    expect(elapsed).toBeLessThan(timeoutMs);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `device.getRuntimeDevice()` was added in Detox 20.18 — projects on older Detox versions must fall back to inspecting the `DETOX_CONFIGURATION` env variable or the device type in `.detoxrc` to infer emulator vs physical device; the `type` field string values are not part of the public stable API and may change in minor releases, so check the changelog when upgrading Detox.

**Pattern 556** — `element.scrollTo('bottom')` + `element.scroll()` Nudge for Lazy-Loaded Long-Form Navigation
```typescript
// scroll-to-element.e2e.ts
import { device, element, by, waitFor, expect as detoxExpect } from 'detox';

describe('Profile settings — long form with conditional sections', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
    await element(by.id('nav-profile-settings')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('profile-settings-scroll'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(3000);
  });

  it('scrolls to the danger-zone section and confirms account deletion CTA', async () => {
    // scrollTo('bottom') triggers lazy-load sections to render
    await element(by.id('profile-settings-scroll')).scrollTo('bottom');
    await waitFor(element(by.id('danger-zone-section')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(3000);
    // Small nudge to bring section header fully into view above the bottom safe area
    await element(by.id('profile-settings-scroll')).scroll(50, 'down');
    await detoxExpect(element(by.id('delete-account-btn'))).toBeVisible();
    await detoxExpect(element(by.id('delete-account-btn'))).toHaveText('Delete account');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Calling `scrollTo('bottom')` on a `FlatList` with `onEndReached` pagination causes Detox to wait for the end-of-list network request to settle before considering the scroll complete — on slow CI networks this can add 5–10 seconds per step; disable pagination during E2E tests via a feature flag (`launchArgs: { paginationDisabled: '1' }`) and use a seeded local dataset so the list length is deterministic.

**Pattern 557** — `copilot.perform()` Natural-Language Assertion for Subjective UI State and Broken-Image Detection
```typescript
// copilot-smoke.e2e.ts
// Requires: detox-copilot installed, COPILOT_PROVIDER env var set
import { device, element, by, copilot } from 'detox';

describe('Copilot-assisted subjective UI verification', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await copilot.init(/* your PromptHandler */);
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true });
  });

  it('confirms the onboarding screen communicates its value proposition', async () => {
    await copilot.perform(
      'Verify that the screen visually conveys a fitness tracking value proposition ' +
        'with at least one illustration, a headline, and a call-to-action button.',
    );
  });

  it('detects a broken image on the home feed', async () => {
    await element(by.id('nav-home')).tap();
    await copilot.perform(
      'Check that no broken-image icons are visible in the feed list. ' +
        'A broken image renders as a grey box with a crossed-out picture icon.',
    );
  });

  it('confirms the loading skeleton is shown before data arrives', async () => {
    // Trigger a slow-network scenario first
    if (device.getPlatform() === 'ios') await device.setNetworkConditions('off');
    await device.reloadReactNative();
    await copilot.perform(
      'Confirm that a loading skeleton (grey placeholder cards) ' +
        'is visible on the home feed within the first 2 seconds.',
    );
    if (device.getPlatform() === 'ios') await device.setNetworkConditions('on');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Copilot assertions are non-deterministic — the LLM prompt handler can produce different pass/fail decisions across runs for visually borderline UI states (e.g., an image that partially loads), making them unsuitable as blocking CI gates without a retry wrapper; treat Copilot assertions as supplementary checks in a separate CI job that posts a comment to the PR but does not block merge, reserving hard `waitFor`/`expect` assertions for correctness gates.

**Pattern 558** — `device.appLaunchArgs.get()` / `.modify()` for Feature-Flag Introspection and In-Suite Mutation
```typescript
// launch-args-introspection.e2e.ts
import { device } from 'detox';

describe('Feature flag introspection via launchArgs', () => {
  it('confirms the dark-mode flag is passed to the app under test', async () => {
    await device.launchApp({
      newInstance: true,
      launchArgs: { featureDarkMode: '1', featureNewCheckout: '0' },
    });
    // Introspect what args are active on the running instance
    const activeArgs = device.appLaunchArgs.get();
    expect(activeArgs).toMatchObject({
      featureDarkMode: '1',
      featureNewCheckout: '0',
    });
  });

  it('mutates a single flag without relaunching via modify()', async () => {
    device.appLaunchArgs.modify({ featureNewCheckout: '1' });
    const updated = device.appLaunchArgs.get();
    expect(updated.featureNewCheckout).toBe('1');
    // The change only takes effect on the next launchApp() call
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: false }); // resume = flag change applied
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `device.appLaunchArgs.get()` reflects the args object as Detox has built it — it does not query the running app process to confirm the args were received; the actual `process.argv` (iOS) or `Intent.getExtras()` (Android) inside the app can differ if the app's `AppDelegate` or `MainActivity` filters or transforms args before passing them to the React Native bridge; validate receipt in the app by exposing a debug endpoint (e.g., `__E2E_FLAGS__` global) that the test can read via `device.executeScript()` or a WebSocket channel.

---

### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha G325: `device.setNetworkConditions()` call is silently ignored on Android Emulator and any physical device — no error or warning is thrown, tests give false confidence that degraded-network paths are covered on Android**
`device.setNetworkConditions()` is implemented exclusively through the iOS Simulator's private `SimulatorKit` framework (`simctl` network conditions command). On Android, Detox's implementation returns `Promise.resolve()` immediately without routing the call to `adb` or `tc-netem`, so the call appears to succeed but no throttling is applied. Teams that add `setNetworkConditions()` calls to a cross-platform test suite and run CI on both iOS Simulator and Android Emulator see the iOS job catch real timeout regressions while the Android job never triggers the slow-network code path.
Why this matters: The Android app's offline/retry logic is never exercised in E2E, giving false confidence that error-state UI is correct on Android. Bugs in the Android error banner (wrong text, wrong icon) survive code review and reach production because the CI Android job always passes under full network speed.
Fix: Wrap every `device.setNetworkConditions()` call with `if (device.getPlatform() === 'ios')`. For Android degraded-network coverage, use a dedicated Docker WireMock container with built-in response delays (`fixedDelayMilliseconds` per mapping) and configure the emulator to reach it via `device.reverseTcp()`, so Android latency is simulated at the stub layer rather than the network layer.

---

**Gotcha G326: `element.tapAtPoint()` coordinates are relative to the element's bounding box, not the screen — passing screen-absolute pixel values from a screenshot overlay causes the tap to land in the wrong location or outside the element entirely**
`element.tapAtPoint({ x, y })` documentation states the coordinates are relative to the element's top-left corner, but teams using screenshot-annotation tools (Figma redlines, BrowserStack App Live tap coordinates) record coordinates relative to the screen (0,0 = top-left of device screen). When those screen-absolute values are passed directly to `tapAtPoint()`, the actual tap is displaced by the element's `frame.x` and `frame.y` offsets — on a large phone where the chart starts 300 px from the top and 20 px from the left, every tap lands in the wrong column of the chart.
Why this matters: The test file appears correct and the coordinates look plausible, but the wrong chart data point is tapped consistently. Because the tooltip still appears (just for a different data point), the test may pass if the assertion only checks that `chart-tooltip` is visible without asserting the correct label — the bug is only discovered when a designer notices the wrong month is highlighted in a screen recording.
Fix: Always derive `tapAtPoint` coordinates by calling `element.getAttributes()` to get the `frame`, then compute the desired tap position as a fraction of `frame.width` / `frame.height`. Never paste screen-absolute coordinates into `tapAtPoint()`. Add an explicit `toHaveText` assertion on the tooltip label to confirm the correct element responded to the tap.

---

**Gotcha G327: `device.clearKeychain()` does not clear Secure Enclave–backed keys on iOS Simulator — keys created with `kSecAttrAccessibleWhenPasscodeSetThisDeviceOnly` persist across `clearKeychain()` calls and survive app reinstall**
`device.clearKeychain()` calls `security delete-generic-password -a` and related commands to flush the simulator's keychain database. However, keys stored with `kSecAttrAccessibleWhenPasscodeSetThisDeviceOnly` are bound to the Secure Enclave simulation and are not removed by the standard keychain delete commands. These keys survive `clearKeychain()`, app deletion, and even `device.launchApp({ delete: true })` — only resetting the entire simulator (Simulator → Device → Erase All Content and Settings) removes them.
Why this matters: Biometric enrolment tests that call `device.clearKeychain()` in `beforeAll` assume a clean slate, but if a previous test run stored a Secure Enclave–backed key (e.g., a biometric-authenticated private key for passwordless login), the enrolment flow detects the existing key and skips the "Enable Face ID?" prompt, causing the `toBeVisible()` assertion on the enrolment sheet to time out. The test is flaky — it passes on fresh simulator environments (CI machines after reset) but fails after the first run on a developer's local machine.
Fix: Avoid `kSecAttrAccessibleWhenPasscodeSetThisDeviceOnly` in the debug build variant's keychain policy. Use `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlock` for the E2E build target so `clearKeychain()` can remove all tokens. If the Secure Enclave policy is required for security compliance, add a dedicated Xcode scheme environment variable (`E2E_MODE=1`) that the app checks at startup to skip Secure Enclave storage and use a standard keychain item instead.

---

**Gotcha G328: `element.swipe('left')` on a `ScrollView` with `horizontal={true}` inside a `ViewPager` tab on Android triggers a page change in the parent pager instead of scrolling the inner `ScrollView` — the touch event is consumed by the wrong responder**
On Android, React Native's touch responder arbitration resolves conflicts between nested horizontal `ScrollView` and a parent `ViewPager` (used by `react-native-pager-view` and `react-navigation` tab navigator) by giving priority to the outer `ViewPager` when the swipe starts near the edge of the inner `ScrollView`. Detox's `element.swipe()` generates a gesture that starts at the element centre by default; if the inner `ScrollView`'s content is fully scrolled to one end, the initial finger-down position is at the scroll boundary, and Android's `onInterceptTouchEvent` in `ViewPager` steals the event, advancing to the next tab instead of scrolling the inner view.
Why this matters: The E2E test for a horizontal image carousel (implemented as a `ScrollView` inside a tab screen) intermittently switches to the next tab mid-test, causing all subsequent `by.id()` matchers to target the wrong screen. The failure is timing-dependent — it only occurs when the carousel is at the last item (scroll position = max) and therefore always passes on the first run through the carousel from left to right.
Fix: Set `startNormalizedX: 0.5` and adjust `startNormalizedY: 0.5` explicitly in the `swipe()` call to keep the gesture origin in the element centre. If the conflict persists, invoke `element(by.id('carousel-scroll')).scroll(width, 'right')` using Detox's `scroll()` action instead of `swipe()` — `scroll()` uses a two-phase (press, move, release) strategy that gives the inner `ScrollView` first-responder priority before the move begins.

---

**Gotcha G329: `waitFor(element).toBeVisible().withTimeout(N)` resolves as soon as the element's opacity becomes non-zero during a FadeIn animation — the resolved promise fires before the element is fully opaque and interactive, causing the next `tap()` to miss**
Detox's `waitFor().toBeVisible()` polls the accessibility tree every ~100 ms and resolves as soon as the element is visible at any single polling tick. For elements that use a `FadeIn` animation (opacity: 0 → 1 over 300 ms), the element becomes technically visible (opacity > 0 → the accessibility layer marks it visible) at the first frame of the animation — approximately 16 ms in. The `waitFor` resolves at this moment, and the next `element.tap()` fires while the element's opacity is still ~0.1 and its touch target is not yet interactive, causing a "tap on non-hittable element" error or a silent miss.
Why this matters: Developers add `waitFor(...).toBeVisible()` before every `tap()` under the assumption that `toBeVisible()` implies "fully rendered and interactive", but `toBeVisible()` only checks the accessibility visible flag, not whether the element has completed its entry animation and has a fully opaque touch target. The failure manifests as a `tap()` that silently does nothing (the touch hits the view beneath), and the next assertion fails with "element not found" because the expected state change never occurred.
Fix: After `waitFor(element).toBeVisible()`, add `waitFor(element).toBeEnabled()` if the element is a button, which is only truthy once the view is interactive. Alternatively, disable entry animations in the E2E build target by setting `UIView.setAnimationsEnabled(false)` in an `AppDelegate` flag checked via a launch argument (`E2E_DISABLE_ANIMATIONS=1`). The cleanest solution is to expose a `testID`-based "ready" sentinel element that the app mounts only after all entry animations complete, and `waitFor` that sentinel before acting.

**Pattern 559** — `device.openURL()` for Deep-Link Entry-Point Testing Without Navigating Through the App Shell
```typescript
// deep-link-entry.e2e.ts
import { device, element, by, waitFor, expect } from 'detox';

// Covers the "open from external app" flow: the app cold-starts via a universal link
// and must land on the correct screen without passing through the home tab.

describe('Deep-link entry points', () => {
  beforeEach(async () => {
    // Terminate the app so openURL triggers a cold-start (not a background resume)
    await device.terminateApp();
  });

  it('lands on the product detail screen when opened via product deep-link', async () => {
    // Trigger iOS Universal Link / Android App Link – Detox routes this through
    // simctl openurl (iOS) or adb shell am start -a VIEW (Android)
    await device.openURL({ url: 'myapp://products/sku-98765' });

    await waitFor(element(by.id('product-detail-screen')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(6000);

    await expect(element(by.id('product-title'))).toHaveText('Wireless Headphones Pro');
    await expect(element(by.id('product-sku'))).toHaveText('SKU-98765');
  });

  it('lands on the order-status screen and shows the correct order number', async () => {
    await device.openURL({ url: 'myapp://orders/ORD-20240512-001' });

    await waitFor(element(by.id('order-status-screen')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(6000);

    await expect(element(by.id('order-id-label'))).toHaveText('ORD-20240512-001');
  });

  it('redirects to the sign-in screen when the deep-link requires auth and the user is logged out', async () => {
    // Ensure logged-out state
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true, launchArgs: { E2E_AUTH_STATE: 'logged_out' } });
    await device.terminateApp();

    await device.openURL({ url: 'myapp://account/settings' });

    // Auth-protected deep-link must redirect to sign-in and then restore the destination
    await waitFor(element(by.id('sign-in-screen')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(5000);
    // After sign-in the app should return to the settings screen
    const storedRedirect = await element(by.id('sign-in-redirect-hint')).getAttributes();
    expect((storedRedirect as any).text).toContain('account/settings');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `device.openURL()` calls `simctl openurl booted` on iOS and `adb shell am start -W -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d` on Android — both require the URL scheme or App Link domain to be registered in the app's manifest / `Info.plist`; in the debug build variant, register a dedicated `myapp-debug://` scheme so E2E deep-link tests never collide with production universal links that require AASA validation on a real web server.

**Pattern 560** — `device.shake()` Followed by `element.tap()` on the Debug-Menu Action for Custom Developer Overlay Testing
```typescript
// debug-menu.e2e.ts
import { device, element, by, waitFor, expect } from 'detox';

// React Native ships a built-in Dev Menu triggered by shake on real devices.
// In E2E builds, teams often expose a custom debug panel the same way.
// This pattern shows how to reliably open and interact with it.

describe('Developer debug overlay via shake gesture', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({
      newInstance: true,
      launchArgs: { E2E_DEBUG_MENU: '1' }, // custom flag that enables shake-trigger in release builds
    });
    await waitFor(element(by.id('home-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
  });

  it('opens the debug overlay on shake and toggles the slow-animation flag', async () => {
    await device.shake(); // simulates device shake via XCUIDevice (iOS) / InputManager (Android)

    await waitFor(element(by.id('debug-overlay')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(3000);

    // Verify the overlay contains the expected developer options
    await expect(element(by.id('debug-slow-animations-toggle'))).toBeVisible();
    await expect(element(by.id('debug-feature-flags-section'))).toBeVisible();

    // Toggle slow animations on
    const toggleAttrs = await element(by.id('debug-slow-animations-toggle')).getAttributes();
    const isEnabled = (toggleAttrs as any).value === '1';
    if (!isEnabled) {
      await element(by.id('debug-slow-animations-toggle')).tap();
    }

    await expect(element(by.id('debug-slow-animations-toggle'))).toHaveValue('1');

    // Dismiss
    await element(by.id('debug-overlay-close-btn')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('debug-overlay'))).not.toBeVisible().withTimeout(2000);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `device.shake()` maps to `XCUIDevice.shakeDevice()` on iOS Simulator (reliable) and `adb shell input keyevent 82` (menu key) on Android emulators — the Android keycode approach works for React Native Dev Menu but may not trigger a custom shake handler if the app uses `DeviceEventEmitter.addListener('hardwareBackPress', ...)` instead; on Android, prefer a dedicated test-only button (hidden behind `launchArgs.E2E_DEBUG_MENU=1`) to avoid relying on the shake emulation which differs by Android API level.

**Pattern 561** — `element.longPress()` with Optional Duration for Context-Menu and Press-and-Hold Action Sheet Testing
```typescript
// long-press-context-menu.e2e.ts
import { device, element, by, waitFor, expect } from 'detox';

describe('Long-press context menu on message bubbles', () => {
  beforeAll(async () => {
    await device.launchApp({ newInstance: true, launchArgs: { E2E_SEED_MESSAGES: '5' } });
    await waitFor(element(by.id('chat-screen'))).toBeVisible().withTimeout(5000);
  });

  it('presents the reaction picker after a standard long-press (400 ms)', async () => {
    // The default long-press threshold is 400 ms in the app; Detox default matches this
    await element(by.id('message-bubble-0')).longPress();

    await waitFor(element(by.id('reaction-picker')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(2000);

    await expect(element(by.id('reaction-emoji-👍'))).toBeVisible();
    await expect(element(by.id('reaction-emoji-❤️'))).toBeVisible();
  });

  it('presents the full action sheet when held for 800 ms (premium actions)', async () => {
    // Dismiss the previous picker first
    await device.pressBack(); // Android; on iOS tap outside
    await waitFor(element(by.id('reaction-picker'))).not.toBeVisible().withTimeout(1500);

    // 800 ms hold reveals Copy, Forward, Delete options on top of reactions
    await element(by.id('message-bubble-1')).longPress(800);

    await waitFor(element(by.id('message-action-sheet')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(2000);

    await expect(element(by.id('action-copy'))).toBeVisible();
    await expect(element(by.id('action-forward'))).toBeVisible();
    await expect(element(by.id('action-delete'))).toBeVisible();
  });

  it('taps the forward action and navigates to the contact picker', async () => {
    await element(by.id('action-forward')).tap();
    await waitFor(element(by.id('contact-picker-screen')))
      .toBeVisible()
      .withTimeout(3000);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: The `duration` parameter (milliseconds) passed to `element.longPress(duration)` maps to `pressForDuration:` in XCUITest and `ViewConfiguration.getLongPressTimeout()` in Espresso; Android's long-press threshold is device-dependent (default 500 ms, but OEMs modify it) — always read the threshold from a launch argument (`E2E_LONG_PRESS_MS`) rather than hardcoding so CI can tune it per device class without editing test code.
